I just have to say that this is one of the best films that I have seen in a while. Paul Haggis has managed to do it again and I think that this movie should definately get a little more consideration come Oscar time. Sandra Bullock was amazing in the three or four scenes that she was actually in, and should come under some consideration for best supporting actress. 
 
The film itself I thought was just kind of unique in dealing with race relations in such a metropolis like Los Angeles. The only thing that I think could have been better was the ending because they left so many loose ends with quite a few of the characters that it was dissappointing that it all didn't get resolved. Other than that the film was really kind of raw and at times emotional and heartbreaking. It was simply great!

This has to be one of the best movies of all time. Thought-provoking, harsh, cruel no holes barred $hit.
 
With all the other over-hyped movies this coming U.s. summer, this movie could be missed by the general public because it didnt have a budget in the excess of $100m.
 
Crash, takes place post 9/11 in LA, and how certain individuals (of deferent ethanicities) collide.
 
Crash is flawless. Performances are genuine and excellent. Screenplay is awesome. The eerie soundtrack just adds to the tension.
 
While the ensemble cast, will not impress everybody, they are all excellent. Including the supporting actors not mentioned in the trailer. Ryan Phillippe and Matt Dillion impress the most. Thandie Newton's character was my favorite, the scene after she gets molested by a racist-cop is a real heart breaker, especially when the scene takes place 10mins into the movie. All the cast impress, even the ones you would never expect a half-hearted performance from, a-la 'Ludacris' and Larenz Tate.
 
What makes Crash work so well, is how ur perception of a character quickly changes through-out the movie. The characters u hate in the beginning, turn out the ones you feel sorry for in the end.
 
All most in every scene in the movie you will ask yourself "What would you do in their situation?".
 
Paul Haggis coming off the success of writing, "Million Dollar Baby" is more so at his best here.
 
With racism such a problem these days, especially after 9/11, this film reminds us just how un-complacent we have become. Sandra Bullock character shows us this the best 
 
Thought-provoking stuff. 
 
[b]Grade: A++[/b]

A District attorney and his wife (Sandra Bullock and Brendan Fraser) is carjacked by two black men (Ludacris and Larenz Tate). Two police officers (Matt Dillon and Ryan Phillippe) stop a wealthy black couple (Terrence Howard and Thandie Newton) only to harass the couple. Don Cheadle and Jennifer Esposito stars as an interracial couple dealing with their own troubles. A Persian storeowner (Shaun Toub[b]) [/b]buys a gun to protect his store. Over the next 36 hours they will all crash. 

Crash is a movie that comes at you with loaded firepower blazing. It is a movie with a mission and a message to challenge the audience to the question of their own prejudices. It is a real revelation and offers an upsetting evaluation of the present state of racism. It is not the kind of film that tells you how to think or feel, on the other hand, it makes you think or feel something. Crash considered as one of the most tasteful and stimulating wake-up calls. It bonds everything together in a rational way, rather than to find answer that do not exist. However, the problem will live on gathering the momentum that we do not need. Crash is a success from all point of views, with a proper script and high-quality acting. Go see this one!

[font=Arial]I love films that pull the blanket from under us, such as, say, when a character we've followed dramatically changes personality and becomes the opposite of what we expected. I don't like to feel jerked around by such twists, like when the change cheats the audience and undermines all that went before. The first half of "Crash" is borderline preachy, providing the audience with the good characters who aren't racist and the bad characters who are. The second half of the movie takes these characters and adds a depth to them that creates a grey zone, where we realize things aren't always this polarized. [/font]
 
[font=Arial]"Crash" considers the reasons for racism as well as showing the effects, and it provides ample coverage of this war zone. Racism does not come down to skin colour, and so it penetrates within every individual culture. As Matt Dillon's character states: "You think you know who you are? You have no idea." He is proved correct.[/font]
 
[font=Arial]From "Million Dollar Baby" scribe Paul Haggis, "Crash" plunges us deep into the city of Los Angeles where the racial and class divisions are evident. The film provides a broad spectrum of characters from all backgrounds and watches as they end up crashing into each other. The reason why they crash, or tangle I suppose, is down to their own ignorance and inability to share the city. The film contains Persians, Hispanics, Latinos, also Chinese andAsian persons among others. One character in the film attacks a Persian because he believes him to be a terrorist from the Middle East. Another incident occurs because a bitchy white woman finds her locksmith is Mexican and presumes he is going to duplicate the key for future use, but we have already seen this individual for more than his suggested appearance. This motif of perception not being reality is key to understanding the film.[/font]
 
[font=Arial]There are too many characters in the film to try to explain how they all interlock, but FBI agent Don Cheadle is the character who links almost everyone. Cheadle is both faineant and melancholic as he indulges in an affair with his partner Jennifer Esposito and sidelines the wishes of his mother to bring her other son home. Terrence Howard plays a black television director who is pulled over by a police car because his wife (Thandie Newton) was performing fellatio. The cop is Matt Dillon, a seventeen year veteran in the force who has been around the blocks so much that he can't overcome his prejudice. He mistakes the woman as being white and decides to grope her when they step out of the car. His partner Ryan Phillippe, whose youthful looks seem angelic, silently protests. Then there is District Attorney Brendan Fraser and his wife Sandra Bullock, who have their car seized by a couple of black youths (Larenz Tate and Chris "Ludacris" Bridges), who aren't racist as they only attack people with white skin, though they are still thugs.[/font]
 
[font=Arial]"Crash" plays out in vignette form, though let's make it clear that this isn't Altmanesque. Take "Nashville," which is episodic and contains ebullient characters. This movie is beleagured by the screenplay to the degree that some of the dialogue sounds forced, though it is all essential. I guess "Crash" is like Altman with all the random peculiarities and meandering moments swept up. The script is tighter than Joan Rivers face, and the actors fit their roles like a pair of tightly stitched gloves.[/font]
 
[font=Arial]We can debate whether the film manipulates the situation too frequently, like when Dillon meets the women he took advantage of again, and Phillippe meets her husband. I see this world in which "Crash" presents to be a sprawling roundrobin of problems that, without any sense of algorithm, will rise to the surface again. You can't bury what you can't hide.[/font]
 
[font=Arial]There are two moments in "Crash" that are going to make people weep. Period. The first occurs when a despicable character is forced to help an individual who earlier was dehumanized by the very same person now trying to help. The other is a moment when a disgruntled character holds a gun to a person who he blames for the loss of his property. They both have different first languages and can't communicate efficiently. As the man pleads for his life, his tiny daughter watches from inside and rushes out to him moments before the pending release of the trigger. What happens, and because of what we've already seen from this family, is as powerful a moment of treasuring humanity as I've ever seen. "Crash" indicates that we all have prejudices even if we don't realize or acknowledge them, and that we will never be able to completely wipe such issues clean. [/font]

   I was taking classes at a city community college and about the same time I was experiencing alot of fear against anyone who appeared to maybe be Muslim.  In one of my classes I got to know a single African-American mother who radiated a very God-like vibe that I picked up on from the get go.  As I went home every night and watched CNN and heard the endless pre- war muslim fear stories, I became even more hateful and fearful of the people who practiced that religion.  One day while sitting in class I told the young single mom that I knew she had such a presence because I could feel God from her.
She bagan to thank me and then told me she was Muslim.  I was astonished.
   She would never know the overwhelming lesson that I learned that day.  I do not talk to her now but I have never forgot the fact that even I, a gay, HIV positive man could harbor such bad feelings toward a group of people just because of the way they believed and let alone looked.  I never in a million years would have thought the beautiful, bright, kind woman I got to know was a Muslim.  Now I am finished rambling but I started with that story for a reason.
[IMG]http://images.rottentomatoes.com/images/movie/gallery/10003654/photo_01.jpg[/IMG]
This film about racism is like no other and is so emotionally charged that at times you just want to get up and stop watching the truth that is being laid out before your eyes. Like the emotion I felt from my own experience, Crash overwhelmed me with even more lessons about myself and those around me. 
    Paul Haggis (wrote Million Dollar Baby screenplay) writes and directs this raw ensemble piece with several weaving stories.  His cast is brilliant and includes Thandie Newton, Matt Dillon, Sandra Bullock, Brendan Frasier, Don Cheadle, Ryan Phillipe, Ludacris, Larenz Tate among others.  There is not one actor who outdoes the other and this is the very BEST ensemble I have ever seen.  It is Magnolia-like in structure but different because the point is clear from the start and nowhere near the length.  
    I am telling you now forget about the predictable summer blockbuster wannabes.  This is what film making is all about.  Run to the nearest theatre and see Crash.  It is one of the most astonishing portraits of today's America ever produced.  Must see!!

I went in expecting a masterpiece. I left the theater looking forward to [i]House of Wax[/i]. This was not the experience I was expecting. Paul Haggis' new film [i]Crash[/i] is excellent - about half the time. The other half is pretty contrived and preachy. The "characters" are Haggis' excuses for bringing up some thought-provoking ideas. But, I am very sad to say, the actual movie falls short. The performances are all perfect, but Haggis just didn't have well-defined characters. You shouldn't have an ensemble piece when all the characters act and sound the same. All the coincidences were just too cute, and the sequences ranged from brilliant to embarassing (some scenes were both).

Crash is a movie that will change its viewers beliefs on racism and prejudice.  The script and acting is tremendous, but the subject matter may leave you with a sour taste when you leave the theater.  It is interesting to see how each of the individual stories come together throughout the film to reveal the ultimate message.  If you want an action flick or fun film, do not see Crash.  It is a serious and disturbing movie that explores the harsh realities of the world we live in today.

There are few films like Paul Haggis' [i]Crash[/i]. I'm talking about the kind of film that speaks so loudly without really saying a lot. I've been thinking about the effect the movie had on me since I walked out of it late Friday night. I have also been thinking a lot about how to even begin constructing a review of the film. I decided that a film like this doesn't deserve a review, because reviews are basically critiques. I don't feel the need to criticize this film because it really never felt like a movie to me. All I can say is that this is most definitely one of the best movies to come out of Hollywood in years, and whether you like it or hate it there is one thing for sure - you will be affected by it and want to talk to someone about it. 

Haggis, a writer for television for some 30 odd years before taking a stab at cinema and powerfully adapting the screenplay for Clint Eastwood's [i]Million Dollar Baby[/i] weaves a tale of emotions to such a masterful extent that it is hard to believe it's his directorial debut. A huge cast of characters ranging from all races and financial areas are set in front of the harsh background that is Los Angeles. There is a way to strongly hate and strongly sympathize for each character through all of their twists and turns. This is an ensemble filled with the most unusual but perfectly orchestrated choices ranging from big name stars like Sandra Bullock and Brandan Fraser to those who have had talent for years but are just now receiving respect and fame (think Don Cheadle). Going into the film I had no idea what to expect from the story or the actors other than the ones I have always liked, like Cheadle, Matt Dillon, Terrence Howard, and Larenz Tate. Haggis has such a strong sense of making his characters real just seconds after we meet them. He is sort of a magician with the pen and makes us forget that it's just a movie, forcing us to care for each and every one of these people, whether they're good or bad or just simply victims of manipulation. 
 
A big surprise in this film is Chris Bridges, otherwise known as "Ludacris". He really proved himself as a legitimate actor in this film, giving a deep and personal performance in a film filled with such roles. Not a person in this is left without development or feeling, and at a film clocking in at just around 100 minutes that is extraordinary. My favorites in the film are Matt Dillon as a longtime member of the LAPD who has been raised around racism, Terrence Howard as a successful African-American who is constantly brought back to his fear of standing up for himself in racial situations, and Don Cheadle as an FBI agent who kind of intersects with each and every character throughout. Cheadle is also a producer on the film and it is very obvious how bad he wanted this movie widely seen. Sandra Bullock gets big respect from me for taking on such a role like this, and with her name on the cast list the film will be allowed a chance in big multiplex theaters as well as the little ones in the coming weeks.
 
This is a film that will without a doubt hit a nerve with many people, and maybe some in a bad way. I can see people walking out of the film halfway through because the movie never holds back, and to succeed as a true and accurate film it can't. I hope people can stick with [i]Crash [/i]until the end, because it most definitely is not a film to bash and point out differences among races, it's a film that unifies all. It's a beautiful piece of work that maybe only comes along once a generation. There have been comparisons to [i]Magnolia [/i]here, but I think that is suggested wrongly. Sure both films deal with awe-inpiring coincidence, but the core of each couldn't be any more different. A more accurate comparison would be to Lawrence Kasdan's amazing film [i]Grand Canyon [/i]15 years ago.

Today I went and saw Crash. This movie has been getting great buzz from critics and word of mouth. I decided I would give it a shot, since I had nothing better to do anyways. I watched the trailer and actually liked what I saw, so off to the theater I went. Heres what I thought.
 
[img]http://images.rottentomatoes.com/images/movie/gallery/1144992/photo_01.jpg[/img]
 
First off, the movie had some terrific performances. Don Cheadle was great (as always). I was also quite suprised with the performance Sandra Bullock gave, she did an excellent job. In my opinion though, Brendan Fraiser was a bit of a miscast in this film. When his character began yelling and spouting off the F bomb, it came off as very goofy to me. Chris Bridges, AKA the rapper Ludacris, didn't do too bad in this film as well. Though it was far from an Oscar calibur performance, Ludacris fit into the film quite well. I also enjoyed Matt Dillion's performance. I haven't seen this guy in a film since There's Something About Mary. Either way, he did a good job.
 
The film reminded me of Magnolia a lot (which happens to be one of my favorite films). It's about a big group of people who all end up in situations that sort of intertwine together. Many of the characters are of different ethnic backgrounds. There are characters of Asian, Puerto Rican, African American, Caucasian, and Arab backgrounds. Each character(s) end up in situations that sort of connect them to other characters, in some shape or form.
 
Crash really focuses on racism. Pretty much every character gets put into some racist situation. Some of them are victims of racism and some of them are the ones who dish out the racism. I like how this film handles it's character's views of racism though. One minute a character will be getting treated like garbage due to his/her race, the next minute that same person will be doing the same thing. This is probably one of the most honest things I have seen in a film this year. I know that this film is trying to give the viewer some sort of message about racism, but I can't quite figure it out. I'm not sure if the writer is simply trying to show us the negative effects of racism (like American History X) or something else. Either way, each story is interesting and moving at the same time.
 
Paul Haggis's directorial debut is a good one. Nice camera work, good gritty style to it, and some interesting shots. Haggis also wrote the film, which he did another great job doing. Crash probably has some of the best dialog out of any film this year thus far. This guy really knows how to write drama stories. Unfortunatly this film and script isn't as good as Million Dollar Baby (Haggis' previous screenplay) but it's far from bad.
 
Even though I'm not quite sure of it's message, Crash is a very good film. I'm sure I would like it a lot more if I knew what the film was trying to teach us, but either way it's a great watch. This has the potential to grow on me in the future with more viewings. I'm not sure if it'll finally come to me when I put more thought into the film, but I'm sure whatever message this film has, it's probably a good message.

With [b]Crash[/b], writer-director Paul Haggis follows up his Oscar nomination for [b]Million Dollar Baby[/b] with a tale of race in modern Los Angeles. Employing the ensemble drama mode with loads of coincidence, Haggis attempts to look at racism from the many different ethnicities trying to get by in the City of Angels. Unfortunately, using an ensemble leads to the most common problem seen in this genre: superficial characterization in the service of a very self-aware story.
  
 Taking place in the span of two days, we see the fine line between race and class in Los Angeles ranging from the District Attorney (Brendan Fraser) and his wife (Sandra Bullock) down to a pair of cops (Matt Dillon and Ryan Phillipe) on down to a pair of carjackers who take the D.A.'s SUV in the opening moments of the film. Coincidences, mostly in the form of car crashes, keep the characters interacting with each other throughout the film. 
  
 Most of the film's conversations revolve entirely around race and that immediately knocks the film down several pegs on the believeablility scale. Not only would most of these characters be nowhere near as blatant about race (I've seen movie KKK members more subtle), but the speechifying makes the characters look more like mouthpieces for different theories on race relations and less like authentic characters. This is often a problem when it comes to films about racism. It can so often be such a subtle problem that many films exaggerate it to deal with it and subsequently shoot themselves in the foot by doing so. [b]Crash[/b] is no different. This film bludgeons you with its theme like a sledgehammer, giving off a pretentious air about it that was a turn-off from the hammy opening line spoken by Don Cheadle's homicide detective. 
  
 That opening line about crashing into each other to feel anything comes off as hammy and even moot given the crazy coincidences of everyone meeting. There were times it felt there were only about a dozen people in L.A. or else the city was the size of my old high school. The coincidental nature of the film is a gimmick and the tone of some of the character interactions struck me as odd, almost like it was black comedy in the tradition of [b]Pulp Fiction[/b]. "There's a Chinaman under the truck!" Yuck yuck. Other times, plot twists come off unintentionally funny, such as when Sandra Bullock takes a spill down the stairs. The pacing of these twists also doesn't help much, since the film climaxes long before you think it should. It moves quickly yes, but it also feels like we're just getting brief glimpses.
  
 Compounding the problem of the film's script and structure is a cast of mostly unappealing characters. Despite the film's simplistic statements about the grey nature of people, I just didn't end up caring for many of them. Matt Dillon is pretty good as an angry cop who, in the film's best scene, gropes a woman during a traffic stop. This scene works so well because while there is an undercurrent of race, it's primarily about power. Dillon's character arc is the best of all because Haggis gets the correct combination of right and wrong. While Officer Ryan may have what he feels is a pretty logical problem, it's his attitude that gets in the way. 
  
 However, just about all the other characters grate on the nerves. The Iranian store owner is just obnoxious, apparently understanding and speaking English only when the script called for another argument. During a fight with a locksmith, he came across as just plain crazy. When the characters aren't bewildering the audience with their behavior, they're pulling stupid mistakes that annoy. For example, a cop picks up a hitchhiker and then getting hostile with him. There's also a little girl who doesn't believe in monsters under the bed, probably has more street experience than I ever will, yet believes some horse hockey about an invincibility cloak. Another time, police witness a violent carjacking only to go after the driver and then never inquire about the two other guys who disappeared.
  
 People are good and bad.  That's essentially what [b]Crash[/b] boils down to (although one could make an argument that the film takes a half-hearted stab at other themes about conditioning and social disconnect). People initially portrayed as good do something that can be seen as bad and once the pattern is recognized, the rest of the film became a grueling task of guess the twist that would give a bad guy a simplistic redemption. Constantly overhead are the strings putting these characters through the ringer, never once allowing a scene to develop with any kind of natural progression.  Like when it snows if for no other reason than to give a visual signal that it's the end of the film. 
  
 At least it wasn't frogs.

It took me about 5 days to fully unpack. I really have too much "stuff". Most of the random objects I have are not even worthy of being categorized as "stuff". Nostalgia is my weakness.
    
     I must say -- [b][i]His Girl Friday[/i][/b] is a bit overwhelming. Witty, sly and fresh, for sure, but I needed to catch my breath sometimes. I expected it to be a hoot, but I was not expecting it to be so gleefully sardonic. Yeesh -- good thing I am not going to be a journalism major anymore. [b]A-[/b]
    
    Although [i][b]Crash[/b] [/i]is ambitious, Haggis commits the sin of having an ensemble cast and underdeveloping the majority of them. Therefore, the characters are basically stereotypes with one sympathetic scene. Perhaps that was deliberate, but it still does not account for a hollw core. Some scenes are tense and very effective, but the film as a whole is only momentarily powerful. Haggis strives to find a way to express racism but his presentation is too overt and preachy. I always thought of racism as being subtle. Haggis isn't sure if he wants to create an observant reflection on society or a hyperbolized depiction which exposes the ugliness of humans. For a film that tries to neatly tie all of the characters together in the end, it doesn't seem to have a strong focus on the themes and narrative. 
       
     When I was watching this film, I could not help but think of it as a mix of [i]Short Cuts[/i], [i]Amores Perros[/i] and [i]Do the Right Thing[/i]; all of which are better films (even though I am not a [i]Short Cuts[/i] fan). One of my minor complaints is the end montage. I really love how it is executed (with the intermittent fuzz and various other unpleasant sounds) but it just seemed a bit derivative to me, without knowing exactly where I had seen it before. Regardless, Egoyan succeeds again in weaving a tale of desire and alienation. [b]B+

[color=#fffacd]"Crash" exploits our superficial racist thoughts and lays them out for us to look at, but not think too much about. [/color][color=#fffacd]The movie is blunt and wastes no time questioning whether or not what the characters do is linked to prejudice. They are. It puts presumptuous thoughts onto the table and reminds us they're in everybody's mind - blacks, whites, Latinos, Asians and Middle Easterners. To me, the message of the movie is that we have a choice to follow up on our instinctual biases or reject them and see people for their true character. I choose the latter, but the movie also says that racism is a force that's hard to say no to.[/color]
 
[color=#fffacd]A friend of mine who worked at Bullseye Entertainment, one of the production companies that developed the film, told me it was pitched as "Magnolia" on the mean streets of L.A. that deals with racism. Anyone who's seen "Magnolia," or "Traffic" for that matter, will find links. In the course of one day, the movie shuffles between many stories, each with intertwining characters. Jean (Sandra Bullock) and Rick (Brendan Fraser), who serves as the district attorney, are an upper-class couple. They're carjacked by two analytical and cynical black men, Anthony (hip-hop star Ludacris) and Peter (Larenz Tate). Matt Dillon and Ryan Phillippe are two cops who pull over a TV director played by Terence Howard, and his wife, Christine (Thandie Newton), becasue they drive a similar SUV. Dillon's character is a bigot who takes his personal troubles out on other people.[/color]
 
[color=#fffacd]In another part of the city, Graham (Don Cheadle) and Ria (Jennifer Esposito) are two detectives who get into an accident with a screaming Korean woman, while Michael Pena is an alarm installer who ticks off a Persian convenient store owner (Shaun Toub) after his store is robbed. How all of these stories connect is, of course, for you to discover, but "Crash" makes for exciting and disturbing drama. The director is Paul Haggis, who wrote "Million Dollar Baby." Whereas that film was slower and more patient with its mood and tone, "Crash" uses brevity as a way to express how quick we all are to judge. Bullock, for example, delivers a line indirectly targeted at Pena's character so that we know how she feels at that moment, which could very well represent how she feels all the time.[/color]
 
[color=#fffacd]The movie ultimately takes us on a familiar journey to our fears, our anger and our shames. It never flinches, reminding us that conflicts like these happen everyday and if we close our eyes or turn our heads, we've missed something. Haggis and co-writer Robert Moresco don't overwhelm us, though. There's surprisingly a lot of humor in the film. It's geared toward everyone who's guilty of being prejudiced and perhaps represents the frivolity of such thoughts that run through our minds. The endless coincidences and connections in the film aren't contrived, but serve as a way to tie together as many races as possible to illustrate how each one has a member who's at fault. [/color]
 
[color=#fffacd]The tagline for the movie is "You think you know who you are, you have have no idea." I think that I'm not racist, but what if a black, Latino or Persian person pointed a gun in my face? Would I put a label on all the others in that group? "Crash" seems to think so. Sadly, it's probably right, but I'm glad it was brought to my attention.[/color]

As the world gets smaller, the more likely well bump into each other. The more likely wed be exposed to people different from us. The more well be dealing with the volatile subject of race. Could this be a good thing? If you see me walking down the street, what would you think of me based on my appearance? If you crashed into my car, what awful things might I say to your face? Are you racist? Am I racist? Who among us is not? The reality is everyone is a little bit racist. Unless youre blind, I dare you to step up and say youre not.
 
Crash interweaves stories of varying ethnic characters in Los Angeles. All of them affected by racism, whether they like it or not. Sandra Bullock is a Brentwood housewife, who is married to the District Attorney (Brendan Fraser). Shes the type of woman who tightens her clutch on her husbands arm the moment she sees two young black men (Larenz Tate and Chris Ludacris Bridges) walking towards them. When she sees a Mexican-American man (Michael Pena) is fixing her locks, she believes the man to be gangster. Don Cheadle and Jennifer Esposito play police detectives who are also lovers. She gets pissed when he incorrectly identifies her Latin origins. A gun store owner insultingly calls an Iranian man (Shaun Toub) Osama because he thinks the client might use the purchased gun for terrorism. A black TV director (Terrence Howard) is pulled over by a white cop (Matt Dillon) and his rookie partner (Ryan Philippe). The cop oversteps his bounds when he frisks the directors light-skinned wife (Thandie Newton) in a sexual manner. 
 
In one way or another, these characters will show up in another characters story. Writer and director Paul Haggis gives them raw dialogue that doesnt shy away with political correctness. For some reason, I cringed when I heard these racial comments on the big screen. It didnt feel right, even though I hear and say stuff like that often. But its not the brash conversations that the movie excels at. Its just plain good storytelling. Crash arrives at familiar moments but refuses to follow movie stereotypes. It has tons of unpredictable moments and it dares you to judge if a character is a good guy or a bad guy. 
 
The colorful ensemble is awfully strong. Matt Dillon and Ryan Philippe probably pull off their best performances here. The most memorable scenes for me involve their police characters approaching dangerous situations. Also take notice of relatively unknowns Michael Pena and Terrence Howard. Theyre absolutely engrossing in their own intensely written stories. Veteran Sandra Bullock is surprisingly effective in a dramatic and challenging role. But the biggest surprise is rapper Ludacris, who displays convincing wit and emotion to his character.
 
Despite many characters populating the film in short span of 100 minutes, the film feels complete. As far as Im concerned, none of the stories failed. Youll be pretty banged up when one story after another hits you on the gut, on the mind, and on the heart. It might take awhile to recover from this beautiful disaster.

It's a rare thing that a wide release film is as intelligent, human, and honest as Crash.  Though technically an "indie" picture (produced by Lions Gate), Crash has enough big name actors that will guarantee it will be seen outside of the usual arthouses and major city theaters.
 
And thank God for that; Crash is one of the finest American productions this year so far.  A sobering meditation on racial and class conflicts, it is also a tremendously acted ensemble film that deserves to be mentioned in the same breath as Nashville and Magnolia.
The characters are numerous, but never get in the way of the story, which is always moving full speed ahead.  Like the best ensemble pieces, this plays like life is unfolding; situations are messy and the players bump into each other.

Don Cheadle plays Graham, a high-ranking investigator in the LAPD whose dedication to his job is hindered by his knowledge that his brother his a street criminal.  Meanwhile, Graham's brother (Larenz Tate) and his partner (Ludacris) steal the LA district attorney's car at gunpoint.

There are other incidents.  A racist cop (intensely played my Matt Dillon) feels up a black woman during a routine traffic stop.  Sandra Bullock, the DA's wife, makes racist remarks about the Hispanic man changing their locks, presuming him to be a gang member when he is in fact a family man.  And an Iranian shop owner is presumed to be Arab, and made the target of anti-Arab slander when in fact he is of Persian descent.

Yet this is also not a simple case of black vs. white racism; each character shows their own prejudices in their actions, and each character shows a form of nobility, sometimes when it is least expected.

While watching Crash, I was reminded of that line in Cool Hand Luke - "What we've got here is failure to communicate."  I think that while this film may show an ugly side of us that we'd rather sweep under the carpet, it would be hard for anyone who sees it to walk out thinking we can't get along better...and then try to do just that.

And that's my two cents.

[i]Crash

[/i]Although Paul Haggis has only been involved in the making of three films, its fair to say that he has made quite the splash. After the huge success of his [i]Million Dollar Baby[/i], how would the writer follow the Oscar-winning surprise? The answer is [i]Crash[/i], a fascinating look at the current state of race relations which offers no easy explanations as most films on the topic have (i.e. [i]Guess Whos Coming to Dinner[/i]). The most common comparison seems to be to other ensemble pieces of today such as [i]Traffic [/i]and [i]Magnolia[/i] however, I would argue that it cannot be truly compared to the two given their inherent differences in structure and style. Although it certainly is akin to[i] Traffic[/i] in that it takes a multi-faceted look at an issue which has yet to be fully defined and explored, [i]Crash[/i] is much more dramatic, more cinematic if you will (which is not to say thats necessarily a [i]good [/i]thing nor is it to say that its a [i]bad[/i] thing), with its characters one can see a strong basis in singular basic themes such as loss of innocence, redemption, and selflessness. As for the [i]Magnolia [/i]comparison, I suppose one could find a few correlations between the two but they are wholly different in so many aspects I honestly dont see it as applicable. The main "flaw" critics seem to continually- and validly- point out would be the number of contrivances throughout its run time. However, this is not necessarily a flaw as much as a different, more self-conscious, style which actually helps the viewer to step back from the film and focus on what its trying to say. Another point of division amongst the two sides which inevitably seem to be forming in reference to this film would be the lack of character development. Again, this is not necessarily bad unless one gives it the context of a normally structured film which it certainly is not. I do not believe that the audience is necessarily supposed to sympathize with the characters themselves as much as empathize with their plights.Certain films must be judged on a much more subjective level given their content and [i]Crash[/i] is one of those films. The acting in the film is excellent with Don Cheadle being a highlight (not surprising given that hes one of my favorite working actors), even normally inconsistent actors such as Brenden Fraiser and Sandra Bullock deliver solid performances. Although it will certainly have its detractors, I was completely enthralled by Paul Haggiss latest and anticipate his future projects.

Perhaps I find it comforting to know that there are people in the world with bigger problems than me. Or maybe it's my voyeuristic side? Whatever the reason, I consider it something special when a film can simultaneously make you think and feel. And it's something all together magic when it can make you reconsider what you thought to be fact.
 
A lot of people have described Crash as "similar to Magnolia", but I'd say it has more in common with a film like Traffic. It takes a single theme and explores it from differing perspectives using parallel storylines. Maybe nobody else drew this comparison in an attempt to avoid obvious car jokes..
 
The only problem I have with recommending this is that it's not the type of film that is made to just be enjoyed. It's a film with something to say and it wants to make sure you get the message. That's not to say it's full of moral and righteousness but it does mean you'll be clear on what the film wants you to think - That is that racism can be hidden or outright and everybody has a bit of it in them.
 
So, who would want to see a film about racism that -if the previews are anything to go by- has everyone crying and screaming at each other? Well, there are three good reasons - Don Cheadle, Michael Pena and Matt Dillon. Yes,[i] that[/i] Matt Dillon. He does a fine job playing a completely corrupt cop (is there any other kind in movies?) who is sexually perverted and harbours overt racist tendencies. He is also singularly responsible for the one scene that made me the most uncomfortable in the entire film. Don Cheadle, who just gets better and better (this almost makes up for his accent in Ocean's 11.. almost) is superb. But, the best of the lot is Michael Pena. I would recommend him as the best reason to go and see this film.
 
Actually, now that I think about it, there is not one bad performance in Crash. That's really saying something when you consider it uses the talents of Sandra Bullock, Thandi Newton, Ludacris and Brendan Fraser. All the performances are completely naturalistic making it disturbing in it's believability.
 
On this point, some people might say the entire film is a little too realistic. Like I said before, this is not cinema that is concerned with providing you with an entirely pleasurable two hours. It has something to say and it's direct. So, if you go to the cinema to escape from real life, avoid this one.
 
Otherwise, this is definitely a film you should try and get to see. Sandra Bullock can actually act! Who'd want to miss that once in a lifetime opportunity?

Like [u]Saw[/u] (2004, James Wan), [u]Crash[/u] grew on me a lot the more I thought about it. I didn't like it much initially, but in retrospect, I dig it. 

It's about several characters, so it's hard to pin them all down into this story, but from memory we have a District Attorney and his wife who get robbed by two criminals, one a Black militant and the other his lighter hearted sidekick. Then there's an affluent Black couple, a racist cop, his young, not apparently racist partner, a Black police investigator and his Hispanic wife, a Persian store clerk, his daughter, a Mexican locksmith and his family, and an Asian couple. All of them interact in a day in which several terrible things happen to all of them, and all of them seem to have some beef with some or a few races who they take it out on. Because that's what [u]Crash[/u] is really about: racism, and how we all fall prey to it at some level at some point.

Let me try explaining my response to this film this way: every individual scene in [u]Crash[/u] is very good. The acting is amazing, and the dialogue is first rate. Paul Haggis's direction shows a lot of promise, as he uses tight close ups and landscapes fairly well. And I even liked how certain scenes played out. But the big "but" for me in [u]Crash[/u] was how they all connected together. I thought it was sloppy, and that bothered me after a while.

See, it's like this: there's no linear plot to [u]Crash[/u]. Everything just sort of crashes together. When it opens, it feels like it's going to be [u]Pulp Fictio [/u](1993, Quentin Tarantino)-esque, with the majority of the film in flashback and then coming back to the beginning. It even has a screen title of "Yesterday" after the first scene to suggest that structure. But unless I missed something (which is possible), I don't know whether that day ever elapses back to that "present moment" or not. I think it does when the Asian lady reenters the story, but even so, there was no need to put her up front to begin with. Move that first scene where it needs to be chronologically and IMO, no one would notice. So because there's no driving plot holding all this together, it's like a collection of scenes that connect via coincidence and plot contrivance. So ultimately the question becomes, do you like those scenes more than you dislike the lack of structure in [u]Crash[/u]? 
 
I personally didn't, but I can see how a lot of people would. Because truth be told, all of the scenes in [u]Crash[/u] are effective. Every character, just about, appears three dimensionally, leaving us with no easy answers and a lot to think about. For me, the moral of the film was that we all have problems, but we're all looking for somebody else to blame for them, and oftentimes use race as our way to do it. Sandra Bullock's character exemplifies this best, I think, but in one way or the other, all of the characters in [u]Crash[/u] do it. When I began this film, it reminded me of my frustration with the race problem, wondering how we were ever going to solve it, but by the end of it, I think I had an answer. [u]Crash[/u] argues that if we paid more attention to ourselves, and our own part in our own misfortunes, we'd realize it's not some boogeyman "out there" that's ruining our life. We're doing it to ourselves.

A strong message, and a strong film. I just wish it would have held together
better.

This might have been better if it weren't a coming-of-age story about Scarlett's character, but just a film about the downfall of Travolta's character.   [/b]Well written, well acted, strong cast. Sure, this is about as unrealistic as you can get, but I was able to forgive a lot of it because the coincidences emphasized the hypocrisy within all the characters. My early favorite for best ensemble movie of 2005. [b]8/10[/b]

[font=Arial]I'm always wary of the handful of films that come out every year that seem to have "everyone" in them. I have to say, CRASH was a most pleasant surprise. It's like MAGNOLIA and BOOGIE NIGHTS (both Los Angeles-set films I loved) on a much smaller scale. In this case, smaller is NOT a negative.[/font]
[font=Arial][/font] 
[font=Arial]Blessedly free of gratuitous violence and restrained in its indictment of Los Angeles (the city where I reside), writer/director Paul Haggis does a fine job of interweaving (and interconnecting) the stories of a seemingly disparate group of Angelinos. Normally I like a few loose ends dangling at the end of a movie but, the fairly neat package we are presented as the credits roll actually works in the film's favor. Indeed, we are all connected even if it is by the most tenuous of threads. Actions do have consequences, words carry weight and things (as well as people) are not always as they seem.[/font]
[font=Arial][/font] 
[font=Arial]It was also refreshing to see a film with racism as a central theme that did not preach and had the cajones spread the "blame" equally. This is not the tired "white people bad" and "black people victims" crap that Spike Lee churns out. Rather, the issue of racism is placed front and center in ALL of its ugly guises. Without pointing fingers and without sparing any of the major characters, Haggis shows that ignorance can be overt (like Matt Dillon's blatantly bigoted character) as well as internalized (like Terrance Howard's character, a TV producer so desperate to fit in that he turns a blind eye to the racist attitudes that swirl around him and the self-hatred deep within him).[/font]
[font=Arial][/font] 
[font=Arial]There are fine performances throughout but, stand-out work is turned in by Sandra Bullock, Thandie Newton, Michael Pena as well as Dillon and Howard. The big revalation in the cast is Ludacris (billed as Chris 'Ludacris' Bridges). As the de-facto "narrator" of the film, his warped sense of logic straddles a fine line between humor and tragedy. As funny as it is disturbing, the chase sequence that finds Ludacris and Howard thrown together (thanks to a botched car-jacking) is truly one of the best film scenes of 2005. Howard's almost emotionless dressing down of Ludacris at the end of the sequence ("You embarrass me. You embarrass yourself.") says so much with so few words. At that moment, you could hear a pin drop in the sold-out show I attended.[/font]
 
[font=Arial]The film is a plea for civility and understanding in a world that seems to have forgotten what it means to be polite and tolerant. I have to admit, CRASH has made me a little kinder, a little more patient and a lot more willing to cede the right of way (with a smile on my face) to my fellow drivers when I am on the road. Any film that can do that is, in my opinion, time well spent.


[/font]

[color=#999999][font=Tahoma]Although it is a huge relief that Jar Jar Binks is confined to a three second cameo, Lucas replaces Binks with an equally annoying General Grievous, an enemy droid that coughs and pointlessly wields around four light sabers against a Jedi that should have been able to dispose of the hunk of junk with just an inkling use of the force. [color=#999999][font=Tahoma][/font][/color] 
[color=#999999][font=Tahoma]Now, it is an undeniable fact that Lucas is a great storyteller, but when it comes to dialogue, the man should be writing for porn. The man couldnt romance a blowup doll if his life depended on it. Luckily, here in Revenge of the Sith, he limits these scenes between Portman and Christensen to a bare minimum, but even so, the evidence of poor dialogue is still there. [color=#999999][font=Tahoma]First Ill say this  Unleashed is Jet Lis best American film to date. Some have criticized this film for Lis performance, but I praise him for it. Theres a reason why it may seem Li might not know how to act in this film and thats because the character hes playing doesnt know how to be human. [color=#999999][font=Tahoma] [/font][/color]

[color=#999999][font=Tahoma]The supporting work is solid as well, with Hoskins turning in a malicious performance  the kind that really gets under your skin and almost has you throwing objects at the screen whenever hes on it. [color=#999999][font=Tahoma] [/font][/color]

[color=#999999][font=Tahoma]If you could picture Frankenstein infused with martial arts, you would have a pretty good idea of what Unleashed is like. There is a story here, a reason for there being the action sequences that there are, which is something many action films lack  a reason for blowing shit up other than it looks cool. [/font][/color]

[color=#999999][font=Tahoma] [/font][/color]

 Words truly have the power to sting in [b]Crash[/b], a stunning new drama from Paul Haggis, the writer of the Oscar-winning [i]Million Dollar Baby[/i] making an amazingly assured directorial debut here. The movie deftly weaves together several interlocking stories about characters living in L.A. (lawyers, producers, policemen, locksmiths; whites, blacks, Asians, Latinos; rich, middle-class, and poor), and paints a vivid picture of urban alienation, cultural disparity, and the unpleasant undercurrent of racism that still exists in that city, and, probably and sadly, others like it. It gives us the theory that in today's metropolitan centres, people are so disconnected from each other that the only way to feel someone's presence is to collide (with cars, with verbal force) with them.
  
 In an early scene, a white couple (Sandra Bullock, surprisingly harsh and unlikable, and Brendan Fraser, convincing as a self-centred district attorney) are walking casually down the street when a couple of young black people - one philosophical and righteously angry (Ludacris, a rapper boasting surprising presence), the other more mellow (Larenz Tate) - pass by them, then unexpectedly hijack their pricey Lincoln Navigator. Then two cops - a virulent racist who's been on the force for years (a searing Matt Dillon) and a rookie who is getting fed up with his partner's behaviour (Ryan Phillippe) - pull over another, different black Navigator, driven by a black TV director (Terrence Howard), and the vet proceeds to harass the driver and humiliate his lighter-skinned wife (Thandie Newton). After her fearful encounter, Bullock has the locks changed in her house by an honest Latino man (Michael Pena), who has a wife and kids back home, then wants them changed again because she doesn't trust the locksmith. An Iranian shopkeeper (Shaun Toub) has communication problems with the same locksmith, and after his shop is ransacked he goes to the man's house with a gun. Don Cheadle plays a detective who has an affair with his Latina partner (Jennifer Esposito), but doesn't even care enough to learn what country she's really from. And you might think Dillon's cop is just abusing his power, but he's got his own problems with his sick father and an HMO representative who denies the father's claim, and who also happens to be a black woman.
  
 And so on and so forth. The characters proceed to crash into one another in various, intense ways, and though Haggis has a lot of complex narrative choreographing to do, he never makes the connections between the characters feel too contrived, and he makes the transitions between scenes smoothly. He and Robert Moresco also craft direct, realistic dialogue that can be potently dramatic, casually shocking, or sharply funny, and that speaks to the ugly racism all of us are capable of, and that can be brought to the surface at any time. The diverse, eclectic cast make for a powerful ensemble, making their roles deep and believable and connecting with each other in unexpected, and often emotionally gripping, ways (the second scene between Dillon and Newton is just breathtaking). It may have its share of convenient coincidences, but [i]Crash[/i] is nevertheless a thrilling, electrifying, starkly funny, thought-provoking, and moving look at society and the way it is now - busy, disconnected, prejudiced, harsh, and violent, and with only a select few opportunities for real intimacy. [size=3][color=#000000][font=Times New Roman]The film tells the story of a group of people of different age, race, and occupation, living in Los Angeles. The lives of these people coincidentally converge together in a dramatic and incredibly heart-wrenching way. It is apparent that many of the coincidences that draw the characters together are perhaps contrived for the purpose of completing the story, and would not actually happen in a real situation. [/font][/color][/size]
 
[font=Times New Roman][size=3][color=#000000]I had a problem watching many of these coincidences because they played out like an old episode of Seinfeld: A set of wacky occurrences that somehow come together in the end and all tie back in with the original crazy plot. [size=3][color=#000000][font=Times New Roman]On the other hand, there were a few times when a couple of the occurrences were some of the most powerful moments I have seen in a film. I cannot deny the devastatingly honest and brutal parts of this movie that convey the true sense of emotional conflict that can occur when living in a world full of fear and hate. Every character seems to show regret in this film, and the most touching scenes show the characters trying to get redemption for their regretful actions. The characters in this movie were connected to the audience in such a profound way. I could not help but feel extreme sorrow for the plight of these people, especially for the Hispanic locksmith and his young daughter and wife. [/font][/color][/size]
 
[size=3][color=#000000][font=Times New Roman]That being said, I do also feel that a few of the characters were portrayed one way in the beginning of the movie and suddenly shifted near the end. One scene in the last part of the film involves a gun-toting car thief and a police officer. In the world of Crash (or the real world) where everyone is filled with anger and lives their lives at the edge of reason, how could the audience expect a gun-toting low-life with prior convictions to be anything more than just that? I will save the scene for you to view, but I cannot help wonder if perhaps Haggis was trying to show that everyone, even criminals, have a bit of good in them. For the purpose of tying the story together, this scene will work, but for the purpose of being realistic, I did not buy what Haggis was selling. [/font][/color][/size]

[i]Crash[/i], set in Los Angeles, is a cinematic demolition derby. Cars, ethnic groups, husbands and wives smack into each other, shattering glass, relationships, and lives. Co-screenwriter and director Paul Haggis, who wrote Million Dollar Baby, traces his inspiration for the film to being carjacked back in 1991. Watch out: hes still mad! This is an ensemble film of interwoven stories, [u]a[/u] [u]la[/u] [i]Magnolia[/i] or [i]Short Cuts[/i], with ethnic, marital and familial strife as the signature spice of the stew. 
 
Detective Graham Waters (Don Cheadle), on his way to a crime scene, tells his Latina partner and lover, Ria (Jennifer Esposito) how people in L.A., insulated in their cars, never get to touch each-other. Bang! An Asian woman rear-ends their cruiser. The women get out. You blake too fast! the Asian woman screams. If you see over steering wheel you blake too! Ria retorts, and, whammo, the racial slurs fly like cat fur. 
 
Two young Black men, Anthony, (rapper Chris Ludacris Bridges) and Peter (Larenz Tate) emerge from a restaurant in an upscale white neighborhood. Anthony, dissatisfied with the service, pontificates on racial discrimination and the potential danger of being the only Blacks in a vanilla milieu. Some danger: theyre the ones with guns. The two reminded me of the pair of wisecracking horseflies in Racing Stripes, though the intellects of the flies were more evenly matched. Peter is dim, naïve, and basically a straight man to Anthonys homie Socrates. The two carjack the L.A. District Attorney, Rick Cabot (a too-youthful Brendan Fraser) and his wife Jean (Sandra Bullock, playing not so nice for a change), with dire consequences. 
 
Cameron (Terrence Howard), a Black television director and his lighter-skinned wife Christine (Thandie Newton) are caught having oral sex in their car by a pair of cops, Sgt. Ryan (Matt Dillon), an angry bigot saddled with a sick father, and Officer Hanson (Ryan Philippe), an idealistic newbie. Things escalate rapidly, leaving Christine violated and Cameron, figuratively, with no balls. 
 
Adding post - 9/11 paranoia to the mix, a gunshop owner addresses a Persian customer as Osama. The ensuing explosion is damped by the Persians daughter, who, like other female characters in the film, balances emotional intelligence and common sense with the testosterone-fueled obduracy of the men.
 
The script is intelligently and perceptively written, with wit and humor that provide needed relief from the pounding that the film administers. The plot involves numerous coincidences. Too many? A matter of opinion. After all, much of the entertainment value of mainstream movies derives from order imposed upon a chaotic universe. Real life is not a movie or reality show: we need our cineplex fix. 
 
The characters are not, pun intended, purely black or white. Despite their prejudices, they are nuanced, and demonstrate their essential humanity in a variety of ways. The film itself is rich in subtext, and director Haggis succeeds in showing, rather than simply telling, the source of the characters' complex emotional palette. 
 
The plot successfully negotiates the no-mans land between improbable coincidence and effective dramatic irony. It looks as though Haggis threw everything he could about race relations into the story, and the characters played by Bullock and Fraser are sketchy. But these are minor gripes. The performances are uniformly excellent, and the music by veteran composer Mark Isham is affecting without being cloying. The film succeeds in making its points in a cumulative manner, as a series of sharp and well-aimed blows that add up to a knockout. Once youve risen from the canvas, Crash is likely to reverberate inside your head for a long time.
 
My rating: **** Healthy

This is a thoughtful movie that exists to make a point about the complexity of human nature and how people can change depending on the situation. It accomplishes its task by using a complex plot structure, weaving together at least six different stories with creative editing. 
 
And in order to more drastically drive home the point, there a a few times when the coincidence factor is high enough to only happen in hollywood. [i]Crash[/i] just might be the most interesting movie up for discussion thus far this year. I'm inclined to like it, love it maybe even, but it has its share of flaws and errors. As the movie began, I was worried about what I'd gotten myself into, with the blatant conversations that screamed, "THIS MOVIE IS GOING TO BE ABOUT RACE!" And sometimes the film is like that, and that's when it's at its weakest. The theme is pushed too hard in places, but in the end, it does make a solid impression. 
 
Strong points in the film are when Haggis's direction is intense and focused in on a scene, such as the car wreck, the important scene with the little girl, etc. Absolutely breathtaking: literally. It ends a little bit more subtley than it begins, and shows its meaning without shoving it down our throats. We're all connected, and sometimes we're all a little bit racist (Avenue Q anyone?). But we're all the same deep down. It certainly means well, and hit me hard, in a good way I think.

[b]Crash[/b] has been described as an intriguing exposition of the undercurrents of racism that are always bubbling just under the surface of apparently thoroughly multicultural, multiracial Los Angeles. This is certainly the jumping board for the movie, forming the thrust and emotional undertow of its dramatic narrative as it unfolds across the lives of a veritable tapestry of characters. Police detective Graham (Don Cheadle) is investigating a possibly racially-motivated killing. Ryan (Matt Dillon) is an asshole of a bigoted cop, who pisses off his younger partner Hanson (Ryan Philippe) when he stops a rich black couple and sexually violates the young wife Christine (Thandie Newton) when frisking her. LA's district attorney Rick Cabot (Brendan Fraser) and his wife Jean (Sandra Bullock) are car-jacked by a pair of black hoodlums (Chris 'Ludacris' Bridges and Larenz Tate). The edgy Jean is suspicious that their locksmith Daniel (Michael Pena) will sell a copy of their house keys to his no-good friends, but Daniel really is just a good family man who goes home to the daughter hiding under the bed, terrified by the bullet that ripped through her window one day. He replaces the lock on a faulty door for Persian shopkeeper Farhad (Shaun Toub), whose family, as we shall see, is discriminated against for being something they're not--Arab.
 
Considering the sheer wealth of stories to get through, writer/director Paul Haggis has pulled off an incredible feat in keeping this movie just under two hours long, while giving us compelling insights into most of the main characters. (And don't even think the list above is exhaustive, as there are secondary and minor characters whose entrance into the movie frequently makes just as strong a point about the prejudices we all carry with us as the leads do.) Haggis does a good job of laying out the preconceptions--and often, misconceptions--that we live with and the assumptions we make, whether consciously or not. Anyone who's been a victim of racism, however mild, will understand some of the pain, humiliation and internal conflict experienced by the characters here: like Graham, when he is asked to lie, or at least omit extenuating circumstances, on his case so as to assure his promotion. Or Hanson having to pretend that he has an embarrassing personal problem to get away from being Ryan's partner, as explained to him by his black superior who has no illusions about how he made it up the ranks of the LAPD--by shutting up and not fighting personal battles that could get him fired. It's not difficult to understand how Ryan's treatment of Christine leaves her feeling violated and lashing out at her husband Cameron (Terrence Howard), who in turn begins to feel less of a man for all the times he's never stood up for himself, including against his diva of a TV star Fred (Tony Danza in a cameo) for wanting the black guy on the show to 'talk more black'. It's interesting that his most vocal mouthpiece in the movie is a black thug who emerges onscreen sounding as literate and righteously indignant as they come, railing against the slightest hint of racism, only to proceed in perpetuating the stereotype in the worst way possible. 
 
But while this is all worthy stuff, my favourite aspect of [b]Crash[/b] is not so much its treatment of the racism, but its intelligent, balanced treatment of its characters wrapped up in their own little dramas, even as these spill out and bleed into the lives of others. No character is uniformly bad or good here--they are flawed individuals, all carrying their own baggage and world-views, all making mistakes and assumptions that Haggis very cleverly suggests to us are perfectly justified ones to make. Take Christine, who, as fate would have it, is rescued from a horrific car accident by Ryan--she first flinches away from his attempts to help her, terrified that he will hurt her... with good cause, given his behaviour the previous evening. Hanson too, until his penultimate scene an apparent hero in a movie peopled with anti-heroes and schmoes, makes all the wrong assumptions one fateful drive back into LA, and yet the hint of steel in the darkness and Haggis' clever tension-filled dialogue all contribute to the audience actually understanding why Hanson reacts the way he does. (Am I being enigmatic and non-spoilery enough? [g]) It would have been easy to give in to stereotypes in creating his multitude of characters, but Haggis instead chooses to give us insight into the strange, inexplicable, at once evil and good human condition, and we too realise that we're making assumptions about people [i]all the time[/i], regardless of the colour of their skin. Ryan has a well of love for his father larger than you would assume motivates a close-minded bigot. Jean's high-strung shrewishness hides a loneliness and estrangement we've all felt, while Graham's devotion to his desparately sinking mother (Beverly Todd), trying to keep her from giving herself over to complete insanity in hankering after her lost son, is wonderfully affecting.
 
So far, all is well and good, with Haggis backed also by an ensemble cast that rises gallantly to the occasion, with standouts being Cheadle and Dillon, and pleasant surprises include Bullock and Newton (both of whom show dramatic abilities so far not hinted at in their careers). The only thing hobbling [b]Crash [/b]from greatness, I feel, is Haggis' missing out on providing a satisfying resolution to some of the main characters' storylines. I'm not asking for a happy ending, god no--that would defeat the purpose of what is really a very realistic movie, depicting real humans rather than movie heroes and matinee idols. But some stories end worse than others: Graham's is a corker, for instance, as is Jean's discovery of her lonely existence. But Cameron's journey of self-discovery is frankly bizarre, culminating in a climactic stand-off wth a host of squad cars and policemen that eventually dovetails into... nothing. (Oooh, pretty snow! Big whoop.) While I greatly enjoyed Daniel's story, when he gives his daughter peace of mind by tying around her shoulders an invisible cloak promising indestructability, and the vengeful Farhad's stalking of Daniel's house was an excellent example of filmic tension, both men ended up with too much of a delusional fairy-tale ending for it to ring quite true. 
 
Nevertheless, [b]Crash[/b] was a good time at the movies. Far, far, FAR from escapist, but a wonderfully-observed study of the human condition that's as big-hearted, flawed and dark as its subject matter.

So much for great expectations. I thought "Crash" was going to be an exceptional movie, sure to give audiences new insights into race relations both in LA and in society in general. And sure it may have had that kind of impact on some even many audience members but if anyone who watches "Crash" really thinks about it, the question becomes - What messages does the movie expose us to that most observant individuals do not already know?
Yes. Racism and prejudice exists, has existed, and will probably always exist in the great melting pot known as America.  But who didn't already know that?
Crash is a pretty unoriginal movie in the way it shows the raical disparities between whites and blacks.  However the movie is somewhat original in its exploration of the racial tensions and stereotypes that play out between blacks and asians, whites and mexicans.  In the movie, all of the characters  are more complicated than they appear, which gets right to the heart of their intertwining stories.  The most interesting and engaging characters are the two black self proclaimed criminals played by hip hop artist/acting rookie Ludicrous and his partner in crime played by Lorenz Tate.  Ludicrous portrays a thug like character who has very strong, extremist opinions about the state of black people in the good old US of A.  His partner in crime is the voice of reason because he is more willing to acknowledge human complexity.  one of the most profound moments occurs when Sandra Bullock's character falls down the stairs and she later realizes that the one person besides her husband who truly cares about her is her Mexican maid.  Her maid is the only one who supports her emotionally immediately after her accident.  This is the same maid that Bullock's character would have quickly accused of stealing only a day before.  It is this kind of character realization and development that really gives the movie depth and quality more so than many of the other scenes in which overt behavior provides the shock value.

I probably wouldn't have seen this if it hadn't been for A. A friend of mine saying he was really pretty sure I'd like it, and B. It was at the cheap seats. 
 
But I'm sure glad I did! I thought this would be one of those ultra-self-important 'hollywoodized' type moralistic films about racism, but in reality, it's quite a bit different.
 
It is self-important to a certain degree, and although it's a Lion's Gate film (It seems to me Lion's Gate has gotten so big as to not really fit the independent mold anymore), it's clearly still a hollywood project, with a ensemble cast of familiar faces, but it isn't a moralizing film, and it's remarkably well done.
 
Some have complained that the film is too riddled with coincidences, and there is some justification to that complaint, but it misses the point: The film is a story with a point, not a moral so much, but a point, and the story is constructed around that idea. It isn't suppose to be a naturalistic film. The characters, by neccesity, need to act like real people, their dellemas and personalities need to be grounded in reality, but the way events unfolds isn't suppose to be naturalistic, it's a ambiguous parable, not a birds eye view of some characters lives. 
 
Anyhow, this film works very well for a series of reasons. The first one, is that it is excellent at setting up moral dellemas and situations that reflect a certain point of reality. It is doubtful that all these things would intersect like this, that is part of the movie construct, but any individual dellema is very realistic and pointed. With one exception (the persian and the hispanic locksmith), they all worked great. 
 
Second, I really liked his textural style. His camera, music, and flow of the film were excellent, kind of like a cross between Paul Thomas Anderson and Michael Mann (and I don't just say this because their films take place in LA too). He uses a variety of different types of music, all to good effect, and the film is always interesting to look at.
 
Third, the performances are universally strong, even from Sandra Bullock. The who's who of Hollywood casting is distracting at first, but by the time the film really picks up speed, you won't notice, the performances and the directing won't let you. 
 
Finally, like 'Do The Right Thing' before it, this film shows racism in all it's forms, yet refuses to damn anyone, or to propose easy, feel good solutions, which few films either have the courage to do, or know how to do. It's characters are facinating because we can always understand them, even when we are horrified by their actions. It isn't a 'big bad racist' vs. 'poor, meek, honest little Black, Irish, Mexican, Asian pick-your-favorite-minority-group-and-incert-them-here,' it's about a bunch of people that are flawed, and how they interact with each other, and continue to exaserbate the situation by not allowing themselves to look deeper.
 
The fact that this film is currently #94 on the IMDB top 250 is utterly rediculous, but it is a very fine film, probably the best one I've seen so far this year, by a hair anyway (Forgiveness, and Land of the Dead are close). It's a film like 21 Grams: Yes, self important, yes big hollywood cast, but still gritty, moving, and impossible to take your eyes off of.

 [/size][/i][size=2]I watched Crash expecting a good film, and finished watching it shellshocked, having watched a [i]great[/i] film. Ever so often, a film of such searing intensity comes along as to drag you along for the ride. Halfway through 2005, Crash is already coming along as one of the best films of this year alongside Batman Begins. 
 
 Crash has this powerful intensity that frankly cannot be described. The film moves on a kinetic framework, drawing on luck and seredipity to potray how the lives of different people, across different social classes and races intertwine and literally crash in the space of 36 hours. And the result is a dynamite of racial prejudice, xenophobia, and at the same time hope for something better. Not quite a masterpiece, but damn close to being one. 
 
 The parallel storyline and large ensemble cast is reminiscent of the likes of Amores Perros and Pulp Fiction, but what this really reminds me of is the little known and underrated Australian film Lantana, which is likewise one of my favourite films. In Crash, we have a solid ensemble cast which bring out the gritty reality of life. Not the sanitised Hollywood version, but the bleak and pervasive sense of racial discrimination in the US. Every one in the film is guility of it, and yet everyone is also a victim of it. It may be a film populated by blacks, whites, hispanics, asians but in the film every character is a shade a grey. There are no moral touchstones in the film, everyone has a side which they may well dislike. A racist white cop who harrasses a black couple at first seems like a jerk, but later, we sympathise with his filial piety and in an ironic twist of events, he would later save the woman he molested. 
 
 Granted, alot of the coincidences would seem too much and even too contrived. But that is the nature of film; some artistic license has to be taken. And yes, due to the many characters populating the film, some of the character arcs inevitably get the short shrift. Sandra Bullock and Brendan Fraser's charcter arcs are truncated and fail be be sufficienctly developed. 
 
 But the many powerful and poignant imagery more than makes up for it. The confrontation between the cops and the black couple and the subsequent meeting between them make more one of the more memorable scenes of the film. As victims and aggressors change place, as the racial complexities of human nature confront us, how will we react? Will we, quite literally crash and burn?
 
 A thoughtful and provoking film, Crash takes a look at race relations and in the process confront us and forces us to look at ourselves, at our prejudices. The characters of the film are realistically potrayed and could well be a mirror for ourselves. In particular, the black couple played by Thandle Newton and Terence Dashon Howard as well as the racist white white cop (Matt Dillion) impress in the film. 
 
 Crash is one of those films that i'm glad to have watched, and i'm richer for the experience.

Intense story about perceptions and prejudices, acted out by an ensemble cast whose characters have intertwining relations.
 
Top character for me was Matt Dillon's racist cop -- great to see Matt in a solid dramatic role.
 
Everyone is not what they seem.
 
After the district attorney's (a smarmy Brenden Fraser) Lincoln Navigator is carjacked by a couple of black guys (a strong Ludacris and Larenz Tate), an alert is out.
 
Dillon and his young partner (Ryan Phillippe) see a truck matching the description, but the plates aren't the same. But the couple in the truck are up to something, so Dillon pulls the the Navigator over, much to his partner's objections.
 
In it are a black director (Terrence Howard) and his light-skinned wife (Thandie Newton). They are giggling, and have an attitude that Dillon finds galling, so Dillon's character steps over the line during a patdown of the man's wife, which causes no end of problems for the couple later on.
 
Later, Dillon is seen at home, worrying over his sick dad, and on the phone, getting vulgar with the HMO and a black woman who works there.
 
But, as I said, all is not what it seems. Is Dillon really a racist? Is Phillippe's character really such a good guy?
 
This is all before another crime scene, where a body has been found and there is talk of how cold it is and that it might snow.
 
Gliding through it all is Don Cheadle, a black detective whose having an affair with his Latina partner, has a junkie mother and a brother gone missing.
 
Meanwhile, the DA's wife (Sandra Bullock) is having problems of her own, starting with the tattooed Hispanic man changing the locks on their home after the carjacking.
 
And that guy has issues of his own, caring for a young daughter and trying to move into a decent neighbour.
 
And still more meanwhile, a Persian shopkeeper buys a gun with the help of his daughter, the store gets robbed and locksmith gets the blame.
 
The stories twist tighter and tighter and everyone tries to deal with who they are and what they are and what they believe about what other people are and who they are.
 
The only people who take it in the ass in all this interracial reflection are the Asians, who come off pretty horribly stereotyped. But then maybe that is another film for another time.

This movie came out ages ago and I had no interest in seeing it. Even after friends told me they'd seen it and liked it, I still had no interest in seeing it. But then last Friday it came down to seeing either [i]Crash[/i] or a two and a quarter hour epic set in a Beijing theme park, and the latter sounded like just too much of a chore. So I peddled my little bicycle to the closest theatre still showing [i]Crash[/i] and took my seat amongst the smattering of others who had chosen to see this particular movie over three months after it was released and wondered just what their excuses were. Couldn't get a sitter til now?
 
As is often the case in films I unenthusiastically see simply for lack of a better alternative, I soon regretted my decision. Fifteen minutes into [i]Crash[/i] and I was considering walking out. Cutting my losses short, hopping back on my little bicycle, riding back home, and writing the shortest review ever. "It sucked. I walked out." 
 
For better or for worse, lethargy got the better of me and I ended up seeing it through to the end. My reward is the seemingly daunting task of writing this review, despite total lack of inspiration, in part due to my week-long procrastination and the resultant dulling of the memory of my initial ire. 
 
So here goes. Quick and painless. Like pulling off a Band-Aid.
 
[i]Crash[/i] has about 47 main characters. I couldn't keep them straight. They all live in Los Angeles, which I hear is a fairly large city, and yet they bump into each other constantly, both literally and figuratively. Almost all of them are blatantly, openly racist. There are blacks, whites, Latinos, Asians and Persians, all living and working side by side and hating each other's guts. 
 
I can somewhat accept the concept that many or even most people have some prejudices when it comes to people of other races, but in our current PC climate, all but the Matthew Hales of the world manage to keep them in check, at least publicly. Not these people. Not only are they extremely racist but they apply no self-censorship whatsoever. They just come right out and call the Mexican locksmith a crook and ridicule the Korean woman who mispronounces words. They accuse the Persian man of being a terrorist and make fun of the black woman's name. 
 
Then, just when the movie has us convinced that almost everyone in L.A. hates and fears people of a different ethnic background, whoa, implausible plot contrivances occur which turn all of the information about these characters that was just jammed down our collective throats upside down. Upside down, I tell ya! The racist cop becomes heroic. The good cop succumbs to prejudice. The black thug really has a heart of gold. And the rich white bitch realizes that her Latina housekeeper is her one true friend. Big hug! Awww.
 
And then it snows. In Los Angeles. Magical! The end. And we're supposed to all walk out of the theatre pondering just what a complex entity racism is and how seemingly bad people can have good traits and seemingly good people can have bad traits. Why [i]can't[/i] we all just get along, huh? 
 
Ugh and double ugh.
 
With such a negative review, why, you may ask, are you giving this movie even a 4? Well, just as a seemingly one-dimensional movie character can turn out to have some good qualities, so too can a sucky movie contain an occasional well-written subplot. Or a smattering of good dialogue. Or a rare compelling scene floating amidst the flotsam and jetsam of raw suckage. 
 
Whoa. That's either the best or the worst sentence I've ever written. Maybe both. I best end now. If you haven't yet seen this movie, you've made the right decision. And if you have seen it and you told me that you liked it and now you're reading that in my opinion it sucks, well, you already knew that I was a contrarian, didn't you?
