[font=Verdana][color=#000000]In the city of Los Angeles, everyone is separated by metal and glass. What happens when these worlds collide? So is the story of Crash. Several individual stories interweave during two days involving a collection of eight inter-related characters. The first involves a black police officer and his drugged out mother who is depressed about her missing son who appears not to exist. The second story involves a pair of car thieves, one who believes there is a conspiracy against his race, and the other who believes theories against his race is one big contradiction. The third story is in regards to a District Attorney and his irritated and pampered housewife. The fourth story is in regards to a racist seventeen-year veteran police officer that is caring for his sick father who happens to lives with him. The next story is about the racist cops younger partner who wants to do right in the world and may be the only non-racist character in the film. The final three stories involve a successful black Hollywood director and his wife who must deal with the racist cop and an inter-racial marriage, while the next story is in regards to an Iranian-immigrant shopkeeper who buys a gun to protect his shop with the help of his daughter. The final story is in regards to a Hispanic locksmith who people are biased against because he has visible tattoos. However, people do not know about his family life that includes a young daughter who is afraid of bullets.

[i]Crash [/i]is an intense film, a whirlwind of characters and dramatic events spanning a day in Los Angeles. The Director, Paul Haggis, had to be inspired by Paul Thomas Anderson's [i]Magnolia[/i]. Both films have interconnecting stories with similar themes, both have a weather related quirk at the end, and both contain musical sequences filled with shots of characters reflecting on their lives. 
 
[i]Crash's[/i] focus is on race, and how communication barriers and prejudices can often take complicated situation's to their breaking point. Don Cheadle is a black homicide detective, having an affair with his Latino partner (Jennifer Esposito). Matt Dillon is a racist white cop, frustrated with a sick father, who seems aware and resigned to his character flaws. Ryan Phillippe is Dillon's partner. A principled fellow, who finds out by the end of the film that perhaps his partner was correct in telling him, "You have no idea who you are." 
 
Ludacris and Lorenz Tate are black carjackers, and offer up some of the film's most hilarious dialogue. Brendan Fraser is a logical white district attorney. His wife, played by Sandra Bullock, is a spoiled, prejudiced, frustrated housewife who is searching for answers as to why she is always angry. 
 
I just realized that it will take forever to list all the characters and their relation to the story, so I'll just quit now, and point out that this is one of the film's flaws. There are so many plot lines, and so many conflicts, that the film fails to flesh each one out sufficiently. Another problem I had with [i]Crash[/i] is that there are an extraordinary amount of highly dramatic situations that arise, that tend to lure the viewer into remembering that they're watching a film, and in a gritty life drama, this can only detract from the underlying message.

And the film doesn't have a preachy air, sometimes difficult to acheive when exploring a subject like race. 
 
[i]Magnolia[/i] is an excellent film to compare with [i]Crash[/i]. Paul Thomas Anderson's film has all of the traits of Paul Haggis', but none of the drawbacks. If you haven't seen either, watch them both, and see for yourself.

Paul Haggis wrote last year's best film with the incredible [b]MILLION DOLLAR BABY[/b], and with [b]CRASH[/b], he has truly outdone himself. This time he writes and directs and proves himself as a powerful director, giving this multi-plotlined film a very natural flow, as well as keeping some shocking moments low-key and using the "less is more" technique, and giving the "glassy" city of Los Angeles an atmospheric feeling that anything could happen with these characters at any time, he navigates through the city with an effortless cool and it feels like you know the place just as well as he seemingly does by the film's end. [b]CRASH [/b]is not only what will probably turn out to be the year's best film, but with Haggis behind the wheel, it's even better than Clint Eastwood's moving masterpiece [b]MILLION DOLLAR BABY[/b].
 
The cast is the most attractive aspect of the film on first glance. Haggis does take a few risks with a couple of actors though. Ludacris and Ryan Phillippe, for example. Ludacris is nothing but a rapper, right? And has Ryan Phillippe ever done anything seriously challenging for his career? Though I had doubts about them before going in, under Haggis' excellent direction both turn in performances of the highest order. Ludacris bringing a sort of "streetwise preacher" feel to his character, and Phillippe both vulnerable and intense as a young cop who gets a bit mixed up in the job, though he has a good heart.
 
The best of the cast's performances come from Sandra Bullock, Thandie Newton, Matt Dillon, Terrence Dashon Howard and Michael Pena. Bullock in particular is amazing, showing range I never knew she had. She is totally convincing as a complete and utter bitch and when her character begins to get underneath her own skin, she almost brought me to tears. Particularly one scene near the very end of the film where she has an embrace with her housekeeper. Whew! Howard and Pena also bring a real heartbeat to their roles, while Newton is given an excellent opportunity to show a woman who hits rock-bottom and doesn't waste it. Dillon is a bastard, but a sympathetic one, and his very questionable actions relate to his dying father - and Dillon's character must feel extremely frustrated that he can do nothing to help his father, this is shown brilliantly in a scene with [b]URBAN LEGEND[/b]'s Loretta Devine.
 
[b]CRASH [/b]is a complex and enthralling film with very serious, relatable issues in today's world - racism and class for example, this film contrasts the differences between upper-class and lower-class people very well, and the racism angle is excellently handled. The film is constantly ignoring or destroying stereotypes, while sometimes staying true to them and showing that they do exist. I'm not explaining this film very well, because it really is just one of those incredible experiences you have to see to understand and formulate your own thoughts on it. 
 
2005's best so far!

Easily one of the better pictures of 2005, this movie focuses around the racism and xenophobia that surrounds all of us, every day. What makes it really special is that none of its characters are good or evil. They are all heroes and are all villains in some way. It is not one-sided. It shows different views of racism, different sides of racism, and different kinds of racism.
 
This movie features a star-studded cast including Sandra Bullock, Don Cheadle, Brendan Fraser, Ludacris and Tony Danza in a small role. Some of these performances are surprisingly good, such as Matt Dillon as a rascist cop and Ludacris as a car-jacker.
 
Paul Haggis wrote the screenplay for 'Million Dollar Baby' (2004 Best Picture Academy Award Winner) and had planned to direct it... until he turned the direction over to Eastwood because he was tied up due to directing [i]this [/i]movie. I think this movie is much better than 'Million Dollar Baby' because 'M$B' only hinted at profundity while this film actually had a point. It said that no matter how unbiased we think we are, we are wrong. Stereotypes and biases surround all of us, all the time. Haggis is becoming one of the most insightful screenwriters/directors I've seen, and I look forward to seeing more of his work.
 
The only problem I have with Haggis' screenplay is that some parts are a little farfetched, although most of the story [i]is [/i]feasible. There are so many characters and so much story to cover that Haggis' direction moves lightning fast, so some viewers might have been left behind as the story takes off. There are so many threads and connections between the numerous characters that it takes some serious focus to keep up. Also, at some points the swearing gets a little out of hand, almost to the point where it becomes unnecessary.
 
Chronologically (by release date), this is one of the best movies I've seen in a long time. It shows both sides (well, really like twenty sides) of the story, displaying every character's biases and bigotry. I highly recommend that you see this movie. It may be too early to say, but I think it may get nominated for Best Picture, and it has a case for winning too. All I can say is MAKE MORE LIKE THIS. Whether or not you agree with it, there's no doubt this movie is thoughtful, compelling and provocative.

Crash is the story of many characters of different races 'colliding' with each other in an event and the effects it has on all of them. It is written and directed by Paul Haggis (wrote the screenplay for Million Dollar Baby).
 
Crash is incredible. Almost done to perfection, it had me hooked from the beginning. This is now one of my favorite movies. In my top 20. Relentless is its telling of the problems of race, but ultimately shows us that we are all of one race, HUMANITY. No one is perfect. Everyone has their own problems. We make rash decisions. But some of us are blessed enough to be given a second chance. 
 
What I loved most about Crash was the excellent characters. The viewer is thrown right into the middle of their life. Just when we begin to judge them (like they do to each other w/o even knowing each other), something happens and we see the other side of the story, and we realize we can't judge them. Even though some of the redemptions are small, they are still effective. And the characters you think are great, you find out later, might not be so great and mess up, just like everyone else. As the credits role, it makes you think about your own actions and how you judge others too quickly, whether it be by race, age, sex, etc.
 
The acting is top-notch. Many big-name stars are involved (Don Cheadle, Sandra Bullock, Brendan Fraser, Terrance Howard, Thandie Newton, Ludacris, Matt Dillon, Ryan Phillippe, Jennifer Espesito, etc.) and even those you have never seen give great performances. Every character is believable. You feel sympathy, anger, disgust, and a fondness for each character displayed, but not too much.
 
The writing is awesome. Never cheesy, never boring, doesn't mince words, always getting the point across with great effect. I don't think the writing could've been any better.
 
Crash is great.  In my opinion, from what I've seen, this one will be a hot contender at the 2006 Oscars.  A perfect pick for Best Picture and Best Screenplay. 9/10

This is a first for me in a long time. Usually, I don't write reviews, full reviews, unless a film completely intrigues me. When I say intrigues, I mean, whether the film is good or bad, if it has me thinking about it afterwards, then it is a film I have to discuss. The film in question today?
  [i][b]CRASH [/b][/i](2005)
  written & directed by Paul Haggis
  Starring:
  Don Cheadle
  Brendan Fraser
  Sandra Bullock
  Larenz Tate
  Chris "Ludacris" Bridges
  Jennifer Esposito
  Ryan Phillippe
  Thandie Newton
  Matt Dillon
  Terence Howard
  William Fichtner
  
  I can't really put my finger on Paul Haggis. I can't get a read on him. [b][i]MILLION DOLLAR BABY [/i][/b]was a film that I genuinely liked and admired. I know he is a talented writer, but is he able to be an accomplished writer/director?
  I'm not sure. The opening of [i][b]CRASH [/b][/i]is quite promising, to be sure. A beautiful credit sequence, followed by a great statement by Don Cheadle's character on the disconnection that people share(or don't share)with one another. That flows right into Anthony(Ludacris)and Peter's(Larenz Tate)exiting of a coffee shop, and Anthony dissecting the behavior of the waitress in the coffee shop. It's an incredibly well-written and acted scene, pointing out some major characterisics of the people around them. When Anthony spots a white woman(Sandra Bullock)clutching her purse in fear, he becomes angry, launching into a diatribe about why he should be the one afraid of her, not the other way around. After all, they are in a predominantly white neighborhood, clearly the minority, so why is she afraid? Because, in a moment of beautiful contradiction, Anthony and Peter carjack the white couple. As I said before, it's a great scene, with so many undercurrents of emotion, and it's beautifully played.
  
 Keep in mind. It is at this point that, for the most part, the film goes downhill.  All of this is not enough, though. Haggis needed more time to expand each of the characters, and because he didn't, a handful of them come off as one-note and emotionless. [size=3][i]Crash [/i]is a tale of interlocking characters in Los Angeles that strives to make a profound statement about race relations in America, but instead comes across as somewhat sophomoric and tidy. Despite having a gritty style highly reminiscent of Steven Soderbergh's [i]Traffic[/i], the film's underlying themes and ideas are as simple as anything in the dreadfully earnest Stanley Kramer "message" movies of the 1960s. The message in this film is basically that we all judge people by their appearances (and more specifically, their race), but they are in fact more complex than we give them credit for. An admirable sentiment, to be sure, but [i]Crash [/i]is never able to turn this theme into a profound and moving film because writer-director Paul Haggis sacrifices character complexity in the service of plot machinations (as he did in his screenplay for [i]Million Dollar Baby[/i]). Despite the best efforts of an all-star cast (including Matt Dillon, Sandra Bullock, Don Cheadle, and Ryan Phillippe), none of the characters are able to transcend their one-dimensional natures...even though Haggis provides backstories that are supposed to shed light on these people (i.e. the racist cop with a sick father, etc.). The film is noticeably-written, but that is not the same thing as being well-written...the characters seem to be speaking the voice of the screenwriter, instead of their own voice. All too often a character will launch into a monologue that is either racist or about racism, and it sounds more like a university thesis than realistic dialogue. In fact, at some points I got the uncomfortable feeling that Haggis was venting his own racist thoughts through the dialogue of his characters. It is the overriding tone of cynicism and misanthropy that gives [i]Crash [/i]its sour taste. In scene after scene, [i]Crash [/i]shows people resorting to racist cliches and snapping at one another, and this is finally as unrealistic a portrayal of race relations as one in which everyone is colour-blind and gets along. I simply did not believe some of the actions the characters take in this film: in a scene that is deplorable for the way it manipulates us, a Persian man hunts down a Hispanic locksmith and appears to shoot his daughter; in another sequence a black TV director confronts police officers in a way that would probably get him shot in two seconds. Haggis will let his characters do entirely unbelievable things just to crank up the drama. Watching the film, I kept being reminded of Lawrence Kasdan's great 1991 movie [i]Grand Canyon[/i], which is also about L.A. citizens of different races coming together. [i]Grand Canyon [/i]was about the courage and difficulty of breaking through barriers of class and race in an urban environment, and its message was essentially a hopeful one (yet one still grounded in realism). In Haggis' film, the characters don't need courage to reach out to one another, they are simply flung together by cosmic coincidences, and the results of their encounters are almost uniformly disastrous. If [i]Crash [/i]is intended to be a hopeful film about the melting pot experience in America, then its hopeful message was lost on me. [i]Crash [/i]deserves credit for tackling an important issue and being reasonably entertaining, but their is a nastiness and simple-mindedness at its core that prevents it from being a good or great film. It is ironic that a film that encourages us to look beneath the surface should turn out to be so superficial.[/size]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]Do you ever wonder about the people who have the most meaningless effect on your life? The person who fixes a leaky faucet, the guy who sells you DVDs at Blockbuster, the salesperson whom you flatly turn down or even the guy who delivers the mail. What do they do, and what effect do they have on the lives of others?[/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]Well, thats what Crash is here to explore, the seemingly coincidental manner in which people relate to each other, while at the same time hitting hard on stereotypes and bigotry. Throw in some superb acting and Crash becomes one of the best movies I have ever had the privilege of viewing.[/font][/size]
[size=3][font=Times New Roman][/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]To describe Crash in its entirety is impossible. Its about a group of people who seem at first to be completely unrelated, but as time progresses, each has encounters with the others which have a profound effect on each other. These characters include two police detectives who are also lovers (Cheadle & Esposito), a hispanic locksmith with a loving family (Pena), a Persian drug store owner (Toub) and his daughter (Soomekh), a heavily racist cop (Dillon) and his rookie partner (Phillippe), two carjackers (Ludacris & Tate), a film director (Howard) and his wife (Newton) and the Los Angeles District Attorney (Fraser) and his angry wife (Bullock). How they all interact is simply brilliant.[/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]Its almost the kind of plot that you would normally expect from a television mini-series. It would work perfectly as a show that develops one character per episode, learning about the characters they encounter later. It works much better as this faster-paced version, however.[/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]
[center][size=3][img]http://us.movies1.yimg.com/movies.yahoo.com/images/hv/photo/movie_pix/lions_gate_films/crash/michael_pena/crash1.jpg[/img][/size][/center]
[size=3][/size] 
[size=3][font=Times New Roman]Some characters definitely are more prominent than others, however. The two carjackers seem to be the central characters of the movie, as most of the other stories branch off directly from them. We also see a lot of Cheadles Detective Graham Waters. On the other hand, while running into many characters, the conclusion for the locksmith feels much more isolated than the others. The D.A.s wife also seems completely separate. This isnt a problem, as it would have seemed forced to make more characters collide directly with each other.[/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]How it all wraps up is literally astonishing. The conclusion of the movie is pretty much the last 45 minutes, with a couple characters ending their story together one at a time instead of cutting back and forth. Its a smart move, making the movie feel much more like five or six different movies in one.[/font][/size]
[size=3][font=Times New Roman][/font][/size] 
[center][size=3][font=Times New Roman][img]http://us.movies1.yimg.com/movies.yahoo.com/images/hv/photo/movie_pix/lions_gate_films/crash/_group_photos/matt_dillon4.jpg[/img][/font][/size][/center]
[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]During all of this, the movie manages to hit on numerous racial discretions and problems. It views from both sides of the spectrum, which includes preferential treatment of minorities as well as discrimination due to race. It also perfectly shows that even the largest of bigots can have their redemption, and the least racist of all still generalize due to stereotypes. The tagline You think you know who you are, you have no idea perfectly sums up the movie, and it will truly cause you to re-examine your views on the issues.[/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]With all this racism abound, youd think that there would be no light at the end of the tunnel. This would be completely false, as while it does hone in on the faults of humanity, there is hope to found within. As opposed to simplistic one-dimensional characters, we get to see both the high and low points of each. Dillon has arguably the biggest character shift, but it occurs to each and every one. Just when hope is lost, a miracle will save the day. The movie may have some tragic moments, but it never appears pessimistic.[/font][/size]
[size=3][font=Times New Roman][/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]A lot of credit has to go to Paul Haggis, who wrote and directed the movie. In most films, the abundance of characters would have left many without any character development and many would have been lost and forgotten. Luckily, despite each having limited screen time, Haggis is skilful enough that we at least begin to understand every major character in the movie, and why they act the way they do. Its no easy feat, but it is accomplished masterfully.[/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]In order to accomplish the beautifully written characters, a hell of a cast would be needed. As opposed to a great cast, we are given a truly Oscar-worthy cast. In fact, deciding which ones would be particularly worthy would be near impossible.[/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]If being the best was a simple matter of surprising me with yet unknown ability, Id definitely have to say that Ludacris was the best of the cast. Despite the fact that he is a rapper, he has some surprisingly good acting chops, as well as some excellent comic relief when he is rambling about racism and stereotypes, yet living up to those exact stereotypes. Its definitely the best Ive seen from a rapper in a movie so far.[/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]As for other actors coming from behind, Sandra Bullock gives what is the best performance of hers I have ever seen, mainly for one single scene in which she demands new locks because the locksmith currently replacing them looks suspicious. Its an incredibly powerful scene that really raised my respect for Bullock.[/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]Terrence Howard also gives one of the films best performances as an emotionally torn producer who is finally forced to come to grips with reality, and his breakdown near the end is exceptional. Thandie Newton is just as good as his wife who has lost faith in him after he stands by during a questionable pull over by Dillons racist cop. Riding the success of Million Dollar Baby, screenwriter Paul Haggis has used his new found leverage to make his directorial debut with Crash. 
     
 It is unfair to say that Crash is a movie about racism, because that would only be confronting the crust of the film. Crash takes racism, takes our social stereotypes, sets them up against the backdrop of the culturally diverse City of Los Angeles, and asks the viewer if these things affect their judgment, beliefs and actions. Racism in this movie is just a tool to show how our stereotypes influence how we react to other people, even of our own race. 
     
 Crash has an excellent cast that includes Sandra Bullock, Don Cheadle, Brendon Fraser, and Terrence Howard. All of them did an excellent job; however, the real stand out performance in this film was by Matt Dillon. He is simply amazing in his role, and a Best Supporting Actor nomination would be well deserved. 
     
 Not everyone will come away liking this film. The context of the story is not easy to digest, the language used may even offend some, but everyone I have come across has been moved by the story. Simply and amazing film.

The two central issues of discussion that come from watching this film for me are as follows...

Second... is it a Magnolia rip-off? Not a controversial topic I know, but I was really wondering going in. It had the formula. Crash is a very good movie. But those who see it should be prepared for a 100-minute musing on racism and social status, about the way we interact with people, and how something one day can affect us the next. It's the kind of movie a filmmaker makes when he gets a specific idea and won't let any air in, and while Crash is executed perfectly, the movie never bothers to explore other territories, and by the end things feel a little boxed in, with the movie's wheels having gone all the way around and returned to familiar territory. But again, it's skillful exploration, and as long as the audience is prepared for a single idea to be cross-examined from all sides, then they'll be prepared for Crash.
 
There really isn't a story in the movie, there are characters. There's Graham (Don Cheadle), who works for the police. There's his work, which he is good at, but there's also his family, such as his mother, thinning and sad, asking Graham to find his brother. Graham is tired, although upbeat when he can be, with Don Cheadle creating a bit of a sad-sack without the implied request for pity. His brother is Peter (Larenz Tate), who hangs out with Peter (Ludacris) stealing cars. Peter extolls all sorts of knowledge about people, which Ludacris handles relatively well with a few stumbles. Tate has energy as Peter but not enough character to make us care very much.
 
Christine (Thandie Newton) and Cameron (Terrence Howard) are pulled over by a shady officer named Ryan (Matt Dillon) and his partner. Ryan feels Christine up while patting her down. She feels violated and angry that Cameron doesn't step in. This leads to two of the movie's best scenes. Newton and Dillon are both note-perfect in a truly gut-wrenching sequence in the movie, in which their characters meet again. I won't spoil it. Howard, meanwhile, vengeful and riveting, confronting Ryan's partner, Hanson (Ryan Phillipe) when the cops pull him over the next day, after a disturbance. The way these characters move and act, especially Officer Ryan and Cameron, are some of the movie's most interesting elements.
 
There is also Daniel (Michael Pena) and his daughter. They have a heartwarming relationship, which is a highlight of a movie with a lot of darker characters, with Pena giving the what might be the film's best performance. He earns sympathy when Jean (Sandra Bullock) insults him within hearing range, not to his face but her husband Rick (Brendan Fraser). She is shaken after the gunpoint theft of their car in the middle of the road. They are a minor note to the movie, but meanwhile Daniel earns our trust as we watch him interact with his daughter, and later, when an angry shopkeeper, after a break-in, confrtons Daniel with a gun, we truly care what happens.
 
Crash moves through these character's interactions and meetings, examining how they react, how people think, through a window of racism and the role of race in society. As good as the movie is at this, sometimes the twists, turns, and outcomes are not as fresh as they pretend they are, and it is sometimes easy to see how the lives of the characters are going to interconnect again. The movie's sense of conicidence is a related sticking point: some will find it goofy, and although the need to use only so many characters throughout the film is understandable, it still seems a bit unlikely and unusual at times. Lastly, there is also a completely worthless character, an Asian woman who mostly screeches and moans, and comes off as over-the-top. Her purpose in the movie is a mystery.
 
Crash is certainly not for everyone. Many will be turned off by the unflinching eye the movie takes towards the way some people think, discrimination, and the like. But there are some powerful ideas here, and there are good characters, formed well in Paul Haggis's writing, brought to life by talented performers and given the soft, solemn tone by Haggis's direction. Ironic that the movie is about people, places and ideas coming together, crashing into one another in order to find something else to touch on, because Haggis's movie is something of the opposite: a single idea, veering around from place to place, lacking enough opposing forces to connect with, and give it deeper meaning.

Paul Haggis wants to teach everyone a lesson that can be summed up as "racism is bad, don't judge people". The film does illustrate several human tendencies: the willingness to overlook people's backgrounds in order to condemn them based on appearance, the willingness to sacrifice 'the right thing' when it benefits oneself the most, and the willingness to let people believe what they want to, thus continuing the cycle of judgement. It's just that Haggis has to bludgeon the viewer by staging the same object lesson with different characters, over, and over. It's like saying "can you hear me now? Can you hear me now?" ad infinitum. Yes, we really got it the first time. There are some good performances that partially elevate the material above its staginess, namely the segments involving Terrence Howard, Thandie Newton, and Matt Dillon. 

However, the film likes to play with fire, without getting dirty. We've seen that each character can be a racist prick, a phrase that the film likes to use repeatedly. When time allows, we also get a little tidbit of their background, for empathetical purposes. It creates characters that are unsatisfactorily two-dimensional, mainly because cramming something so sprawling in under two hours so that people don't get insufferably impatient doesn't allow for it. It wants us to empathize with the characters' plights, but is willing to deride them at the same time with off-the-cuff mockery. The film likes to put characters in jeopardy, but there has to be a couple pseudo-contemplative, self-congratulatory musical montages at the very end to make you feel better, whose cloying saccharineness is truly infuriating, mocking itself all the while. Then it rams home the point one more time. Comparisons to [b]Do The Right Thing[/b] are inevitable, and if you want a film that unflinchingly displays the depravity that racial tension can unleash, see it. This film wants to make the audience feel good about "oh, I get it now!" It appears that when not within the constraint of adapting existing material, as with [b]Million Dollar Baby[/b], Haggis can't help piling on didactic hamfistedness.

4/10

It's not very often a film as powerful as 'Crash' comes around, and when it does, it can't afford to be missed. The story that 'Crash' tells is an important one to tell, and it couldn't have come at a more perfect time when nobody is safe from other people's prejudices. It's a conflicting story of how strangers affect strangers without a conscious effort. It's one of the best films of the year, and one of the most powerful film in some time.
     
     [center][img]http://images.rottentomatoes.com/images/movie/gallery/1144992/photo_01.jpg[/img]
     
     [left]'Crash' takes place in Los Angeles and consists of compelling stories of citizens of various race, all in different walks of life. A troubled housewife and her DA husband. A Persian store owner confined by language barriers. Two police detectives involved in a relationship. A black television director and his wife who come face to face with police brutality. A Mexican locksmith trying to support his family. Two car-jackers. Two cops, one a rookie and another one a seventeen year veteran. A middle-aged Korean couple. All strangers, yet in 36 hours their lives will collide in unexpected and tragic ways.
     
  'Crash' is a prominent ensemble cast, in every sense of the role. It's not every day you're going to find a film with such enormous talents than that of Sandra Bullock, Don Cheadle, Brendan Fraser, Matt Dillon, Ryan Phillippe, and Thandie Newton. More surprising, however, comes from rapper Ludacris, who delivers a knockout debut performance in the role of a two-faced L.A. citizen. Together, the cast works magic. They're roles that are untreaded by most of the actors, which require emotionally charged performances, which ultimiately is key to the film's success.
     
  It's a film about race, a story of realism. It neither feels forced nor contrived when the character's stories intertwine with each other, which happens to be a huge achievement. It digs at an ugly truth, and isn't put off by the blunt racial issues involved. It's the things that bubble beneath the surface, the thoughts that cross all our minds, yet in 'Crash' they all come bursting out. It asks the question 'Why do we do the things we do?', and is a bold movie for taking such a step. 
    
  Courtesy of a multi-layered and powerful script that makes for such strong drama, it's masterful filmmaking in the hands of director and screenwriter Paul Haggis. It lingers far after the credits have rolled, and the haunting issues are not too soon to leave. It refuses to be shy around the edges, or else it wouldn't have had the same effect as it so profoundly does. It's an ambitious movie, one that could have failed, but instead is capable of spuring serious conversation that's presented to us with a sense of urgency. It's beautiful. It's powerful. [font=Courier New]This is the film that all of my peers have been hailing for a long long time. Most of them say that they were stunned when the film was finished - begging for more. I don't exactly feel the same. I thought [i]Crash[/i] was a decent film in terms of execution, definitely above the average fare, but definitely not awe-inspiring. I think aggravating and insulting better describes this film.
 
 The main problem I had with the film focused around the first half. The problem with ensemble films such as this one is the requirement to introduce all the characters accurately. But being a film about racism, all the characters are in some form racists. Most take this to the extreme. Thus the film feels very overdone. You get bombarded with racial slurs and constant yelling. The film is too angry for its own good. In this way, [i]Crash[/i] almost becomes laughable since it takes itself so seriously. It portrays an outlandish world were everyone hates everyone else solely for the reason of ethicity. The racism issue that is central in the film becomes annoying.
 
 But, when the car crash scene with Matt Dillon's officer and Thandie Newton's violated wife arrives, everything that came before pays off (though I still think that the first half is overdone). This is one of the most powerful and emotional scenes I have ever witnessed. With few words, Dillon and Newton show reactions that tell so much more than the hateful words that preceeded. Suddenly, there are so many layers to racism and it all expresses itself on Newton's face. Her fear, her hate, her relief, her vulnerability, her strength, her honor. It is a scene to remember.
 
 The rest of the film tries to build on the opening scene of the second half. And while they are noticably stronger than those in the first half, they cannot surpass Dillon's and Newton's scene. But they do add complexity. Of the final group, the only other scene I would point out would be Ryan Phillippe's. Not to give anything away, his repressed fear is so evident and understandable that the film's final twist seems all too natural.
 
 Of course, [i]Crash[/i] had to end on a sentimental note - with a song and a medley of images meant to show reflection in all the characters. And this works, sort of.
 
 In the end, though, [i]Crash[/i] does not say as much about racism as it thinks, and many others think, it does. It's portrayal of racism is so far fetched (with the exception of Ryan Phillippe's character) that the film edges on insulting. It preaches and preaches and yells and yells but never says anything all that insightful. In terms of execution, [i]Crash[/i] succeeds. Everywhere else, the film fails. The overdone and unrealistic racism actually simplifies the issue. All in all, [i]Crash[/i] is a technically well made film that dies in its desperate attempt to say something important. It is this last thing that makes me hate this film. [/font]

Keeping an online journal is hard work when you have a deadline looming for a 17-40 page paper on James Joyce, college graduation, a bar to finish building, a job, a fucking math class and suffer from persistent laziness as a result of the crushing pressure of multitudinous responsibilities. I finally made a list, which is a big step for me, so I'm going to take some time and look back on what has been my life for the last month and a half. I need to get back in this thing, but I put a greater amount of effort into writing entries than posting and I haven't had the time to invest in any creative writing appropriate for the space of Mankiw, but now I do, and you all get a long entry to feast upon. After this, I'll finish my NPR review.
 
 I went as Danzig for Halloween this year. A picture will be up soon. I bet you're excited.
 
 Most of my mental meanderings have been focused on [i]Ulysses[/i], especially now that I'm plowing through the end of the book so I can start writing my paper, so much so that Joyce has become an evil ghost in my own life, haunting me and playing tricks on me. It started early in the semester. My roommate lent me his favorite novel, Italo Calvino's [i]If On A Winter's Night, A Traveler[/i]. I read a page of it, became interested, and set it aside for a time when I'd have the opportunity to guiltlessly read it. The next day in class my professor alluded to a passage on page 333 of [i]Ulysses[/i], telling us to turn our attention to something or other Joyce was subtly returning to. I found that I didn't have page 333 in my book. In fact, I was missing pages 324-340, which were replaced by reprints of pages 300-316. My professor told me that those were important pages and that I'd better find a way to get my hands on them. I went up to him after the class to have a little laugh about it. He said that the same thing happened in that book by that Italian guy, If On A Winter's Night,...
 "A Traveler," I finished for him.
 "Yeah, there's a printing error in the first chapter and the novel completely restarts itself."
 This was obviously not a laughing matter. I told him, astonished, "My roommate just lent me that book yesterday, but haven't been able to start it."
 "Well then it's your fuckup," he told me matter of factly, "for letting him give it to you," and walked out of the room.
 My fuckup, indeed. I was assigned [i]Portrait of the Artist[/i] last semester in England, but blew off reading it at first and skipped the class on it to go to Dublin. When I finally read the book, I realized that the route Stephen takes to his University was nearly the same route that I took several times while meandering around the city: down Gardiner Street, to O'Connell, across the bridge, past Trinity College and the Bank of Ireland, up Grafton and through Stephen's Green ("Crossing Stephen's/ That's my green" (Joyce SOME PAGE). I thought it was cool, but I began to realize at the moment of this printing error and the events which have followed that Joyce has transcended the page and is intent on haunting and mocking me for an indefinite period of time.
 It's scary stuff. We read Shelley Jackson's hypertext essay [url="http://www.altx.com/thebody/"]My Body: An Autobiography Plus Lies[/url] in my Ethnography class, and the author mentions [url="http://www.altx.com/thebody/vagina.html"]her Vagina rewriting Joyce.[/url] As soon as my Revolution in Russia class moved into the section on Tsar Nicholas II, I was reading [i]Portrait[/i] and Stephen says of him, "He has the face of a besotted Christ." Then shit really started to go downhill. A couple of weeks ago, we watched a documentary in Primate class about Ring-tailed lemurs, and in it an infant has a distended stomach. I had the word distended on my mind all evening. Distended The next day, I was reading [i]Ulysses[/i] when the narrator in the "Circe" episode described the "distended belly" of a pregnant woman. That freaked me out and I told all my friends. They laughed at me and thought it was a joke. The next day, in my readings, the narrator said "distended" again, later in the book. I don't know if Joyce is talking about the way he's going to murder me my infecting my GI tract, but the narrator the next day made it personal and referred to "The O'Donoghue's of the Glen fighting the Glens of O'Donoghue": O'Donoghue is the root of my less adorned Irish surname. As most events in Joyce anticipate a later fulfillment, I fully expect to from self-inflicted hari-kari wounds, an overbloated stomach caused by a print-ink borne pathogen or some incident involving an ashplant and British army privates.
 
 We've been discussing the masochistic elements of the artist, Leopold Bloom and even Joyce himself in the class. Fascinating stuff. I shall report more on this at a later date. For now, just know that I am afraid.
 
 Joyce has taken up so much of my academic endeavors that I'm three books behind in my American literature class: Henry James' [i]The Europeans[/i] (of which I've read about half), F. Scott Fitzgerald's [i]The Great Gatsby[/i] (which I read in high school) and Sarah Jewett's [i]Country of the Pointed Firs[/i]. I'm supposed to have started Willa Cather's [i]O Pioneers![/i] by Thursday, but we'll see how it goes. I have to write a paper doing some sort of comparison between James and Fitzgerald, which is ripe territory for a matriculating English major such as myself. [i]The Europeans[/i] is, like many of James' works, a novel of manners, exploring the differences between the moneyed puritans of New England and the poor nobility of Europe. It's funny, which I didn't know James was capable of being, and written by one of the best prose writers in American history. I'm sure everyone read [i]Gatsby[/i] in high school, but I'm excited to do a fresh and well-crafted essay comparing the two. I'm not sure where that paper will go, but I was thinking about how much Christopher Isherwood's Berling novels ([i]Goodbye to Berlin[/i] and[i] Mr Norris Changes Trains[/i]) [i]Gatsby[/i] is: the postwar lamentation, the straightforward honesty of the writing style ([i]Goodbye[/i] begins with the narrator telling the reader "I am a camera"), the homosexual undertones. I hope he goes for it, since it's an American lit class.
 
 I'm very interested in [i]Country of the Pointed Firs[/i]. I only have a few classes of discussion and about four pages read, but I'm fascinated with the way Jewett dispenses with plot and instead sets out ot create a series of sketches, reminiscient of, and perhaps an influence on, Garrison Keillor's fictional Lake Wobegone ("Where all the women are strong, the men are good looking, and the children...are above average") from his fantastic radio series [i]A Prairie Home Companion[/i]. It's a quiet novel, but radical, too, in the matriarchal anti-capitalist utopia she depicts (which further recalls Lake Wobegone), and I'm psyched to get into it, even though pre-1900 New England fiction usually bores the shit out of me.
 
 I saw that a guy (named Bo Scaife) who I played football with in high school, and who grew up two blocks from my parents' house, a god at my high school, the massive, smart senior (when I was a froshie) who went to Texas, is now a tight end for the Tennessee Titans. Go Bo.
 
 As for the movies, [i]The Usual Suspects[/i] has a cool plot, some good lines and a good piece of Spacey acting. The cops are a little hammy, but so what. It's a good flick.
 
 I liked Crash more immediately after I saw it than I did upon reflection: it's a good movie, but overly stylized and obsessed with its own importance. I didn't feel a lot of depth in the characters. Whatever. It's a pretty good movie.
 
 Typing up Joyce took a lot more out of me than I thought it would, so I'm gonna sign off and go finish [i]The Europeans[/i]. Sayonara, and keep me in your thoughts and in your prayers as I try to deal with the possibility of a Joyce-smack.

[left]Not many filmmakers are willing to deal with the topic of racism as directly as [b]Crash[/b]. It's a very sensitive issue and many comedies have tried to trivialize it in a distasteful manner. However, in the real world many Americans are still being influenced by racism. In most parts of the country citizens don't deal with racism as directly as people have in the past; but the subtleties are still there and many individuals are being affected simply by the color of their skin or social class.[/left]
 
[center][img]http://us.movies1.yimg.com/movies.yahoo.com/images/hv/photo/movie_pix/lions_gate_films/crash/sandra_bullock/crash1.jpg[/img][/center]
[left]Taking a cue from [b]Magnolia[/b], amongst other films, Haggis weaves together a very diverse cast with unique circumstances that occur over a two-day period. For a film that has as many characters as [b]Crash[/b], Haggis does a fairly good job giving all of them sufficient screen-time for the viewers to connect to. In fact, some of these characters that only have approximately 15-20 minutes of screen-time in the entire film are easier to relate to than some main characters that star in 2-hour movies.[/left]
 
[left]Haggis turned some heads after co-producing and co-writing the screenplay for [b]Million Dollar Baby[/b]. Now after [b]Crash[/b], his name will be hard to ignore. This film is far more personal and will undoubtedly rub some viewers the wrong way. It even makes reference to the 9/11 attack and how all Arabs are to blame. Haggis does not hold back one bit and just totally lets loose on anything and everything that's stereotypical about ethnic backgrounds. Some of the dialogue was so offensive that there were occasional "oooooo's" from various viewers in the theater.[/left]
 
[center][img]http://us.movies1.yimg.com/movies.yahoo.com/images/hv/photo/movie_pix/lions_gate_films/crash/_group_photos/larenz_tate7.jpg[/img][/center]
[left]All of the characters depicted here are seriously depraved. However, we see enough of their lives to be able to empathize with them and not to pass judgment. In fact, as uncomfortable as this may sound, some of these characters may remind us of ourselves in certain areas of our lives.[/left]
 
[left]With a fine ensemble cast such as this, it's very difficult to pick a favorite actor. Everyone has done a superb job playing their roles. While some of these characters can make you mad, you can't help but to respect the actors for portraying their animosity towards other races so disturbingly well.[/left]
 
[center][img]http://us.movies1.yimg.com/movies.yahoo.com/images/hv/photo/movie_pix/lions_gate_films/crash/ryan_phillipe/crash1.jpg[/img][/center]
[left]Nothing is certain when watching this film. When you think you have established the characters for which they are, you'll see a completely different side of them in the next act. Those who appear to be good will become villains and those you may initially hate will do something that may win your heart. As the movie deals with the topic of racism--judging others by what you see on the outside--Haggis forces us to deal with our own presuppositions about these characters even before we really get to know them.[/left]
 
[center][img]http://us.movies1.yimg.com/movies.yahoo.com/images/hv/photo/movie_pix/lions_gate_films/crash/michael_pena/crash1.jpg[/img][/center]
[left]This is a solid tale from an emotionally raw standpoint. I can't recall off the top of my head right now any other recent film that has dealt with this issue so head on. This is an ambitious commentary that conveys the psychological paranoia that a lot of people have towards others due to their exteriors. [b]Crash[/b] does a good job balancing out the stereotypes. Some of the paranoia is warranted and you see that manifest in the movie; but there are other cases where paranoia is nothing but paranoia. It's a monster in the closet that some of these characters have created on their own.[/left]
 
[left]I just want to reiterate on how very direct this film is when it comes to stereotypes. I want viewers to go into the theaters prepared on knowing that no one will be escaping the racial labels here. Every viewer will be hearing the "you people" dialogue directed towards their own ethnicity. In almost every scene there is something along the lines of "What is it with you black/white/Mexican/Asian/Middle Easterner people?" The labels are blunt and cruel. Viewers who are sensitive to insults may find themselves angry and exasperated with the film's relentless stereotyping.[/left]

[left][b]Crash[/b] is a perfect illustration of how bad things happen to good people as surely as good things happen to bad people. It's an unfair deal in the world we live in today; but this movie shows the harsh reality that no matter how good or bad a person may be, he or she is still capable of charitable and evil acts. We cannot pass judgment on these characters. For to do that we would be judging ourselves.[/left]

Crash was a film that i was sort of avoiding since its theatrical run. The film was hyped so much by everyone, and in the middle of all the hype was the constant voice of people saying how important the film was, and how it was a must see for anyone affected by race. The film was going to make us change the way we look at life and at our fellow man. It's a shame that this film did neither for me. 
 
From the very beginning of the film we get a lot of dialogue, 98% of it dealing with race, religion, or ethnic stereotypes. Every single race. No one was safe, no one wasn't covered. I had deep hesitations about the rest of the film and i was only about 12 minutes in. So far it seemed to be heavy handed and far too much like it was trying to be important.
 
The film then progressed and let us get to know the characters a little. I say a little because the film is not even 2 hours long and we have to meet numerous characters. Far too many. The emotional impact this film could have had was lost the moment they throught it would be a good idea to introduce 3 extra storylines. The film could have been much tighter and much more emotinally charged had Haggis narrowed his view and focussed solely on a few stories, giving the resonance. The great thing was that not all the stories winded up weaving themselves together at the end. It would have been far too easy to have all the characters affect each other in some way by the end of the film. 

What Crash gives us instead are a few stories that will tie together, other stories with characters walking in and out of the scene, but nothing where every single last person touches the life of the others in some way.
 
Crash has been hailed for its performances, and rightly so. The only problem is that the actors don't get enough time to show their craft. For once I didn't fully hate Ryan Philleppe or Matt Dillon. Terrence Howard was superb, but then again, when hasn't he been in the past year. Some of the weeknesses were Thandie Newton, Brendan Fraser, Sandra Bullock (very out of place here) and Don Cheadle. Cheadle is a good actor, but we have seen this role out of him before, in pretty much every film that he does.
 
The main thing that does not allow me to rate this film any higher is the endings. The way each story wraps up. We see that something bad is going to happen to pretty much every cast member, and it is pretty much just a matter of time until it does happen. My problem with this again lies in the fact that there are far too many story lines. The emotional impact that would be felt for a character is lessened when you see something bad happening for everyone. It might not even be bad things, just things that will change their lives in some permanent way. A better ending would be to have some people get off without being touched. This would be far more realistic than the ending we get. Everyone is affected and has the most profound day of their life. Sounds like something out of a movie.

An epic film if you ask me.There are no words to categorize this film.  Haunting, intense, provocative, startling, raw, and incredible are all understatements.

The ensemble remains one of the best ensembles ever assembled for a film, IMO.  They are individually and uniformly spectacular.  The best has to be Sandra Bullock who really shows her acting stripes in the (surprisingly) few scenes she has.  The "lock changing" scene in which she goes on a rampage about having the locks in her home changed after being car-jacked is simply phenomenal.  She is so powerful and so real and so emotional in this one scene you feel as though you either want to jump through the screen and clap for her or jump through the screen and strangle her.  She is wonderful.  Thandie Newton is another standout.  She takes what probably looks like, on paper, a simple, one-layered character and just as if by the push of a button, she creates layers upon layers upon layers for her character by doing something as simple as changing her facial expression or putting her hands a certain way.  Her performance isn't only remarkable because of her acting but also because of the simple quirks and little, tiny, somewhat unnoticable movements that make her character so interesting and so complicated yet relatable.  

There is one scene in which *SPOILER* a cop (Matt Dillon--also delivering a great performance) saves a woman (Newton) from an overturned car soon to catch on fire.  What makes this scene so spectacularly moving is that at the beginning of the film, Dillon molests Newton, and now, he is saving her life (or attempting to).  I wont try to spoil much, but the way the scene plays out and ends will leave you reaching for the tissue box and un able to catch your breath.  Its an undescribably wonderful scene.*END SPOILER*

This movie has moments in it where you may cringe (a lot *A LOT* of racial discrimination is approached in this film in a manner that, at first, may seem unsatisfying and sudden but soon turns out to be smoother than you thought and really perfect).  But, while you may cringe or feel uncomfortable during these scenes, think why.  I can tell you why you probably will right now.  Because you've felt these things.  You may not have said them outloud, but you've thought them.  You've mumbled them to yourself when you're alone.  You contemplated saying it.  You may not admit it, but you have.  And its a subject that has NEVER been approached until now.  And what  an excellent way of approaching it.  With no sugar-coated, candy-colored moments.  With realness.  It's done impecably and suddenly.  It's said flat out and not subtely.  It's not the way most would have approached this (being the first to do so) but it works.  You may not think so at first, but it does.  And it's quite remarkable.

All in all, this movie will blow you away on so many levels.  What I felt when I watched Crash was that (like most movies nowadays) it wasn't trying to express a feeling like love or hatred or passion or whatever.  It's not trying to show how you miss those who are gone or what you learn by coming of age or anything about your friends or family members.  It doesn't mean to go deep.  It doesn't want to.  It just wants to skim the surface which resonates within you and you, on your own, dig deep to find the purpose of a scene or the significance of a line.  The movie doesn't want to change you.  And it doesn't.  It mearly starts a feeling that changes you.  You will finish this movie and feel changed and different and moved.  But not totally because of the movie.  Not really.  Because the movie struck a nerve or a feeling that made YOU come to certain assumptions or made YOU come to certain realizations about yourself.  And I've never seen a film that has been able to do such a thing.  It may sound confusing and I may not be expressing it in the best manner, but basically, because of the way you leave the theater (changed by yourself, not the film) Crash is a masterpiece pure and simple.

[font=Times New Roman][font=Verdana][size=2]Having found that my retrospective outlook on the movie [i]Crash [/i]had become much too clouded amidst end-of-year heaps of both praise and criticism on the movie, I saw it fit to revisit it so as to better formulate my own views. My original review ([url="http://www.rottentomatoes.com/vine/journal_view.php?journalid=267176&entryid=277999&view=public"]linked here[/url]) was negative, having found the film, which looks at racial and ethnic issues amongst a group of about a dozen intersecting characters, didnt address its material with the right sincerity to make it anything more than a Hallmark card to people who felt bad about racism. A second viewing was kinder to the film on the ouset: while it is still too naïve regarding the varying causes and effects of racism in society (it approaches the many events with an overly wishful all things considered equal attitude), it does serve as an occasionally touching look at the basic shared humanity between all these different people in the midst of their conflicting lives. However, for both supporters and detractors, the ultimate effect of a movie like [i]Crash [/i]is cumulative, and it isn't until it reaches its peak that its very prominent, underlying flaws, reach their offensive apex. The cloying and hackneyed elements are almost besides the point: the overly emphasized title metaphor is unnecessary, and diminishes the impact its depicted racial clashing would otherwise provide if the intended subtext was allowed to be deferred rather than outright stated. And, call me elitist, but [i]Crash [/i]takes it way too easy on white people to truly be effective as an examination of racial relations in todays world; the many poignant moments of intended emotional realization notwithstanding. The film is more concerned about not offending its intended primary audience than actually enlightening them beyond the obvious surface material, most notably in the what-the-fuck? denouement of intended euphoria that comes almost immediately after the climax of depicted racial misunderstanding has reached its most tragic. If I didnt know better, Id think the movie was celebrating the fact that one of its black characters had just been killed. Because the movie relishes in some sort of completely unmerited revelry upon its conclusion-less ending, it undermines much of what it had otherwise effectively set up beforehand. Racism is a very, very bad thing, but you dont need to worry about it [i]that [/i]much. Especially if youre white.[/size][/font][/font]

I watched [i]Crash[/i] last night. I was fairly riveted, but afterward the film just didn't sit well with me. It was disturbing in sections, obviously, but what bothered me was that it didn't feel authentic. Even though things didn't end perfectly, they were still wrapped up too neatly. The interconnectedness of the characters felt far too contrived. I feel the film's purpose was to prove a point, but I think to address racism, sexism, etc. you need to dig a little deeper into the realm of realism. 
I did think the acting was pretty solid. It had a huge ensemble cast of well-known actors. In particular I enjoyed Don Cheadle and William Fetcher's performances. I also enjoyed what little we saw of Jennifer Esposito's character. She was all around smooth. Her speech, mannerisms, etc. and to me, it felt authentic. I wish she had a larger role in the film.

[font=Tahoma][font=Trebuchet MS][i]Spoilers within.
  
  Crash[/i] has been one of 2005's big controversies; clearly and unabashedly a picture with "something to say", it's been praised and hated in equal measure. It's direct approach to the conflicts caused by race has been seen by some as blunt and heavy-handed, and some as brilliant and bracing. The problem is that [i]Crash[/i] manages to be both; with the various, intertwining plot threads with various Angelean characters, it has an unfortunate tendancy to shift in tone, with some powerful moments, such as the moving car-rescue scene, sitting uncomfortably alongside manipulative scenes like the "shooting" of a child.

  The film has an undoubtedly starry cast, who have all been cast in roles one doesn't often associate them with (Sandra Bullock is particularly impressive, as a hard-nosed, frightened and cruel wife of a politician), but Paul Haggis, the writer and director of [i]Crash[/i] (coming from his similarly uneven script for [i]Million Dollar Baby[/i]), writes most of these characters as stereotypes, and containing only one-note each. Each character is written as, over the course of the two days the film takes place in, having a shift in character, which in some cases seems positive, others negative. But closer examination shows us that these people never really shift at all. Bullock's character finishes her small character arc by realising that her only friend is her foreign maid (Yomi Perry), but this only shifts her perception of herself, not her attitude to race. Matt Dillon saves the women (Thandie Newton) he had previously molested, but this doesn't change his racist attitudes (the film tries to vindicate Dillon's character by giving him an ailing father who Dillon must care for, but what excuse is this?). If Haggis was trying to suggest that racism is not going to simply vanish after one experience, then fine; this would be a downbeat but acceptable conclusion. But Haggis then attempts to redeem his characters by having white, purifying snow float down upon them; not only is this illogical (apparently, it hasn't snowed in L.A. since 1949), but it seems almost offensive; none of these people have redeemed themselves, but Haggis seems to think they have.

[i]Crash'[/i]s characters, as I've mentioned, are mostly stereotypes, and every single one of them seems extraordinarily quick to anger. I have no experience of L.A., or indeed America, but do people really immediatly seize on people's race? Haggis' seems eager to rush each interaction to get to the point of race, but this means he misses out on the realism he so desperately desires. James Muro's striking digital photography, which paints the world in hues of black and blue, is certainly praise-worthy, but it's realism sits uncomfortably alongside the race-orientated spiels that spout from these people's mouths.

[i]Crash[/i] is not, however, without it's merits, which mostly stem from it's cast, who are, on the whole, very capable, and generally manage to enhance the rather flat characterizations given them by Harris. Bullock's performance may be the best she's ever given, and certainly the darkest; in contrast to her fluffy, lovable klutz characters we usually see her as, this bitchy portrayal is striking and vivid. Dillon, an underrated actor who never seems to lift himself out of mediocre films, gives a performance edged with sympathy and pain; he makes his father scenes seem less hollow and more human. Terrence Howard, in his breakout year, is also impressive, while Newton, as his wife, is extraordinarily powerful in her scenes with Dillon, yet fluctuates wildly otherwise. Michael Pena, who features in the manipulative scene where his young daughter is shot at by an angry Persian shopkeeper, maintains a beautiful humanity and softness when he's on-screen with his fictional daughter.

  But [i]Crash[/i]'s characters are ones stuck with double-standards. The Persian shopkeeper is angered by the insults thrown at him by a gun salesman, but then is similarly cruel to Pena's locksmith. Lucacris' young character bemoans the "humiliation" of travelling by bus, but carelessly insults the "Chinaman" he runs over. Don Cheadle is angry about the treatment of black men on the police force, but insults his girlfriend's (Jennifer Esposito) culture without care. As a film about the effects of race, [i]Crash[/i] can be a powerful experience, but, ultimately, it's composite characters are stuck in Haggis's limbo and a world it's hard to believe exists.[/font]            
  [/font]

So what was that? I spent an hour and a half in a cinema crowded with idiots, and some of them were drunken enough to imagine they've got an poignant sense of humour, and what did I get as a refund? Nothing special I tell you, though it's no use denying the movie raises (or rather reminds us of) some problems that have a vital importance for us. 
   I don't live in the US and can't say in my country the problem of racial intolerance is as evident as here, but I can't state there's no racism here. I guess it exists everywhere where there's at least two cultures which try to stay separated as much as possible and at the same time they have to deal with each other. In my country there are two languages: Russian and Ukrainian, and the latter one is the only state language though the former is rather widespread, especially in industrial centres, which creates a great problem when Ukrainian is implemented in everyday life in big cities. People who don't speak Ukrainian have to learn it 'cause otherwise it's quite difficult to fill in papers, watch TV and read ads (by law they have to be in Ukrainian), help children about homework and so on. It's usually the favourite topic of the opposition 'cause every time an election campaign is conducted they promise to make Russian the second state language and never deliver on the promise 'cause it's the minor language in our country (about 30 per cent). It causes hatred and lack of understanding between the Ukrainian West and the Russian East. I live here and I feel 'cause if you speak the wrong language in the region you're sure to be at least insulted. At least...
   Why did I make this digression? It's just the same as here in Los Angeles where the scene is laid. There are some groups of people with quite different racial backgrounds: Det. Graham Waters (Don Cheadle) and his Hispanic partner, DA Rick Cabot (Brendan Fraser) and his wife Jean (Sandra Bullock), Sgt Jack Ryan (Matt Dillon) and his yound partner Tommy Hanson (Ryan Phillippe), the TV director Cameron Thayer (Terrence Howard) and his wife (I'm not sure), two local stickup men - Anthony (Ludacris) and Peter Waters (Larenz Tate), Det. Waters' brother, and the Asian couple. If I missed someone I'm sorry but you must understand it's quite difficult to remember all of them. All the characters have to deal with each other from time to time, and these connections are virtually always colored with racial stereotypes, and these ones do impede mutual understanding.
   It's just impossible to retell the plot. It's related in retrospect when Graham Waters arrives at the crime site where the young man's body was found. Meanwhile his partner argues with the Chinese woman, and their talk soon acquires racial coloring. And then we see a series of racial-colored scenes: Jean Cabot and her husband become victims of Anthony and Peter who steal their car at gunpoint; Rick Cabot gets angry that this may ruin his campaign 'cause Anthony and Peter happened to be Afro-Americans; Jean is afraid that the Afro-American locksmith may sell their keys to the local gang; the salesman doesn't want to sell the gun 'cause the buyer is Persian (the salesman thought him to be Iraqi). Jack abuses by his treatment an Afro-American couple who did nothing bad, and many others. Each scene is filled with racial Angst of the one who differs from you, and the natural reaction of people in such circumstances is to protect oneself by insulting first. 
   Frankly speaking I didn't see anything special in the movie though I understand the problem raised is important, and sometimes it's really necessary to bring it on screen if it's possible to teach at least some people. But the thing is that I never evaluated movies only on educational grounds. For me it must be something more than just a piece of information, it has to be aesthetic in a sense. Not so long ago I saw "Lord of War' which is highly acclaimed and praised because of antimilitary content, but I don't think the film was really that good due to lack of emotion and action though I don't think these two elements are of primary importance. Everything should be measured. "Crash" is just a series of interwoven plotlines and occasional meetings which doesn't excite much. Of course if racial intolerance is a case with you it's really exciting, and I see the film has educational force and social meaning. The problem is that something is lacking here, and content comes to the fore shadowing all the rest. It's a good film to see and think of, but not to adore and remember. That's my point of view.

Para cualquier guionista, que un director de la talla y el talento de Clint Eastwood realice tu guión es todo un honor en todos los sentidos. Y si eres un guionista con la intención de dar el salto a la silla de director, como era el caso de Paul Haggis, no puede haber mejor escuela de dirección que ver trabajar a un maestro como Eastwood. Aunque Million Dollar Baby no ha sido la única colaboración entre estos dos hombres, ya que repitieron en la esperadísima Flags of Our Fathers, visión norteamericana de la Batalla de Iwo Jima. Dos jóvenes afroamericanos, que pasean por una de las calles más selectas de Los Ángeles, están a punto de desencadenar una ola de acontecimientos que afectará a todo tipo de personas. El asalto a una aterrorizada pareja y el robo de su coche tendrá unas consecuencias totalmente inesperadas. 

Crash es una historia sobre la necesidad de contacto del ser humano, de cómo lo busca por todos los medios; sin embargo es también una historia del racismo que aún impera en la sociedad estadounidense, en especial en la policía y la alta sociedad. Se trata de una extraordinaria visión a vuela pluma de una gran cantidad de personajes, que personifican a la sociedad americana al completo. Es una trama dura y desgarradora, cruel en varios momentos, en la que el azar juega un papel fundamental sobre los personajes y sus actos. Paul Haggis sumerge al espectador en un turbulento viaje sin cinturón de seguridad, y mientras dura la travesía, el cineasta canadiense muestra una gran sensibilidad y un buen hacer dignos de uno de lo grandes (es más que evidente que Haggis aprendió valiosísimas lecciones de cine de Clint Eastwood). 

Prácticamente todas las virtudes de la cinta se encuentran en el magnífico guión de Paul Haggis y Robert Moresco, pilar central sobre el que se sustenta todo el conjunto. A la solidez de ese conjunte contribuyen notablemente todos y cada uno de los intérpretes de Crash, aunque destacan Don Cheadle, Terrence Howard y Matt Dillon. 

¿Cómo puede sintetizarse la vida misma en poco más de dos horas? Algo que parece tan imposible, Paul Haggis lo ha conseguido en Crash, y si no lo creeis, acudid al cine más cercano.

[left][i]Crash[/i] is one of the best films of 2005 and one of the most truthful, uncomfortable, yet necessary films I have viewed. In this film about intersecting lives and racism, you will not only see an accurate photograph of 21st America but also a frightening look at yourself. A black detective and his Hispanic girlfriend, a racist cop and his father, a black television producer and his fed-up wife, a district attorney and his bigoted, lonely wife, a Hispanic locksmith and his young child, a Persian shopkeeper and his daughter, and two thugs intersect and crash into each other with their racist thoughts, words, attitudes, and actions. Rather than examining racism at the institutional level, writer/director Paul Haggis ([i]Million Dollar Baby[/i]) chooses to weave a lyrical web of how what individuals say and do causes the loss of identity, shame, guilt, and even death. The film works as an essay about the fragility and coincidence of human connection as well as about the importance of interpersonal responsibility. 

Most notable about the film are the amazing performances from normally B-grade actors such as Matt Dillon, Sandra Bullock, and Brendan Fraser. And even in a miniscule role...Tony Danza! Don Cheadle continues a streak of strong roles, which will hopefully be recognized one day, and Terrence Howard gives a performance of [i]Hustle and Flow[/i] quality. My only real complaint about the film, which is full of contrived situations so well-written that they seem truly coincidental, is that it doesn't know how to end; it seems to have two endings, but unfortunately, the last one is silly and tonally inappropriate.

Paul Haggis's Oscar-nominated [u]Crash[/u] has turned out to be very divisive, earning near-universal praise from critics while seeing a backlash of scorn among many RT members. With its theme of racial sterotyping and its (often unlikely) intermingling of many different storylines, my first thought after seeing [u]Crash[/u] was that it was as if Spike Lee had made [u]Magnolia[/u].
 
Haggis sets up what he sees as the underlying message of the movie in an opening monologue by Don Cheadle. Cheadle expresses the view that Los Angeles is a unique city in that nobody there walks anywhere. Everybody drives. This lends the city's inhabitants an isolation from their neighbors that no other city can. Cheadle's character (a successful police detective) theorizes that much of the city's violence is actually people trying to "crash" against each other, just to feel [i]any[/i] of the human contact that denizens of other cities feel every time they walk down the street. Personally, I found the movie's underlying message to have been better summed up by children's author Lemony Snicket: "People are like chef salads, with good stuff and bad stuff all mixed together."
 
This is one of the reasons I liked [u]Crash[/u] as much as I did. Haggis pointedly refuses to let any of his characters be simplified into either all "good" or "bad." While some of the coincidences of the movie may stretch credibility, his characters, at least, are painted as realistic human beings with both typical human failings (generally various forms of racial hatred and prejudice in the context of the movie) and also capable of nobility. The lone excpetion is Michael Pena's "Daniel," a Mexican-American locksmith who, despite being mistrusted by his customers and suffering racist abuse from both Whites and immigrants, has managed to move himself and his daughter out of the Projects and into a safer, better neighborhood, keeping a polite and warm outlook on life and his work against all odds.
 
Throughout the rest of the film, most of the many other characters are shown as either being guilty of racism or being guilty of living out the very racist stereotypes leveled against them. However, by the movie's end each one of these characters is brought to an understanding of their ignorance and petty "evil" through an interaction with someone of a different race. In most of these cases, we feel hopeful that the lesson learned will stick.
 
And, above all else, hope seems to be Haggis's message. He wants to convince us that there [i]is[/i] hope for improved race relations in America... but that it is likely to occur on an individual level and not without a lot of blood being shed along the way until each of us gets to [i]know a little[/i] about a person we blindly and negatively stereotype.
 
I can't wrap up without saying something about the cinematography in [u]Crash[/u]. This is another reason I was reminded of [u]Magnolia[/u]. However, cinematographers James Muro and Dana Gonzales teamed up to surpass [u]Magnolia[/u]'s beautiful look by a large leap. Never has LA looked as lovely as in this gorgeous movie. Muro received a BAFTA nomination for his work, and I find it criminal that he was ignored by AMPAS for Oscar consideration.
 
If stark realism is essential to your enjoying a film, then you may want to give this one a miss. Ditto if you need a straightforward storyline with a beginning, a climax and a neat denouement. But if you don't mind a looser ensemble piece in the vein of a Robert Altman movie or [u]Magnolia[/u], and if you are willing to accept some plot contrivances in order to deliver a powerful and hopeful message, then you may well find [u]Crash[/u] one of the best movies of 2005.

Without kitsch or wrong sentimentality, director and writer Paul Haggis tells stories about various people living L.A. who meet each other within 36 hours. Even more enjoyable is the fact that the movie does NOT seem overconstructed, which is given through the excellent screenplay.
