[b][size=4]'Crash'[/size][/b]
 
[b][size=4]Racists get equal opportunities to hate in this awkward drama.[/size][/b]
 
By Carina Chocano
Times Staff Writer
 
May 6, 2005
 
I'm not sure the best way to kick off a movie that wants to expose the dark heart of the [i]true [/i]Los Angeles is to contrast it with "real cities" where "people walk, you brush past people, people bump into you," but that's what writer-director Paul Haggis does in the first few moments of "Crash," a grim, histrionic experiment in vehicular metaphor slaughter.
 
Graham Waters (Don Cheadle) and Ria (Jennifer Esposito), two detectives in love, are rear-ended on their way to a murder scene, and no sooner has the dazed Graham delivered his soliloquy on urban alienation ("I think we miss that sense of touch so much, we crash into each other just to feel something") Ria and the other driver, a middle-aged Korean woman, start loudly trading racial slurs without even a four-letter preamble. So much for the urban brotherhood of man: In "Crash," there's no getting through a fender bender, casual conversation, business transaction, phone call to mom or naked love romp without someone's ancestry taking a nasty beating.
 
From here, Haggis, a veteran television writer who wrote the script for "Million Dollar Baby," weaves no fewer than nine sets of characters into a suffocating tangle of ham-fisted ironies and belief-beggaring coincidences designed to reveal the latent racism that festers in the souls of all those who ever laid claim to a 310, 323, 213 or 818 area code. (Yes, you too.) The movie's structure has drawn comparisons to "Short Cuts" and "Magnolia," though it'll feel familiar to anyone who submits to regular cudgelings by "hard-hitting" network TV dramas that wield messages like bludgeons.
 
Every conflict in "Crash"  even lovers' quarrels  is racially motivated, and having hit on this key to human inhumanity, the director pursues the line with extreme (sorry) prejudice. There may be a million stories in the naked city, but there are something like 20 principal characters in this movie, and they expend 90 minutes of screen time on roughly one topic of conversation.
 
What really makes you want to screw up your eyes, clap your hands over your ears and belt out a show tune, though, is the nagging feeling that Haggis, a Canadian who has resided in this city for most of his adult life and who suffered a traumatic real-life encounter with a pair of armed carjackers a few years ago, seems to have experienced some misplaced guilt over his lingering low opinion of the gentlemen who took his car, followed by anger at the guilt, more guilt at the anger, and so on. I'm only guessing, of course, but upon meditating on the lives of his assailants  what were they like in their free time, when they [i]weren't [/i]sticking guns in people's faces?  the director has written them a funny valentine. They are reborn in his imagination as a couple of charming, clever, philosophical, socially committed young car thieves who, when not busy jacking SUVs, enjoy ice hockey, Merle Haggard and liberating smuggled Asian sweatshop workers into the free market wonderland of downtown L.A.
 
Anthony (Chris "Ludacris" Bridges) and Peter (Larenz Tate), black men in their 20s, come out of an Italian restaurant in a ritzy neighborhood where Anthony gripes that the black waitress has treated them shabbily. When Peter points out that black men have a reputation for being bad tippers, Anthony confesses that he didn't leave one. This is just the first of about 1 1/2 hours worth of Buddhist conundrums on the nature of racist stereotypes. Anthony, a philosophical sort, sees racism lurking in every corner, even in the gesture of a white woman who takes her husband's arm as they pass.
 
"We're the only black people surrounded by a sea of over-caffeinated white people and a trigger-happy LAPD," he says. "Why aren't we scared?" It sounds like a good question, until the considerably more chilled-out Peter ripostes with: "Because we have guns?" and within seconds, Jean (Sandra Bullock) and Rick (Brendan Fraser) are scuttling along the sidewalk, having been divested of their Escalade.
 
If a generalization falls in the forest, and somebody who fits the description confirms it, is it really true? In the case of Rick and Jean, at least, it is. Rick happens to be the district attorney of Los Angeles County, a man apparently incapable of experiencing anything except through the prism of how it will play in the media. After the carjacking, the couple repair home to change the locks and spin the story. Rick frets that being robbed by black men will cost him either the black vote or the law-and-order vote and instructs his aides to locate an African American on whom he can pin a medal. The lonely, bitter, pathologically angry Jean, meanwhile, newly freed from the worry that her racism might have been unfounded, freaks out at the sight of the locksmith, whom she loudly takes for a gang member. Then she snaps at the maid.
 
It's around this point that the theme of the movie, neatly summarized by one of its characters and encapsulated in the tagline, begins to emerge. "You think you know who you are," the racist cop Officer Ryan (Matt Dillon) tells his green, uninitiated partner. "You have no idea." Actually, in "Crash," you do. Whatever flimsy layers cover the characters' raging 24-hour xenophobia are swept away by the slightest breeze. It's painfully clear to anyone but Jean, for instance, exactly who Jean is. The sensitive, sloe-eyed locksmith, meanwhile, like the warm and friendly domestic, bears his symbolic nobility like a cross. Daniel (Michael Peña) bears Jean's insults silently, then goes home to comfort his traumatized child, who sleeps under the bed for fear of stray bullets. Soon, Daniel and his family will be victimized by a high-strung Persian patriarch, Farhad (Shaun Toub), driven to the edge by constant (and geographically inaccurate) race-baiting.
 
Add to this daisy chain of bigotry a Korean who sells illegal Thai and Cambodian workers to sweatshops, a black HMO worker who denies coverage to a sick man because the man's son is a racist, a white cop on his third African American murder, and a member of the D.A.'s office who wonders "what it is" with black people who "can't keep their hands out of the cookie jar," and the film's characters stop seeming like they've been culled from a random cross-section of the citizenry so much as cherry-picked from the top of the class at the Pat Buchanan School of International Relations.
 
The few characters who aren't culprits are victims, the most discouraging among them Cameron (Terrence Howard), a successful black television director. Cameron and his wife, Christine (Thandie Newton), are returning home from an awards show when they're pulled over by Dillon's racist Officer Ryan and his conflicted young partner, Officer Hansen (Ryan Phillippe). Ryan, a virulent racist, humiliates the director and his wife by viciously molesting her under threat of arrest.
 
At home, the couple implode. After hanging up the phone without reporting the assault ("Do you really think they'll care about what you have to say?" says Cameron), Christine lashes out at her husband. "The closest you ever got to being black was watching 'The Cosby Show,' " she yells. And he: "At least I didn't watch it with the rest of the equestrian team!" Of course, what with all this horseback riding and "Cosby Show" watching, you'd think they'd have a lawyer too. But "Crash" is too heavily invested in the idea of race as class to allow these two even the slightest sense of security, entitlement or surprise at being so crudely mishandled by the establishment of which they are a part. Instead, Cameron quietly unravels as his whole life reveals itself for the sham that it is. Even Tony Danza, who plays an actor on his show, cows him into humiliating a black costar. How's that for rock bottom?
 
As another critic once said about another movie bearing the same title, " 'Crash' isn't plotted, it's programmed.' " The logarithm is fairly simple: Money plus power plus a pale complexion equals total inhumanity. (Jean learns the hard way that her only friend in the world is the woman who cleans her house.) Power plus pallor minus money fares slightly better. (Ryan's bigotry is motivated by the suffering of his sick father, who lost his janitorial company when the city began giving preferential contracts to minority-owned businesses, and he gets his moment of slo-mo redemption.) Pallor minus power minus money plus small-town idealism (as embodied by Hansen) gets a kick in the head.
 
Any glimpse of emotional honesty comes courtesy of the actors, who manage to do a credible job despite the material. The smart, sexy spark between Esposito and Cheadle is all but extinguished by the airlessness of the script, and Cheadle manages to squeeze in some quietly affecting moment as the unloved son of a drug-addicted mother. Howard, an actor who radiates intelligence and sensitivity, fills out his maddeningly reductive character as best he can, though he's never given the chance to do anything but react to the trumped-up pressures around him.
 
Similarly, Newton is never allowed to come down from the ledge of hysteria, just as Bullock is systematically barred from entry into the human race. Tate and Bridges, as the loquacious carjackers, provide the only breath of fresh air in the movie, but given the film's bird's-eye point of view and its pretensions at objectivity, their charm feels assigned at random. The cast members more than pull their weight, it's just too bad they had to get together for this.

I am angry all the time and I dont know why. This is the statement Sandra Bullock comes out with halfway through [i]Crash[/i], and she could be speaking on behalf of every character in the movie. Everyone in this film is angry, frustrated and unhappy. Oh, and racist too. [i]Crash[/i] opens and closes with a car crash (hence the title) and during the intervening two hours every character - Black, White, Hispanic, Asian, Arab - will reveal the bigotry they manage to keep under wraps most of the time.

Set over the course of a day in Los Angeles, [i]Crash[/i] is an ensemble drama following a dozen or so characters who cross paths (often in ludicrously contrived fashion). Matt Dillon is a bigoted cop who pulls over a black couple and molests the woman (Thandie Newton), much to the horror of his partner (Ryan Phillippe) and her husband (Terrence Howard). District Attorney Brendan Fraser and his wife Sandra Bullock are car-jacked at gunpoint by two black youths (Chris Ludacris Bridges and Larenz Tate) and she starts to have suspicions about any minority, including kind-hearted locksmith Daniel (Michael Pena). Don Cheadle is a local cop who finds himself being used as a political pawn. These characters repeatedly crash into each other throughout the film, resulting in scene after scene of anger, hatred and prejudice.

Paul Haggis, a successful TV writer for many years, is best known for his Oscar-nominated screenplay for [i]Million Dollar Baby[/i], and [i]Crash[/i] marks his first attempt at directing a feature. His film is ambitious in scope, tackles an important theme and features a starry cast, many of whom deliver their finest work in years. Unfortunately, Haggis is guilty of taking a preachy, heavy-handed approach which makes [i]Crash[/i] feel like less than the sum of its parts. Given the nature of the films structure, [i]Crash[/i] inevitably draws comparisons to the work of PT Anderson and Robert Altman, but the comparisons do Haggis film no favours. Anderson brought an epic grandeur and operatic sweep to [i]Magnolia[/i] which helped make the often incredible coincidences and contrivances more palatable to the viewer, something [i]Crash[/i]s more realistic approach doesnt manage, and while Altman filled his films with numerous themes and ideas, [i]Crash[/i] has one thing and one thing only on its mind - racism.

The opening car crash sets the scene with Jennifer Esposito asking the Chinese driver in the other car if she couldnt see over the steering wheel or see her blake lights properly. The next scene features a Persian man being called Osama by the owner of a gun shop and told to plan the Jihad on your own time. It seems every person in this vision of LA resorts to racial stereotyping when pushed to the edge and Haggis just keeps it coming. In the opening half hour every scene seems to end with some kind of racist insult being hurled and it all becomes a bit wearying before too long. It doesnt take long for the minor shock value of such robust racial language to dissipate and after that you have to ask Haggis what else have you got?.

The answer, depressingly, is not much. Haggis hammers home the same point with every scene, an approach which simply dilutes the power of the issue. Hes careful to paint every character in a shade of grey, with each of them shown making racist remarks as well as being on the end of prejudice themselves. Haggis is lucky that his well-chosen cast give such committed performances as they manage to raise his material a notch or two. Matt Dillon gives his best performance for a long time and shares two electric encounters with Thandie Newton, Sandra Bullock plays against type effectively, and Michael Pena is a soulful presence as the closest thing to a truly good character in the film.

Haggis struggles in the second half to ensure that all the disparate characters interact in some way, resulting in some ridiculous coincidences and plot developments which will strain audiences credibility to breaking point. Two of the films big moments - one involving an overturned car and one with a gun being fired - are handled in overblown fashion by Haggis, with syrupy music and slow-motion laying it on far too heavily. Finally, despite the writer/directors intent to provide a gritty, edgy portrait of racism in contemporary USA, he goes soft at the end, and the film climaxes to the sound of many I love yous and plenty of hugging.

[i]Crash[/i] is undoubtedly very watchable, mainly thanks to the first-rate cast, but it never fully engages the viewers emotions and is nowhere near as brave or important as Haggis clearly thinks it is. Haggis loses the fight by trying much too hard, which is hugely disappointing as he can stage an effective scene when he takes his foot off the race pedal a little. The most compelling sequences in [i]Crash[/i] are the ones that have the least to do with colour, a scene between a father and daughter or a mother and son, and show glimpses of what the film could have been, but such delicate moments tend to be swiftly lost under the juggernaut of Haggis overriding theme.
 
With its broad strokes and ridiculous plotting [i]Crash[/i] would probably work best if you dont take it too seriously but - theres the rub - [i]Crash[/i] simply demands to be taken seriously. It likes to think of itself as being some sort of great statement on the issue of racism but, while it tries to say everything about race, it ends up saying nothing new.

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]            I saw this film just a few days before I was told I had to see it for a class assignment because I decided to see as many Oscar-nominated films from 2006 as I could, before the awards took place. I had the misconception that Oscar-nominated films were always boring and just not cool, but this movie has proved me wrong in a way I never imagined. In the first minute of the movie Don Cheadles character [i]Graham [/i]says: [i]You brush past people, people bump into you. In L.A., nobody touches you. We're always behind this metal and glass. I think we miss that touch so much, that [b]we crash into each other, just so we can feel something[/b]. [/i]That last phrase got to me, it clicked something in me: I felt completely identified with the words he just said. It made me question the way people behave.[/font][/size]
 
 [size=3][font=Times New Roman]            From where I'm from, people have this always fed-up, angry-at-life kind of mood that makes us scream at each other and fight with the first person that crosses our way for no good reason. Could it be that were trying to connect with people, with anyone, but the only way we feel we can do that is by behaving like that? I think thats the point director Paul Haggis is trying to make. Hes trying, in a very realistic way, to make us come to our senses and make us see the unnecessary things we do to feel touched, to feel alive, when all we can do is ask for it. [/font][/size]
 
 [size=3][font=Times New Roman]            Something I really liked in this film is the way it treats racism. Its cruel but its real and even if it [i]is[/i] shocking, thats what counts, its what makes you see things the way they really are. If he wanted to make a movie about racism, Haggis couldve just done what other movies have done: go around the topic and treat it in a sublime way. But no, he chose to do it the mean way, the real way. At times, the movie can shock you and you can feel what the characters are going through. For example, when Sandra Bullocks character [i]Jean[/i] is saying to her husband that she wants the locks from her house changed again in the morning because she doesnt trust the man thats changing them at that moment. She says that hes a gang member just because the man has a shaved head, pants around his ass, (and)prison tattoos. Right after she stops talking she realizes that the man has heard her. Michael Peñas character Daniel (the gang member  actually a Mexican locksmith) stood there, still changing the locks but looking at her. You could see how indignant he felt because of her comments. At that moment the movies just beginning, so you cant really tell if hes good or bad, but in that moment you feel like hes a good man, you feel sorry for him and terribly angry at Bullocks character. Its ironic that we can feel like that about a movie, but in real life weve all thought and acted, at some point, exactly like [i]Jean[/i].        [/font][/size]
 
 [size=3][font=Times New Roman]            Racism is something that is so inside our culture, inside our lifestyle, that we tend to see it as something normal, something acceptable because everyone behaves like that. The truth is that, even if we criticize it, we all contribute to racism whether consciously or not. [/font][/size]
  
 [font=Times New Roman]            [size=4]In his well-deserved Oscar-nominated film, Haggis tells stories of everyday-racism and interconnects them to show us just how human we are, even if our actions contradict themselves. By behaving like racists we dehumanize ourselves because were supposed to love one another, but by crashing with people were just looking, yearning to feel touched, to feel alive and [i]thats[/i] what makes us human.

NOTE: This is a Film Review that I wrote as a class assignment for my English Class.

[/size]If each of us were merely the personification of a vehicle, then Henry Ford would not be happy with how things have progressed. The roads are populated with human versions that come in a rainbow of colors. Crash, a film by Paul Haggis, is an ensemble drama that follows the journeys of a dozen or so Angelenos, snarled in a traffic jam of proportions that rival the 405 at rush hour.
 
 
Bookending (or should I say front- and rear-ending) the film is the scene of an accident. With clues and debris strewn about Don Cheadle as detective Graham Waters investigates the cause of the wreckage. This is the safest we'll feel over the next 100 minutes as nearly each person we meet eventually jumps the curb to a conclusion that spins their frustration with life further out of control.
 
Flashing back through the day before, we traverse the landscape of contemporary urban Los Angeles, itself a society at the boiling point in the ethnic melting-pot experiment that is America, in its 221st year. From our eye-in-the-sky position, characters at first appear flat and two-dimensional at best, simple stereotypes like symbols on a map. Then from a different view, the topography begins to reveal texture and range. No one is just good, or just bad, but a curious mixture of the two. As much as our knees tend to jerk in only black, or white, there actually are a lot of other shades inciting reflection.
 
From the affluent white housewife and the buppie television executive, to the first-gen Persian convenience shop owner and the throwback cracker cop, the participants in Crash represent models of humanity manufactured carefully to specification at the factory, now at various stages of wear and tear, replete with the inevitable dents and scratches incurred along their routes. Some attempt to hide evidence of their higher or harder mileage with a hand-rubbed polish, others with Bondo and a cheap paint job. But under the Armor-All each of this hard-driven lot is rendered inoperable due to the high rate of self-absorption at in which they travel.
 
On the surface, Crash shows a grid of intersecting stories that deal with racial themes. Black and white may offer the highest contrast, but Crash also explores how racism, or bettercultural prejudice, can skew our point of view and shade the way we perceive and treat women, the elderly, teens, the poor, and yes, even the "rich." People in the film tend to live down to the expectations of others, thereby confirming their initial assumptions. Yet the harsh but valid message is that the disrespect we have for others is but a manifestation of the loathing and dissatisfaction we have for ourselves.
 
Opposing attitudes, like particles of matter, can't occupy the same space at the same time without a collision. There has to be some form of compromise. Realistically, the film portrays the fact that we may actually not have much in common with other folk, and it is those differences that terrify us. To be sure, there is some commonality, however small: at their core, these people believe they are right in their perspectives-- yet are able to change if inspired to give it enough thought. That change does comes at a price, most often that of leaving something behind. If the mind can be opened, one can see that it's easier to move around with less baggage.
 
Values may be a composite of culture, but if you believe in Free Will, we are not simply the sum of our past experiences. We can choose where we go from here. The characters in Crash are more often than not, given second chances to deal with their perceived demons. At every crossroad, every turn, they choose the direction to take. Some take the road less traveled, some play a dangerous game of chicken, and some make U-turns.
 
Like the stereotypical "man who won't stop to ask for directions," people don't like being told what to do, especially by someone they consider to be the "opposition." Crash suggests that a more satisfying way to solve problems within cultural niches is for those within the culture to manage themselvesthat being your brother's keeper should be strongly encouraged, but keep it in the (cultural) family.
 
The intersection of diverse lives may at first seem too neatly choreographed, but far from resorting to the deus ex machina that pops up in most Hollywood fodder, Haggis uses the connections for convenience and economy. Greek myths, the most enduring stories the world has known, are riddled with recurring characters, coincident, and overlapping story lines, but were presented as parables for the sake of metaphor, or to teach a lesson. Modern folk go to movies for identification and resolutionto observe the actions of others who share questions or problems similar to ours. We are forever optimistic that the characters will make the right decisions. And when they don't, we can sit back in the safety of our own tinted-windowed, safety belted, reinforced radialed, air-bagged selves and thank God our own near misses didn't kill us.
 
It's human nature to slow down and rubber-neck when we see the results of a crash on the highway. Perhaps this is nature's built-in way to have us take personal note of the dangers of driving recklessly through life.

I'll never catch up on my film reviews, but here are five more fairly recent views. I'll start with two Oscar Winning films of 2005.
 
[b]Crash[/b], written and directed by Paul Haggis, was an upset winner for Best Picture of 2005, beating the favored [i]Brokeback Mountain[/i]. [b]Crash [/b]seems to be a movie that people either love or loathe, and very few people take the middle ground on this film, which I kind of do. Set over a two day period in Los Angeles, [b]Crash [/b]is a study of race relations. A large ensemble cast including Don Cheadle, Sandra Bullock, Terence Howard, Matt Dillon, Thandie Newton, Ludacris, Brendan Fraser, Ryan Phillippe, Larenz Tate and Jennifer Esposito literally "crash" into one another during the course of the film, and each new scene reveals something about their racial prejudices and attitudes. I won't go into much plot detail as most are familar with this film, instead I'll focus on what I liked and disliked about [i]Crash[/i]. 
 
First my dislikes. My biggest problem with this film was not the message (a good one) but it's bombastic delivery. Almost every scene produced some confrontation or high drama, like Haggis was trying to outdo what we had seen ten minutes earlier, and over the course of the film it just diluted the strongest scenes in the film and it's overall message. This film needed more emotional peaks and valleys instead of trying to be so melodramatic in every scene. Yes the script needed a rewrite, and the film some serious editing. I would have removed some characters entirely and focused more on the characters that did work. And I would have had added more restrained scenes so some of the very powerful scenes (and there were some) did not become diluted. Also, some of the characters were just too stereotypical or one dimensional. It was a severly fragmented film that seemed to go from brilliant to ridiculous at any given moment.
 
What I liked? Despite the over-the-top melodrama of the film, it was quickly paced and enertaining, albiet maddeningly frustrating at times. There were scenes of brilliance (Dillon molesting Newton in front of partner Phillippe or the sidewalk scene with Bullock, Ludacris and Tate), and scenes that were just ridiculous (any scene with Cheadle's mother). Another plus was the performances of a few of it's stars. Matt Dillon was phenomenal as Jack Ryan. I also thought Terence Howard, Thandie Newton, Sandra Bullock, Ludacris and Ryan Phillippe were very good. Had this film concentrated on a half dozen characters and shown more restraint it would have been a great film. As is I found it frustrating, yet at times very engaging. A mild recommendation for a film that could have been much more.
 
[b]Hustle & Flow[/b], written and directed by Craig Brewer, received a couple of Academy Award nominations, one for Terence Howard as best actor and winning for best song. D-Jay (Howard) is a low level pimp and drug dealer. living with three women, Lexus, Shug and Nola (Paula Jai Parker, Taraji Henson & Taryn Manning). Now in his mid-30's, D-Jay is unhappy with how his life has unfolded and decides to give his love of music one last shot. He runs into old high school friend Key (Anthony Anderson) who helps produce shows at a local church. Although Key has a wife and leads a respectable life, he's as unhappy as D-Jay, so he agrees to work with D-Jay. A skinny geeky white guy named Shelby (DJ Qualls) is brought on to help with the beats. When the men complete D-Jay's tape, he arranges to meet with national Rap Star Skinny Black, a former native of Memphis. Skinny Black thinks D-Jay is there to sell him drugs, but D-Jay hopes Skinny can get his tape to the right people.
 
[b]Hustle & Flow [/b]rises above similarly themed movies due to excellent writing and an outstanding performance from Howard. It would have been easy to stereoype D-Jay, but Brewer did not make him flashy at all. D-Jay drives a beater with an AM radio, doesn't dress well or wear any jewelry, and most importantly isn't enamored with his chosen profession as a pimp and drug dealer. Although he's no angel (afterall he's a pimp) he does have a conscience and sees his women as more than merely property. He may not be book smart, but D-Jay is highly intelligent and extremely philosphical. He has enough depth that we can sympathize with his plight despite the line of work he's in. The supporting cast is also very good, especially Taryn Manning and Ludacris. The cast also features Memphis soul legend Isaac Hayes. I didn't expect much from this film and was pleaseantly surprised. I have not seen enough 2005 films to pick a Best Actor, but as of now Terence Howard leads the pack. 
 
[b]Dirty Pretty Things[/b], directed by Stephen Frears, is one terrific little film. Set in London, [b]Dirty Pretty Things [/b]is the story of illegal immigrants, trying to make a life working low wage jobs while trying to avoid Immigration authorities. Okwe (Chiwetel Ejiofor) is A Nigerian immigrant working two jobs, one as a ataxi driver and the other as fron desk clerk at a hotel. He was a trained doctor in Nigeria. His roommate Senay (Audrey Tautou) is a Turkish immigrant who works as a maid at the hotel. She yearns to travel to New York. One evening Okwe receives a call from Juliette (Sophie Okonedo) a prostitute working out of the hotel. Her toilet is clogged. Okwe soon discovers what has clogged the toilet, a human heart. Due to his illegal status, Okwe cannot call the police so he begins investigating this mysterious discovery himself. He soon finds out that night manager Sneaky (Sergi Lopez) is running a business out of the hotel that offers visas or passports to illegal immigrants in exchange for body parts. Sneaky tries to blackmail Okwe after he finds out about his medical training, but Okwe wants no part of the deal until Senay seeks a visa through Sneaky.
 
What a script! [b]Dirty Pretty Things [/b]is unbelievably well written. What could have turned into an exploitive thriller never does. This film never takes the easy way out, and it's story of the struggles of illegal immigrants is as poignant as it is realistic. The film shows in numerous ways how these people are exploited. It's well written, well acted, and never allows the thriller aspect to go over-the-top. Highly recommended.
 
[b]High Fidelity[/b], also directed by Stephen Frears, is a romantic comedy drama starring John Cusack as Rob Gordon, the owner of an independent record store. Rob's current relationship with Laura (Iben Hjejle) is failing, giving Rob an excuse to review his "Top 5" failed relationships of all time. As the whiny Rob rambles on we see his past loves and why those relationships failed. Mmm look in the mirror Rob! Life at the record store is much more fun as friends and co-workers Barry (Jack Black) and Dick (Todd Lousio) are music snobs, which leads to some interesting conversations about, well music! Unfortunately these scenes are the best part of the film, leading to my very few laughs. The love stoy between Rob and Laura simply doesn't have enough sparks, and I found Rob's whiny meanderings to be neither funny or insightful. Run Laura run! Some ridiculous subplots (Tim Robbins as Laura's New Age lover and Rob's discovery of the punk kids) only drag this film down further. Jack Black brutally butchering the great Marvin Gaye didn't help either! I thought this might be one of those lightweight but enjoyable films, but I was wrong. The cast also features Joan Cusack, Lisa Bonet, Lili Taylor, Catherine Zeta-Jones, Sara Gilbert and a cameo from Bruce Springsteen. 
 
Lastly we have [b]Spun[/b], an absolutely wretched look at our drug culture. Directed by Jonas Akerlund, [b]Spun [/b]is billed as a "dark comedy" but it's about as funny as a nosebleed or throwing up in a toilet. Like most honest adults under the age of say 50, I've been there and done that. No hypocrit here as I had some good times and some bad times. Sure I saw some casualties along the way, but most people survived and became quite normal, even hypocritical of their own pasts! Hey I'm not ashamed to say that dancing to Front 242's "Quiet Unusual" is much better on ecstasy. Okay this movie was about meth or speed or crank or crystal or whatever trendy name it has today. It's still a wretched film. I was sober when I watched it and doubt I would have enjoyed it even if under the influence. As far as drug films goes this was the worst I have ever seen. Obviously the screenwriter wasn't on drugs when this was written as it would have least been funnier. The dialogue was insipid, the worst I have heard in a long, long time. The characters so ridiculous and unfunny that I wonder if the actors actually read this thing before signing on. And the film did have a (somewhat) capable cast which included Jason Schwartzman, Mickey Rourke, Mena Suvari, John Leguizamo, and Brittany Murphy. I guess including cameos of Deborah Harry as a lesbian phone sex operator and Rob Halford as a porn store clerk (reading gay porn no less) constitues clever casting. And plot? What plot? We have Mickey Rourke cooking meth while watching wrestling on television. We have Jason Schwartzman handcuffing a girl to the bed, taping her mouth, and leaving her in a hotel room while he drives Rourke around. We have a green dog. We have a geeky informant that gets shot in the balls. We see Mena Suvari take a dump. We see John Leguizamo beat off and then put a sock on his wee-wee. I'm still waiting for my first laugh and I returned the DVD a week ago. Oh did I mention the editing? Edgy and hallucinatory of course. Heads spinning, close ups of eyes and computer graphics of stuff going up noses. Stupid, stupid, stupid film. Worst drug movie ever! You will have more fun listening to "Bela Lugosi's Dead" backwards, that's if you still own a record player. Or ever owned a record player!

Personal review of "Crash"
 
* * *
So, I was curious if the Best Picture winner of 2006 really was that good.
 
Sounds strange, but I think that Crash somehow is a comedy. A very twisted one; none that makes you laugh, but one that makes you chuckle over mankind's stupidity. 
 
The movie is full of irony[size=1] (or black humour... sorry for the pun :P)[/size]. The young white cop who is so offened by his rassistic partner ends up shooting a young black guy who only pulled a holy figure out of his pocket (and no gun as the cop thought). The rassistic cop who saves the life of the very same woman, he humiliated the other day just because of her skin color. The arab who 'shoots' the little mexican girl with blank cartridge - the girl who got the 'invisible bullet-save cloak' from her dad just the other day. And so on. In the end, everyone got their nice or not so nice little christmas messages. 
 
So, what do I think about Crash? It's an interesting mixture of several short stories which all stay on their own and yet are connected by certain elements. Kinda reminds me on Sin City which used the same storytelling-effect (but that is, of course, the only similarity between these two movies).
The characters were very exaggerated and some stories were a bit over-dramatised. 
 
All in all it was an okay-movie. Nice popcorn-entertainment, but nothing I would buy on DVD. Nothing that keeps me thinking days and weeks after I watched it. It was a bit too blatant for that.

[i]Crash[/i] is a film that sets out to address the ever important societal issue of racism through the telling of a series of seemingly unrelated events during a 36 hour period in Los Angeles. We follow the chaotic events that engulf a wide array of characters and all of these situations spell out the evils of stereotyping and racism in general. At least, thats the intent.

As noble as the intentions of this film may be, the point is ultimately failed to be reached in a successful manner. Precisely why this so is more than a bit ironic. This film leans so heavily on stereotypes to prove the ever-important point that it ends up undermining it quite successfully.

The biggest problem is that [i]Crash[/i] continually betrays the audience and its own characters. The best example of this occurs in the second scene of the film when wee are introduced to Anthony and Peter, two young black men who have just dealt with racism against them in a restaraunt. Anthony then breaks into a monologue that hits the nail on the head about the situation concerning the treatment of young men like them. They are continually disrespected, not trusted and irrationally feared as Anthony points out. At this point I genuinely felt for these characters because they were victims of stereotyping. Then in the blink of an eye the are brandishing guns and stealing an SUV at gun-point. Wait a second, was what that point about being irrationally feared? Yeah, all credibility just got shot to hell! Not the best way to make the point. In fact, it is the worst way.

It wasn't long after that scene (only the second of the film) that I really lost interest when it became very apparent that absolutely every character in the film was going to be racist in a completely exaggerated way. EVERY CHARACTER! Apparently, if two people have an altercation, they immediately resort to racial slurs and jokes. Now, I don't argue that this occurs in the real world, but certainly not at the very drop of a hat as portrayed in this movie. [i]Crash[/i]'s approach is so heavy-handed and exaggerated that it isn't even plausible, much less an effective way to illustrate a point. It also doesn't help that every character is a dicotomy in the extreme. Everyone (like Anthony) has a scene where you are supposed to sympathize with them only to have them suddenly become super-racists. That game is up very quickly and the effect is lost.

Because [i]Crash[/i] systematically betrays every character in this fashion, the film makes a stronger case for stereotypes (which, right or wrong, are born out of some element of truth, sad to say) which is unfortunate. What really surprised me, however, was that I haven't seen a film with a message this important fail so miserably in memory. In fact, some of the portrayals and situations actually made me laugh (example: the Asian woman seen in the first scene and again near the end). Aside from Anthony, who turns out to be a complete fake after his opening monologue, none of the characters are really protrayed as intelligent except for Daniel, who I would say was the film's best character. That fact raises a big question with me: Why weren't they portrayed as being more intelligent because I know people and have met people from these ethnic groups who are very intelligent?

It would be safe to say that the creators of [i]Crash[/i] chose caricature as the means to illustrate their point about racism. However, caricature, while often meaningful and significant, isn't always the best choice for doing that. Recent global events demonstrate that truth very clearly.

I lost interest early on in the film when it became apparent that absolutely everything was beyond caricature. Is racism alive and well in America. Yes. Does a movie prove a point by reinforcing stereotypes in its story while trying to say that they are bad? No. Not to me.

Ah what a tangled web we weave.  Isn't ironic that every action or decision will affect others either advertedly or inadvertedly. Chaos theory in action.  This is some heavy thinking that would make men go mad trying to solve this riddle.  [u]Crash[/u] takes a look at how the lives of ordinary people of different race, ethnicity, and class intertwine in the social-racial-political melting pot that is Los Angeles in a twenty-four hour period.
 
This movie is a philosopher's dream come true.  From the get go we can tell that this is no ordinary movie.  The viewer is automatically drawn into the different worlds of the people of Los Angeles.  As Shakespeare once said we a re all puppets on a stage, and this movie demonstrates that truer words have never been spoken.  
 
With an all-star cast this movie is surrounded by talent from all different genres of cinematic history.  Some actors like Sandra Bullock, and Ryan Phillipe give what is perhaps the performance of their lives.  They are able to go beyond their traditional typecast and test the merky waters of different personas that they are not familiar.  Let's not forget that this cast also include no-name actors as well as the long forgotten.  Matt Dillon for example was a staple of eighties cinema and I completly forgot he exsisted, sometimes to be confused with Matt Damon.  [u]Crash[/u] brings his career to a new level earning him a much deserved Oscar nomination for his portrayal of a veteran cop with racial ideals of society.  Including when he conflicts with Star Jones, whome you can never picture in such a movie.  From Don Cheadle to Brendan Frasier to Jennifer Esposito there is no wasted talent, and the actors are able to push them selves to memorable performances.
 
The problem with [u]Crash[/u] is that it could take forever analyzing the film on different levels of thinking.  Sociology, history, philosophy, filmography, political science, can all be argued as the main themes of the film.  Truth be told they all fit in nicely to the epic story of the film. Expect this movie to be analyzed, disected and discussed in the classroom.  
 
Much deserved of its' Academy Award for Best Picture, [u]Crash[/u] sends a message that everything we do can affect the life of another.  If we choose to acknoweldge a higher power then we are all part of an intrigate design, that can never be understood.  We each serve a purpose in life and the outcome will never be known.  Perhaps as you spent the last ten minutes reading this review your life and the life of those around you have forever changed.  That my friend is thinking outside the box.

So, essentially, Crash is a film about racism.  You can't get away from it; every other line is about race in some manner and it gets a bit too monotonous.  I don't like being preached to.  I don't like having Hot PC Topics stuffed in my face when I want to watch a film, and unfortunately, that's just what Crash does.
 
The one thing that redeems the movie is the acting.
 
Sandra Bullock being non-Annie from Speed is fantastic.  She's not being Miss Congeniality either, but a bored rich housewife, a role that doesn't quite suit her but works anyway.  She's showing a hint of versatility and should be encouraged.  Brendan Fraser's always good, Thandie Newton deserves her praise, everyone acts brilliantly, but most of all they all manage to make the non-twists in the plot work.
 
This is no small thing.
 
The non-twists I refer to are the bits of plot where you know what's coming.  You know who's going to get shot.  You know who's going to die.  You know who's going to crash and who's going to suffer.  Except you don't.  The thing that this film manages to very well is unpredictability.  You're so sure so-and-so is going to die, but then the scriptwriters pull off a nice little trick that isn't so unlikely - you've seen the hints leading up to it, as in the case of the Turkish man's gun, but what actually happens is entirely not what you expect.
 
So for clever film making and acting that allows the script to work brilliantly, Crash is fantastic.  But making it a vehicle for a message about racism doesn't quite work.  It's too obvious, compared to the subtleties of the script.  The Oscars can award the gritty, real-life films all they want, but I've seen many better films in the past year and although Crash is great for the attention to detail and so on, it just doesn't quite seem worthy of so much hype.  Maybe I miss out having never been to LA or, indeed, the US, but as a good film it's a good film.  Not entertaining and too much moralizing to my taste - but then there are worse mistakes it could have made.

Crash is a very interesting, very haunting and very deep look at racism in America. This isn't a film that simply caters to a specific type of oppression or stereotype that needs to be exploited, but instead takes a look at both sides of all racism. There are no protagonists or antagonists. Only complex people who try to live based on their experiences are present in the film.
 
The story consists of several different characters. Don Cheadle plays a cop who comforts his heart-broken mother and shows little respect towards his Puerto Rican girlfriend played by Jennifer Esposito. Sandra Bullock plays the wife of a district attorney, played by Brendon Fraiser, who bares a hatred towards other ethnicities after being car jacked. Ludacris plays a small time thief who believes he has the whole world's agenda nailed down and preaches it to his sympathetic partner, played by Larenz Tate. Matt Dillon plays a dirty, racist cop who has to take care of his sick father. Terrance Howard plays a cowardly producer who is accused by his girlfriend of not acting black enough. There is also a Persian store owner who bares hatred towards others who accuse him of being a terrorist, a Mexican locksmith who watches out for his daughter and an Asian man who makes shady deals for some friends to come into the country. All of these character directly and indirectly affect each other in this complex tale.
 
Crash is not a film about how racism is bad or how all racists are actually pretty good people. It's about how people have several layers to them and how the world is not always black and white. One day, you're a racist biggot or a law abiding citizen. The next day you could be a hometown hero or wanted for murder. The dialogue of the film is also a big plus as it forces uncomfortable, infuriating and sometimes darkly comedic discussions. For instance, there is a scene where Sandra Bullock's character argues of why it is screwed up that if you don't feel safe around black people you're a racist.
 
Paul Haggis has directed a film that works on so many situational levels that ties in with the all-star cast and great acting. There are a few who believe this a ficticious and slanted film that is not going to end racism by displaying how racists are still still good people. Crash does not display this, although it can be interpreted that way, and it certainly isn't a film that is going to end racism. However, it is a film that forces you to see other people as people, even if they are blinded by hate.

Whether white, black, Asian, Hispanic or any other ethnic group, as presented in this film, everyone is full of prejudice against the other race. And not only the members of the other race, even the same race. Everyone seems to be in a turmoil. But hey, this is LA, city of angels and angels are not only white, as we know. [/color]

Therefore, the store owners daughter is also the pathologist, the screaming Chinese (or Japanese or Thai, it doesnt matter in a Hollywood movie) lady from the hospital is also the Chinese (or Japanese or Thai, read above) lady who hit Jennifer Espositos car at the beginning of the movie, or how Loretta Devine, whom you thought youd not see in this film again, as her character is really unimportant to the story line and is limited only to a brief cameo, appears at the very end in, yet another car crash; or even how the police officer Matt Dillon, who at first finger-fcuked Thandie Newton, becomes her life savior  in a scene filled with more sexual tension than the sex between Esposito and Cheadle. I had to trick my husband into seeing this movie. I didn't tell                      him that this movie is about everyone basically being racist,                      which could be true, but is still a horrible thought. I knew                      that once my husband realized that every character was unlikeable,                      he would start to hate everyone in the movie. I asked him                      about 20 minutes into the movie if it was making him mad and                      it was. He did watch the entire movie though.
 
                    I didn't realize how many people were in the movie. I knew                      it was an ensemble, but didn't really pay attention to who                      was in it. When the credits started, I was surprised to see                      Sandra Bullock, Ludacris, Ryan Phillippe, Don Cheadle, and                      Brenden Fraser. I seemed to only remember Thandie Newton and                      Matt Dillon were in the movie.
 
                    The movie starts out with Don Cheadle's cop character talking                      to his partner, played by Jennifer Esposito, while they are                      at a murder site, but just got into a fender bender while                      pulling up to it. He is talking about how everyone is so disconnected                      nowadays that sometimes the only human contact happens when                      they actually crash into one another. It was the kind of statement                      that might be said by someone at the end of the movie or not                      said at all, but the sentiment would be taken away from the                      movie if it did a good job telling the story. The movie told                      me what I needed to think right away and I really didn't like                      that. Jennifer Esposito looked at him like he was crazy and                      then went on to yell at an Asian lady while making wonderful                      racial slurs. 
 
                    It is what starts the racial slurs and stereotypes that continue                      throughout the rest of the movie. Some of them are too obvious,                      like Sandra Bullock's character not trusting the Hispanic                      locksmith at her house since she is sure that he will make                      copies to give to his hoodlum friends to steal from her later.                      Having her scream this through the house so he can hear is                      just too obvious. There are other scenes where it is more                      subtle and I think that are truer to life. Sure, there are                      people that are that blatant in their racism, but people that                      really think they don't believe in stereotypes while thinking                      that the black man might shoot them when he reaches into his                      pocket, is more interesting to watch. 
 
                    My favorite character in the movie was Ludacris's character.                      He said what he thought other people were thinking about him                      and his friend, which was funny and true. Then they acted                      on some of the things they knew people were thinking about                      them. He was so angry at what everyone automatically thought,                      but then didn't see a problem doing what others expected.                      It was too funny.
 
                    By the end of the movie, it seemed everyone changed their                      thinking, if only slightly. It was a realistic way to end                      a movie since not everyone is going to realize they are stupid                      and change how they think of other people immediately. It                      was little things that maybe made them rethink how they act                      since they want to actually be decent human beings.
 
                    I didn't think this movie was the best movie of the year,                      which is recently was declared by Oscar voters. I think it                      had serious flaws, but was a decent movie. I just don't think                      I have the need to watch it again, except for the scenes with                      Ludacris.

There are two films that Crash reminds me of.  One is Magnolia, the other is House of Sand and Fog.
 
It reminds me of Magnolia because of its structure.  We have ourselves an ensemble of characters whose lives seem completely unconnected but, as the film progresses, they slowly become weaved together.  Like Magnolia, none of the characters could be said to be the leads as we spend roughly equal time with all of them.  Unlike Magnolia, there isn't the boldness in the editing and pacing giving a sense of ordinary lives moving towards a moment of common transcendence.  Crash is more of a "slice of life" kinda thing with the film concluding in pretty much the same place as where it started.
 
Not that the characters don't change.  In fact, that is what the thing's about.  Each character represents one stereotype or another.  We have black hoods holding guns sideways and jacking cars.  We have a white yuppie terrified to leave the seclusion of her upper-class home.  There's the racist cop, the rookie cop, the upper class black couple accused of being too white.  We have an east-indian family fighting anti-terrorist paranoia.  We have a poerto rican man trying to bring his family out of the ghetto and a black cop wondering if he isn't doing enough on the homefront.  All of these characters have a specific world view and every one of them has it challenged as they clash with one another.

[left]That brings me to the second film, House of Sand and Fog.  Both these films are really and examination of perspective and racism.  About making assumptions about the other people that we collide with and forgetting that they too are coming at us from their own unique perspective.  Unlike Sand and Fog which presents the miscommunications and downright bigotry that exists between us as tragic, Crash seems to almost celebrate them in the end and that's where I have my only real problem with the film.  Instead of challenging us to be better and to question the way we see others, Crash seems to just shrug its shoulders and grin, "hey, we're only human."[/left]

[font=Palatino Linotype]Naturally, since I wrote a review the other day ([i]Love Actually)[/i] that referred to [i]Crash,[/i] it makes sense that I should do a review so that you could put them in comparison, and actually know how I feel about this film. Well, I loved it. It's brilliant, simply put. It delivers on every front. The ensemble cast work nicely, and the interweaving stories are brilliant. It takes real skill to be able to pull of all these branching stories, and some movies fail miserably when it comes to this. [i]Crash and Love Actually[u],[/u][/i] are a few that succeed.[/font]
[font=Palatino Linotype][/font] 
[font=Palatino Linotype]The theme in [i]Crash[/i] is racism, and it deals with the many stereotypes that are very real, and very much a problem in our culture today. This film isn't necessarily a happy one, and it really just depends on which storyline you're following. Some are beautiful and touching, like Daniel's story, with his little girl. It's so sad, touching and moving. I read mommiezombie's review of [i]Crash [/i]awhile back, and she thought this one spoke to her, because she was a mother. Well, yeah I  can see that, but you don't have to be a mother for this one to speak to you. I was moved and I'm just a young college punk. Cameron and Elizabeth's story was really moving, but in a different way. It was just miserable to see Cameron (Terrence Howard), having to go through this, and he's just put through so much shit, that's undeserved. Just because he was black and made something out of himself.[/font]
[font=Palatino Linotype][/font] 
[font=Palatino Linotype][i]Crash[/i] is visually a treat as well. The camera angles and shots are beautifully shot, and well-thought out. The music, likewise, is haunting and melodic. Everything fits in the film, and it's easy to see why so many critics loved this film. Any attention [i]Crash[/i] received, was well deserved. The characters are wonderful, and they really stick out still, which is something not easily said about ensemble pieces. How often do you go into a film with a dozen main characters, and come out enjoying all of their stories and arcs, and relationships? Well, not often, if you're like me. So this is another reason which I loved [i]Crash [/i]and [i]Love Actually [/i]so much.[/font]
[font=Palatino Linotype][/font] 
[font=Palatino Linotype][i]Crash[/i] is definitely not the feel good hit of the year, but what it is, is a powerful drama, with a complex and balancing story, that shows racism in pretty much every aspect. Many of the character-arcs are a little cliched, like Sandra Bullock's character Jean, but then the dialogue and the acting make up for any cliches. Just as in [i]Love Actually[/i], Haggis takes a theme that has been done to death in cinema, something usually cliched, and makes it new and original. [i]Crash[/i] succeeds on every level and doesn't disappoint. Highly recommended![/font]

Crash is a thought provoking, moving, incredibly written and acted film. The interweaving plots and storylines work perfect, if a little unlikely. The point of this film is not to show a 24 hour period of people's lives (although that is part of it), but to show how racism affects our lives and how we are all looking for someone to hold on to.
   I really can't stress how good the acting is. The best of the best would have to be Michael Pena, who gives just a heart wrenching performance as a Spanish locksmith who is stereotyped as a "gangbanger" and cares for his daughter who's scared of getting shot at. He gives her an invisible cloak that he says will stop anything from hitting her, like a bullet or a knife. This leads up to a fantastic, moving, chilling scene, which brought tears to my eyes because of the amazing acting from Pena. Every actor makes you feel bad for them, makes you feel what they're feeling - an incredible feat that made this movie stick with me weeks after I saw it.
   All the other performances are terrific too, with Matt Dillon as a cop who transforms into an almost caring cop, Terrence Howard as a man tortured by the fact his wife was molested by a police officer and he didn't do anything about it, Ludacris as a gang member who also undergoes a transformation after a few events. 
   Simply put, the writing and directing is nearly flawless, and the acting is by far the best of the decade. Deserving of its Best Picture win? Completely.

So finally I watched Crash.  After all the "I hate Haggis" or "Crash rules!" talk around the block I wasn't sure how I would like it.  I tried to go into the movie completely neutral, and I think I did.  So since everyone already knows what the movie is about I'll explain it for you.  The film tries; yes [i]tries[/i], to exploit racism in LA for what it really is.  Racism is silly and this film tries to show that, but does it succeed?  Hardly.

The film starts us with two black fellows in a white neighborhood.  One discusses a very biased thought of them having to be scared in the white person area of the city.  "It's us who should be scared," he says.  Then he proceeds to completely void everything he had just said and steals a car.  Right at that moment the first eyebrow was raised.  Continually throughout the movie there are what [i]should[/i] be eyebrow raising moments, but after the first few times one of the characters uses an awful stereotype it just gets silly.  

This is a movie that is meant to be taken seriously, but by having some of the more over-the-top dialouge in recent memory it cancels out any hope it had of me taking it seriously.  As I said before Haggis, by making the dialouge kind of "out there," tries to show how stupid racism really is.  I think Haggis actually outdid himself and got in a bit over his head so to speak.  

But enough flaws.  Let's talk about something that went right in this film.  The one thing that pops out to me is the use of the montage.  The final montage is one of the better one's I've seen in a while; possibly rivaling the House: Season 1 finale.  So all in all the film isn't bad so to speak, it just isn't very good.  It tries to make a big civil statement about racism, but it turns out silly and I couldn't take it seriously.

There are a few things that go with a film like this that may not be considered a good thing. Here is a quick rundown.

1.Emotions become too much- Sometimes the emotions portrayed in these type of films arent realistic enough, the actors show to much pain and suffering and it becomes unbearable.

2.Short Cuts- these are scenes designed to show little clips without revealing to much. Sometimes they are two small and dont show enough of the scene to reveal anything and sometimes crucial information is skipped

3.Little Character development- Sometimes with so many characters they forget to develop some of the littler characters. This did happen in this film. Christine and Camerson werent defined as people and they didnt feel right, they just seemed to be two people who landed themselves in what was an awkward situation.

4.Acting- Sometimes the actors dont really have big enough scenes to get themselves established and none of them really seem to nail it in. With the exception of Penas deliverance of his vocations and words with clear execution the rest of the cast had some drama, but it didnt capture really great

5.Storyline- sometimes the story fails to catch a theme, fails to progress because they cant progress the lives of the characters and they cant progress the story line without progression of the climatic drama.

6.Intensity- The intensity as well as the storyline can be lost amungst the shift because of the short cuts

7.Romance- Romance in a film of intertwining people can often seem really cheesy because they dont have enough time to explore exactly why these people love each other.

8.The ending- A lot of times a film tries to end positively but the entire film has been negative. A film cannot change its outcome of emotions in the final 10 minutes, it just doesnt seem like the right thing to do. Through out an entire film there has been sadness for 10 people and then all of a sudden a world of epiphanys come to the people.

9.Conclusion for all- Sometimes not all the characters get the conclusion that we had hoped for or we dont even get to see their conclusion at all. [FONT=Book Antiqua]There are several problems inherent in last years inexplicable winner of the Best Picture prize. For starters, the dialogue is weak, the emotions are forced, and all events are far too coincidental. But another significant problem is obvious: Los Angeles and the surrounding areas simply arent all like the way they are depicted here. With notable exceptions like the 1992 riots over Rodney Kings court case (which were frightening), people generally get along. LA is one of the most racially diverse cities on the face of the planet, if not the most. To the simplistic mind of Paul Haggis, this should mean that there is a perennial state of fear and distrust between Middle Easterners and Hispanics, Blacks and Whites, Asians and Hispanics, and so on. But it isnt so, at least not in the simplistic, feel good angle that [I]Crash[/I] takes. 

OK so Haggis isnt honestly recording what Los Angeles is actually like, so what? Well that might be forgivable if the material seemed believable, or if it even rose somehow above the aforementioned mistakes in the film. It clearly doesnt. And Id expect much better from Haggis considering that he wrote 2004s Best Picture winner, [I]Million Dollar Baby[/I], a film that absolutely blew me away with its insights into the human character. [I]Crash[/I], unfortunately is relentlessly superficial and plays more like an aimless urban opera than a compelling drama.

[IMG]http://www.weekinrewind.com/images/Crash.jpg[/IMG]

Don Cheadle, an actor of talent so immense that I would watch him in any given venue, speaks the first words in the film. The chimerical premise of his thoughts on car crashes in LA (we miss the that touch so much, that we crash into each other just to feel something) is a good indicator of things to come. For the next one hundred and ten minutes nothing improves; people behave not like human beings, but like written characters. Sometimes the dialogue is so self-aware that it reaches the point of laughable (any conversation involving Ludacriss character is a great example). 

Some of the performances here are excellent, mostly Cheadle, Matt Dillion, and Terrence Howard. The rest arent as noteworthy, as the actors are crushed by the over seriousness of their lines. Take for example Sandra Bullock, who received some accolades for her performance as the traumatized wife of the DA. Really she doesnt deserve any praise, her acting here is cheap and like most of the movie, way over the top. She isnt believable, likeable, or really even vital to the story. So why is she there?

Bobby Moresco, a producer and a co-writer of the script, has said that they fought their own fears over defying the rules on political correctness and decided to make it as ugly as necessary in parts. He could not be more wrong. The moments in [I]Crash[/I] that actually work are not the moments where individuals from different races hurl insults at each other like baseballs, but where the film takes a step back. The scene where a black tv producer played by Terrence Howard is advised that one of the actors is sounding less black (racist code speak for smarter) is quieter and more introspective than the rest of the film. If more of [I]Crash[/I] was like it, the movie as a whole would be resoundingly effective. Instead we get too much ugliness, not enough insight. And even worse, the creators seem to be of the opinion that we arent smart enough to comprehend their message if they dont make it very clear. It is one thing to have everything spelled out for you in a film. Its another thing to be beaten over the head with a brick for almost two hours.

Many are now calling [I]Crash[/I] the worst film to win the Best Picture prize in the entire history of the Academy. I dont disagree. And while I usually dont concur with the Academys choices in that category, I generally dont detest the movie that wins. Heres an exception. And for the record there were several films that were worse last year ([I]Dirty Love, Dukes of Hazzard[/I], and [I]Aeon Flux[/I] all spring to mind) but the difference is none were celebrated at any awards shows (except maybe for the Golden Raspberrries). More importantly there were several films released last year that were far better. [I]Brokeback Mountain[/I] (which is simply one of the best films I have ever seen), [I]A History Of Violence[/I], [I]The Constant Gardener[/I], [I]Syriana[/I], [I]King Kong[/I] (none of those last four films were even nominated), [I]Walk the Line[/I], and [I]Capote[/I] were all far superior films in ever sense of the word. Yet the Academy embraced the film that mercilessly threw them around in a dishonest and rambling mess. They should all be embarrassed. 

Years from now, if remembered at all, [I]Crash[/I] will be thought of as the Oscars second greatest shame (the first is obvious: its continuing failure to award the greatest living American director, Martin Scorcesse). This is an overly theatrical thriller and a colossal mess with a misguided message. [I]Crash[/I] says nothing, but insists on declaring it loudly and ineloquently, what could be worse?  

Grade: [B]C-[/B]

How this film won it's Oscars is beyond me. Crash is a tale of racism and karma in the everyday life of everyday people and gives insight into how strangers can affect the path of a person and their demeanor in general. Crash is an ensemble piece and this factor works enormously in it's favour, it never pushes any single character further ahead than any others, instead giving equal weight to the cast. However, Matt Dillon and Terrence Howard prove to be the true standouts in this proportioned picture as they each give their roles the layers and depth that ultimately resonate further into the audience than any of the corresponding stories or characters. And, it is through this scripted tale of corresponding stories, that we feel for and connect with each of the characters on quite an intimate level; but this is also achieved through some fine camerawork and editing. However, as good as the script's movement and film's pacing may be, it ultimately is a good example of how shoddy dialogue can ruin a movie, shown especially through the cringe-worthy scenes of Bullock and Ludacris, who serve the racial tension of this film on a silver platter. And it is this ease of thought, where the film never provokes any further intellectual response  from the viewer, that ends up dragging this film far down. This is a film that begins very, very badly with horrid speech and simplistic overtones, but eventually works into quite the moving tapestry; we could only wish though that Haggis knew the definition of subtle.

[font=Times New Roman][size=3][color=#000000]Crash is, if nothing else, a triumph of editing. Weaving a dozen storylines and a giant ensemble cast together over the course of 36 hours in Los Angeles, the movie grows increasingly powerful as you watch the stories intersect and crash together. The frustrating part comes from my personal annoyance at having 30% of the words in a movie be the F bomb. I ranted on this in my Negotiator review if you really want to hear me go. For me, to have stunningly insightful passages of dialogue collide with characters just shout the F word at each other for 30 seconds is jarring. It took me out of the movie. Its insulting to my intelligence, and I hate when filmmakers do it. Its actually a credit to how well everything comes together because this movie was cruising on a 5 or a 6 with me for the first hour. I have now seen two of Paul Haggis's movies and have thoroughly been captivated by each film. The first is Million Dollar Baby (which he only wrote) and the second is Crash, the movie I'm reviewing. I liked Crash more. I didn't enjoy it more, but Crash was a better movie. Either way, he has two Best Pictures under his belt and Flag of our Fathers is looking pretty sweet, too. But onto the film...

I love LA. I love UCLA, I love Hollywood, I want to be in LA for the rest of my life. Crash shows the fuglier side of Los Angeles. And that's where the strengths are in the movie - the ability to show the sides of people. That's what I got most out of the movie; the fact that there is no such thing as only bad people and only good people. In the film, for every life a character ruined or even ended, that character saved another life. Maybe I totally missed the message, but that's what I got out of the movie along with a few deeper thoughts that would be too hard to type out.

The movie is very performance driven. It has an ensemble cast which includes Don Cheadle (good as always), Matt Dillon (solid performance), Terence Howard (very very good), Thandie Newton (awesome job), Sandra Bullock (blah), Ludacris (his character was annoying, but he suprised the hell out of me), Larenz Tate (not great, but good), Ryan Phillippe (awesome, as always), Michael Pena (best performance of the movie), Brendan Fraser (dead-weight, but still okay), and Jennifer Esposito (nice tits, okay acting). The movie doesn't have a single bad performance, and this makes the movie as good as it is.

Not to mention Crash is visually stunning. The settings are very real. It's not the glitz and glamour LA, it's the gritty and mean LA. The movie only cost 6.5 million, but it looked like a huge budget movie. The screen is filled up with breathtaking cinematography. Paul Haggis knows this shit.

In conclusion, Crash is a very strong movie. Despite a slow start, the movie is a very powerful, very thought-provoking film.

Years later, I still can't get over the fact that this drivel won the Best Picture Oscar over Brokeback Mountain. If I could give a film zero stars, I would here. And no, that's not just because of the Oscar controversy. I remember coming out of the theatre long before awards season feeling like I'd just been slapped in the face.

The acting is decent, I'll give it that much (I guess the half-star has to count for something). But any actor can be great if you give them such simplistic, wrenching material as this. The characters are horribly underwritten, each one only gets one or two scenes to shine. None of the storylines are connected in any way, except by the very loose racism theme, and most of the time it can't even broach that subject with any intelligence. They are all overwrought, and they hit you over the head again and again with the preachy "message" it's trying to deliver. Once would have been plenty!

Then it's all strung together with cheap, hyped up TV-style editing. With Paul Haggis background in television writing, it doesn't surprise me that the dialogue in this film is also very pedestrian and obvious. This could have been a half decent movie of the week at best, but it certainly doesn't sit in the same league as Brokeback Mountain, or any of the nominated (or even the not nominated) 2005 cinematic gems.

[font=Comic Sans MS]OK let's start off by dispelling the misconception that [i]Syriana[/i] is an action movie. Yes the trailers showed off explosions and high tension sequences and all that, but in reality those scenes take up about 1% of the movie. The remaning 99% is bogged down by convoluted storytelling riddled with characters that we never quite get to know and care about the way we should.

When two oil companies in America planm to merge to become a massive force in the industry, it sets in motion a series of events that links corruption from the board room of one of the companies to Washington, D.C. all the way up to Middle Eastern royalty. The problem is the story gets so wrapped up in its own exposition and whatnot that you can hardly remember who's who and what each character's objective is. The reason I compare it to [i]Crash[/i] is because both films use the concept of interweaving different subplots and the characters therein until all the different stories become one. What makes [i]Crash[/i] better is the fact that all the stories really do come to a head and there's enough action to compliment the phenomenal performances that it's very difficult to lose focus. [i]Syriana[/i] never quite brings everything together and the lack of substantial action makes it much more difficult to watch and appreciate.

This is not to say that [i]Syriana[/i] is a complete waste. The acting is stellar virtually across the board. George Clooney is very much deserving of his Oscar, and Matt Damon as the analyst-turned-fianancial adviser to Prince Nasir (Alexander Siddig) is stunning. Furthermore the message of the film comes through just enough to make viewers appreciate the effort. The story just kept this one from being a truly phenomenal film.

The initial dark qualities that surrounded the opening 30 minutes of this film made me wonder whether I wanted to continue watching it. But I did. And I'm glad I did. 

The story is about an interlinking section of lives between people of varying ethnicity, working backgrounds, and class and how one little event can effect the lives of those they've never met. 

Racism rears its ugly head early and often in the film, and does so in the bright light of day. Nothing is hidden or candy-coated for the audience. And all of the characters have depth and emotion and love and hate and fear and hope balled up inside themselves. 

A cop, who cares for his ailing and aging father in a very loving way, is also a bigot and uses his power as a policeman to exact revenge on those (i.e. African Americans) he sees as causing many of his and his father's problems. 

A district attorney who gets his SUV car-jacked one night, tries not to stereotype those black men who stole it, but also has to deal with what "the black vote" will think when this news comes out. He also has to handle the sudden panicky fear his wife feels toward any minorities they meet (including their long-time, hispanic housekeeper). 

A hispanic man who installs locks for a living must deal with the prejudices people feel toward him because of some gang tatoos that peek out from underneath his clothing. But he's also a loving father with a little girl at home who fears that something bad will happen to her; they used to live in a very tough neighborhood where gunshots were a common sound. The scenes with this father and daughter never ceased to grip me, especially when some of the girl's fears appear to be coming true. 

A Persian immigrant who owns a store must fight to understand and to be understood in a land where he feels hatred at every corner because of the Sept. 11th attacks. And he responds in kind by buying a gun to protect his store's property, much to the dismay of his wife and daughter. 

...And the list of characters go on, each event folding over and effecting the others. It's an awesome spectacle to behold, and the end is like a piece of interpretive art. There's no definitive message to hang on to other than that we're humans, flawed and greatness in equal quantities. 

The all-star cast was also pretty impressive: Sandra Bullock, Brendan Frazier, Don Cheadle, Matt Dillon, Daniel Dae Kim, etc. 

I've read some other reviews here that comment on the "sterotyping" of the racist characters. But that is completely and utterly untrue. The fact that the characters often knew the stereotypes surrounding them, and commented on these, helped bring the screenplay to an entirely different level. And if, as a viewer, you felt offended by the film, you might want to ask yourself why that is. 

Although the film uses race to deliver the message of hate, fear, and shallowness, the ending is surprisingly up-beat as some (but not all) of these great characters grow internally.
