Crash felt like a bad 80's after-school special on racism. The character study relied on and believed so much in its own conception of racism that characters did not in fact develop or grow. The dishonesty of the script is grounded in the fact that each persona was chained down by the theme of the movie, which almost seems to want to tell us that we are all racist, even if and when we don't think so. The character motivation is spelled out in infantile and preachy gestures of race relations, seeming to have been set up to appeal to the minds of junior high students. The reality of racism is mocked by the utter failure to represent race relations in an honest light. The film seems almost to perpetuate racial stereotypes by writing its characters into those social constructs. The racist L.A. cop. The sell-out black producer. The police chief who got where he was by ignoring racism. The hardworking ex-gang-member Latino. The middle eastern small business man. The white politician afraid of losing the black vote. The young black thugs waxing fancy on their roles in society. These cliches are trying to help us realize how racist we are? Or, is Crash more racist than its audience and the streets of L.A.?

A plot so contrived in its nature that it denies us suspension of disbelief. Characters who are more cliche, corny, and liberal mind soothing than real. No amazing direction. A waste of an ensemble cast. An insultingly preachy message. The attempted, yet awfully predictable, "Oh My Gosh" moments in which Characters, so underdeveloped and overwritten, deny their own supposed nature. The white racist cop saves the black woman he molested! Oh my! The goody goody do-right cop reacts in racist fear! Oh my word!

The truth behind the subtle nature of racism disappears. No real or useful commentary of social construct emerges in the end. The film-makers want to guilt trip us and appeal to our emotional ignorance and insecurity to make a successful impact. They're hacks.

And to pretend that this is revolutionary or mind-opening, or brave is ridiculous. If it was any of these things, it clearly would have never won best picture.

Crash strikes me as a movie devised purely as an Oscar-nabbing vehicle. I found the constant onslaught of racist outbursts and histrionics from the various characters just too over-the-top. Having never been to L.A., I can't comment on whether this is an accurate depiction of everyday tension there, however I simply found the situations that director Paul Haggis has concocted overly contrived, tiresome and improbable. Subtle he ain't, and that appears to be his intention. 

The intersecting characters/story-lines approach has been done before, and in far-superior films, most notably Robert Altman's "Shortcuts". I found two scenes in particular utterly ruined this movie: First, the coincidental nick-of-time arrival of scum-bag cop Matt Dillon to gallantly rescue Thandie Newton, was beyond "clumsy plot device" status. It's as if Haggis has taken a cocktail party conversation far too literally: "Yes, that Matt Dillon character may be a corrupt racist, but given the chance, he wouldn't hesitate to risk his own life to pull a woman from a burning car". Gosh, wasn't it awfully convenient that there was such a burning car (which happened to have Thandie Newton in it) the very next day to prove this? I felt truly embarrassed for Haggis by this scene. Are we supposed to understand that this is an allegory, is too fantastic to actually occur, and that this is Haggis' ham-fisted way of making a point about people's duality?

The other high cringe factor scene is Terrence Howard as the successful television director who gets pushed too far, and winds up in a stand-off with LA cops. OK, so he's had a frightening and humiliating episode. This is presumably enough to push him over the edge and go from level-headed TV professional one day, to suicidal, gun-brandishing desperado the next? Sorry, I don't buy it. (Terrence Howard is great in other films, such as Hustle and Flow). 

To be fair, I think Haggis' subject matter is crucial and definitely requires examination. His intent (other than Oscar-related) is noble; however his sledge-hammer execution is inept and wholly unsatisfying. In the end, I found myself cringing twice - once after sitting through this movie, and again when it won the best picture Oscar.

[color=black][color=#d1d168][font=Tahoma][color=darkorange]With our wedding and moving lately I haven't had much chance to write reviews or watch many flicks. I now have a few moments so I'll write a bit on what I've watched in the past little while.[/color][/font][/color][/color]
 
[color=black][color=black][b][color=#d1d168][font=Tahoma]Spirited Away[/font][/color][/b][color=#d1d168][font=Tahoma] is another Miyazaki animated film with more wonderment and imagination than anything Ive seen since, well, the last Miyazaki film I watched. This ones got more story to it than the last one (Howls Moving Castle) and makes more sense. Its has an Alice in Wonderland feel as its about a little girl who wanders into a surreal alternate universe where she must learn to fend for herself without any parental guidance. I watched this a while ago so its hard to remember specific examples of what I liked about it but was very thorough and detail oriented where little facets added up to an amazing whole. Visually stunning but sometimes overwhelming.[/font][/color][/color][/color]
 
[color=black][b][color=#d1d168][font=Tahoma][color=silver]Elizabethtown[/color][/font][/color][/b][color=#d1d168][font=Tahoma][color=silver]. Milusha and I watched this last night and its confounding. I didnt realize that it was a Cameron Crowe film until the credits rolled. Its one of those films where the ingredients just dont add up to a whole. You watch an Altman film and its about individual characters going on with their individual lives and they intersect with each other at opportune moments to create drama or comedy or whatever. I think this film tried to do this but it didnt really go anywhere or make any logical sense. It feels like an essay where you think you understand the point theyre trying to make but the supporting arguments are pretty weak. There were some good moments here and there but the screenplay was very forced and hard to comprehend; in terms of dialogue and plot direction. Kirsten Dunsts Southern accent was like a magic trick, it kept disappearing and reappearing.[/color] [/font][/color][/color]
 
[color=#d1d168][font=Tahoma][color=yellowgreen]We also finally saw [b]Crash[/b], the film everyone was talking about last year. Don Cheadles monologue at the beginning of the film mirrors David Cronenberg/J.G. Ballards film (also called Crash) so Im, again, slightly confused. He says that people run into one another to feel something again because our society has become so distant and impersonal. This is basically the entire thesis for Cronenbergs erotic thriller but he uses sex as the ultimate in car crash connections whereas this ones a vehicle (vehicle, crash, get it? ha, ha Im so witty!) to live out our inherent racist tendencies. This being an American film makes this a different viewing experience as a Canadian. If this is truly representative then I think Canadians are more progressive with our racial cohabitation than Americans are. I found it a bit overly blunt, somewhat simplistic and gloomier than it needed to be. It seems to follow this formula most of the time 1.) set up a nice, happy immigrant or differently cultured/coloured family situation, 2.) ensure audience knows they are NOT a racial stereotype and 3.) the family ends up being the victim of racial stereotyping or must act out in a racial stereotypical manner because society has forced them into it. I dont want you to think I didnt like the film as it has some good things to say and has the guts to try and give us the many faces (and languages) of racism, especially those we dont always realize were using. Yes I believe some small part of us will always have a profile in our heads as this is unfortunately very human to do but I think the film centered on nothing but the negative and everyone had melodramatic racial faults. Where were the redemptions? Moments leading us into redemption fell completely flat. Where were the ones trying to end the circle of prejudice? Despite the fact that so many of us posses biases it doesnt mean we never think about them or try to right this wrong thinking. I guess the film wants us to know that it will just continue and stay the same and racism will persist as long as people live together and cant understand each others accents. I dont have a problem with this line of thinking, per se, as I dont reserve much hope for racism stopping anytime soon either, I just think a character or two living comfortably within the reality of multi-centralism would have been pertinent.[/color][/font][/color]

Wealth/Poverty?  Power/Submission?  Were these themes not noticed by anyone else?  Perhaps the most profound theme of all was that of hope and progress.  Even Roger Ebert agrees:

It's urban Los Angeles where seemingly unrelated lives collide during the course of a two-day period. An array of stars portray individuals whose diverse lives meet at the intersections of coincidence, fear, racism, drug abuse, loneliness, violence, and death. 
 
I have never seen a stronger Sandra Bullock performance; albeit a brief one, her role as the angry wife of a DA is an indication that she needs and deserves a good movie to showcase her real talent. Don Cheadle, Thandie Newton, Matt Dillon, and Terrance Howard also play memorable roles that strengthen this excellent film.
 
We see only cameos of each of their lives, but in these brief slices of life, we recognize the complexity of emotions and the contradictions that define human existence. It is an existence that blurs the lines between good and bad, insensitivity and compassion, anger and regret, and innocence and the loss of innocence; we watch the survivors stumble forward to gain some measure of self-realization, appreciation for the plight of others, and an awareness that very little in this world can be interpreted in simple black and white. 
 
One of the most graphic illustrations of the complicated and unexpected intersection of lives is that between a racist police officer and the wife of a television director. A day after Matt Dillon runs his hands between Thandie Newton's legs during a humiliating, abusive, and racist body search (with her husband watching helplessly), he pulls her from a car that has crashed and is ready to explode, saving her life. Even in the midst of her hatred of him, she recognizes that he has saved her; for the viewer, his doing the right thing to perform a heroic act can be added to our own appreciation of his compassion for his ill and aging father.

The officer's good action does not diminish the bad but it certainly demonstrates the difficulty in judging anyone stereotypically. There are other illustrations of how the lines between good and bad are blurred by the complex nature of human beings. In truth, that such blurring is the norm is a point that is made repeatedly in the movie and it feels a bit manipulative; nevertheless, it is a good point and [b][i]Crash[/i][/b] makes it effectively within the context of the everyday lives of these urbanites. 
 
Certainly, the movie is full of numerous forms of racism directed at all kinds of people. If such attitudes truly are so prevalent in our society, then we can expect that the intersections of our lives will result in numerous such crashes. It is artistically satisfying that the movie begins and ends in a collision, an obvious but appropriate metaphor for what we can expect.

Well I sat down to watch the film not knowing what to expect, and I got this rather complicated, but clever and well made film. I was impressed with the effects used in the film; the budget must have been rather high, and I found the directing quite superb! Basically the film follows a few stories of families or individuals living in LA who face life's challenges and try to cope. Filled with quite a bit of profanity; this is not a film for kids, and the detail of how they show LA is rather sickening at times. The film also carries a few messages about racism and how the black people cope with being called black or being targeted for racism. Of course there's a bit of violence but not much, thank god. I think that this film could have benefited from less profanity and more heart, perhaps a better taste in music too. Overall a pretty good movie; well made, the story is well written but with a little less profanity and a little bit of cutting could have made this better. I don't know how the Academy chose this for Best Picture over other great films of 2005, although I will admit it deserved the Oscar WAY more than 'Brokeback Mountain'.

This well intentioned story of intertwining lives in the cultural melting pot that is Los Angeles is an ambitious attempt to explore the grey area outside of political correctness. Nearly all of the characters display racism to various extents but it's done so in a way as to create three dimensional characters without demonization. It's sensitively directed and well played by all concerned with Terrence Howard in particular bringing depth to his black studio exec who suffers humiliation at the hands of the LAPD. Paul Haggis cut his teeth on TV comedy drama and it is very apparent here; the unlikely series of coincidences that unites the characters seems overly contrived and there is one too many of the kind of pop music montages that are the hallmark of lightweight American TV drama. It is well meaning and nicely executed but the need Haggis shows to tie all of the themes up in a nice big bow for the audience seems just a little patronizing.

Take the pop-cultured infused socio-political discourse of a  Spike Lee movie, the glossy grit of a Michael Mann LA crime story, and the compelling mosaic story-telling technique of a Paul Thomas Anderson film, and you'll get the "feel" for Paul Haggis' stunning directorial debut. To boil a film like "Crash" down to such terms, however, would do it severe injustice. Powerful and thought provoking, this is the most accomplished and compelling film since "21 Grams" premiered back at the end of 2003.

"Crash" brilliantly shows through intertwining vignettes, that are often blazingly funny in their brutal honesty and fascinatingly gut-wrenching in their melodrama, how subtle racism (often guised in nervous humor) and overt prejudice (often exasperated by sudden irrational violence and an overabundance of readily available firearms) completely permeate our culture and everyday interactions within society. A hyper intelligent script showcases not characters, but brilliant representations of real people, people we know and pass in the street every day, people not unlike us. People who at first seem to be lost causes in the war against racism (witnessed in Matt Dillon's harried beat cop and Sandra Bulluck's spoiled District Attorney's wife) can often become the most unlikely solutions to the problem, while people who ride in on their high horse (witnessed in Ryan Phillipe's noble young police officer) can turn against the tide in the blink of an eye. No one is immune to it no matter how hard they try to rise above it (witnessed in Don Cheadle's quietly tragic detective).

In the end, everyone is flawed, the racism is inescapable, and the audience feels a twinge of sympathy for just about everyone. Perhaps that is what Haggis is hinting at to be our answer. Showing empathy and being able to relate even on the most remote level to every human being out there is the first step to that true brotherhood of man. Because the film offers no real solution, the discussion and discourse it creates in the minds of the viewers is the first step in solving society's ills. We can't tackle everything at once, but we can open a dialogue, and hopefully, one person conversing with another will be the first step to our salvation. It takes a bold film to raise such questions, and an even greater one to compel an audience to talk about the potential answers, and that is exactly what "Crash" accomplishes.

Yendo al grano, "Crash" de Paul Haggis, es un film decepcionante y manipulador que trata ineficazmente de pintar el estado de las relaciones raciales entre los residentes de los Estados Unidos. Haggis, quien sin ninguna duda pasará a la historia del cine por haber escrito uno de los mejores guiones de la historia con "Million Dollar Baby", lamentablemente falla al sentarse en la silla como director, y en Crash su trabajo está más en línea con el efectismo de su creación televisiva "Walker, Texas Ranger", que la excelente cadencia de la obra de Clint Eastwood.


"Crash", parece una película bien intencionada, pero peca de ignorante y sensacionalista, sacrificando el verdadero estado de la unión, en pos de una visión que cuando menos pretende ser desatinadamente didáctica.

En el film una retahíla de actores de segunda mano, interactúan en un Los Angeles nocturno y triste, a través de situaciones que Haggis entremezcla a duras penas sin ninguna credibilidad. La razón, "Crash" está lejos de ser original, y parece estar coreografiada sobre el plano de "Short Cuts" de Robert Altman o "Magnolia" de Paul Thomas Anderson. Especialmente esta última  con la cual comparte un final que raya en el plagio. En "Magnolia", Anderson termina el film con una inexplicable lluvia de ranas, su visión bíblica de un clímax cinematográfico (en realidad un homenaje al final sísmico de "Short Cuts"). En "Crash", nieva en Los Angeles pocos minutos antes de rodar los créditos con una música de fondo demasiado similar al excelente soundtrack de Aimme Mann en "Magnolia".

Pero el problema no está en las influencias de Haggis. Es difícil mencionar un film que de una u otra manera no haya sido influido por otro que le precedió. Pero donde algunos directores como Anderson, reinventan y personalizan premisas, Haggis toma el camino fácil de copiar y pegar. El resultado es un film diferente pero sin alma, novedoso solo para aquellos que desconocen sus orígenes.

En el proceso, se pierde todo lo que caracteriza el film de ensamble a la Robert Altman, donde la historia gira alrededor de personajes bien definidos, no al revés como en "Crash", donde con excepción del personaje de Don Cheadle (y ni siquiera), los protagonistas son meros esbozos de verdaderos seres humanos.

Esto debe haber sido obvio para Haggis, quien ni siquiera trata de corregir el rumbo, y en vez de rescribir sus personajes, los presenta como elementos simbólicos y generalizados de la población estadounidense (el árabe, el negro, el latino, los chinos), que como tales son guiados a situaciones extremas representativas de lo que el director presente exponer, creando situaciones incendiarias que en vez de ser aleccionadoras, se ven falsas y carentes de ningún significado.

Además, donde Altman o Anderson o cualquier otro director de talla se alimentan de la capacidad de los actores que contratan, Haggis parece contenerlos dentro de su guión que deja poco espacio para el histrionismo, luciendo curiosamente aprensivos y desgajados. Soltando diálogos filosóficos y erróneamente ilustrados que no armonizan con lo mundano de los personajes. Esto quizás a lo intrincado del mismo guión que gasta demasiado tiempo en paneos dramáticos ineficientes e innecesarios, que se comen el espacio que Haggis debió utilizar para describir a sus personajes.

Lo cual inexplicablemente es uno de los más elogiados logros del filme. Cada protagonista en "Crash" apenas tiene tiempo para proyectarse, sin embargo, sus actores han conseguido nominaciones para cuanto festival existe en la tierra incluyendo una inmerecida nominación al oscar para Matt Dillon.
En cuanto a la versión en DVD, el filme no nos presenta nada nuevo, aunque nos revela inconscientemente el origen de los fallos fundamentales de "Crash".

"Crash" no es una comedia, y tampoco es particularmente entretenida. Sin embargo durante el video clip de cómo se hizo el film, los productores, incluyendo Haggis y Cheadle, insisten en como ellos querían enviar un mensaje a través de situaciones hilarantes. ¿Hilarantes?

Cheadle, que trabajó para Paul Thomas Anderson en "Boggie Nights", insiste en esto como si estuviera hablando de otro film y quizás lo está haciendo. El que el pretendió emular y no salió.

Y es que "Crash", con todo su discurso sobre racismo, se nos presenta demasiado racista en si misma. En los comentarios del DVD Haggis afirma que lo que él quiso exponer fue la forma en que la gente piensa de verdad. Pero "Crash" no fue escrita ni por árabes, ni por latinos ni por negros, sino por dos hombres blancos basados en lo que ellos creen piensan los demás, exponiendo sentimientos encontrados que incluso se cuelan en el casting.

La amante y compañera de Cheadle, una oficial portorriqueña/salvadoreña, en vez de ser actuada por una latina, es presentado como el mito femenino hispano típico del hombre anglosajón, una mujer exuberante y exótica como Jennifer Esposito.

Cuando más, Crash es un experimento negligente que puede servir de trampolín a guiones con mayor profundidad y menos petulancia que indague sobre las tensiones sociales en los Estados Unidos sin terminar siendo un regalo para audiencias en búsqueda de opciones "interesantes" y "cultas" que al final suelen ser meras telenovelas de alto presupuesto.

Canadian director-writer Paul Haggis (he was behind the screenplay for Million Dollar Baby and Casino Royale) is in Altman/Paul Thomas Anderson territory in this ensemble piece that scooped the Best Picture Oscar in 2006. Ensemble pieces often polarise opinion so I was not overly surprised to find a lot of spleen-venting over Crash being awarded the top prize although I understand that it's the first Best Picture winner since Rocky in 1976 with only three Oscars in total (most secure four or more). That said it's received another 56 nominations and 38 wins, so the Oscar glory was hardly an aberration. An ambitious piece, that this movie cost just $6 million to make and went on to wow the Academy is incredible. To put it into Hollywood perspective, that was Sandra Bullock's take home pay for A Time to Kill, or double what she got for the execrable Speed 2. After reading the script, Bullock was so eager to participate that she paid for her own flight to LA. Thandie Newton won the Best Supporting Actress BAFTA for her role, and while it rivals Dame Dench's Shakespeare in Love award in terms of brevity hers is a pivotal part of the arc of Matt Dillon's racist cop role. Any movie that opens up a debate on how individuals view themselves and others is a worthwhile exercise and many of this film's naysayers appear to have got the words worthwhile and worthy mixed up. This is a movie where prejudices are shattered and incredible coincidences occur. Chance meetings and confrontations send characters on tangents that defy predictability and it's refreshing to see a movie not tied by the bounds of political correctness portraying the often terrible truth of how human beings treat one another. With this and Million Dollar Baby back to back Best Picture winners (the failure of the nominated Letters from Iwo Jima broke this run) his career's come over all Highland Games with Haggis firmly in the ascendent. And seeing Matt Dillon in a police uniform reminds you of the Fairytale of New York video.

Sounds complicated? It should be, but director Paul Haggis has brilliantly made the film so everything falls into place simply and perfectly.
'Crash' boasts a great cast including Don Cheadle, Sandra Bullock, Matt Dillon, Thandie Newton and Brendon Fraiser.

Other than the Sandra Bullock/Brendan Fraser storyline (which didn't really go anywhere), this is basically a perfect movie. Most impressive to me were Don Cheadle, Thandie Newton and Michael Peña, though this film features a great ensemble performance. Some scenes will bring you to tears, others will leave you shaking, and one made me howl with (highly inappropriate!) laughter. These are all reactions that it's the film's goal to provoke as it asks the characters (and the viewer) to confront their prejudices. And sadly, for this (expertly plotted) group of (loosely) connected characters, this is all in a day's work in contemporary Los Angeles. People say that Robert Altman's Nashville did this first, and did it better. I'll watch that one and see. The reason why I didn't like this film is because it is condescending, dishonest, and it lacks subtlety.

The condescending argument has a lot to do with the way the film spells out complex situations. The film is too verbose for its own good in that it explains everything to a point where it is almost didactic. The beginning monologue with Detective Graham sums up the entire movie, therefore not really allowing the audience to come up with their own conclusions. The same goes for Anthony's monoloque and how he verbalizes the atrocities of racism towards blacks. Instead of hinting the audience to evaluate the situations, Haggis is insistent on telling us how to feel and think. 

Crash is unrealistic because everything about it is so formulaic. Everyone has a complete 180 as if to prove a point. Haggis suspends reality for the sake of proving a point which in my opinion is a very poor decision. In the world of Crash, everything falls in place so perfectly so that Haggis can teach us all lessons about racism. People argue that coincidences happen but everything felt so forced and planned out. Instead of dealing with everyday situations that occur, Haggis decides to use his sock puppets and puts them in the most unlikely of situations just to get a rise out of the audience. So are these "revelations" that the audience feels pertinent to the racism of our own society or to the simulated atrocities in Crash? The fact that Crash isn't an honest depiction of our own society is justification that it doesn't do a good job with handling its subject. 

As for subtlety, instead of mirroring how an average person would react in a racial situation with the utmost reserve and subtlety, Haggis goes in overdrive and delivers an overdramatic punch. If Crash were indeed a recent depiction of our own society, the suspension of reality wouldn't be the right approach because it isn't truthful. The reason why Haggis employs characters from all different races and backgrounds is because they are supposed to reflect us. But with all the exaggerated reactions and unlikely situations, this social commentary fails to deliver a message in which the audience hadn't already known.

When I watched the film Crash (which, if you haven't seen it already, is about the lives of people who are affected by racism in Los Angeles), I realized something. No, it wasn't that everyone is a racist. No, it wasn't that everyone as a stereotype. And no, it wasn't that the film beats you over the head with it's foolishly simple message. Instead, I realized that this film accomplishes ABSOLUTELY NOTHING. Forget about whether this film has any soul or not, because it doesn't. At the end of this film, the audience is no better off than when they first started watching it.

Let's talk about the characters. For one thing, almost every person in this film is a stereotype of popular cultures. Whether it be the racist white cop, the screaming and incoherent Chinese crash victim, the two African-American men who rob people (and I'll get back to that in a second), the police partner with a heart of gold, the Latino man who everyone mistakes for a gangster, the cop who has to sacrifice his ideals to get ahead, or even the fat Italian mechanic, they are ALL shallow and predictable characters. There is absolutely no one in this film I can relate to. Everyone is a shell.

Let's talk about the plot. Here's an example of the story: two African-American men are eating out at a fancy L.A. diner. They complain about how people are treating them unfairly, that they shouldn't be judged based on their skin color, and then they proceed to rob people at gunpoint. Gee, thanks for setting back race relations hundreds of years, guys. And what about the racist cop who molests an African-American woman for no reason, then proceeds to save her life the next day, and realizes the error of his ways. Would you like me to beat the "racism is bad" symbolism into your head some more? How about the cop who is forced to conform to a white person's beliefs to get a promotion at work? Still not enough? And then there's the Persian storekeeper who goes after a person who he supposedly thought robbed his store, and shoots a gun at him in broad daylight? Christ, the plot is so messed up that it's not even funny.

That brings me to another area of the movie: the characters. You tell me, when have you ever seen a white police officer launch into a rant about "you people" to an African-American customer service woman? Or when have you ever heard a policemen talk about black people like they are a nuisance? No one in this film talks like a normal person. It's ALL hackneyed dialogue designed to elicit a response from us, the viewers. Even the character behavior is all out of wack. As I said before, who talks about the mistreatment of their race and then proceeds to act in a stereotypical representation of their culture? Who decides to go out in broad daylight to shoot a man in front of many witnesses, and how do you not realize you were firing blanks? Better yet, why would you practically molest a woman in the middle of a crowded street? And there's even the part where a car chase occurs, and no one even bothers to fill out any paperwork or anything. These characters are all hopeless idiots.

And then there's the ending, where we find out one of the carjackers is suddenly Don Cheadle's brother, despite the fact that we haven't seen anything that proved he was even related to Don Cheadle's character, RYan Phillipe's character shoots a man and leaves the scene of the crime even though he is a police officer, the Persian shopkeeper honestly believing he had been saved by "an angel" when he shot blanks at a defenseless child (he was really shooting blanks, or was he too stupid to realize this?), people talking while a person is singing in the background(???), Chinese illegal immigrants stuck out in the streets, and hey, just for good measure, we find out that the African-American female receptionist is also a racist. Not to mention that it's SNOWING IN LOS ANGELES. Champ job, guys.

This film is a tired, preachy mess that is designed to pander to the lowest common denominator. Don Cheadle says in the beginning of the film that everyone is disconnected. What a load of bull that is. We only have twelve stereotyped characters making stupid decisions and interacting in idiotic ways.

This is the first movie to ever make me cry. Easily one of the best movies to come out in this decade. There are so few films these days that actually try to make a real statement. And even fewer that try and succeed. This is a fantastic movie with very few cons. Among those cons being a few (key word FEW. as in like two) minute-long cheesy moments which really don't hurt the movie too bad. What makes this movie so great is how it makes you think about the society in which you live. We all place stereotypes on people whether its based on how they dress, how they act, or (in this case) what someone's skin color is. The film presents character's which seem to at first like racial stock characters, but as the film progresses, those stereotypes are dismissed, marking the characters who placed those stereotypes on certain characters as being ignorant. The way in which the character's lives are all intermingled into one another's and how some will ultimately crash into others, keeps the viewer intrigued throughout the film. Its hard not to get attached to each and every character as you learn more and more about their stories. I would also like to point out that the cinematography is fantastic. Every angle and every shot brings the film to life and you really can get lost watching it. I freaking love this movie and would recommend it to anyone and everyone.

Like Titanic before it, Best Picture-winning Crash has become a punching bag for movie snobs. While about as subtle as a series of left jabs from Hilary Swank, Paul Haggis's ensemble race drama is a watchable effort with some fine acting and a few truly moving moments.

I think Crash's biggest problem is that it tries too hard, often sacrificing believable dialogue and characters for the clever, preachy and faux-profound varieties. Aside from a few miscasts (Encino Man as the L.A. district attorney?), the actors are able to rise above the overly...scripty script. Thandie Newton and Terrence Howard  give standout performances.

But my favorite characters, the films least clichéd, are the Hispanic locksmith and his daughter. My favorite scene in the film is probably the only one not centered around race: the one in which he comes home late from work and gives her an invincibility cloak that will protect her from the neighborhood gunfire. It's a tender moment amidst the heavyhandedness.

Is there much about Crash that is hard-hitting, bold or over-the-top thought-provoking? In 2005, not really.

But I still liked it.

Crash is the film equivalent of a beauty contestant's plea for world peace. Although not a false claim, it is so reprehensibly simplistic that the claim's sincerity is invalidated. Additionally, the context in which it is being professed undermines the claim and makes it come off as a pandering and manipulative tactic used to exploit the emotions of the gullible. Although this scenario can be likened to "Crash", it is not to say that Paul Haggis does not have honest intentions and doesn't whole-heartedly believe in what his film purports. It is rather that his impassioned views have caused the film to get so caught up in its own rhetoric that it becomes morally and thematically ineffectual. For the most part, the only positive  response this film elicits is a hollow self-approval within viewers who already denounce discrimination. So, instead of offering insight and solutions, Haggis's film merely precipitates moral indignation from most viewers. For those who can see past the ethical smoke and mirrors, they view the film's underdeveloped and naive core, encased by cheap tricks and moral heavy-handedness. To sum up, Haggis's film, although propped by lofty ambitions, merely scratches the surface of complex and nuanced issues and because of its complete failure to really make a real assertion and cause viewers to see racial issues in a different light, it just perpetuates self-righteous voyeurism.

Keep your eye on Paul Haggis as the next great writer/director. His academy award nomination of writing Million Dollar Baby got people?s attention and his emotional thriller, Crash has got me hooked on him. The movie is brilliantly intense and emotional. The characters are fantastic and believable. The acting throughout, starting with Oscar nominee Don Cheadle, all the way through Matt Dillon, whose performance was fantastic, Ryan Philippe and Sandra Bullock was great.  Brendan Fraser was even able to deliver a line well, only one though. The highlight performances came from lesser-known Terrance Howard as Cameron, whose wife is taken advantage of by a police officer during a routine traffic stop. Chris Ludicris Bridges was very good as well. The movie is very powerful and courtesy of its similarities to Magnolia, widely entertaining. The flaw of the film was its opening dialogues. As an audience member, I was a bit overwhelmed with the racism. It was certainly getting the overall point across, but the film did that well without overdoing anything. This and the last coincidental shot that ended the film were the rookie director?s only real mistakes.  This is and will be one of the best films of 2005.

For those of you too young to remember Diff'rent Strokes was a Situation Comedy. Crash is a serious 'Oscar Winng'??!!?? Drama. This film enraged me so much. Self important and preaching dialogue - people don't really talk like this. Over long scenes with music to build tension, but there is nothing tense occuring to warrant the soundtrack. The characters are cliches and stereotpyes, the actors do the best they can, but the script never allows for them to become fully formed emphatic beings. As a result I never felt any emotinal connection with them or cared about their situations. It is not that I lack intelligence or that I do not enjoy films of this genre. I usually do, arthouse drama is my genre of choice. Self important and utterly patronising rubbish. Haggis attempts to objectify the issue of racism in LA but fails miserably bringing a paint-by-numbers arthouse drama with a script worthy of Sesame Street.

More than being a risky venture in terms of box office results for Hollywood producers, perhaps the subject of racism in films isn't very common because it is so difficult to depict in an objective way. Even some of the best features that have seemingly flawlessly executed an anti-racist stance often fail to look at every angle of the problem, either because it clouds the over-riding message or because the filmmaker does not feel comfortable depicting a contrary thread which they cannot relate to as easily, much less represent in an accurate fashion. The new motion picture Crash is a brave stab at the complicated subject of racism, particularly when one considers that all of the characters, to one extent or another, exhibit racist tendencies themselves towards any number of minority or majority groups. It begs the daunting, unshakable question, Can anyone truly claim to be otherwise? And worse, with the world in the dubious shape that it's in right now, can some kinds of prejudicial thinking actually be beneficial under certain conditions? Our kneejerk reaction is to say no, but the film pushes the debate a step further. 

Crash doesn't dare answer any of the myriad questions it raises, but that it dares to ask them in the fair place is certainly to be commended. We are introduced to an ensemble of people who live in downtown Los Angeles. There's Graham Waters (Don Cheadle), a police detective investigating a high-profile case but is sleeping with his female partner (Jennifer Esposito) on the side. Elsewhere in the police department, rookie Officer Hanson (Ryan Philippe) has been paired with a chauvinistic veteran Jack Ryan (Matt Dillon), a cop whose racism gleans a shinier badge than anything the LAPD could have issued for his uniform. When the patrolling officers arbitrarily pull over a young African-American couple (Thandie Newton and Terrence Dashon Howard, in my two favourite performances), Ryan violates the wife in plain view, assuming himself to be above reproach or the law. In another storyline, two African-American youths (Chris "Ludicris" Bridges and Larenz Tate) rob the car belonging to the district attorney (Brenda Fraser), and his wife (Sandra Bullock). As a result, they engage a locksmith of Mexican descent to bolt their front door (Michael Pena). The tattooed locksmith becomes mistrusted by many, including an Iranian small business owner (Shaun Toub), but it turns out he is not the "gangbanger" he is accused of being and is actually a loving husband and father from the suburbs trying to make ends meet. Slowly, the stories begin to overlap and converge, and the results challenge the fundamental assumptions and beliefs of the characters, as well as the audience. 

Strange how so many people in real life spout the expression "things happen for a reason", but when unique coincidences happen to people in the movies, we cry foul and pan the device. Crash's effectiveness really does hinge on a suspension of disbelief in terms of how often the storylines of the characters intersect. However, if you buy into it, then the movie, including its sharp dialogue, gripping situations, and combustible subject matter, works very well. And because writer/director Paul Haggis establishes the identities of the characters so clearly at the onset, when the criss-crossing of story arcs does occur, the result is heightened drama because we are so familiar with the people in this small universe he has created. If Haggis had opted to write new characters into the screenplay in midstream, the result would have been a lot of scenes that aren't nearly as electrically charged as we observe. 

Of note is a specific scene about midway through the film that really stuck with me, where the lives of two characters are at stake, and they must trust each other in the midst of a nearly impossible situation. It's shot with such confidence and precision that it sinks in and resonates. That scene is matched a bit later by another intense scene, and yet another, until the bittersweet conclusion, which shows each of the characters in a montage similar to the interlude-like one in Magnolia. 

It is in these moments that Crash rings the most true. In other parts, when the characters discuss race and prejudice issues among themselves in almost a platonic dialect, the results are a little more mixed. Although Haggis benefits immensely from a seasoned cast, sometimes the blunt debates seem too forced to be effective. Nevertheless, the film takes risks at almost every turn, and what we get is an intelligent, literate, and often affecting exercise in exploring a volatile topic that we take for granted so frequently that it rarely gets the heated, or at least passionate, debate it deserves. Here's a film that's been a long time coming.

I went into this film with high expectations and left wondering...well, wondering why the hell I had such high expectations for it. This heavy-handed film by first-time director Paul Haggis (screenwriter for Million Dollar Baby, creator of WALKER, TEXAS RANGER [that is not a joke]) attempts to shockingly unveil racial issues in modern-day America. Haggis insults his viewers' intelligence by repeatedly beating them over the head with his message, refusing to let them draw any conclusions of their own. The shock of the characters' comments begins to lose its edge once you discover that ALL of the characters in this film are racist...but (and here's the kicker) they're racist in DIFFERENT WAYS. How's that for variety? White people racist against Latinos! GASP! Black people racist against Asians! SAY IT AIN'T SO! Arabs getting called terrorists! SINCE WHEN?! Haggis acts as if we don't know that these issue still exist in this point in time. And on top of that, it almost feels like he knows how weak his script is, as he tries to give the dialogue weight and meaning by assigning big-name, likeable actors to the parts. Sandra Bullock says she doesn't like black people? HOW COULD MISS CONGENIALITY DO THAT?! Despite the stunt acting, the cast does (for the most part) do a great job with what they are given (which is...a god-awful shitstorm of a script). But good acting does not a good movie make (as the f'ed up saying goes), and when the time comes for each of the characters to have their "moment of revelation" where they all turn "nice" (Sandra Bullock momentarily appreciates the company of her hispanic maid! Awwwww! Ludacris decides to NOT keep the Asian slaves pinned up! What a sweetheart!), I found myself crying not tears of sadness, but of laughter. And I think that, in itself, is rather telling.

Something so complex, and deeply ingrained into history, environment, and culture, that simply just taking a step back  and "seeing it from the other's POV" isn't enough.  The root of prejudice cannot be boiled down to  something like, "Oh I've seen that black or white or brown guy commit this crime... or get that job over me... or blah blah."   Crash treats it like its that simple, but honestly, why wouldn't it?   The charachters are archetypes, "the racist cop", "the uncle tom black man" "the self involved rich wife" and racism in this film is treated as just the same.  Gee guys, its really easy!  Its just one big misunderstanding!  Thats ridiculous.  All this movie does is flip stereotypes to make its vapid point.  The cop who's racist... turns out to help the black woman.  The cop who isn't racist... SHOOTS the black man!  The black guys who are educated... ARE stealing the cars!  And so on and so forth blah blah blah blah.  In Do The Right Thing When Spike Lee picks up the trash can and throws it through Sal's window, its not an easy choice.  Its not one he seems to agree or disagree with, what we get is moral ambiguity.  The audience is left to wrestle with the conclusion of that film on their own.  Crash does not realize, or worse,refuses to acknowledge that in reality there is no convenient "flip the problem find your answer" situations.

"We're Losing Touch." That's one of the very first lines spoken in the new great film by Paul Haggis. It is spoken by Don Cheadle's police detective, Graham, after a head injury resulting from a car crash caused by an overly eccentric Chinese lady. He's babbling all this random stuff, but it's not so random. That line is pretty much the whole basis for 'Crash'. We as a society are losing touch of each other. We don't care about each other anymore, and the day and age of chivalry has died in 2005. When we see someone in need or down on their luck we just turn the other way. We aren't involved with each other and we've become so callous and self-absorbed. We are torn apart the the racism, prejudices and differences of each other, that we almost don't even care anymore. 'Crash' takes that idea and spins a handful of interesting and beautifully layered vignettes that take place in the slums of Los Angeles during the course of two days.

The two days the film is set over follows eight different situations all eventually interlocking with each other. The first situation is about two detectives, Graham (Don Cheadle - Hotel Rwanda) and Ria (Jennifer Esposito) investigating the murder of a could-be dirty cop, and Graham helping his heroin-addicted mother find her hoodlum son. The second situation follows two L.A.P.D. police officers, Ryan (Matt Dillon - Drugstore Cowboy) and Hansen (Ryan Phillippe - The Way of the Gun), Ryan struggling with his dying father while Hansen struggles with having Ryan as a partner. The third situation follows a rich black television producer, Cameron (Terence Howard - Hart's War) and his wife, Christine (Thandie Newton - The Truth About Charlie) who try to keep their marriage together after an upsetting run in with two police officers. The fourth situation follows a wealthy and smug D.A., Rick (Brendan Fraser - The Mummy) and his self-centered pedantic wife, Jean (Sandra Bullock - Miss Congeniality) and how they deal with life and the political hardships that follow Rick after he's assaulted and car-jacked by two black street thugs. The fifth situation follows the two black street thugs/car-jackers, Anthony (Chris 'Ludicrous' Bridges - 2 Fast 2 Furious) and Peter (Larenz Tate - Dead Presidents) as they roam the streets of L.A. in the newly stolen SUV. The sixth story follows a lower-class Hispanic locksmith, Daniel (Michael Pena - TV's The Shield), who's trying to make ends meet while supporting his wife and daughter. The seventh story follows a Chinese-American couple in the ghettos of L.A., while the eighth story is centered around Islamic citizens, Farhad (Shaun Toub) the owner of a pawnshop and his emergency room doctor daughter, Dorri (Bahar Soomekh) as they try to get through life without being discriminated against. It's a very complex plot, but that's not an insult, it's actually a compliment. These days, it's good to see a film that actually requires you to think and examine life, then some mindless action lackluster of a film starring Britney Spears or Jennifer Lopez. 'Crash' is a unique opportunity to see a though-provoking and heart-wrenching suspense tale that you can learn a lot from.

'Crash' has some wonderful qualities to it. The acting of the film is spectacular with stand-out performances. Sandra Bullock actually turns in a good performance as the nasty housewife (for the very few screen time she has). Don Cheadle is absolutely brilliant in his role as a conflicted L.A.P.D. police detective, following his startling turn in last year's Oscar contender 'Hotel Rwanda'. Matt Dillon turns in one of the best performances of the film, as the bigoted and emotionally scared police officer, and I can't remember Dillon turning in a finer performance since 1989's 'Drugstore Cowboy'. Jennifer Esposito is good as Cheadle's partner, while Brendan Fraser is kind of so-so as the District Attorney of Los Angeles. For me, he wasn't very believable in that role. Terrence Dashon Howard turns in a very powerful performance, while Ludicrous does an actually all-right job with acting (I was a bit skeptical because he is a rapper, not an actor). Thandie Newton was amazing in perhaps the best acting performance of the entire film, and Ryan Phillippe and Larenz Tate played their roles with staunch authenticity and passion for the craft of acting. The newcomer, Michael Pena (who can be seen every Tuesday as the latest cast member of 'The Shield') does a surprisingly fabulous job, along with Shaun Toub. The film also contains bit parts played by Loretta Devine (Boston Public), Keith David (Barbershop), William Fichtner (Black Hawk Down) and most notably Tony Danza in a thirty second part. Paul Haggis does a phenomenal job writing along with directing. Haggis provides a script so rich and elaborate in that it keeps you deeply focused for the entire runtime of the film. His directing is exquisite and impressive, but not too flashy or pretentious. The only real flaws that are present in 'Crash' are that it is somewhat unbelievable or confusing at times. Like I said, you really have to pay close attention to detail while watching the film. It isn't one of those movies where you can take a trip to the restroom in the middle of it, come back, and ask the person sitting next to you, "What did I miss?". Because in those few minutes you spent in the bathroom, you most likely missed a plot revelation or new set-up. A lot of people will be turned off with how involving 'Crash' is, but for the few who truly appreciate the art of film, it will be like a dream come true. I enjoyed almost everything the picture had to offer, but I couldn't help but feel the ending was a bit inadequate of what the whole film was seemingly heating up for. In conclusion, I highly recommend 'Crash' even though it's ending was rather disappointing. Grade: A-

Pun intended in my title. "Crash" attempts to create a message about the "race" issue that had supposedly occurred because of the backlashes of Sept 11, 2001. 

In its attempt, it focuses on various characters of various nationalities and presents all of them as racist hypocrites who stereotype others or are overly sensitive about everything around them ending up becoming racist.

Where is this movie set in? None other than Los Angeles, a city filled with an extremely racially diverse population.

From here, the character development goes as follows:

It tries to turn an African American gangstah thug (who steals and robs) into some kind of on intellect on the historical and sociological inferences as to the root causes of racism.

It makes a racist cop, who is apparently misunderstood because his father's janitorial company went out of business because of affirmative action money going to minority owned businesses.

It pairs Brandon Fraser as a horribly casted (and paired with Sandra Bullock) District Attorney who looks at everything he does from the point of view of being Politically Correct.

It creates a Persian family and makes white store clerks (in Los Angeles) become overly boastful about anti Arab sentiment.

It takes a cop who is having an affair with a Mexican female who only looks at her from her stereotypes as if matter-of-fact racist "wondering alouds" is still chic and apparently was too focused on sexual relations with her to even realize that she was part Puerto Rican and El Salvadoreno by stereotyping her as Mexican.

and there are other countless examples of this. With all of this fed to us immediately right off the bad, the dialogue become annoyingly pretentious and undermining. As a viewer, I feel as if I am being shallowly preached to about something I already learned from Martin Luther King and in a much more effective manner: racist stereotyping is bad.

The dialogues written must have been by a college freshman who took his first Ethnic Studies course.

90-95% of the dialogue's involved racial tension, when, in myriad interactions in my own personal daily life here in the very diverse San Francisco Bay Area, I can only think of a handful of racially tensions in the past five years, and they were miniscule at that!

Because of this, I really found the story to be exaggerative, unconvincing and unbelieveable. It reminded me of John Singleton's "Higher Justice"; another movie that had no expertise in how races sociologicize. Singleton was brilliant in Boyz in the Hood and Poetic Justice because he focused specifically on the African American's viewpoint, but his knowledge, like the direction in this movie, of the dynamics of how races interact was flawed. Why is it flawed? Because he can only write from an African American's viewpoint.

The only writer that could effectively write a dialogue for a movie involving racial tensions would have to be a consortium of African American, Arabic, Mexican, Caucasian, Chinese, Filipino writers each writing the dialogue for the character's of their nationalities.

That obviously was not done here. And as a result, the movie was a failure despite moments of brilliance.

The beauty of the film was noticeable. It had a somber electricity to it similar to Lost in Translation or Collateral. But beauty is only as good as the sound from the dialogue.

I think the director tried too hard to disturb and did very little do the necessary research in order to dispel his/her naivity to tell a story that would be worth watching.

Because all the characters were rather one-dimensional and unreal, I could not, in the end, take this movie too seriously.

I don't recommend it.

This is today's epitome of 'issue'-filmmaking. It has tokens in place of characters, and its message is simple-minded earnestness masquerading as depth. So on the way to New York, I didn't really have a clue what to do to pass the time. I've got 145 songs on my iPod and enjoy listening to them all, but three hours of music? I like my music plenty, but three hours is just too much. Luckily, my father came to my rescue, and with quite a surprise. He gave me the Netflix envelope of Crash and his laptop and said I could watch. I was shocked, and I asked him if he realized it was Rated R. After triple-checking to make sure that he didn't mind me watching, I gave in and started watching.
 
And I was deeply disappointed. For such a rare opportunity, I do wish I'd been given a better movie to occupy myself with. Crash has high ambitions and a noble enough goal, but it is hopelessly hamhanded and a drag to watch. Racism is a pertinent issue, but the movie just dumps it on. It's like nachos and cheese. Nachos are good with cheese, but you don't [i]smother[/i] them with it. Just a good healthy dip does it. Crash completely missed the ball, and the racism comes across far more strongly than it needs to. There are at least seven different narratives here, and they converge and diverge at the blink of an eye. Each of the people in these stories ends up facing some enormous racially-motivated argument. Crash makes it look like all the world's people hate one another, so strongly is the racism message sent.
 
First off is the problem that there are precious few characters even worth supporting. Racism is just a flaw some people have, but even without it, pretty much all of these people are awful people. Brendan Fraser's wife was especially loathesome; not once in the movie did she even evoke any small bit of sympathy from me. I was halfway toward cheering when she fell down the stairs, since she was just so obnoxious and hateful. Besides her, though, almost all of these people got on my nerves. The Persian father just deeply bothered me (the guy was yelling at the locksmith because he wouldn't fix his door. Locksmiths do locks. They don't do doors. Sound simple? Well, it is. But apparently it's not to this guy.), Cameron's wife was irritating, and the two gangsters were just awful people.
 
While on the subject of the gangsters, though, I think I'll express how I'm getting tired of how filmmakers are trying to underline the fact that ebonics is bizarre. I forgave them in ATL for wondering why they talked the way they did. It wasn't too serious and it was just in good fun. But here, the one gangster was going on and on and on about how the use of the word 'nigga' makes absolutely no sense to him. ATL handled that discussion decently, but this was just ridiculous. There are better ways to denounce slang than this (but even then, why bother? What's so wrong with this particular branch of slang? I don't get it.).
 
The only racism here that was even partially justified was coming from that cop who half-raped Cameron's wife. He complained to this black secretary that his father had lost a lot of money when the city started focusing on the minority. There's not a whole lot of credibility to that, and even if there was, it doesn't really justify hating an entire race, but at least there was an attempt at justification there. The rest of the people were just idiots for the sake of filling roles. 
 
Then comes the final act, where pretty much everyone ends up having to atone for their sins. And this act fails [i]spectacularly [/i]because the characters suffering are all terrible people by and large, and it doesn't affect you at all when they get into accidents or car crashes or whatever. The only person I felt sorry for was the Hispanic guy with the daughter. The bond between the two of them briefly demonstrated earlier in the movie was heartwarming, and when it seemed like the Persian man had shot the little girl, I felt a distinct sense of sadness.
 
That scene ended up being a total copout. In the aforementioned scene, the Hispanic man tells his daughter about an 'invisible cloth' that prevents the wearer from ever being shot or stabbed or mortally wounded. He passes this cloth on to his daughter to make her feel more scure, and she's 'wearing' it when her father is confronted by the Persian man who is irate both about the locksmith not fixing his door and the consequent vandalism of his store. He shoots, and it appears as though the little girl was hit. And apparently she was. But there's no gunwound or any damage done at all. The explanation? Well, the invisible cloth of course! That completely blew me away. The one poignant death scene in the entire movie, and it was just tossed aside. Wow.
 
EDIT: Oh, hold the phone! Apparently the Persian shopkeeper had a box full of blanks. Well that makes it all just the slightest bit better. I know nothing about guns, because the only ones I've ever seen are in movies and TV shows, so I couldn't tell the difference between blanks and real bullets. But...well, this makes up for that scene just a little bit. At least the girl isn't bulletproof as I thought she was. Stories from her father are fine, but in the real world, there is no such thing as a bulletproof cloak. However, that does sort of take away from the scene, now I think of it. If no one's in any danger at all, then the alarm is completely gone. The only gripping part of the scene would be the fact that the daughter actually believes the gun is lethal and that she alone can protect her father. That's sweet of her, but if she's not in any danger in the first place, then...Blegh. Either way, the scene was poorly executed.
 
Also, I am not in favor of this tactic used during the movie's dramatic scenes. This tactic would be "let's take out all dialogue and sound effects and insert some foreign song in instead." This is obviously meant to bring out the [melo]drama of the scene, but it's used far too often because there are far too many dramatic moments. And every last one of them falls flat.
 
So overall, this movie fails in far too many ways to count. The characters you're obviously supposed to sympathize with come off as abrasive jerks. The soundtrack is redundant, and although the music choice is sort of nice, it gets terribly boring after hearing it five times or so. The movie is positively hamhanded and incapable of expressing what a problem racism is in the modern world. I don't care about the R Rating; sex scenes are only a problem when other people around, only absolute prudes even care about language anymore, and violence is absolutely necessary in this sort of movie. 
 
If anything, I'm glad for the R Rating. This way a lot less people will be forced to suffer through this bleak and bothersome movie. Crash has good intentions, but I just couldn't shake the feeling that it was being racist simply for the sake of being racist. The resolution fell completely flat and the message was ruined in a big mess of chaos and injury. I give it a 2, and even that's probably more than it deserves. It's a monumental failure, and I hope someone will come along someday and express the core issue here the way it should be.

Paul Haggis, the writer-director-producer-songwriter of "Crash", also created the Chuck Norris TV series "Walker, Texas Ranger" and the "kindly mountie in America" series "Due South". I mention these to place this film in its appropriate, lowbrow context. "Crash" is the sort of film that rather desperately wants to be edgy and provocative, but never quite earns the plump portentousness that wobbles onto the screen. 

Confusingly sharing a title with the leg-shagging JG Ballard adaptation, "Crash" is a look at racial stereotypes and attitudes in contemporary Los Angeles. Narratively, the film comes from the "more is more" tradition of "Magnolia" and "Love, Actually". Roughly thirty stories (roughly) weave in and out of each other, building up a picture of confusing times in American race relations:- 

Black people are no longer slaves, white people are confused about this. 

Except it's more complicated than this; white people hate black people, black people hate white people, black people hate other black people, white people hate Hispanic and Persian people because they're a bit like black people, Persian people hate locksmiths and insurance representatives, and white people hate themselves. 

So, it's not really that much more complicated. In fact, it's much, much more simple. Everyone hates everybody else. 

The film begins with a rather noble speech by the great Don Cheadle:- "In LA, nobody touches you. We're always behind this metal and glass. I think we miss that touch so much, that we crash into each other, just so we can feel something." LA is obviously meant to be a character in the film, but it comes across as a rather horrible character, a huge uncle that sits in the corner of the room and really depresses you. In this way, "Crash" is an excellent advert for upping sticks and moving to a "free love" hippy commune in the middle of nowhere, where you can just, you know, get along with people. 

In this film, everything is 'complicated', and the film wears its 'complicated' colours with pride. Two young black men have an intelligent discussion about how they represent educated black youth, and how white people in the upper-class area they find themselves in should not be afraid of them, and THEN STEAL A CAR! A rich white woman is openly dismissive of her Hispanic home-help, and THEN SAYS THAT SHE'S THE ONLY FRIEND SHE HAS! A black police officer is offered a promotion BECAUSE HE'S BLACK and then is blackmailed into saying something against some guy BECAUSE THE GUY IS WHITE and if the police officer doesn't say it, HIS BROTHER WILL BE TOTALLY ARRESTED because HE'S BLACK and his MOTHER IS ON DRUGS and HAS NO GROCERIES! This constant pride in being 'complicated' is exceptionally wearing. This is even before we get to the racist white policeman rescuing a black woman he had previously molested from a fire, which could probably have been a fun episode of "Due South". 

Rather than being insightful, the film's fragmented narrative allows some really sloppy writing. Characters are reduced to stereotypes, as they need to be brought in quickly and finished quickly. Stories tend to follow a pattern:- the person is unhappy, they are shot or they shoot somebody, they are more unhappy as a result. The story that resonated most for me was the deeply odd story about the Persian man trying to get his revenge on a locksmith, but that wasn't really about racial tension, it was more about the trials of being a locksmith. Quid pro quo. 

One fortunate thing that the film does is make you not hate its cast. If someone suggested you went to see a film with Ryan Phillipe, Sandra Bullock, Brendan Fraser and Thandie Newton, you'd probably expect a horribly bland comedy, but none of these are given much time to be offensive. Don Cheadle is welcomingly passive, and there's a standout performance by the rapper Ludacris, who has a nice speech about how hip-hop demeans black people. Oooh. Irony. Apparently Tony Danza from "Taxi" and the woman who plays Deanna Troi are also in this film. I have no idea where. 

So, yes. "Crash". I probably enjoyed it more than watching someone shagging a leg, but I enjoyed it less than "The Wedding Crashers", which - considering how important the film wanted to be - is a rather damning state of affairs.

I love this movie. It's interesting how many people I've talked to about this movie have entirely different, sometimes even opposing, perspectives on the characters and their actions.  The movie urges the audience to look at their own prejudices.  People have complained that the movie is too simplistic and obvious in its stereotypes.  While stereotypes may come across strongly, they are realistic, and they serve a key purpose: to play on the audience's own prejudices.  The movie pulls the audience in, creating an environment where they are likely to make judgments of their own on the characters they are watching, many of which will later turn out to be wrong.  I feel that realizing our false judgments and becoming aware of the prejudices we attached to those judgments is a key element of appreciating the value of this movie.

While I agree with the reviews that have given this film an F, I can't give it that low of a rating with a clear conscience. The film is fun to look at, with a clean, TV-esque style. But, what's going on in the film is not clean, not pretty. It has the same stylistic problem Lord Of War had. Magnolia had style, but it was so chaotic that it perfectly mirrored the characters' situations.

Story-wise, Crash has all the subtext of a motorcycle license pamphlet in the DMV lobby. In this universe, someone pouring a bowl of cereal could inexplicably lead to a tirade about how Mexicans are thieves and we should be ashamed of racism. OF COURSE WE SHOULD! Anyone who's going to rent Crash knows that already. I wouldn't even go so far as to say the film is admirable. The film doesn't care about its characters, it just provides a bunch of talking heads to discuss what Paul Haggis wants, then frowns on them or gives them a moment to be sorry.

Hopefully this will not be the template for future ensemble pieces, but I'm afraid it will be positively compared to the superior works of Soderburgh, Altman, and P.T. Anderson.

If I started citing the most memorable performances, I'd start with Terrence Howard, then Matt Dillon, then Thandie Newton, then Ryan Philippe--and I'd end up listing the entire cast. From the muck of racism, I certainly did not expect a fashioning of humanity. I didn't expect to see beauty, certainly not when the movie started. Is racism really like a car crash?  No, stupid.  This film marks the point these interconnected-storyline films (Magnolia, Traffic, Syriana, Babel, Bobby ad nauseum) truly jumped the shark.  Each separate plot reeks of Hollywood feeling rather sorry for itself.  Although the acting is, admittedly, very good, all scenes seem remarkably contrived (including its name, which, apart from being referenced in the first line of the film, has no bearing whatsoever), with some very nonsensical, emotionless, slow-motion (oh dear) finales to each plot strand that just ring incredibly fake.  This ultimately stems from poor direction on the part of Haggis who disappointingly uses very conventional imagery, slow-motion (fool) and tries to find symbolism where there plainly isn't any (like that meaningless Christian doll that the younger brother has).

This, of course, would be excused if the stories were any good (and Haggis' strengths are definitely as a screenwriter - just look at the brilliant Due South) but that doesn't cut it here.  Other than the Ryan Philippe character, who made me reflect once on the dangers of pretending to be morally righteous, there was nothing original in this film.  The story structure was also meaningless, with no satisfying conclusions and no overall message or stance (except maybe that shit happens) - this film stays on the fence to the extreme.  Add to this that Haggis gets his issues mixed up - racism is linked to min-wage labour and inequality, but they are not the same thing.  And at one point he seriously expects us to sympathise with people-traffickers (the Koreans).  Really.  The film suffers from being issue-tastic, not really dealing with any of them successfully or originally.

I think the first thing I need to mention are my preconceptions before first seeing this movie. I do this as I think your view of a movie can be affected by your preconceptions. For example I am sure I do not rate Gladiator as highly as it deserves due to the fact I caught it late on DVD after I had heard and read people raving on about how great it was, I was disappointed at least partially due to my expectations being overly high.

With Crash however although I did not catch it until after it had won the Oscar I was not convinced it was going to be a great movie as I was indifferent about the cast and on reading the cover I could see it looked like one of those movies which would either work or just be an incoherent mess. Besides "Gladiator" and "A Beautiful Mind" had won Oscars in recent years both of which I do not rate that highly! I was slightly worried by the opening scene, it features Cheadle (probably the actor involved I rated highest before seeing this movie) but seemed to contain awkward dialogue, was not particularly visually inspiring and bottom line just failed to grab me. However the scene was just a setup scene out of context as the movie quickly moves into the true first act set a day before within the time line of the story.

The story quickly progresses to show various characters from different walks of life within the city of Los Angeles living through the previous 24 hours. All of the stories involve the subject of racism and all end up being intermingled in the style of previous films such as the brilliant Magnolia.

The script is often funny whilst at other times heart breaking and even though it has the sense of being contrived with the aim of getting an emotional response from its viewers it can be forgiven for this because at the end of the day it does work.

For me a major revelation was Matt Dillon, he is one of those actors I had not seen much of before for whatever reason and he shone for me in a truly first class believable performance.

I won't spoil the plot for those who are yet to see the movie but the road accident scene involving him and Newton is plain awesome and I love the interaction between them in the car and the way although his prejudices are wrong they do not in themselves define him as a bad person - just a messed up one.

The film is not without its critics and many think it is Hollywood dribble with no clear or relevant message. I believe it shows none of us to be without prejudice of some form or another even if this is sometimes hardly a conscious thing.

Ignorant, shrill, hysterical, contrived, and completely over-the-top, this isn't a movie about racism; it's a movie about what people who don't know any better think racism looks like. It's nothing more than a bunch of people ridiculously screaming and yelling at one another. 

The acting is terrible, from Ludacris, whose facial expression doesn't change once; to Sandra Bullock, who comes off as borderline retarded due to the fact that she just wails and waves her arms around in the air in each scene; to Thandie Newton, who shrieks and screeches at such a painfully high pitch that at times I am sure only bats can distinguish her sentences; right down to the inexplicable cameo from Tony Danza. And don't even get me started on Shaniqua, who in the last scene of the film reprimands an East Asian woman for not "speaking American." Did it not occur to anyone that Shaniqua would have grown up during segregation and that her ancestors were shipped to the USA to work as slaves? And yet we are expected to believe that a black woman living in Los Angeles would have the gumption to be prejudice towards someone for not speaking, of all things, what she calls "American"? 

The premise of this film is not that "everyone is slightly racist on the inside," it's that "everyone is a tempermental bigot with a heart of stone except for the Mexican guy." How on earth do people take this movie seriously? It shouldn't be called "Crash" it should be called "Trainwreck." I'm all about movies that abolish prejudice, but a film where Sandra Bullock falls down the staircase and is cured of racism is outrageous. Honestly, did racism itself push her? Is this a joke? What the hell was the Academy thinking?

And what about when that little girl gets shot with a blank bullet while wearing the magic cape? As if that scene wasn't manipulative and just plain stupid enough, did it not occur to anyone that A HUMAN BEING CANNOT GET SHOT WITH A BLANK AND WALK AWAY UNHARMED?!?!?! That little girl would have been injured (unless, of course, that magic cape her dad gave her is real). Just because a bullet doesn't doesn't come out of the gun, a blast of heat due to chemicals and a really hard force of air does. This type of lazy, sloppy, ignorant direction and writing which completely disregards actual human life and gives us a manipulated vision of the world that doesn't really exist is an insult to the human race and should NOT be applauded, let alone win Oscars. And believe me: the instance with the little girl getting shot is just one of many, many examples of Paul Haggis' being a lacklustre, seemingly uneducated, and out-of-touch  writer and director which the film provides for us. 

This film does not deliver its message so much as it pounds it into our faces with a shovel. Crash does not relate to real life at all. People need to understand that just because a Hollywood movie portrays something, it doesn't mean that it's lifelike. I have never seen anything so bombastic, pretentious, and full of itself in all of my life. This is film-making at its very lowest. Words cannot possibly describe how much I hate this movie, but I'll give it half a star for trying.

Crash is a film about lives coming together, being torn apart, failing, succeeding, and how those lives create complex emotions which are often to much to bear.  The film tackles the issue of racism in today?s society, and how little we concern ourselves with how we view others.  Overall, this film is about emotions of the human character, and how we deal with them.

	Films that are based almost solely on acting and storyline have a great possibility of failing miserably, because if one aspect is bad, the whole movie goes down with the ship.  Similarly, if one aspect is superb, or if both are as the case is with Crash, the film succeeds.

	The main difficulty people had with this film from what I can find is that it is far too similar to others that have come before it.  Wait, have I just not seen them?  I?m confused, because never before in my life have I seen a film that takes on the issues of racism and bigotry, and looks at the human emotion with such success as Crash has. 

	The success of this film is all in the acting, because no matter how well written and/or directed a film is, it certainly does not mean the film will be a success.  The ultimate responsibility lies with the actors.  It is also important not to underplay the importance of the casting agency in the analysis of the film as well.  After all, if the parts don?t fit, how can the actors be expected to succeed?

No film, I repeat, no film thus far has ever completely torn me to pieces like this one did. It was just so impacting in so many ways and exceptionally made. Its subject matter is of course highly controversial as it always is when dealing with race. The sheer intolerance of society just appals me and it is highlighted ever so specifically in this film. Handling its issues and messages with intelligence and strength not seen often enough, Crash addresses the issue of racial intolerance head on. One of the things I appreciated the most about this film was its ability to handle its numerous interwoven stories from many points of view. Whilst this can be criticised as simply a western view of racism, I still felt the film held its own and dealt with so many elements of the racial debate with equal integrity. One of it's best features is the way in which is does present the stories with elements of truth. Also in the way there is no holding back here. Every issue, every racist remark, every indecent act, every encounter, is thrown onto the screen one after another, rarely letting up even for a moment. The first half sets each circumstance up, to be broken and addressed in the later half. The concluding minutes are perhaps the most impacting of all, because though many of us may deny being racist on any level, and we do our utmost to prove we are tolerant, truth is, we can utterly shock ourselves. By the film's conclusion, some characters were potentially redeemed, others, torn to pieces. In actual fact, it almost turns on its head in the sense that the characters you would assume to act in a certain way, do not, while those that do surprise you. It just goes to shows how impacting stereotypes are on us. And actually, the way certain stereotypes were dealt with in this film, and in some circumstances broken, prove how unfounded and damaging stereotypes are. This film hit me emotionally again and again and again. I was almost reduced to tears on two occasions. Whilst it was not necessarily easy viewing, I still urge you to see this, for the themes, for the messages, for the awakening it can give you and for the impacting film that it is. It truly was exceptional. It's the sense of touch. In any real city, you walk, you know? You brush past people, people bump into you. In L.A., nobody touches you. We're always behind this metal and glass. I think we miss that touch so much, that we crash into each other, just so we can feel something.
