I think the first thing I need to mention are my preconceptions before first seeing this movie. I do this as I think your view of a movie can be affected by your preconceptions. For example I am sure I do not rate Gladiator as highly as it deserves due to the fact I caught it late on DVD after I had heard and read people raving on about how great it was, I was disappointed at least partially due to my expectations being overly high.

With Crash however although I did not catch it until after it had won the Oscar I was not convinced it was going to be a great movie as I was indifferent about the cast and on reading the cover I could see it looked like one of those movies which would either work or just be an incoherent mess. Besides "Gladiator" and "A Beautiful Mind" had won Oscars in recent years ? both of which I do not rate that highly! I was slightly worried by the opening scene, it features Cheadle (probably the actor involved I rated highest before seeing this movie) but seemed to contain awkward dialogue, was not particularly visually inspiring and bottom line just failed to grab me. However the scene was just a setup scene out of context as the movie quickly moves into the true first act set a day before within the time line of the story.

The story quickly progresses to show various characters from different walks of life within the city of Los Angeles living through the previous 24 hours. All of the stories involve the subject of racism and all end up being intermingled in the style of previous films such as the brilliant Magnolia.

The script is often funny whilst at other times heart breaking and even though it has the sense of being contrived with the aim of getting an emotional response from its viewers it can be forgiven for this because at the end of the day it does work.

For me a major revelation was Matt Dillon, he is one of those actors I had not seen much of before for whatever reason and he shone for me in a truly first class believable performance.

Written and directed by Paul Haggis, this Best Picture-winner (an undeserving upset over Ang Lee's terrific Brokeback Mountain, a much more noteworthy allegory of human discrimination) drowns in its belligerent vanity and does so pitilessly, nearly pulling the well-intentioned genre -- self-romantic as it is here -- to the cooker with it. In its defense (a half-serious attempt at reconciliation for those who have mounted it as a "classic") it took a couple viewings for me to grow repelled by it -- to be honest, I, like most, was initially swept into acceptance of its audacity by its pinnacle moments -- but, even as soon as the opening frames of my first rehash, the musty stench of its arrogance engulfed me and I was again scooped by the product, this time ashamed at its malice and bewildered by its vindictive nature.


Structurally, Crash is a resounding example of unconformity (though its rearranged chronology is an ever-growing theme and its multi-focal yarn is an age-old cliche of priggish cinema, yet not always implemented by films of such). It is likely to become the template by which many subsequent mystery/thrillers are drawn, though that wouldn't be all that bad: it hooks its audience by immediately proposing a problem to which the answer comes together, piece-by-piece, as the story -- which jumps backwards, then proceeds in real-time, ending with its opening scene -- progresses. As we the audience travel alongside the film's event timeline, our attention is maintained thoroughly by its three climaxes, which are evenly distributed within the film's last half. Yet what is unrealized by a majority of viewers is that while their emotions have been forged and manipulated by these peaks, the movie's story -- and more specifically its script (co-penned by Bobby Moresco) -- runs amok in a cesspool of racially-directed propaganda, which is grossly mistaken for morally-motivated and "necessary" exposure to the cultural/ethnic differences that set aside and bring hardship to the diverse citizens of America (or, in this particular case, Los Angeles).


Crash is a textbook example of exploitation, presented with a slew of disgustingly (and abnormally) xenophobic characters, each of whom spit bigoted slurs as if they were the letters of the alphabet. Simply put, when it tries to address intolerance (which occurs with just about every interaction -- an unfortunate truth), it is smothered rather by its own impudence, which appears more political than it does substantial. In fact, Crash is packed so tight full of asinine stereotypes that, if it exploded into a million pieces, its fragments would have enough false piety in them to supply their own feature-length pictures. The film's self-importance swallows all of its positive qualities (which admittedly are not in short supply and include winning efforts by Don Cheadle, Matt Dillon, Terrence Howard, and Michael Pena) and amasses to an indigestible cinematic experience without the uplift of conciliatory sensitivity or social spotlighting, which it almost embarrassingly thinks it embodies (and forever will, thanks to its three Oscars and national acclaim).

I've always gotten into arguments with my friends over what makes a great movie. I know people that will watch a masterpiece like Tarantino's Pulp Fiction or Gilliam's Brazil and say "I don't like it," simply due to some element of the storyline. I walk out of the theater and hear people talking about how this character should have done this or how that character was a jerk, and I want to bang my head against a wall. A movie, I argue, isn't a story; it's a work of art. It doesn't matter that you didn't like the ending of, say, Brazil because 1, you don't get the real meaning behind it and 2, it doesn't matter in the first place if the ending is unpleasant that makes the movie unpleasant, Brazil is a directorial masterpiece, with so much ingenuity and vision that it comes very close to quite litterally blowing the mind. So, with this mindset somewhere in the back of my mind, I start watching Crash. It's got nice, flashy, modern directing, which is something I always like; it's got great acting from all cast members; it's got a weird Fripp-ish soundtrack that helps move things along; and it's got one of the worst scripts I've ever seen turned into a movie. Each character is a stereotype who harbors stereotypes, and at some point realizes the errors of their ways by being saved by the very stereotype they hated so much to begin with. This is more sickenly politically correct than Remember The Titans, which leads to the bigger, more imporant question than anything in the film itself raises: how far can a movie go with a horrible script? To what extent is the script essential for a movie to be great, or even good? Crash has proven to me that a script is more important than I had realized, though a film can survive without it. This movie, despite brilliant filming and whatnot, can't stand on a shallow, show-this-to-junior-high-kids-so-they-learn-to-accept-each-other plot. A group of diverse people living in Los Angeles are interconnected by racial discrimination and prejudice as their lives are traced and affected in dramatic fashion within a 24 hour period.  It's hard to pinpoint one standout performance in the movie since we're dealing with an enriched cast of well known actors with the exception of Ludacris, known more for his work in the music scene but shows his comfort level and credibility as an actor here, playing a carjacker who's convinced the world is out to get black people simply because of the color of their skin.  His carjacking victims are a DA (Fraser) and his racist wife (Bullock).  Don Cheadle plays a detective and Jennifer Esposito is his Hispanic partner.  Another pair in the movie is a black couple played by Thandie Newton and Terrence Howard whose characters get into a tense fight because she felt her husband should've stopped a corrupt racist cop (Dillon) from violating her.  Ryan Phillipe plays the partner of Dillon's cop and struggles with the realities of what being a cop entails.  Michael Pena is a Hispanic locksmith who everyone suspects is a gang member.  "Crash" is one of those movies where just about every character is at fault for something or has done the unforgivable yet there are no villains because there is something good and redeemable about each and every one of them.  This is explored throughout the film, even using coincidences and contrived situations to get that point across and it works wonders, making for some emotionally gut wrenching scenes.  The theme of racism is dealt with honestly and to some extent realistically, showing that although these characters are different in skin color and ethnic background, they all think alike and are more similar than we realize.  The movie allows us to witness two sides of the story; that racism can bring out the bad side in all of us, leading to destructive patterns of behaviour and that underneath it all, we are all given a second chance to make things different and for the better.  More than anything else, the movie shows us that regardless of race, people can share the same fears no matter where they're from.

At the 78th Academy Awards in March 5, 2006, Crash was nominated for six Academy awards. It battled it out with strong contenders like Brokeback Mountain, Good Night and Good Luck, and Memories of a Geisha, and went on to win Best Motion Picture, Best Writing-Original Screenplay, and Best Achievement in Film Editing. 

Premiering in 2004 (in Canada) and released internationally in 2005, from 2005 ? 2007 Crash earned a further 61 nominations and 40 wins at various film awards ceremonies around the world. It was financially successful, with a budget of 6.5 million it went on to gross nearly 55 million at the USA box office.

Written, produced, directed and scored by Paul Haggis it was his debut film. He had been in TV before Crash directing Family Law and Ghost of a Chance amongst others. A recognised talent he went on to write Flags of our Fathers, Letters from Iwo Jima and Casino Royale and has just completed directing In the Valley of Elah and is busy on Honeymoon with Harry.

Crash features an incredible gathering of acting talent, amongst whom were Don Cheadle, Sandra Bullock, Matt Dillon, Jennifer Esposito, Brendan Fraser, and Ryan Phillippe, to name a few. This powerful ensemble cast drove the movie to unexpected heights with profound character performances, which firmly rooted the story in a gritty reality that could not be denied.

Set in the streets and homes of Los Angeles, USA, yet echoing in the familiarity to any large multicultural city, Crash firmly explores contemporary urban society. Leaving no rock unturned, it highlights concurrent themes of urban life through gang violence, car hijackings, sexual assault, robbery, car accidents, discrimination, corruption, and plain pure survival. The uniting theme is the crash of cultures and Haggis takes pains to explore the reigning and arising perceptions in each culture?s viewpoint of each other. His master stroke is the portrayal of the complete uncertainty and unpredictability of real life and experiences; he gives out hope in the ability of people to change in a second no matter their history. All ordinary people in extraordinary situations have the choice to rise to the demand of the occasion and choose the right positive thing to do.

?We crash into each other so we can feel something,? -Don Cheadle as Detective Graham Waters in Crash.

It is also unreasonable to attack the integrity of the screenplay or writing. Many may call the writing contrived, but I suggest you take a look at the movies you enjoy yourself. On the surface, this film is a set of short inter-connecting stories which all have a theme of racism on different levels. In reality, it is a whole lot more.

The film follows the lives of several groups of people living in L.A. and how their lives all link together - whether they are aware of it or not.

I could spend all day here going through each story and explaining how it linked to the others but I still would not get across the whole scope of the movie. Instead, I think the best explanation comes from one of the opening lines of the movie. "It's the sense of touch. In any real city, you walk, you know? You brush past people, people bump into you. In L.A., nobody touches you. We're always behind this metal and glass. I think we miss that touch so much, that we crash into each other, just so we can feel something."

The rest of the movie using these interlocking stories shows how that statement is wrong and how people do touch each others lives, even if only briefly.

No not the Cronenberg movie about the couple getting off on car accidents, this the best picture winner from director Paul Haggis, who co-wrote Million Dollar Baby. In this Crash, the things colliding with one another are racism and it's participants, all in one thirty-six hour time span in Los Angeles. Haggis and co-screenwriter Bobby Moresco present many stories into one massive narrative. For me, there are too many stories presented. Thankfully he has a bevy of gifted actors who make sure the rage stays and has an impact, and lace it all with real emotion. A district attorney (Brendan Fraser) and his wife (Sandra Bullock in one of her best roles) are carjacked at gunpoint by two black men (Ludacris Bridges and Larenz Tate), leading to wife to demand the locks be changed, and then changed again because a Mexican (Michael Pena) did the job first. A black television producer (Terence Howard), getting a blowjob from his wife (Thandie Newton) on their drive home are pulled over by two white cops (Matt Dillon and Ryan Phillippe), one of which (Dillon) gropes the wife, while the other watches. A Persian shopkeeper (Shaun Toub), constantly thought to be an Arab, purchases a gun for protection. In the center of it all is Don Cheadle as a detective who ties everything together when he finds a body on the side of the road. The acting is just electrifying, notably in the scenes between Dillon and Newton, who have a shocking second encounter. Is the film preachy? Hell yes and then some. But it has enough dynamite energy and acting going for it that hating on it for being ambitious is pointless. It's a knockout.

It's funny- the Academy and I don't agree too often. They say the best picture of 1991 was Silence of the Lambs, I say it was T2. They say Scorsese's best work was the Departed (after all, it was the only one he got an Oscar for), I say it was Goodfellas (and I've heard great things about Cape Fear). But I'll be buggered if, in 2005, we didn't see eye to eye at last. You see, while I could go on and on about how Batman Begins is the best movie EVER (and thus also the best film of 2005), I am a rational man, and also a man of taste, and so I can see that, in the theaters of 2005, there was nothing that could hold a candle to Crash. Crash is a well thought-out, well executed trip through the less savory side of life in America. It gives us a glimpse of evils that some people consider things of the past, and that some must deal with on a daily basis- racial tensions, discrimination, hate crimes- but at the same time, it takes our preconceived notions about these subjects and turns them on their heads. This is a movie that delights in ambiguity, developing its characters in one light and then, quite adeptly, playing with the preconceptions that you form about these characters as a viewer, thus both enriching and providing depth for the characters on-screen and forcing you to think differently about how you view other people. The ensemble cast is pitch perfect, filled with both name actors and relative unknowns, and this plays further into the film's dynamic as most known actors are played against type (try finding one other movie that features Sandra Bullock as a bitch). Matt Dillon, whom I've never had that high of an opinion of, finally knocked my socks off as a racist LAPD cop. Michael Pena's Hispanic locksmith has possibly the most moving tale, and the sincerity he brings to the part- and his relationship with his daughter- is a huge part of what makes it work. In fact, all of the actors in this film are impressively believable, and as their solo vignettes weave slowly around each other, we are painted a dark, imperfect, but ultimately hopeful and strangely beautiful portrait of the lives of these people and the prejudices they all face, whether they are the prejudices of others or those of their own. It is one of the few Oscar winners for Best Picture that I side with the Academy on- How Green Was My Valley was NOT better than Citizen Kane- and with damn good reason, too. It's a movie that makes you think, it makes you feel, and it changes the way you look at the world (and if that's not the definition of art, I don't know what is). I honestly cannot heap enough praise onto this picture- if you haven't seen it yet, just go watch it!

Redefines overrated.  Cinematically, this is one of the most insipid films I have ever seen; it looks, on the whole, like any network television police drama.  The acting is generally decent (Don Cheadle, Matt Dillon, William Fichtner, Terrence Howard, and Shaun Toub are all quite good), though there are no astoundingly grand performances (excluding Michael Pena and Ashlyn Sanchez, who create the most accessible and likeable characters).  The crux of the film is its apparently searing view of racism and prejudice in modern America.  What it certainly does have is a pile of competing stereotypes (from bitchy [white] society dame to cruelly racist [white] cop to faux egalitarian [black] carjacker/rapper) - very tired stereotypes.  For an interesting film about the motivations and effects of racism, watch Lars von Trier's Manderlay or Bruce Beresford's Driving Miss Daisy, and let Paul Haggis' Crash collide itself away...

"Crash" is simply one of those films that will never be forgotten.  Beyond the acting, script, and cinematography lies an overwhelming theme that has a lot more meaning than the film's Oscar for Best Picture.  "Crash's" portrayal of racism in Los Angeles is raw, real, and emotional.  While it is easy to see that the film shouts "racism is bad," it operates on a different level at the same time.  As this intricate network of interconnected stories wraps up, the film reveals that looks can be deceiving (Ludacris doing the right thing, the true vocation of the Chinese man, etc.).  Although the film's message is more important than anything, it is brought to life by a talented ensemble cast that includes Don Cheadle, Sandra Bullock, Brendan Fraser, Terrence Howard, and Thandie Newton.  Many of the characters have a duality to them, tempted to conform to the bigotous ways of our society while motivated by their consciences.  While I don't enjoy Matt Dillon as an actor (and think that he only received a Best Supporting nomination due to a weak Oscar class), he excels at disgusting the audience with his character's racist intimidation.  This is imperative to plot's climax when he must risk his life for a woman who wants help from anybody but him.  Even more important is Michael Peña's heartwarming father-daughter dialogue, which sets up the emotional climax of the film.  "The scene" will surely have you crying, further driving home the effects of hatred and introducing a message of hope.  The little details throughout the film, like the ignorance in the ammunition purchase and the Saint Christopher statues, set up the films biggest surprises without us even knowing it.  The script (which won Best Original Screenplay) is perfection as it weaves together so many characters in so many storylines without leaving a single plot hole.  Not only is every character important to the transformation of at least one other character, but each character also facilitates the theme of the film.  The culmination of tension and idea of racism as a learned worldview is driven home as Ryan Phillippe buys into the hatred that surrounds him.  "Crash" is stunning and you will surely realize that as you watch the credits roll by, sitting in silence and unable to move as the whole picture comes together and the levity of the theme sets in.

I found this movie to be extremely annoying due to its self-satisfied tone and heavy-handed treatment of racism. The characters don't seem like real people but rather stereotypes constructed with the aim of drilling in the main thesis of the movie, that racism is bad and all people are horrible racists. (And in case you don't get it the first time, this is pointed out again and again in the movie.) I was also exasperated by the dialogue because it comes across as unnatural and lacks any subtlety whatsoever. For example, characters will often launch into preachy, long-winded speeches about their views of race in America during a casual encounter with another character. Characters also have the annoying habit of providing too much information about their personal backgrounds to each other; such self-disclosures ring false because they are tangential to the conversation at hand and seem included mainly to force the viewer into an understanding of the roots of that particular character? s racism. Whatever happened to the notion of show don?t tell or allowing viewers to piece together things on their own? The movie is also melodramatic in a bad way, relying heavily on coincidence in order to connect the main characters in the different plot lines. In the end, the movie comes across like the effort of an overly-zealous adolescent who is eager to tackle big issues but lacks the subtlety or maturity to execute it.

This is the rare American film really about something, and almost all the performances are riveting. It asks tough questions, and lets its audience struggle with the answers. The stunning, must-see drama Crash is proof that words have not lost the ability to shock in our anesthetized society. Haggis writes with such directness and such a good ear for everyday speech that the characters seem real and plausible after only a few words. His cast is uniformly strong; the actors sidestep cliches and make their characters particular. What makes Crash so gripping--so terrifying in spots, so moving in others, and even a little funny at times--is how nothing happens as we think it will. Crash fools around with chronology in a Tarantinoesque way that brings its story full circle. You could argue that as events, and people, merge, Haggis' spiky screenplay (cowritten with Bobby Moresco) gets to be, quite simply, too much. A haunting, perceptive and uncompromising examination of controversial subject matter, expertly written and directed by Paul Haggis and characterised by excellent performances from its starry cast. VERDICT: "Instant Classic" - [Positively Acclaimed Reaction] Usually I give this rating to a movie that I believe is absolutely outstanding and has little to no flaws in it. Frankly, I'm completely mystified as to how Crash won an Oscar for Best Picture in 2005.

Paul Haggis' parable of racism in modern America is all concept and no substance; trying desperately to be heart-wrenching while forgetting to imbue its characters with any detail or realism. A better cast certainly could have helped, although Don Cheadle's forgettable performance proves that you can't pin all the movie's shortcomings on the actors. Haggis' script is so clunky, awkward, and transparent that the movie never really has a chance to hit home in the way it should.

The saddest part about Crash is how much potential is wasted here. Fifteen years after the Los Angeles riots, racism is arguably as prevalent and divisive a problem in America as it was then. As referenced rather bluntly in the film, the fear of Middle Easterners and Mexicans has risen to negate whatever slow progress had been made between blacks and whites. Though changing viewpoints and increased media pressure have helped purge some obvious bigots from government offices and police departments, their effect has probably only served to make prejudice in most people more subtle, and therefore harder to weed out. It's this less tangible racism that is perhaps the most harmful, and the most worthy of examination.

Haggis has moments of unearthing these truths, such as when Ryan Philippe's relatively altruistic character still ends up shooting a black acquaintance for fear that he's carrying a gun. In nearly every other instance, however, the film turns to unnecessarily direct racial insults to prop up its dramatic tension.

"Who gathered all those remarkably different cultures together and taught them all how to park their cars on their lawns?", Cheadle's character says after his girlfriend tells him she's from Puerto Rico, not Mexico. The audience cringes, but I'd say they do so equally because of the fact that Cheadle has no plausible reason to deliver the line. He is exposed as a pawn of the writer, something that shouldn't be so conscious in a well-made film.

At just under two hours, Crash feels more like a cheesy corporate anti-discrimination video than an important cinematic statement, and its magnetism is just as weakly compelling.

Tragic, Beautiful, Intense. "Crash" tells interlocking stories of whites, blacks, Latinos, Koreans, Iranians, cops and criminals, the rich and the poor, the powerful and powerless, all defined in one way or another by racism. All are victims of it, and all are guilty it. Sometimes, yes, they rise above it, although it is never that simple. Their negative impulses may be instinctive, their positive impulses may be dangerous, and who knows what the other person is thinking?
The result is a movie of intense fascination; we understand quickly enough who the characters are and what their lives are like, but we have no idea how they will behave, because so much depends on accident. The movie presumes that most people feel prejudice and resentment against members of other groups, and observes the consequences of those feelings. A brilliant ensemble cast especially Matt Dillon and Ludacris.

I have really mixed feelings about this movie. When I first saw it, way back in May of 2005, I felt it had the emotional resonance of American History X with the wide scope of intertwining characters I first saw in Traffic. Like the former movie as well as Spike Lee's Do The Right Thing, it actually examines race relations intelligently and points the finger at, depending on your perspective, everyone and no one. I can also appreciate the deep questions the movie raises about the peculiar cultural variety in America, and Los Angeles in particular. While historically our country has been referred to, both idealistically and derogatorily as a "melting pot," Crash, as its title suggests, paints instead a kind of violent mixture, sudden and its elements too inherently dissimilar to slow down and fuse together softly or at least coexist harmoniously, they crash and people suffer. Crash is realistic and understands that respect for others and adherence to cultural identity are often incompatible and that we sometimes express our anger in ways that are mindless and tragically off-topic. As interesting as these questions are and as much as I admire the ambition of the screenplay, there are a number of moments and lines that feel a little heavy-handed and the new age-y score just did not seem appropriate to me, though admittedly, I cannot imagine exactly what sounds would work right in the background. I share the opinion that this did not deserve its Best Picture Oscar, although unlike most in this boat, I felt Munich and Good Night and Good Luck were stronger contenders than Brokeback Mountain, another movie for which I have an imbalanced admiration. A good film whose deep social implications outweigh its aesthetic merit, and it is this proportion that prevents it from being truly great.

And you will find characters, such as Matt Dillon, that make you want to fuckin scream one minute and give them a hug the next minute.  A classic, and worthy of the Oscar it won, which I don't say with regularity.

Today the world of cinema revolves around Hollywood and America in general providing the oomph to film, much as it does to the world, and it is, as ever really, down to the more-often-than-not capable hands of the European flick to provide a genuine feel, a true emotion that doesn't feel tacked on and if anything, is more real and touching in the purity that often comes with European cinema, than in the actual words that come from the actors mouths.

If I can give Crash anything it's that it genuinely tries. It's an American film that literally tries to leave the ballpark of general mainstream American cinema. Unfortunately it forgets that another of America's flaws when it comes to cinema is over-earnestness and a distinct lack of subtlety. But arguably, Crash does try.

There are one or two stories in Crash that resonate strongly, but for the most part the others become something of a tangle. The black woman pulled from her car by the same cop that had felt her up the previous night on a routine stop, was sadly complete Hollywood cheese. However the cop himself has one of the better aspects of Crash in having to deal with his aging father's ailments. The other story of note for the wrong reasons is the young latino handy-man who's daughter potentially gets shot. The moment he grabs her after this incident is so full of pomp, gusto, and the fact that it tries to pull on the heart-strings so hard that it ends up pulling the wrong one and ends up seeming silly and completely unsympathetically emotionless.

There is simply no point in the utterly useless Sandra Bullock being here, other than to attempt to draw in the crowds. Had it have been an up-and-coming actress rather than a crowd puller 'purely because it needed one', then it would have been considerably better than her ronsealed acting (that's wood that's been hardened).

However, Don Cheadle is excellent as ever and has a compelling life story-line, one of the few redeeming features of a mess that tries to prove a problem which it actually just emphasizes: we understand that racism is there, but the film has no point and no direction.

Surprisingly for an American film it didn't end well, or bad for that matter, and it didn't try to offer some kind of solutions, which is one of the only genuinely none American things about this film. Other than that and a few select performances and story-lines, Crash lives up to it's ironic title...no direction, no point and consequently, no feeling.

This is at it's best, a compelling human drama.  At it's worst, it's an after-school special, or perhaps "Fox Presents Racism's Greatest Hits".
The structure is standard interwoven ensemble fare; a genre which is almost by necessity highly Dickensian (particularly when many of the characters are not connected at the beginning, as is the case here).  Spectacular coincidences and twists of fate bring people together to confront their own racism in ways which range from subtly tasteful (Sandra Bullock's admission of friendship to the housekeeper she so scorns) to patently ridiculous (Young Black Carjacker Decides Not To Enter Slave Trade).  
There are moments of this that really struck me, largely because I feel they were powerful in a context of pure story.  Two scenes in particular in Matt Dillon's arc- the disturbing and provocative scene in which he molests a black married woman during a roadside stop, followed by his responding to an accident in which her life is in danger (forcing him to view her as a real person, helpless and vulnerable).  The good parts of this film are wrapped up in watching people struggle with dilemmas,  particularly when the dilemmas take center stage and the overriding message of the film is shunted aside for a few precious moments.
This is heavy-handed, make no mistake.  It's as though Paul Haggis can see us nodding yes, clearly moved by his staggering vision, his clear and unflinching examination of modern, day-to-day racism on all sides of our culture.  Here's the problem with that:
I already knew about it.  
If you are a person who struggles to examine all the various sides of each issue in our culture; who is enamored of the study of history, of literature, of an understanding of the world around you; if you reject the party line and choose to LEARN about your world it is inconceivable that you don't know this goes on.  I didn't need to be beaten upside the head with it for two-thirds of this film.  I imagine much of America did, which is probably why it was so critically successful.
I found it pedantic more often than not, which disengaged me from the story and caused me to be less forgiving of the improbable elements to the story- of which there are many.
There are many very nice scenes and moments, some fantastic performances by a superb cast, and a real effort to create three-dimensional characters who are represented in their entirety (or who's redeeming- or condemning- layers are revealed to us as the story progresses).  However even this grey area seems to me too universal, and ultimately subverted from impartiality to a deliberate part of the message:
"We're all the same, and we're all kind of racist."
I know, Mr. Haggis.  I know.  Just tell the story.  You're quite good at it, when you get down to business and focus on your craft.

Crash happens.  It happens at the most inopportune times.  It happens when we're just minding our business.  Racism and prejudice happens.  And it happens a lot in Crash.  A movie that intertwines different racial confrontations, Crash is no holds bar.  It does not sugar coat.  Exposing the crooked cop for what he really is and the good cop for what he isn't.  It makes a man out of "men," like when Terrence Howard, a prominent "white" director, turns a blind eye to the fingering of his wife, played by Thandie Newton, at the hands of a cop, then attempts to retaliate.  Howards pulls a gun on a cop, hoping to finally stand up for his wife and his race, but he sees the bigger picture.  His wife comes to forgive, not only him, but the crooked cop, who saves her from a burning car.  Crash shows what happens when we can't communicate.  When fear paralyzes us into submission and we take matters into our own hands, like the persian store owner, whose store is vandalized.  His english may be bad, but he's no dummy.  He knows about 9/11 and he knows what the world thinks of him.  He also knows that he paid good money to get the store's door fixed, but little does he know.  Ignited by anger, he retaliates, against the mexican locksmith and also the world.  He shoots an innocent girl, but she survives.  The owner's daughter knew.  Knew that if he had a gun, he'd misuse it, so she put blanks in it.  Don Cheadle, who plays a police detective, isn't so lucky.  As he fights crime, his little brother, played by Larenz Tate is fighting.  Fighting to fit into a world that won't accept him. His stubborness and need for vindication causes his demise.  A good person at heart, he wants to spread joy by way of his dashboard ornament.  As he catches a ride from an off-duty "good" cop, he notices the ornament on the dashboard.  He goes to pull out his own, but, just like the rest of his life, his actions are mistaken.  He's shot down.  These and other racial stereotypes are illuminated in Crash.  In the world we live in, Crash shows how accidents happen; some which can be prevented and some which can't.

I can believe that Muslim store owner accuses the locksmith of cheating him out of money and later attempts to murder the locksmith with blanks. I can believe that one of the young black car jackers loved hockey and had a deep understanding of the world around him. I can believe that the nice-looking Chinese couple was smuggling illegal Chinese immigrants. I can believe that the racist asshole of a white cop loved his dad and suffered through his father's prostate ailment. I could believe most of the stories in this movie. And I [i]could[/i] [i]have[/i] believed this movie and its message.
 
But is 100% not believable that a police officer, who waged a moral battle within his department--a department institutionalized with racism, who petitioned to have his partner assignment changed under the embaressing pretense of bad gas, who put himself and his career on the line in front of his racist partners to prevent a motorist from being a victim of racial profiling, would act the way Ryan Phillipe's character acted in the last 15 minutes of the movie. There is no way a cop, whose character was built up to have such a strong moral code and righteous view of himself and others, would panic the way he did and shoot a black hitchhiker in the face, especially one acting as jovial and friendly as the one Phillipe's cop picked up.
 
This ending was so completely unbelievable that I lost all respect for the movie and its 'message' right then and there. I was truly disgusted and angry and disappointed.

It's no longer news that even the America has a race relations problem (see an analysis of a recent Washington Post poll  (http://tinyurl.com/ebe5z) for an example).  Yet Crash rated an Academy Award and a double-clap from me because this country is still not, and maybe never has been the melting pot we imagine.  Through a collection of interlocking stories, Crash keeps in sharp focus how racism and ethno-centrism pervade our relations.  Each of the stories has believable bigotry, both gross and subtle, and almost no one comes off as entirely virtuous or evil.

The overt bigotry is infuriating.  A white cop gropes a black woman during a routine traffic stop.  A white gun shop owner says, "Hey Osama, make up your mind" as an Iranian with limited English skills buys a gun.  The Iranian accuses a Latino man of cheating him because of the language barrier between them.  A white DA's white wife, carjacked with her husband by two black men, boils over at her him, berating both of them for not altering their route the moment they spotted the men.  She then goes on to mistreat the Latino who's installing a new security system, suspecting him of keeping keys to copy for a later robbery.  

The subtle bigotry, however, is some of the most startling.  For example, a black male cop and a female Latina cop are dating, and a call from the man's mother interrupts their sex session.  Annoyed, he tells her that he's busy screwing a white lady, and could she call back later.  The woman, insulted, jumps up from bed and begins to dress.  He explains, "Hey, I'd have told her the truth, but I thought calling you white would piss her off more."  If you think about the scene, it reveals bigotry in *all* the participants.  In a second example, the rookie white partner of the bigoted cop approaches the black precinct captain about the molestation incident.  The captain comments on how amazing it is that the bigoted cop's actions could have gone undetected all these years, especially when he was under the captain's direct command for 11 of them.  The rookie looks confused, so the captain spells it out:  If the rookie complains, it makes the captain look (a) incompetent for at least 11 years, (b) like he hates blacks.  Both of these implications would spell the end of the rookie's career.  You can see the "Oh shit" look register on the rookie's face, and you're left wondering, "Why on earth didn't the captain bust the bigoted cop much earlier?"  In a third example, the DA, a model of political correctness, just after his wife's outburst, cooks up a scheme to "pin a medal on a black man" to keep his image race-neutral.  And I won't even go into what the husband of the black woman molested by the cop does after his wife dresses him down for not standing up for her -- see if you can pick up on all the layers of internalized and external racism.

The performances are uniformly excellent, so the I'll single out just Matt Dillon and Sandra Bullock, whom I didn't know could do such a good job.  There are enough ironic plot twists to make you do several double-takes, but without the movie losing credibility because of them.

I thought I was under no illusions about how much racism pervades this country.  Yet, after the movie, it occurred to me that I had just been indulging in a bit of stereotyping of my own, judging a white musician harshly for trying to "sound black."  It hit me that bigots on both sides of the race line leveled that charge at Elvis Presley and Eminem.  Then there was the opposite attack on the early 20th-century black singer Paul Robeson, for trying to enter the white bastion of opera.  And last, there was the acceptance of Nat "King" Cole by the white community precisely because he sounded "white." Who was I to condemn an artistic styling on the basis of my preconceptions of race?  I set that aside, and the musician's music grew on me.  

See Crash, talk about it with your friends, and see what it brings up for you.

Crash is a thought provoking movie that asks the viewers to question their own prejudice that they may have against a person different than themselves. That is the beauty of this movie. It will undoubtedly rouse up much conversation about ourselves, our nation, and who we consider less than human. The fact is that all of us have some kind of prejudice, small or otherwise, and Crash is a great showcase into the deepest, most discriminating parts of our minds, despite the film being slightly over the top and very coincidental.

Crash tells the story of a handful of people, all of them with some kind of prejudice against another certain type of people. The different characters discriminate against everybody from African Americans to Middle Easterners to Latinos and even back around to Caucasians. Having African American characters in the film with a prejudice against white people is a bold move, but an honest and truthful one that could have been taken in a different connotation had it not been for the blatant "this is how our world is" message attached. However, the fact that the film never delved into discrimination against homosexuals is odd, especially with the increasing intolerance in the last few years.

Outside of the lack of a homosexual discrimination element, I only have one problem with this film. I know a lot of films rely on coincidence to carry on their narrative. For instance, in a lot of romantic comedies, the lead male and lead female will just happen to be in the same grocery store or whatever at the exact same time. But Crash took coincidence to a new level. There are close to a dozen people in the film and they all cross paths with multiple other characters numerous times, despite the majority of them having no direct affiliation with one another. It would take me hours (and perhaps much longer) to type up every coincidence in this movie, but it is absolutely absurd to think that all of this would actually happen in real life.

However, everything else in the film is near perfect. The acting is outstanding across the board, with the sole exception being the mediocre Ludacris. I was astonished to see the usually terrible Brendan Fraser act as well as he did. Sandra Bullock was also a pleasant surprise. When I think of Bullock, I think of happy little bubble gum pop princess movies like Miss Congeniality, but she played her part pitch perfect and it was nice to see her act a serious part for once. With other excellent actors like Matt Dillon, Terrence Howard, and the great Don Cheadle rounding out the experience, I can honestly say this is the best acting I've seen in a long time.

Crash started out as a compelling study into the human psyche, but began to rely too heavily on coincidence to get its message across. As a thought provoking film, it is a great success and a masterpiece for the directors, actors, and writers. But the realm of believablity slowly dwindles down as time goes on. But don't let that stop you from seeing it. Crash is a top notch drama that isn't so much interested in telling a story as it is in questioning the very hearts and minds of the people of our beautiful nation.

I liked it the first time, but then I was 15. The thing about Crash is that it has nothing to say. Nothing, except that racism is bad. Which I knew before I went in. And...that's fine if you're going to do something with it, but this doesn't really do much. It's a very safe movie. Way too safe for its own good. Like "Do the Right Thing" with its balls cut off. And maybe it isn't fair to compare this to the other movie, which is a towering achievment in movies. But where one offers real people with tension actually building, Crash offers people who snap really quickly without much reason. And I suppose there are some of those people. But to have a full movie of characters who are unrealistically unreasonable and pretty much nothing else seems a little silly. 

The cast is good, for the most part, but very little rings true. The problem with this movie is that it views racism as a really simple subject. "It's bad and we shouldn't have it". That's about it. It's not very well written or presented, nothing seems real, nothing seems more than just a bunch of caricatures and cardboard cut-outs. The biggest problem? This movie doesn't examine race relations and social conflict so much as it's...sympathetic towards it. That's all. It's pretty much a safe movie about racism to make white people feel better about themselves. Literally. Paul Haggis wrote it after getting carjacked. And I admire that he's being sincere, but he's not particularly interesting to listen to.

To sum it up, you can get pretty much all of Crash's points out of the song "Everyone's a Little Bit Racist" from the musical Avenue Q. And, to quote a much better movie on this subject, that's the truth, Ruth.

(Sigh), I really don't like this movie.  (ok, get ready for my ramble.)  Just because a movie sends a great message, it doesn't make it a good movie. The idea was phenomenal and I was really looking forward to the movie at first, but in the end it felt so forced, and with each viewing, I like it less and less.  Sure, I watched it in a psych class and it sparked good discussions, but the whole movie was just so forced and fabricated.  Haggis managed to turn racism into a Hollywood ideal and I hated it.  I hated that they jipped Asian American actors again by giving the "China-man" a negligible role, his mom only one line, and they didn't even bother to cast a real Latina in the role of Ria (Esposito is freakin' Italian and she's playing a Salvadoran).  I did like the story-line involving the Persian family, but that was it.  And what really really bothers me is that this film is like an Indie film for people who have never seen Indie films, and that's full of mainstream actors.  Viewers are like "Oh, I saw Crash, it was a good movie and I got the message" and they think they're not racist anymore cuz they've learned their lesson.  If you want to see a better film that explores the same theme, Spike Lee's "Do the Right Thing" is so much more satisfying, and I love "Babel".  Now THAT movie should have won Best Picture, not "Crash".

[font=Times New Roman][size=3][color=black]Do you feel you're being stereotyped or are you the one stereotyping others? How are people being viewed or how do people view others in today's American society? Well, through its characters, dialogues, and symbolism, the film [u]Crash[/u] shows how Americans stereotype different ethnicities and cultures. The different plots that take place in the film show the different situations in which Americans can and will be stereotyped. [/color]
 
[color=black]The characters in the film [u]Crash[/u] see themselves differently. Thus, by seeing themselves differently, it results in the stereotyping of others who are not the same but just slightly different. The characters stereotype each other because of their different races, cultures, and as well as skin colors. In the film [u]Crash[/u], the police officer views others differently just because he is a typical white male who think he's above the law. This fellow police officer judges others by race and skin color. He believes that minority races that are on welfare takes up his tax money, so these races and groups are the ones causing all the problems within the cities. Another example is that the wife of a white couple stereotyped a Mexican locksmith by the way he dresses. The Mexican man dresses in baggy clothes and has tattoos all over his arms. Thus, the Mexican man's look automatically makes him a target, and he then gets stereotyped without knowing anything; but to only finish his job of fixing this white couple's door lock. [/color]
 
[color=black]The dialogue in the film [u]Crash[/u] is also a big factor to how the characters stereotype each other. They use racist remarks, slurs, and languages to show that the other ethnicities and cultures are not equal to that of their own. In one scenario in the film, a typical white husband and wife are arguing about the fact that their locksmith is a Mexican man. The wife disagrees and is not satisfied with this Mexican man's work stating that this individual is a bad person who will in return burglarize her house because he's "Mexican." Another example is that the white police officer calls the black man that he had pulled over on the street, a "nigger." Such language can be offensive in today's society. Yet, due to the police officer's authority, he can careless of what is said to others. [/color]
 
[color=black]The symbolism that is used in the film [u]Crash[/u] portrays the lifestyle of minority characters. Yet, other characters in the film show disapproval of such symbols that reflect these minority characters. In the film [u]Crash[/u], the black minority man who drives a nice brand new vehicle is stereotyped for being someone who isn't worthy enough to drive such an expensive vehicle according to the white police officer. The other characters think differently of this man, stating he deals drugs or is tied into some sort of illegal affiliations in order to afford such an expensive vehicle. The vehicle symbolizes the life style of the black man by showing the audience that he who is thought to be poor can too live a wealthy life. Yet, he is targeted and looked down upon because others stereotyped him to be just another poor black man that can't afford such a vehicle. [/color]
 
[color=black]All in all, the film [u]Crash[/u] portrays the typical American stereotyping of others regardless of ethnicities and culture. The uses of characters, dialogue, and symbolism in the film [u]Crash[/u] defines and portrays the ways a person can be stereotyped. The film [u]Crash[/u] shows that stereotyping of others will just be part of the American society and lifestyle in spite of what others think. This film explored the grey areas of the black and white. I liked this film. And I did not expect that I would.

"We're Losing Touch." That's one of the very first lines spoken in the new great film by Paul Haggis. It is spoken by Don Cheadle's police detective, Graham, after a head injury resulting from a car crash caused by an overly eccentric Chinese lady. He's babbling all this random stuff, but it's not so random. That line is pretty much the whole basis for 'Crash'. We as a society are losing touch of each other. We don't care about each other anymore, and the day and age of chivalry has died in 2005. When we see someone in need or down on their luck we just turn the other way. We aren't involved with each other and we've become so callous and self-absorbed. We are torn apart the the racism, prejudices and differences of each other, that we almost don't even care anymore. 'Crash' takes that idea and spins a handful of interesting and beautifully layered vignettes that take place in the slums of Los Angeles during the course of two days.

The two days the film is set over follows eight different situations all eventually interlocking with each other. The first situation is about two detectives, Graham (Don Cheadle - Hotel Rwanda) and Ria (Jennifer Esposito) investigating the murder of a could-be dirty cop, and Graham helping his heroin-addicted mother find her hoodlum son. The second situation follows two L.A.P.D. police officers, Ryan (Matt Dillon - Drugstore Cowboy) and Hansen (Ryan Phillippe - The Way of the Gun), Ryan struggling with his dying father while Hansen struggles with having Ryan as a partner. The third situation follows a rich black television producer, Cameron (Terence Howard - Hart's War) and his wife, Christine (Thandie Newton - The Truth About Charlie) who try to keep their marriage together after an upsetting run in with two police officers. The fourth situation follows a wealthy and smug D.A., Rick (Brendan Fraser - The Mummy) and his self-centered pedantic wife, Jean (Sandra Bullock - Miss Congeniality) and how they deal with life and the political hardships that follow Rick after he's assaulted and car-jacked by two black street thugs. The fifth situation follows the two black street thugs/car-jackers, Anthony (Chris 'Ludicrous' Bridges - 2 Fast 2 Furious) and Peter (Larenz Tate - Dead Presidents) as they roam the streets of L.A. in the newly stolen SUV. The sixth story follows a lower-class Hispanic locksmith, Daniel (Michael Pena - TV's The Shield), who's trying to make ends meet while supporting his wife and daughter. The seventh story follows a Chinese-American couple in the ghettos of L.A., while the eighth story is centered around Islamic citizens, Farhad (Shaun Toub) the owner of a pawnshop and his emergency room doctor daughter, Dorri (Bahar Soomekh) as they try to get through life without being discriminated against. It's a very complex plot, but that's not an insult, it's actually a compliment. These days, it's good to see a film that actually requires you to think and examine life, then some mindless action lackluster of a film starring Britney Spears or Jennifer Lopez. 'Crash' is a unique opportunity to see a though-provoking and heart-wrenching suspense tale that you can learn a lot from.

'Crash' has some wonderful qualities to it. The acting of the film is spectacular with stand-out performances. Sandra Bullock actually turns in a good performance as the nasty housewife (for the very few screen time she has). Don Cheadle is absolutely brilliant in his role as a conflicted L.A.P.D. police detective, following his startling turn in last year's Oscar contender 'Hotel Rwanda'. Matt Dillon turns in one of the best performances of the film, as the bigoted and emotionally scared police officer, and I can't remember Dillon turning in a finer performance since 1989's 'Drugstore Cowboy'. Jennifer Esposito is good as Cheadle's partner, while Brendan Fraser is kind of so-so as the District Attorney of Los Angeles. For me, he wasn't very believable in that role. Terrence Dashon Howard turns in a very powerful performance, while Ludicrous does an actually all-right job with acting (I was a bit skeptical because he is a rapper, not an actor). Thandie Newton was amazing in perhaps the best acting performance of the entire film, and Ryan Phillippe and Larenz Tate played their roles with staunch authenticity and passion for the craft of acting. The newcomer, Michael Pena (who can be seen every Tuesday as the latest cast member of 'The Shield') does a surprisingly fabulous job, along with Shaun Toub. The film also contains bit parts played by Loretta Devine (Boston Public), Keith David (Barbershop), William Fichtner (Black Hawk Down) and most notably Tony Danza in a thirty second part. Paul Haggis does a phenomenal job writing along with directing. Haggis provides a script so rich and elaborate in that it keeps you deeply focused for the entire runtime of the film. His directing is exquisite and impressive, but not too flashy or pretentious. The only real flaws that are present in 'Crash' are that it is somewhat unbelievable or confusing at times. Like I said, you really have to pay close attention to detail while watching the film. It isn't one of those movies where you can take a trip to the restroom in the middle of it, come back, and ask the person sitting next to you, "What did I miss?". Because in those few minutes you spent in the bathroom, you most likely missed a plot revelation or new set-up. A lot of people will be turned off with how involving 'Crash' is, but for the few who truly appreciate the art of film, it will be like a dream come true. I enjoyed almost everything the picture had to offer, but I couldn't help but feel the ending was a bit inadequate of what the whole film was seemingly heating up for. In conclusion, I highly recommend 'Crash' even though it's ending was rather disappointing. Grade: A-

As I write this, [i]Crash[/i] is sitting at number 153 of IMDB's top 250.  And you know, I'm okay with that.  This is . . . wow.  The word that springs to mind for it is [i]stunning[/i].  

Note, this is the 2004 [i]Crash[/i], not the other one.  This is the one about racism, not fetishists.  These are very different movies that you should under no circumstances confuse.  I also very strongly suggest not showing either movie to children.  That would fall under Very Bad Ideas.

I'm not going to give a plot summary, here, because that would be a very [i]long[/i] plot summary.  For one thing, let me introduce you to the term "ensemble cast."  Matt Dillon got a Best Supporting Actor nomination (he lost to George Clooney, which is not a phrase I had ever expected to use about the Oscars).  However, I'm not sure how they determined that [i]he[/i] was the guy in this deserving of the nomination.  He does a pretty good job, especially given that he's playing a human guy that we're supposed to hate, but Don Cheadle, Terrence Howard, Brendan Fraser, and especially (number two of "phrases I never thought I'd say") the man here credited as "Chris 'Ludacris' Bridges," whom I had previously loathed because of how he spells his stage name.  But arguably, he gives us a better performance.

I am not exactly unfamiliar with many of the attitudes held by people in this film.  I know someone, for example, who won't ride the bus because "only poor people ride the bus."  I've never felt like getting into a debate about his socioeconomic status when he says that.  And, yes, I've known racists and sexists and those tedious people who think only white people can be racist.  (They're wrong.)  I know people who don't even realize how racist they are, which is probably the most common kind.  Brendan Fraser, for example, plays a DA who simply never considers how racist he's being, probably because his wife is that much worse.  (Sandra Bullock, in what is actually a pretty good performance.)

This movie is not for everyone, and I want to make that very clear even as I grant it status on a Top 250 list.  (Not that I've ever put my personal one together, largely because it would keep changing as I watch more and more movies.)  This is a very intense movie, and there is no feel-good message here.  Every character we are presented with is deeply flawed; every character we are presented with has redeeming value.  This is an [i]intense[/i] movie.  You have to be willing to really think in order to watch it, and it will probably make you really think about yourself when it's over.

Crash is an excellent production that kept me rivetted with its twists and turns.

A timely film about the fallibility of mankind and the dangers of gun ownership, set against the background of racial prejudice and conflict, the film was careful to keep a neutral position when it comes to racism (up to you to decide how successful it is at that). Meet cops, politicians, wives, children, small business owners, petty criminals, of various races as the movie explores the tense interactions between them.

Smoothly cutting in and out of the various sub-plots, it slowly draws out a map of inter-connecting karmic relationships between events that when examined in silo (from the standpoint of the characters), would seem unrelated to each other. However, it is when they continuously crash into each other's lives and realise the consequences of their actions, that they learn more about themselves and lose their convictions and moral standpoint.

At some points, Crash may seem an over-dramatised film with racial stereotypes. Perhaps no movie has generated more Oscar controversy than Crash's 2005 win. Many claim that anti-homosexual elements in Hollywood conspired to usurp Brokeback Mountain's projected victory. Politics aside, to me the most worrying issue is how anyone could be duped by what is perhaps one of the most disingenuous movies about racism ever released. Crash thinks it's important. Crash believes that it is saying something bold about racism in America. However, the movie is so unbelievably infantile, so embarrassing in its desperate attempt at tugging emotions, and most shockingly, so covert in its own treatment of race that it cannot possibly be conceived as a realistic critique on racism.

From appearances, Crash intends to challenge the viewer by presenting a series of characters from different ethnic backgrounds and reveal the tensions and complications through the intersection of their lives. That sounds like a reasonable premise, and perhaps in any other director's hands, it would be. However, Haggis infuses his script with such heavy-handed, moronic obviousness that it obfuscates what is essentially a simple and trite message: we are all capable of racism and we should not stereotype. The movie never grasps the complex social, political, and cultural forces that shape our current perceptions of race. Unlike the excellent Killer of Sheep or Do the Right Thing, it offers shallow stereotypes from a Hollywood that is unimaginably removed from the reality of American ghettos and immigrant neighborhoods. But in the spirit of fair play, I will assume that Crash never had any intention of exploring racism along macroscopic social or economical levels, however real or interesting that may be. We are then left to decide whether the interaction of its characters constitutes any form of critique.

Unfortunately, none of the characters are conceived as real individuals, people whom we could probably encounter in real life. Yes, we all stereotype other races in some fashion, and all of us have, to a certain extent, racial prejudices. The key point is that we don't easily lash out our racism at the slightest provocation. This is precisely why Crash rings so unbelievably false. For instance, while on the phone, Matt Dillon's character finds out that the operator is Shaniqua Johnson, and shouts a racially charged invective against the laziness of black people. Are you serious? In another moment of sheer stupidity, Don Cheadle's character is sleeping with an extremely beautiful girl whom he has mistaken to be Mexican. She is actually from Puerto Rico and El Salvador. If you were Don Cheadle's character, would you respond to a phone call from your mother (in the middle of having sex!) to say you are busy banging a Mexican? Part of the problem is that Haggis is so focused on sculpting racially charged situations that he loses track of what is credible and what is not. Haggis feels that the best way to discuss racism is to put in full display, in all its gross and ugly manifestations. That may be true, but Haggis' conceptualization of racial tension is having stereotyped characters shout overtly dumb and juvenile accusations at each other.

People may argue that unlike a book, in a movie you cannot clearly show a character's motivations or thoughts. I beg to differ. In the beginning of the movie, Sandra Bullock's character grabs her husband's arm as two black men approach. Her move was defensive, silent, and instinctive. While certainly a shallow display of racism, it nonetheless, strikes me as a more plausible and realistic scenario. Perhaps this scene escaped Haggis' larger manifesto. One could easily imagine what he could have done, had he realized the opportunity that was presented there. Instead of having a silent, instinctual grab, he would have probably had Sandra Bullock say, just within earshot, that "I do not trust those black people" only to have them turn around and engage in another mindless diatribe.

Crash is more than a failure of script. Even as a series of vignettes, it does not achieve the fluidity of P.T. Anderson's Magnolia or the economy of Soderbergh's Traffic. Dramatic situations in this movie become exploitative and over-the-top. Consider the scene in which an Iranian shop-owner decides to shoot Michael Pena's character, only to miss and hit his daughter. But wait! She doesn't die, because the real bullets were removed by the Iranian shop-owner's daughter. It's another one of those excessive "Gotcha" moments that litters this movie. Each character intersection in this movie is painfully contrived and false. As a result, none of the characters become developed in any meaningful way. Instead, they become reduced to mere examples, talking points about the ugliness of racism. Perhaps a more linear approach would have served the story better, but with a script this awful, its impossible to tell.

There are some highlights in the cast, particularly Terrence Howard, Matt Dillon, and Michael Pena. The cinematography is sound, but to what end? Perhaps most bizarrely, the movie was nominated for Best Film Editing, which is indicative of the Academy's equivocation of "best" with "most." Crash isn't plotted, its programmed. Scenes are edited in structurally obvious ways. When character X comes to sham epiphany, use long frame on the face. When character X is in an emotionally intense scene (Michael Pena's scene with his daughter or Matt Dillion's scene with the burning car) use slow motion saturated with bombastic orchestral music to evoke pseudo-poignancy.

Basically, Crash is one of the most arrogant movies I have ever seen. It exhausts all its narrative tricks to advocate the perverse Hollywood conception of "global" values. Crash does not conceive of race as a product of one's environment and experience. Race just is. When characters have a supposed change of heart, it is never because they felt compelled to do so. Rather, they are merely shadow puppets in an inexplicable "crash" of events; their epiphanies reify the inescapable constraints that race imparts on what they can and cannot do. For all its false pretenses, Crash doesn't do anything other than reinforce conventional stereotypes. Its lofty aims of deconstructing racism are exactly antithetical to the importance that it attaches to race as a defining category. It is the complete disingenuous nature about the whole enterprise that is most damning. One cannot walk out of this movie thinking of it as anything other than colossal insult. Haggis believes that because he has peppered this film with accomplished stars, burnished locations, and the right number of cheap histrionics, that he can somehow hide Crash's Victorian-era conceptualization of race. Crash is bottomless drivel, on par with the antics of Carlos Mencia and other race pundits, and is one of the most terrible films I have ever seen.

A couple of punches are pulled, and the music rather emphatically underlines all the emotional scenes - the MOR rock song that closes movie, feels like it's wandered in from the moral wrap up section of an episode of Scrubs.  Really, television does this kind of multi-character story best nowadays; and though it may seem like damning it with faint praise, I mean it as a compliment when I say that at times it's as good as an early episode of 6 Feet Under.

It seems like nobody hated Crash until it picked up all the Oscar heat, but in some ways it's almost a harsher insult to call it mediocre than to call it awful. Crash is a painfully "OK" film that severely shoots itself in the foot by grasping so nakedly for awards when Haggis' script is just not mature or timely enough to be as important as it makes itself out to be. It's the worst offender of the "what an amazing coincidence" brand of cliched filmmaking, and the way it piles on the plot contrivances makes up for a rather juvenile exploration of race relations that occasionally feels like it's taking the civil rights movement backwards a step. Still, despite a goofy, oversimplified screenplay, the endless parade of great actors really step up to the plate and make do with what they have, and create a lot of really nice moments that would work fantastically well if you took them out of the context of the film, which lightly cheapens their impact by laying them all on top of one another and masquerading them as a raw, cutting glimpse into modern human nature. I hate blatant message films and I hate all this tableau bullshit, but once you get past that, it's not a completely worthless film.[/font]

Crash was originally marketed as an action movie.  To a point, it somewhat lived up to this angle.  But the reality is that it is more of an argumentative piece that could double as a college term paper for a Sociology or Communication class.  The topic of the argument:  racism.  The paper in question would likely start out something like this:

Racism breeds racism.  And until humans learn tolerance and understanding, racism and violence will continue to destroy humans.

So, now that we have our topic for the paper out of the way, let us go ahead and analyze the movie.  By the way, if any Communication or Sociology students are out there, the topic and this argument are my work.  Write your own paper.  That's meant to be taken jokingly, by the way.  Okay, back to the movie.

This wonderful, thought provoking movie takes a look at the argument about racism and its effects.  It does a wonderful job of doing so, too.  Director Paul Haggis and his writers have crafted a story that looks at a group of characters whose lives intersect through the stereotypes, which every ethnic group has created about one another.  The movie avoids the simple black-against-white storyline, opting instead for a story that has a variety of people of different ethnic backgrounds intersecting with one another.

One of the most intriguing pieces of this story comes near the end.  It involves one of the white police officers.  The other centers around a Hispanic repairman and his daughter.  Haggis and co. set up a scenario that audiences know is coming, with an astounding result that will leave audiences shaken far after the sequence is over.

For those who are looking for an in-depth, detailed look at just how damaging racism and violence are to humans, this movie is an excellent start.  Even if not for a paper, this movie is recommended for any college Communication or Sociology class.

In a drama strikingly reminiscent in style and tone of P.T. Anderson's film Magnolia (1999), the narrative in Crash shifts between 5 or 6 different groups of seemingly unconnected characters, whose relationships to each other are only revealed in the end.

Not to be confused with the David Cronenberg feature of the same name, this Crash is the feature-length, studio-released directorial debut of veteran Canadian TV writer/producer/director and two-time Emmy-winner Paul Haggis. An in-depth exploration on the themes of racism and prejudice, cause and effect, chance and coincidence, and tragedy, "crash" is a metaphor for the collisions between strangers in the course of day-to-day existence. Set over a 24-hour period in contemporary L.A., it is a social commentary on the interconnectedness of life in the big city.

Crash features a top-notch ensemble cast which includes: Sandra Bullock, Don Cheadle, Matt Dillon, Jennifer Esposito, Brendan Fraser, Chris "Ludacris" Bridges, Loretta Devine, Thandie Newton, Ryan Phillipe and Larenz Tate. All put in superb performances in a tight script which is at once gritty, heartwarming, shocking, tragic and witty, and which will ring true with viewers of all demographics.

Centering around two disturbing car accidents, a carjacking, vicious workplace vandalism, and the suspicious shooting death of one police officer by another, the drama is set against the backdrop of a racist LAPD and Los Angeles justice system. Action shifts between the various characters, whose lives collide with each other in unpredictable ways as each faces their own moral dilemma, and tries to cope with the consequences of their resulting decision made or action taken. Each of the dozen or so main characters undergoes some type of a personal metamorphosis as the various story lines head toward a striking, common conclusion, which succeeds at being both cathartic and unsettling.

Crash is backed by a solid and varied, original soundtrack and excellent cinematography. Sweeping, wider shots alternate with disjointed camera angles which convey the chaos and confusion of the characters and the unpredictability of life. Occasional lingering close-ups -- on occasion without sound -- capture the actors' facial expressions, which suitably detail key moments of the characters' aching pain, fear, anger, bitter anguish, remorse or grief, far better than any dialogue could.

This breathtaking film is destined to be a critical smash and box-office hit

This movie certainly isn't the worst thing I have ever seen, but I have never wanted to puke so desperately than when I saw it win Best Picture.  It's sickening to see the Academy get duped into nominating a shitty movie because it deals with the controversial issue of racial tensions.  "Oooo, this movie has both black AND white people in it, it must be really edgy!" *NEWSFLASH* There is nothing controversial or edgy or provocative in this film, other than how such a ridiculously clumsy script can be sold, directed, produced, and then go on to win fucking Best Picture.  "People in LA don't touch each other... so... we crash into each other... just to feel something."  No, idiot, Angelenos crash into each other because they can't fucking drive.  "I want the locks changed, because his homies are gonna come and break into our house because we're rich white people and they HATE US!!!"  Yeah, except your recent attack came from two African-American street criminals, so your sudden, abject fear of a Hispanic locksmith makes perfect sense.  While you're at it, why don't you take your anger out on your Hispanic housekeeper, despite the fact that you're too damn lazy and privileged to do your own dishes, you stupid bitch.  "Yeah, anger, it's nice to see it sometimes!"  You know what also makes a really good movie?  Being completely obvious about personality conflicts between characters!  "Mommy, he doesn't have the cloak!"  We always venerate child characters in film because they're supposed to have some sort of innocent wisdom that solves all our problems.  Why do we do this?  Children are gullible and stupid.  Anyway, stupid lines aside, this movie is basically a glitzified mash-up of an after-school special, a soap opera, and a sensitivity-in-the-workplace training video.  There may be something akin to creativity in the intersection of so many different lives; but this is just good treatment, not good writing.  The characters are still idiots running around aimlessly like Roombas, bumping into each other and saying, "Omigod!  I don't know how to react to you!  Your skin has a different melanin quality than mine!"  But what about the message (or whatever)?  Intriguingly enough, at the end of the film, we see a character exhibit mild, humorous racism towards another motorist in a fender-bender; this character, however, was seen earlier in the film as both a victim of racism and a wall of defense against it.  But here she is, telling an Asian person to "speak American" to her.  It would appear that this film is simply giving the limp-dick message "People are racist."  But what it is actually saying is, "People are racist.  Oh well."  After the initial nausea of seeing the producers accept their award for Best Picture, I realized the hilarious irony of the situation; the teary-eyed, cheering crowd, all the people I talked to who loved it, the sparkling reviews of the hope and beauty this movie offered--ÂÂno one, not even the filmmakers, ever realized that they had made an utterly nihilist film.

A wonderful ensemble cast with nary a weak link flesh out this hyperlinking story about race in the postmodern city. Slipping into cliches and preaching on only a couple of slight occassions, the film veers away from having an obvious message about race by complicating each and every example of race/racism: racist characters can perform good deeds and good characters can perform racist deeds. Does that then mean that this film actually condones racism? I prefer to think that this film is actually more about the cyclical nature of racism, neatly and microcosmically summarised in Ludacris' waitress story from the beginning of the film: she gives him bad service because he won't tip, and he doesn't tip because he receives bad service. This reflects the film's themes of how people are treated because of their race and how they subsequently react. The complications of the issue are also reflected in the story's very sructure: complicated by a number of interwoven tales (and also yes, ultimately a cyclical one). Most definitely worth watching.

Crash is a passion play about how complete strangers weave in and out of each other'ÂÂs lives--and ultimately collide, changing their lives forever. From the wreckage of these collisions is a provocative and very real look at the racial and class prejudices that exist in urban Los Angeles--the crucible of multi-cultural, multi-ethnic America. There is no clear good guy or bad guy in the film, only people who are all conditioned by latent racial prejudice, sometimes even animosity. Out of these dramatic experiences, this film demonstrates the ways racism is propagated and perpetuated, sometimes even showing how these prejudices and stereotypes become self-fulfilling prophecies.  This is a fantastic film. The story is gut-wrenching and moving, and its brilliance comes from the way it seeks to elicit strong emotional reactions, making them apart of the viewersÃ¢ÂÂ aesthetic experience as they are taken on this journey into the depths of the human condition.
