Definitely one of the best movies I've ever seen, and bound to become a classic, in my opinion. Instead of one storyline, this film contains three or four or more "different" storylines that are all linked together somehow. Through these storylines, the movie tells a story of racism, and how almost all of us exhibit it in some way, even if we maybe don't mean to, such as the incident between the "good cop" and the black hitchhiker, who is also an important character. Through these seemingly random encounters we are shown how the lives of complete strangers can collide into each other with such force, how stupid our racist stereotypes and prejudices are, and how much our lives really are just leaves in the wind, bumbing into each other and causing each other to change direction. Although some of the jokes made in this movie feel out of place, they all serve their purpose of making us think about what we are laughing about. Lastly, while this movie may not be incredibly subtle in a few places, it makes up for that lack of subtlety with incredibly emotional and often slightly ironic scenes, especially the ones involving the car crash and the one with the locksmith's daughter at the end. The latter scene can make you cry even after two or three times, and the movie as a whole is probably one of the most emotional I've seen.

Graham: "It's the sense of touch. In any real city, you walk, you know? You brush past people, people bump into you. In L.A., nobody touches you. We're always behind this metal and glass. I think we miss that touch so much, that we crash into each other, just so we can feel something." Issues of race and gender cause a group of strangers in Los Angeles to physically and emotionally collide in this drama from director and screenwriter Paul Haggis. Graham (Don Cheadle) is a police detective whose brother is a street criminal, and it hurts him to know his mother cares more about his ne'er-do-well brother than him. Graham's partner is Ria (Jennifer Esposito), who is also his girlfriend, though she has begun to bristle at his emotional distance, as well as his occasional insensitivity over the fact he's African-American and she's Hispanic. Rick (Brendan Fraser) is an L.A. district attorney whose wife, Jean (Sandra Bullock), makes little secret of her fear and hatred of people unlike herself. Jean's worst imaginings about people of color are confirmed when her SUV is carjacked by two African-American men -- Anthony (Chris Bridges, aka Ludacris), who dislikes white people as much as Jean hates blacks, and Peter (Larenz Tate), who is more open minded. Cameron (Terrence Howard) is a well-to-do African-American television producer with a beautiful wife, Christine (Thandie Newton). While coming home from a party, Cameron and Christine are pulled over by Officer Ryan (Matt Dillon), who subjects them to a humiliating interrogation (and her to an inappropriate search) while his new partner, Officer Hansen (Ryan Phillippe), looks on. Daniel (Michael Pena) is a hard-working locksmith and dedicated father who discovers that his looks don't lead many of his customers to trust him. And Farhad (Shaun Toub) is a Middle Eastern shopkeeper who is so constantly threatened in the wake of the 9/11 attacks that he decided he needs a gun to defend his family. Review From the opening monologue by Don Cheadle, to the finale, this movie is a masterpiece. The acting is very well done by most, however, there were a few exceptional performances, such as Terrence Howard and surprisingly, Ludacris. The story is overall well written, there wasn't a moment when I wasn't enthralled by the whatever was going on. Paul Haggis is a visionary who stepped into where most big-budget directors dare not tread. His dedication to this film is amazing, I mean, the man had a heart attack, but still refused to let someone else direct. Overall, this film is well worth the watch. I recommend it to any avid cinema fan.

Then the characters are just brushed off (the Hispanic people disappear from the movie and the Islamic guy was like "that girl's my angel").

[font=Arial]Two black men talk about some bad service they recieved in a cafe, one of them feels that they have been racially profiled by the waitress, who also happens to be black. The other man finds this rather funny, especially considering that his friend is upset about a coffee refill he really didn't want in the first place. The conversation turns around about a white woman who bundles up to her husband upon sight of them, again one of them upset by the initial perception that they are going to rob her or harm her in any way (even though that is exactly what they are going to do). They steal the white couple's car, not knowing that he just happens to be the District Attorney. 

This is a scene that happens early in Crash, the new film by Paul Haggis (recently screenwriter of Million Dollar Baby). Crash is part-ensemble drama, part-morality tale. And as of this moment, the best film I have seen this year so far. This is a film that tears deep into your conscience and your fears and orchistrates a series of scenes that put you on the front lines of high racial tension. This is also one of the most daring films to tackle racism, not by playing on it's brutality, but on it's day-to-day application. This film sees racism as a matter of fact, and one that everybody is guilty of. 

The film starts off with a series of scenes including the one I started my review with, as well as a random traffic stop by two L.A. police officers (Matt Dillon and Ryan Philliappe) that ends up as sexual misconduct when one of them feels up the wife of a black television director (Thandie Newton and Terrence Howard, respectively). We also follow two detectives (Don Cheadle and Jennifer Espesito) who are investigating a police-on-police shooting this isn't as it seems. The two carjackers (Chris "Ludacris" Bridges and Lorenz Tate) get themselves involved in a hit and run as well as a botched jacking in the next 36 hours. The two officers run into the couple one more time in to completely different situations as they attone for what happened the previous night. And one of the detectives is called upon to play city hall politics to possibly frame an innocent man for a race crime. And belive it or not, but these are just a few of the stories. 

But one of my favorite parts of this movie involves a hispanic locksmith (Michael Pena)who is not blasted on racially once, but twice. They see him as a thug when he's actually a family man doing everything he can to keep the mean streets of LA from terrorizing his daughter. There are two scenes with this duo and both of them are the best scenes in the movie. Both will put you to tears for completely different reasons that I'd be evil for spoiling. While most of the people in this story have both a good and bad side, it's nice to meet some just-nice people who we can feel sympathy for. Especially after you meet people like the D.A.'s wife (Sandra Bullock), whose natural reaction is to lash out at people for no good reason. 

Without a doubt, we are seeing some top-notch performances from the key players, but it's the smaller performances that steal my attention. Don't get me wrong, Bullock, Fraiser, Cheadle, and Dillon earned their paychecks with a healthy bonus on top. But the real eye-opening performances came from Terrence Howard and Thandie Newton for their great volitile chemestry. Another excellent performance is my sure nominee for Best Supporting Actor, Chris "Ludacris" Bridges as Anthony. I love his performance as a man who feels deep resentment for his treatment by white America while being the stereotype that white people make him out to be. I love characters that find balance in contradiction. Just watch the scene of him on the bus.

As for Paul Haggis, this is his best film that I'm aware of. He has mastered how to place perspective in his storytelling and in his angles. He knows which stories need to be told and places stress on scenes that get to the bottom of their issues. You see behind the labels, see who they are under the masks. 

All in all, this is a movie that I think people need to see, not just because of the strong ideas that this film brings out, but because it is deeply moving and even tragicly personal. This is one of those movies you can talk about for hours at a time and get many new ways of seeing what this film is about. Like much of great cinema, the points of interest for this film varies on your expiriences (and in this film, even your nationality).[/font]

However, there are worse message movies out there. Give it a shot - see where it takes you.

Issues of race and gender cause a group of strangers in Los Angeles to physically and emotionally collide in this drama from director and screenwriter Paul Haggis. Graham (Don Cheadle) is a police detective whose brother is a street criminal, and it hurts him to know his mother cares more about his ne'er-do-well brother than him. Graham's partner is Ria (Jennifer Esposito), who is also his girlfriend, though she has begun to bristle at his emotional distance, as well as his occasional insensitivity over the fact he's African-American and she's Hispanic. Rick (Brendan Fraser) is an L.A. district attorney whose wife, Jean (Sandra Bullock), makes little secret of her fear and hatred of people unlike herself. Jean's worst imaginings about people of color are confirmed when her SUV is carjacked by two African-American men -- Anthony (Chris Bridges, aka Ludacris), who dislikes white people as much as Jean hates blacks, and Peter (Larenz Tate), who is more open minded. Cameron (Terrence Howard) is a well-to-do African-American television producer with a beautiful wife, Christine (Thandie Newton). While coming home from a party, Cameron and Christine are pulled over by Officer Ryan (Matt Dillon), who subjects them to a humiliating interrogation (and her to an inappropriate search) while his new partner, Officer Hansen (Ryan Phillippe), looks on. Daniel (Michael Pena) is a hard-working locksmith and dedicated father who discovers that his looks don't lead many of his customers to trust him. And Farhad (Shaun Toub) is a Middle Eastern shopkeeper who is so constantly threatened in the wake of the 9/11 attacks that he decided he needs a gun to defend his family. Crash was the first directorial project for award-winning television and film writer Haggis.

This movie was well-produced -- very well-done technically, good acting, good story line. I even liked the concept of "crash," whereby we are so disengaged from each other and so car-identifying, unit-identifying, that it takes such extreme  encounters in order to see each other. For that, I give this film props. However,the film does not say much interesting about race, as it proclaims to. What we get instead is a very safe presentation of the issues around race, issues that are already acceptable to talk about, and can be presented in a tidy, polished storyline, characters, and movie release. The race discussion in this film is not at all the complex thing that is race, as it exists in America. Case in point: the portrayal of the Asians are stereotypical and lead to no understanding at all of what  the Asian characters go through as complex human beings. If you want to make a story about race, you can't talk about race in some cases and refuse to address it in others. This film is an example of the trade-off or diluting the content for the slickness of the final production. It's an ok movie, but then, why make a movie about race that doesn't add to the discussion?

A movie that has 10-11 obvious arcs that all have to do with your life.  I felt compelled to write this review moments after finishing this movie, Crash was a book that I just couldn't put down.  I watched it at a period when I couldn't watch it all the way through and I HAD to finish it (even when I had homework).  It had all the right moves performed in all the right ways.  This movie takes itself VERY seriously, it takes racism VERY seriously, it takes fear VERY seriously.  It does make some mistakes (little things like the Hollywood-esk girl saving her father, snow in L.A., etc) but is easily forgivable by how personal it gets with you.  This movie brings you into the home of many people who are just angry.  Americans, hispanics, pakistanis, chinese, this is a movie about racism but it does NOT take the normal white man racist towards everyone road.  Crash is titled so because there are people from all kinds of different backgrounds and cultures being racist towards each other.  This is what makes this film work the most, because it doesn't become an anti-white man film, it is an anti-fear movie.  And this is summed up in the finish of the movie.  It isn't that we fear people of other cultures or races, it is that we fear the unknown.  Many of us just don't know enough about everyone else that we fear them.  The issue of trust is a big deal in this movie, but it never really gives the solutions.  It doesn't tell us to go pick up hitchhikers anytime we can, but it does tell us that everyone is a person.  Fear was the central theme of the movie, but ANGER is what the movie is all about.  If you notice, everyone in the movie becomes angered with something in their life.  The anger leads to racism and depression, which leads to assumptions and more anger.  The crash that we have with cultures comes from anger.  And this isn't anger from other people, this is anger about ourselves.  Our racism stems from our own hatred.  I won't even go into the whole pride thing, but anger is pride.  I could go on and on about this, but I got this movie, and this movie got me.  I walked upstairs and laid down next to my half Puerto Rican son and pondered what people would think about him because of his skin color and heritage.  I wasn't fearful for him, but I decided to trust people.  Trust that their anger will not carry over into our world.  People aren't always to be trusted, but trust yourself, and let your fear fade into your happiness.  Wow, that's deep and I'm not sure I get it.  See this movie.  My vote: 7.

Definitely one of the best movies I've ever seen, and bound to become a classic, in my opinion. Instead of one storyline, this film contains three or four or more "different" storylines that are all linked together somehow. Through these storylines, the movie tells a story of racism, and how almost all of us exhibit it in some way, even if we maybe don't mean to, such as the incident between the "good cop" and the black hitchhiker, who is also an important character. Through these seemingly random encounters we are shown how the lives of complete strangers can collide into each other with such force, how stupid our racist stereotypes and prejudices are, and how much our lives really are just leaves in the wind, bumbing into each other and causing each other to change direction. Although some of the jokes made in this movie feel out of place, they all serve their purpose of making us think about what we are laughing about. Lastly, while this movie not very subtle, it makes up for that lack of subtlety with incredibly emotional and often slightly ironic scenes, especially the ones involving the car crash and the one with the locksmith's daughter at the end. The latter scene can make you cry even after two or three times, and the movie as a whole is probably one of the most emotional I've seen

Everyone is a little bit (or a lot) ,racist, no matter
how well intentioned, or what ethnic background,
according to the thought provoking if somewhat slow
paced âCrash.â 

Written and directed by Paul Haggis who also penned
the Oscar sweeper âMillion Dollar Baby,â âCrashâ is an
ensemble piece with some intertwining, and some stand
alone stories of struggles and biases.

The film is not for all audiences, as it is very
unapologetic, and embraces many racist jokes, slurs,
and stereotypes.

That is the point however, to make audiences question
and think about their own biases, and to show that no
matter how far we think we have come as a society,
racism is still in everyone, and in some ways it is
almost more rampant than it once was- it is simply
better hidden.

The cast consists of many familiar faces such as
Sandra Bullock, Brendan Fraser, Don Cheadle, Ryan
Phillipe, Matt Dillon, and Larenz Tate.

There are also some moderately known actors such as
Thandie Newton, Terrence Howard, and Jennifer
Esposito. Rapper Ludacris also appears and does a
surprisingly good acting job.

Many of the unknown actors give the better
performances, most notably Michael Pena as Daniel, a
hardworking and caring father who is constantly
wrongly perceived for being Hispanic and tattooed.

Ethnic groups represented in the film are Caucasian,
African-American, Hispanic, Asian, and Middle-Eastern.

The Caucasians are portrayed as the most racist and
cruel, save Ryan Phillipeâs character, who is the best
intentioned of the bunch, but still makes a terrible
move as a result of an unrecognized prejudice.

The African-American ( a term not used much in the
film) characters are very ranged, from successful and
career driven, to stereotypical car jackers and street
criminals, to junkies. The successful are all accused
of âdenying their blacknessâ and the criminals spout
about âthe white man.â These issues have been
addressed in many many movies before, but do
intertwine well in the story, and all actors do an
excellent job in these storylines.

The Asian characters have minimal screen time, and are
very much pigeonholed into stereotypes (bad drivers,
immigrants) There really is no voice or point of view
to fairly represent this group.

The Hispanic characters get some of the best
representation in the film, showing a hardworking
honest loving family, in which the father (Pena) is
constantly judged wrongly based on race, and the
daughter grows up in fear of gunfire near her home.
This family is the only set of characters in the film
not necessarily racist towards another group.

In a separate plot, Jennifer Espositoâs character is
constantly called Mexican, when she is of Hispanic
descent, but not Mexican.

Similar assumptions are made about the Middle-Eastern
characters, also well represented, as a loving
struggling family from Persia who are assumed to be
Arabic, and violent.

Excepting Daniel and his family, every character in
âCrashâ good or not, misunderstood themselves or not,
has an outright bias and prejudice of their own
against another ethnic group.

Many characters succumb to the stereotypes presumed
about their race.

The characters in the beginning who are the most
hateful tend to learn a lesson by the end, and the
ones who seem to be the most caring end up discovering
their biases or being filled with hate and rage.

These elements are predictable, but the plot twists
themselves are not , overall.

Again the best plot involves Daniel and his daughter,
in the most engaging scene in the film.

None of the filmâs messages are all that new, but they
are important none the less, and âCrashâ does raise
many thoughts and questions of its audience, and puts
a new spin on the message of racism in todayâs world..

It is also good that this film focuses more on Middle
Eastern characters, as most films of this nature have
not done so.

The film is very draggy in a few places, and it is
definitely not for children.

Many audiences will be put off- it is not Sandra
Bullockâs typical romantic comedy, or Brendan Fraserâs
usual fall down antics. Audiences who base movie
choices on the cast and what those actors have done
previously may find themselves a bit shocked.

For those who know what the film is going in, âCrashâ
is well worth it for the stellar performances
throughout, and the important if not grim message.

It is also the only good movie Jennifer Esposito has
ever been in.

I don't care what anybody says, this movie is phenomenal. I used to say that this was a film driven on the theme of racism.  However, upon viewing it again, I have changed my opinion.  This is a film about real people put in dire situations.  And the characters are forced to choses between the right way, the just way, and the selfish way.  And, what Paul Haggis has accomplished so brilliantly is the ability to portray the notion that there is no right way.  It's all grey matter.  The people are real, the situations are real, and if you cannot feel for at least one of them, them I am forced to believe that you have not even the slightest bit of compassion in your mortal soul.  There is no story line left un-decided, no plot line left up in the air.  This is a solid, thought provoking, and, above all, emotional film which I will defend until the end.  It deserved that Academy Award.  The End.

One-Sentence Review
"Although the isolation and interconnectedness of automobiles and traffic are one of the driving metaphors of Paul Haggis's film Crash, the experience of the film's characters is more like a roller-coaster, where random strangers are thrown together through twisters and turns of a journey out of there control" (Racism film never been this powerful.Race is paramount in this film, and all our preconceptions of who people are get twisted and turned through the intricate plot. With each new additional character we find another assumption, another stereotype, and then watch as that preconception is obliterated as the character develops. It is a credit to the deftly written script, tight direction and exceptional acting talent that every one of these many characters is fully realized on screen without ever feeling one-dimensional.The all-encompassing theme of the film is racism, and it is dealt with bluntly, honestly, and without reservation. Every single character participates in the perpetuation of the ugly cycle but also suffers because of it. Where racism makes for an interesting enough subject for an already provoking and fairly experimental film (I was surprised to see this get wide release), it's only the catalyst for a deeper, resounding story of redemption and the universality of our lonely situation which the movie becomes during its second hour. It switches from a somewhat depressing contemplative amalgamation of moments about racism in everyday life and how destructive it is, to a throbbing, intense web of choices and consequences -- life and death, vivifying or soul killing - and the chance at redemption.)

I knew nothing about this film when it was first released, and to be honest, it was because I wasn't all that interested.  The theme of the movie seems to be an attitude aggressively against racism, xenophobia, and guns--but I can't fault the film for sticking to tried-and-true material.  Usually, when you go into a film that's based on assumptions like "guns are bad because they sometimes kill good people," the film suffers because it's trying to be preachy, but I see none of that here.  The plot works thusly: through a series of miscommunications and unfair assumptions on the part of some characters (and sometimes just plain bad luck), others end up in dire straits: in the first ten minutes, when everyone was being introduced, I wondered why everyone seeme dto be such a-holes.  What I took away from the movie was that we all need to slow down a bit more and listen to each other.  And you might expect that a film involving so many characters would flow irregularly, or cut uncomfortably to another scene, but the pacing is truly excellent.  No character is wasted--everyone there has a definite purpose, and it all leads up to a chilling but satisfying conclusion.

"Collision" en VF. J'ai achete le DVD en promo apres avoir lu des bonnes critiques et vu quelques extraits qui me semblaient prometteurs. Au final, je suis reste un peu sur ma faim. Sur la forme, il n'y a rien a dire, c'est pro, carre, belle photo, bons acteurs (Matt Dillon en particulier), c'est bien monte avec une tres bonne fluidite dans l'entrelacement des differentes intrigues. Je trouve juste que le film peche par exces de "didactisme". On sent que Paul Haggis a voulu faire un film a message, engage, pour denoncer l'etat de peur permanente dans lequel vivent les Etats-Unis depuis le 11 septembre, la guerre de tous contre tous, l'"incommunicabilite" entre les etres, le racisme,  les armes en vente libre, le systeme de sante foireux, les assureurs proceduriers, etc, etc...  le probleme, c'est que tout est surligne a l'exces, ce qui donne le sentiment d'une intrigue pretexte car trop theorique. Quelques facilites scenaristiques viennent  plomber le realisme et la credibilite de l'ensemble, deja fragilise par des personnages ultra-stereotypes, pour ne pas dire grotesques (le couple bourge Bullock/Fraser, la famille iranienne...) ce qui est un comble dans un film qui condamne les prejuges sociaux et raciaux. "Collision" n'est pas pour autant un mauvais film, c'est plutot plaisant a regarder et on ne s'ennuie pas. Mais, sur des themes assez proches, je prefere largement la spontaneite, l'impertinence mais aussi la pertinence d'un Spike Lee dans des films comme "Do the right thing", "Summer of Sam" ou "la 25e heure".

I had no idea what this movie was when I first rented it. I had never heard of it. I didn't know who was in it or even what it was about. I just knew that, when I worked at Blockbuster Video, everyone was asking for it when it came out. So, I decided to see what all the hype was about. After I had finished the movie, I was impressed. I thought it definitely lived up to all the talk I had heard. It had a terrific cast with a story that never slowed down. It provided a strong, emotional look at the racism running rampant. We are reminded of how everything we do affects the lives of those around us. One of the aspects I loved about this film was that it inspired thought after the credits began to roll.  This movie follows an ensemble cast and has multiple small story lines weaving through it. Don Cheadle and Jennifer Esposito play detectives investigating the murder of a black LAPD officer who was shot by a white colleague. Terrence Howard and Thandie Newton play a couple whose lives are changed after they are pulled over by the police and things go wrong. Brendan Fraser is a DA who, with his wife (Sandra Bullock), is carjacked by Chris 'Ludicrous' Bridges and Larenz Tate. This is only a sampling of the stories involved; each one colliding together in a 24 period.  Paul Haggis did a great job with his movie. Each of the case does a spectacular job. I enjoyed watching actors/actresses working roles I had never pictured them in, namely Sandra Bullock and Brendan Fraser. I wasn't used to seeing them in such serious roles and it was cool to witness the range of their abilities. Ludicrous really surprised me with how well he did in this movie. With so little acting experience, he really seemed to put 100% into his role and did well. There really weren't any weak spots in this film's casting and it would take forever to mention how well they each did.  There seem to be a lot of people who really don't like this movie, but I fail to see why. Each of the stories is developed enough to enjoy, despite having so many in one film. The acting is great and the flow of the story keeps from boring its audience. It's emotionally powerful (my wife STILL cries when watching it) and it sends an important message. As I said before, this movie also shows how much people effect each other in their daily lives. This is definitely a 'love it or hate it' movie and I think it's worth giving it a shot to find out where you stand.

The film is set in Los Angeles over a period of 36 hours, during which the lives of the various characters will all intersect in some way. A paranoid Brentwood housewife (Sandra Bullock) and her DA husband (Brendan Fraser) are car-jacked by two black teens (Chris Ludacris Bridges and Larenz Tate). The Mexican locksmith (Michael Peña) who changes their locks has a horrific encounter with a Persian store-owner (Shuan Toub). A black television director (Terrence Howard) and his well-to-do wife (Thandie Newton) have a humiliating experience at the hands of a pair of cops (Matt Dillon and Ryan Phillippe) and later meet them again in different circumstances. Meanwhile, another pair of detectives (Don Cheadle and Jennifer Esposito) attempt to deal with the strains of their interracial relationship.
    Without giving too much away, the film sets out to reverse your expectations of the characters at every turn, specifically in regard to their various attitudes concerning race. The first time this happens it shocks you but makes you laugh simultaneously; then you realise it's pretty much going to happen to everyone. Whether you like the film will very much depend on how much you're prepared to go along with this and accept the various coincidences involved.
    In the hands of another director this could have been horribly preachy and mawkish, but Haggis gets terrific performances from his cast and the dialogue is both well written and believable. Dillon is probably the stand-out - it's one of his best performances - but there's equally strong work from Thandie Newton (better here than shes ever been), Terrance Howard and Michael Peña.
William Fichtner has a great cameo in which he comes across as a sort of mini-Christopher Walken. Surprisingly, Bullock and Fraser are hardly in it and the characters you come away remembering are the ones played by little-known actors.
    There are some terrific scenes here. Highlights include Dillons two very different encounters with Newtons character and Peñas scenes with Shaun Toub. Its also beautifully shot, with impressive cinematography by J. Michael Muro.
    In short, Crash is an engaging, provocative and thought-provoking drama with an intelligent script and terrific performances from its ensemble cast. Itll be interesting to see what Haggis does next. Highly recommended.

Crash (2005) Directed by Paul Haggis Starring Don Cheadle, Mat Dillon, Terrence Howard, Michael Pena, Brendan Fraser, Sandra Bullock, Chris "Ludacris" Bridges, Larenz Tate, Ryan Phillipe, Tandie Newton, Shaun Toub, William Fichtner

«Graham: It's the sense of touch. In any real city, you walk, you know? You brush past people, people bump into you. In L.A., nobody touches you. We're always behind this metal and glass. I think we miss that touch so much, that we crash into each other, just so we can feel something.»

Crash is somewhat complicated to review without intentionally revealing most of the film. It is a story of a 36 hour time period in Los Angeles, mostly concentrating on the racial problems between different kinds of the people that live in LA. It also tells us about the corruption, prejudice and family problems that occur between the people of different races.

The whole idea of racism in LA is somewhat an example of how bad the racism problem can get. Los Angeles is the second largest city in America, and its one of the most glamorous cities in the world. It is home of Hollywood, the ultimate place of fame. There are thousands of people that dream to live there. And the fact that the city is full of corruption and crime is somewhat truthful. If such a glamorous city became a victim of racism, what could the other cities possibly be like? If there is no respect for a coloured director or a police officer will there ever be any respect for a normal person?

The story is somewhat extraordinary. It is very emotional and extremely sad in many ways. The characters in the movie all connect together and it is somewhat hard to describe them all without revealing much. The acting, the beautifully haunted music, and the cinematography it is all combined perfectly in this movie.

Main theme of the movie is that prejudice prevents people from seeing the actual things. Whenever it's a Persian man being mistaken for an Iranian, or a Spaniard woman being mistaken for a Mexican, all is due to the high prejudice and people's behaviour towards somebody who is different from them in some way. Even the people that are completely unknown to you is judged badly, would it be a locksmith who is falsely mistaken for a "gangbanger" just because he might dress like one or simply when he is in fact a family man, or a pair of black kids that might sound like typical stereotypic black kids when in fact they are just a pair of normal African-American kids that are scared of the society that kills people like them.

This behaviour also makes the characters say exactly what they think which eventually leads to some bad consequences. A wife of the district attorney is so frightened that she calls a false alarm and takes whatever is necessarily to protect her from the danger that doesn't exist. A white cop accuses a black woman worker from HMO of not doing all the possible in order to help his dying father and being racist towards her in the process.

It may also look as it is perfectly scripted out by Paul Haggis and yes it is. The directing he does and the choice of the cast is amazing. I particularly liked the story of a racist white officer John Ryan (Matt Dillon) who looks after his dying father. He stops a black rich couple for something they shouldn't be doing while driving and sexually molest the women while her husband has to watch all this because he cannot do anything against cops - they have guns and they are the law. His partner officer Tommy Hansen (Ryan Phillippe) watches everything and has no choice but to assist Ryan, but he also cannot help but feel guilty for what is happening. This shows Ryan as a vile and disrespectful person, but we see the better side of him later when he is carrying for his sick father and trying his best in order to help him.

Ironically, later in the film both cops find themselves in the different situations and locations, saving the lives of the director and his wife. Is it really ironic? Perhaps, but it also have a deeper purpose and meaning; the characters learn a lesson from their behaviour and move on to do better things. Perhaps not always because one of them makes a crucial mistake that changes his life forever as we learn later in the film.

Don Cheadle as Detective Graham Waters, whose family problems stops him from doing the right thing, gives an extremely powerful performance. The rest of the cast is also amazing, especially, Terrence Howard, Michael Pena and Peter Waters. The music connects perfectly with the movie. Just when you think it can't get any better, the music comes in and completely changes your opinion about the movie and the whole scene that you are watching at the time. The cinematography and the editing have been done to the state of perfection, and it is a hard job to connect a complex movie like that and they did great job by completely nailing it.

Crash may be cliché and predictable but in the end its not the suspense or originality that serve the purpose, but the whole idea of what you do and how it affects your life. The movie is trying to teach you a lesson, sometimes by acting on our emotions and making obvious statements but it works for some of us. If it doesn't work for you, then carry on living your normal life. Eventually you will come across one of the situation you saw in the movie and maybe then you will understand how important this movie is.

First off, let's get things straight: this did not deserve to wind Best Picture over Brokeback Mountain. It's easy to see why a film about a 'serious' issue would win over something just as problematic in America, if much more subtly done. Maybe that's why, but I'll come to that later.
This 'Crash' is far removed from the literal titling of David Cronenberg's 1996 film, as explained by Don Cheadle's cop in the opening scene. It's more metaphorical, in that the lives of the conflicting characters happen to 'crash' into each other, much to their own chagrin. And here, in the film's very name, is the big flaw that stops it from being anywhere near as good as 'Brokeback'. Whereas 'Brokeback' is quiet, casual and sober in its demonstration of prejudice and hatred, 'Crash' is so blatantly obvious in intention and agenda that it's more of an essay than a thriller attempting to hold suspense in terms of plot and narrative. It brings to mind Spike Lee's 'Do The Right Thing', in terms of having characters represent morals and viewpoints, but Lee's film makes the characters develop their opinions into a fiery climax; 'Crash' already sets everyone up as a racist or with having racial prejudice, even going so far as dedicating 2/3 of the film into filling in everyone's profile through dialogue. It's this condescending structuring that, rather than provoking the (American) audience into thinking about their stupid prejudices, it just shows a group of racists increasingly winding each other up. And over such a short period. Even people outside the US won't be convinced that people so racist could become so interwoven in so short a time, especially without any major incident to spark things off. If this is a slice of life it's a wonder these characters have managed to live so long being under such radical and dangerous minds.
The film works best in the final act, when less is said with words than actions. In a single scene we see how racism is truly represented, with Ryan Phillippe's cop succumbing to stereotype and prejudice in a second's thought, rather than the laboured set up of him as a good guy. It's this spontaneity and subtlety that strikes home much more convincingly than the constant rants that permeate the beginning. This end resembles more of 'Magnolia' with its collection of damaged individuals finally too exhausted to speak any more, but just exist as they are. But then another spanner has to be thrown into the works with Matt Dillon's GP (or the American equivalent) spouting off in a contrived manner to so-called immigrants who can't speak 'American'; no doubt to remind the audience that racism still goes on and that we should wake up and realise it and blah blah blah. Is this kind of simple-minded stuff really worthy of Best Picture? Or maybe that says more about the Academy's standards nowadays.
There are powerful sequences and it's well made and acted, but ultimately it tries to make us swallow to much. Ludacris helping out those Asians? His sobriquet speaks for itself.
If you can ignore the ethno-centric moralising it's good entertainment, but nothing intellectual, certainly not to the other six and a half billion people on Earth who are not American.

Crash is probably one of the most thought-provoking, well-written and beautifully acted films I have seen; it is outright brave! In a collage of collisions, traffic and human, the disturbing underbelly of racism in America is exposed in all its forms, each plot line producing outrageous events and even more surprising resolutions. With a cross-section of the public, multi-ethnic characters, cops, the advantaged and the disadvantaged, Crash manages to reach beneath the smooth exterior of everyday life, revealing the fractures that run through day to day relationships, the cherished prejudices, offensive remarks and outrageous attitudes that often go unchallenged, perpetuating more of the same misinformation. The acting is finely nuanced, Don Cheadle's disaffected police detective, Graham, Matt Dillon's jaded and racist cop agonizing over an ill father at the mercy of an uncaring health provider, a bickering black couple (Thandie Newton and Terence Howard), who are humiliated by police officers (Matt Dillon and Ryan Philippe), the husband's manhood put to the test and found wanting, an Iraqi shop-owner, confounded by his new country and a language he cannot navigate. Brilliantly scripted and acted, this film is an example of the quality Hollywood should be providing instead of trite comedies and lackluster superheroes, as potent as Spike Lee's Do the Right Thing, exposing, transforming, confounding in every scene. With all the obvious disaffections of our society, absolutely nothing is predictable, the characters challenged at every turn, their precious beliefs transformed by changing events. Stereotypes abound, as do personal epiphanies, death defeated by a fickle choice, an astonishing exercise in the vagaries of fate and the promise of hope, no matter how spectral in the broader perspective. There are no facile answers and all issues aren't resolved, but the film is a wake up call to those deadened by the endless cacophony of daily defeats and the helpless rage that accompanies almost every endeavor. In moments of personal challenge and an almost overwhelming failure to achieve harmony on even the most elemental level, Crash reminds us of our humanity and ability to transcend our basest responses to crisis. Only months after winning an Oscar for his overwrought but strangely popular screenplay to Million Dollar Baby, Paul Haggis struck back with a movie that took the histrionics and emotional manipulations of Baby to a whole new level. Crash attempts to take on the issue of racism in America by stringing together scenes so over-the-top, unrealistic and sometimes laugh out loud funny that you'll come out believing that only crazy people and overacting Hollywood stars feel even the slightest twinges of racial prejudice. After all, have you ever been so overcome by hated of African-Americans that you were unable to walk properly and fell down the stairs? Probably not, but it happens to Sandra Bullock in one unforgettable scene. Maybe you were so enraged about affirmative action you decided to sexually assault the wife of an African-American television director. And then save her from a burning car while still sexually assaulting her. No? Well, perhaps you were so worried about minorities robbing your convenience store that you decided to point a gun at an adorable little Hispanic girl. When racism is portrayed in such a cartoonish fashion, it becomes easy to forget that racial biases and misconceptions exist within every man, woman and child and often manifest themselves in subtle ways. It's unlikely you would ever point a gun at a minority figure, but you might decide that you are more comfortable living in a neighborhood where everyone looks more or less like you, leading to the de facto segregation in housing and education we see in America today. Making a film about issues like this might help viewers to confront and slowly overcome the unique forms of prejudice they keep buried deep within their own hearts. However, that would require taste, talent and imagination, and these are not Mr. Haggis' strong suits. He prefers to present a 100 minute cavalcade of overheated confrontations to lull audiences into the false assumption that anyone who doesn't run around hurling racial epithets and sexually molesting African-American women is immune to racism. This is truly a contemptible film and easily the worst Best Picture winner in the entire history of the Academy.

A major disappointment. I was hoping (and expecting, given the praise) for a clever, intertwining character driven plot that would leave me pondering more about the state of our world similar to the way Traffic & Syriana left me feeling.. What I got was something that resembled me being given an urban racial education via Sesame Street. This is the perfect film for people who can't walk out their front door and see the real racism in the world. 

The film's script was so heavy-handed - I felt I was bludgeoned over the head with such OTT racist characters that for most of its running time, none of it rang true, and they seemed more like caricatures than real people. The technique to try and show what's dwelling inside each of them and bringing it to the forefront without subtly as some kind of mirror failed for me. Let alone most of the character's issues and plights. I'm not saying that it's not an accurate reflection of racial issues within the States (how would I know living down here?), but there's something to be said for subtlety in a film dealing with such issues. It's like everyone was thinking out loud. I didn't buy it.

It's actually no surprise it won a best picture oscar. It's perfect mainstream fodder taking a serious issue of racism into a film for that people who don't live with their head in the sand. Maybe it should be praised for that reason alone, but I found it hard to sit through due to cringe inducing scene after scene. Even though it does look pretty, has a good score and a handful of interesting performances (Sandra Bullock and Matt Dillon come to mind), it was almost insulting. I personally don't need a film to speak to me like I am ignorant - which I felt like it was doing. 

In the end, if I can watch Do the Right Thing or Mississippi Burning, I don't need watered down stuff like Crash.

While the Oscar winner might take you breathless with the span of its message(s), it seems like a rehash of the same style used in the not-so famous movie, "Magnolia".  Magnolia (Tom Cruise was actually good in this movie!) when it first came out, was well praised critically, but did not fare that well in the box office. Magnolia deftly fused seemingly disparate emotional life situations of different characters, and at the end (with the music slowly evolving to not unlike a sad denouement but with closure and purpose), every character realizes that they are all part of the big circle of life. The ending of Magnolia involves a weird scene of falling animals, shocking and at the same time, mysterious, like the movie that it portrays. 'Crash' on the other hand is more hard-core and deals mainly with the interaction of races in the proverbially diverse Southern California. We see the interaction of everyday people with cops, high power politicians with cops and everyday people, minorities that mingle with the society and how the seemingly 'white' establishment view them, when they are backed into a corner, or how the same establishment uses them to further their own agendas. 'Crash' is a rich 'melting pot' of hidden norms that can only excite people who live in diverse neighborhoods. While it allows racial situations to provide closure, the movie seems trite, seems forced, and seems almost preachy (check Ludacris' almost incessant banterings). We have cops who redeem themselves, but we also have cops who cause more pain in the process of helping these 'misguided' minorities.  Race relations is a powerful agenda, and Crash uses it to the extreme. Sometimes, it does overdo and overkill the obvious, and we are left wondering whether we live in such a disparate country of cultures or are we merely pawns to racial hysteria and we are left blind to the minority struggle of having 'to belong'.   Go see "Magnolia" and compare the movie styling. Compare the musical scores and the ending scenes. It is shockingly similar.

Among the many criticisms one could give this film the one that I haven't much heard but I think must be said is that it misses its own point.  We have the title and opening line to set it up:  Don Cheadle's character muses, "In L.A., nobody touches you. We're always behind this metal and glass. I think we miss that touch so much, that we crash into each other, just so we can feel something."

It may come as a surprise to many, but this movie was not specifically meant to be an exploration of racial tension and prejudice in America.  Instead, it was originally intended to be a negative "pay it forward"; an exploration of the butterfly effect in human interaction; how all our lives are inexplicably intertwined and how perhaps subconsciously we long for that interaction, though it might be painful.  Racial prejudice, negative stereotypes, and ethnic fears were all meant to be dominant catalysts for human interaction.

However, such volatile subject matter quickly takes such strong control over the narrative that the "interconnectedness" of the plot is de-emphasized from the film's point to one of its devices.  And as with any hyper-linked narrative, you'll either appreciate the cleverness of the inter-connectivity or be put off by its artificiality.

Even if one accepts the fact that the original intent of Crash is irrelevant to what finally was produced, it must then be asked, what's the point here?  Crash means well; it unabashedly states that everyone, regardless of intent, upbringing, or skin-color is racist as an intrinsic condition of being human, and then asks us to examine ourselves to know that when we've reached the breaking point of our normal politeness we might become something we never thought we were.

However, implicit to the point is that belief that there are no innocents, everyone is just as guilty as the next.  The movie does little to offer anything in the way of hope or solution and while it makes its point forcefully, by doing so its characters come off as exaggerations.  Accordingly, it becomes a film that racist people can feel good about watching without having to do much soul searching.  White people can now say, "Hey I have a black friend, AND I've seen Crash."

Personally, the film came off as too preachy with too hollow a message for my tastes.  I would have preferred a narrative that stayed closer to the producer/writer's original intent and examined the interconnective nature of human interaction and how we long for it (without such a strong moral agenda).  The ethical overtones made the structure seem artificial and turned the characters into caricatures.  I can appreciate the movie for (hopefully) the conversations it will generate, but I didn't particularly like or find it helpful.  If anything, by calling everyone a horrible racist bastard, it presents a nice way to alleviate some of my white guilt (nearly a complete subversion of its intent, I'm sure).  Whoops.  

Anyway, this is ultimately a better film than the non-Oscar winner of the same name, but not by much.  (Hope you catch this Adam - I love you man)

Several stories interweave during two days in LA involving a collection of inter-related characters, a police detective with a drugged out mother and a thieving younger brother, two car thieves who are constantly theorizing on society and race, the white district attorney and his irritated and pampered wife, a racist white veteran cop (caring for a sick father at home) who disgusts his more idealistic younger partner, a successful Hollywood director and his wife who must deal with the racist cop, a Persian-immigrant father who buys a gun to protect his shop, a Hispanic locksmith and his young daughter who is afraid of bullets, and more. My friend Ali recommend me this movie and the way he portrait it to me, i thought it must be a great movie, cause he hardly can miss in rating movies. It was award winning picture movie of 2005, and also one of the best reviewed movie. For me it turned out to be a big mistake on "everyone's" part. In the first 10 minutes I wanted to quit watching, but I thought its not fair, give the movie a chance and watch it full. I think the main problem I had with Crash was that it just wasn't believable, at all. A serious dramatic movie isn't worth crap if it isn't believable. If people really acted like they do in this film, LA would be in a state of war. I know there was the whole Rodney King thing in LA, that got a LOT of attention. The events in Crash portraits racism on a scale so ridiculously. I'm never convinced at any point in the film that these events could really happen. Now a days people of various nationalities seemed to get along with each other just fine. sure, there's racism out there, but Crash is about as accurate on racism as Rambo is on war. All the dialogue is pretty horrible, too. Totally unconvincing. I couldn't imagine a single character being an actual person in real life. Crash had too many of those oh-so-dramatic scenes where every line is something flowery and deep, and if you actually heard some one say it in real life you would laugh your head off. (Examples- the scene with the gun with blanks,) Some scenes were actually moving, like the car wreck, as hard to believe as it was. but these scenes were overshadowed by all the bad scenes. In the first half of the movie, almost every character was portrayed as a stereotype. I think this was done on purpose... I don't know if the point of that was for them to overcome the stereotypes. Even if they do overcome them, you have an ugly, offensive, and extremely weak first half of the movie. There's a lot to like under the surface of Crash... sure, lots of characters overcoming their inner demons, and fun stuff like that. but almost nothing on the surface to like. "Crash" shuns political correctness with an enthusiasm rarely observed in modern cinema: its characters say exactly what they think and feel providing for an uncomfortable but uniquely edgy experience. What Haggis seems to be saying is that we're all prejudiced in some way or another no matter how broadminded we like to think we are and his film takes a look at the aftereffects of that ignorance, of all that bottled-up resentment and intolerance. Bullock's character Jean sums the incendiary situation up best when she says she wakes up angry every morning and doesn't know why. It's because L.A.'s racial boundaries are so clinically defined, so stringent that the city's rich melting pot of inhabitants rarely comes into physical contact with one another on its bustling, dangerous streets. Bottom line, Crash is a masterpiece, thought provoking film that encourages dialogue on racism and ignorance. Given the tumultuous state of our current society this is indeed a positive thing.

I am struggling here, struggling to comprehend why on earth Paul Haggis thought he could pull off such an ambitious film in his debut film as a director. Struggling to comprehend how the actors managed to do well with such pathetically written characters, struggling to comprehend at how it treats the audience with absolutely no respect or intelligence whatsoever and how blind it is to its own faults which invalidates the attempted seriousness + realism of the entire film. It's no struggle to know why it won Best Picture: Because it's about racism and the fact that racism is bad, something simple enough for the average movie-goer to comprehend without putting too much thought into it, and because it touches on a risky subject only a few years after that fateful day people think it's a brave film, but there is a thin line between bravery and stupidity, Paul Haggis picks up that line and smashes you in the face with it every chance he gets.

The entire tone of the film is set by Don Cheadle's policeman at a crime scene very early on, as he explains how "we're all so disconnected that we have to crash into each other to really connect". Explaining the title of a movie within the first 5 minutes? I know that's a hard concept to wrap your head around but don't worry, by the end of the film Haggis will have tied up every loose end and explained literally everything, as various characters of different races all within L.A all bounce off each other: There's a persian shop owner with a wife and daughter, a politician who only cares what the public think and is married to Sandra Bullock, two young black guys, an old black guy married to Thandie Newton, a racist cop and his rookie partner and a couple other characters I couldn't care less about. Very few of these characters get properly fleshed out, they are all purposely written as stereotypes to make us question whether people actually do fit those stereotypes (only in this film they do, very rarely in real life they do fit). Is that smart writing because he's assuming that we can only fix certain stereotypes and cliche's to various races to get a better understanding of them? No it's actually purposely lazy writing which prevents him from dipping too much into all of the characters who don't get enough screentime to get enough light shed on them. 

What's even worse is the number of times these people meet up in L.A. you'd think that there are only a dozen or so people in the whole of that area. Getting characters to meet up via fate and chance is very hard to translate into film because so often it just seems a bit too much like coincidence that these characters met up at the same time or that it was convenient for the plot. The only director who managed to make sense of an idea of fate or chance without fully explaining it was Krzysztof Kieslowski who had an open-ended narrative style which could have been read in various different ways. But after the first couple of coincidences which you let slide in "Crash", the number of times the people meet at each location just becomes farcical as Paul Haggis actually explains how everyone is related + connected right at the end of the film, it's good to see he's learned the art of subtlety in his storytelling.

But the major theme of the film is racism, and it doesn't actually tackle racism, the entire film involves various races of people shouting and screaming racial slurs at each other every 3 seconds. The film basically turns into a 2 hour long lecture which smashes you in the face with the phrase "racism is bad" over and over again, it gets tiresome after a while to the point where you just lose interest in the characters. And yet the cast does so well with their meagre roles, with Terence Howard, Michael Pena + Matt Dillon being the standouts and everyone else doing decent with literally nothing to work with (although Sandra Bullock is still annoying Sandra Bullock). 

The absolute biggest fault of the film is Paul Haggis: It's not just the poorly written, unrealistic, hugely contrived, preachy and unsubtle screenplay and dialogue, it's the way he constantly goes for the easy way out, the quick emotional payoff, the tearjerking gimmicks (there is one scene where one character gets shot and Haggis actually uses a Hitchcock zoom to push the victim to the foreground and the background out to emphasise the point that someone getting shot is a big deal), the over-reliance on explaining everything and never letting the audience figure something out for themselves, he simply doesn't trust his audience or give them any respect whatsoever, it's utterly ridiculous, this is a ridiculous film that does a lot of barking but has absolutely no bite. It borrows from so many other great films and tries to bring everything together but winds up being a shallow, manipulative, blunt, utterly fake and utterly idiotic film that takes itself way too seriously. 

If you want to see a film with large ensemble casts, go watch something by Robert Altman. Something involving the ideas of fate and chance? Something by Krzysztof Kieslowski. A film about racism? Try La Joven by Luis Bunuel, or those classics 12 Angry Men, Do The Right Thing & To Kill A Mockingbird (American History X & The Believer are also good). If you want to see a film that involves a large ensemble cast AND ideas of fate and chance? Try Magnolia. Please avoid this repetitive nightmare, it's just pathetic.

The reason I thought I didn't like it could be found in the first five seconds -- the part furthest from the footage I'd seen. Normally you can tell a good movie from a bad one by the ending, and that was my fault. Don Cheadle's monologue-esque speech in the very beginning about why everybody in LA crashes into one another. It sets the tone for the entire film. When you have those words in mind, all the seemingly go-nowhere vignettes become entwined in a way that wouldn't do so otherwise, and it's extremely beautiful when they do. They come together to form a vividly touching tapestry depicting the lives we affect, and the people that affect ours, and then you realize what jerks we all are, and that if we'd take a breath and drop our prejudices there are no bad people but ourselves, and therein lies the biggest crash of all -- when we see ourselves acting so petty all the time.

Racism is a ubiquitous condition in the United States. Only rarely these days does it appear in its most virulent forms, like when a swatzika is crudely spray painted on a Jew's home or a rope is tied in an intimidating noose on the branch of a tree in a black family's house. No, often it just rears its ugly head as a racial slur, a crude joke, a humiliating act, and even a left-handed compliment tainted with prejudice. It can even be found within an ethnic group, defined and marginalized by tints of a person's skin color. And sometimes it is a weed growing within, which in spite our best attempts to eradicate, keeps sprouting until it chokes the life of what is good in us. Racism keeps us in ignorance, it keeps us blind, it keeps us angry and uptight, but most of all, it keeps us living in fear. Racism can lead us to behaviors we may find abhorrent if we were on the outside looking in. Sometimes those behaviors lead us to tragedy, sometimes a Universal Force intervenes to avert us from such tragedy, and once in while, these behaviors will ultimately even lead us to redemption. Such is the theme of "Crash" a montage of several interconnecting characters and stories taking place over a forty-eight hours during a Los Angeles December. Directed and co-written by Paul Haggis, who wrote the nominated Oscar-winner Million Dollar Baby, it employs a very capable ensemble cast featuring Brendan Fraser and Sandra Bullock as an ambitious district attorney and his wife; Shaun Toub as a Iranian shop keeper; Michael Pena as a Latino locksmith; Don Cheadle and Jennifer Esposito as a couple of plain clothes detectives who are having an affair while also partners on the job; Terrence Dashon Howard and Thandie Newton as an upper middle class black couple; Matt Dillon and Ryan Philippe as two partnered uniformed police officers; and finally Larenz Tate and hip-hop star Ludicris, as a couple of black youths who prove that looks can indeed be deceiving. Added to these central characters is an assortment of Asians, Latinos, Indians and the rest of the racial spectrum that makes up Los Angeles, and to a larger extent, America. All the performances are extraordinary. The biggest surprise is that Ludicrus can act. The second biggest surprise is Bullock can act. There is not one scene or character in the entire film that comes across as either contrived or manipulative. "Crash" is the real deal, unapologetic and un-preachy. And there is one particular scene that is the most intense I've ever seen since Uma Thurman was resuscitated in Pulp Fiction. Crash is powerful, thought-provoking and emotionally draining. It is the best film I've seen so far this year. While this distinction may not necessaruly sustain by the end of December, it will remain one of the most important movies I've ever watched. For that reason, you have to see it. Now. I order you!

The Oscar-nominated screenwriter of Million Dollar Baby takes the helm of his own project in Crash, an ensemble study of race relations in Los Angeles, which uses the city's daily preponderance of motor-vehicle collisions as a central metaphor. The film recalls the work of Robert Altman (Short Cuts) and Lawrence Kasdan (Grand Canyon) in its attempt to interweave different segments of the city's socioeconomic and ethnic landscape, but uses a blunter hammer stroke to drive home its points. The film's many supporters led to surprising Oscars for best picture, screenplay and editing, as well as a 55-million-dollar box-office take. While some viewers were undoubtedly drawn to the unfiltered language and uncompromising intensity with which racism is depicted, others found that the film veers into contrived territory. As the characters are more often symbolic types than fleshed-out individuals, they butt up against each other according to what will create maximum incendiary dialogue and the potential for explosive conflict. Whether it's Dillon spewing anti-affirmative-action rage, Sandra Bullock spraying racial epithets in as many directions as a lawn sprinkler, or an Iranian business owner and a Latino locksmith using their mutual preconceived notions to block off communication, most of the scenes play out at the highest possible emotional pitch, with mixed results. While a number of scenes work well individually -- most notably Dillon's creepy frisking of Thandie Newton -- their coincidental interconnectedness undermines them enough to seem gimmicky. Even if some viewers found the material preachy, there's no denying that Crash reached a wide audience, its fans identifying a forthright frankness on race relations that they hadn't seen since Do the Right Thing.

While pointing out the ridiculousness of racism is important, that is all the film does. It points out that racism is bad. It doesn't invite the viewer to take an interest in trying to fix racism (obvious I'm not saying the movie should have eradicated racism, that'd be stupid). What I mean is it doesn't invite the viewer to learn more about different cultures nor does it dispel certain stereotypes about cultures. If anything, the film reinforced some of the stereotypes.

Also it was a bastardization of the Altman form. A lot of the stories/situations/characters could have been edited out as they were too similar to each other. The genius of the Altman form comes in the interconnectedness of the characters. That interconnectedness seems like an after thought or for cheap emotional manipulation. If the film used each individual story as a way of exploring racism instead of using racism to tell a story, the film could have been interesting. ie Don Cheadle's relation to his family; Matt Dillion as a racist and his father who is not or the 'Chinese' immigrants experiencing culture shock. 

Technically speaking the film is a bore. Cinematography/editing could have improved and be used as a tool to further the racial themes. Look at Taxi Driver: every time Travis Bickle sees blacks, they are walking in slow motion. This forces us to see and think like he does and become repulsed at those thoughts. The music was misplaced and only fed the exact stereotypes Haggis was trying to point out as ridiculous. The script tried to have natural dialogue but it ended up as a very obvious imitation of natural dialogue presenting itself as actual natural dialogue. The acting inherently suffers from this and by Haggis' adherence to stereotypes.

Watch Cronenberg's '96 Crash instead. Though it is completely different.

I know this movie is highly popular and very well regarded, so I will try to explain my rating of this movie. 

First, the movie succeeds admirably in its theme. The depiction of racial bigotry as a cross and intracultural problem is administrated beautifully. The character changes from complete assholes one scene to good people in the next beautifully illustrates the true nature of people. 

In that being said, this movie was an abysmal failure for me. Movies should draw you into a story, with anticipation of what is next, and an interest in the future of the characters. This movie lacked this in entirety. I personally found nearly every character destestable and found absolutely no caring for what was going to happen to them next. In fact, I was almost tempted to turn the movie off at several points (which is almost impossible for me to do unless its a movie on TV) because I just couldn't care for the characters or their stories. The mass multitude of stories with little to no connection between them was terrible given the nature of the characters. It came across as a disjointed mosaic of bigotry and hate given the semblance of a story. However, this is not to say mosaic themes do not work. Look at Paul Thomas Anderson's "Magnolia" which is the reverse side to this coin showing that even the worst and most selfish  people can show love to one another, which was accomplished beautifully, and is a personal favorite of mine. 

All in all, Crash is an ambitious movie that tackles a huge cultural problem thematically, but did so in a manner which was very terrible. It does not fit the mold. and maybe thats why it is liked, but for me, it was nearly impossible to watch this movie.

Crash : (4.0 / 4.0 stars)

A story about racism in America and how peoples lives intertwine, Crash delivers as the best movie of 2005 without question.  With so many interesting storylines all connecting by the end of the film, we are entrapped by the realization that these events probably occur everyday in the United States.

All of the main characters have one problem to deal with throughout the movie.  Brendon Fraser and Sandra Bullock had their car stolen at gunpoint by two black males on the streets of Los Angeles.  This begins the first of many chain reactions.  Bullock has Fraser immediately change the locks on every door in their house.  The mechanic to come do the job is of Mexican race, which causes Bullock to flip out.  It takes her some time to realize that she can not be mad at everyone all the time whenever she wakes up in the morning, especially her racists comments and thoughts.

While Bullock is dealing with her problems, the two black males are already on the other side of the city.  They end up running over a Chinaman and leave him on the side of the road near a hospital.  After trying to sell the car to an old friend for cash, the two men leave to find more trouble around the city.  The Mexican who helped change the locks at the Bullock house had a call to fix a lock on a Persians back door to the owned store.  After an argument that the lock was not the problem it was the door, the Persian ends up leaving the store without paying the Mexican one cent.  When he arrives at his store the next morning, the Persian realizes someone had broken into the back door, stealing many supplies.  He feels so angry against everyone else, he takes it upon himself to find revenge.

As this is occurring, two police officers are trying to understand how not to be as racist, a black couple is trying to understand that being black is not as bad as they think, the two black males who stole the car become tangled up with the police, a detective is trying to find out what has happened to his long lost brother while supporting his mother at home, and the detective wants to learn why people can be so cruel in the world.

This film really does document what occurs around the world every day.  It shows how racist one person can be, to cause the next person to be just as racist against someone else.  Besides the plot, the direction and cinematography was perfectly executed.  All of the actors and actress put excellent performances on the big screen and deserve two big thumbs up.  The freshest tomato of 2005, a well deserved award-winning film.

There are some good things in Paul Haggis's Academy Award winning statement on racial relations. There are a few moments of insight and quality peppered throughout. It's a shame that so much of the time Haggis settles for preachy, contrived situations and interactions that are supposed to enlighten but just put off a markedly ugly vibe from the start. Crash is a bad film with numerous cringe inducing moments from the shrill scenes with Brendan Fraser and Sandra Bullock to the silly lines uttered by a barely-there Ludacris and the suffocating melodramatics. Haggis, who wrote the screenplay for Million Dollar Baby, is much more of a writer than director and frankly his grasp of direction is questionable (the various stories are supposed to be linked together with some magical pixie dust sheen a la Magnolia, but I find it dreary and droning and poorly focused). As a commentary on race in America, it is relentlessly didactic driving home it's message with brick over head determination. How could anyone who has seen Spike Lee's Do The Right Thing see this as anything but a third or fourth rate revision?  Crash is alive though, in a way that touches a nerve for its admirers and infuriates the detractors. Worse things could happen.

'Crash' won the Best Picture Oscar at the 2006 Academy Awards, and ever since that night, the film has sparked controversy and has been heralded as one of the most overrated of all time. I can now echo those sentiments, having seen the film. Many argue that the favourite, 'Brokeback Mountain', was snubbed of the award, due to discrimination towards homosexuality by members of the Academy. I have not seen 'Brokeback Mountain', so I can't voice an opinion on the matter. 

The film essentially explores racial relations in Los Angeles, a heavy topic, indeed. I don't intend to be racist or xenophobic by saying this, but I feel that 'Crash' was far too American. It's not that I can't enjoy a film that is 'Americanised', but when the film is specific to the United States, such as this one, it's rather difficult for a foreigner to relate to what the film is preaching. The film was allowed to be very American, just as films are allowed to be too (insert other culture here). But my problem is that a film that is 'too American' won the Best Picture Oscar. Everybody around the world should be familiar with the Oscars, and the film that wins Best Picture should be one that is able to be embraced by all cultures. Even films that contain the word 'American' in their title aren't as American as this. Take Sam Mendes' 'American Beauty' for example. It won five Oscars in 2000, and happens to be my favourite film of all time. Why, you ask? It educates us on how society works as a whole, and how individuals contribute to that society. Personally, the film changed the way that I see the world, and the people within it. 

'Crash' just has this two-dimensional feel to it. Its first half an hour or so was actually promising, but everything just seemed to go downhill after that. The film was directed and written by Paul Haggis, whose screenplay for Clint Eastwood's 'Million Dollar Baby' I adored. The dialogue in 'Crash' didn't impress me too much. The film was made as if it was meant to make an audience cry. While there were many moments in the film that were designed to touch an audience, I didn't feel the least bit moved, in all honesty. This is because I didn't care about the characters. The best thing about this film would have to be the performances (that's performances, NOT characters). The film has a strong cast, and they do their roles more than enough justice. The performances are great, in that it doesn't look like the actors are acting, but the characters who the actors portray seem too similar to me. Not similar in looks or background, but similar in terms of their purpose in the film. To be blunt, I feel that they are quite dull, even with excellent performances by the actors, and that's saying something.

One of the most surprising and  worst movies of recent years to win the Oscar for Best Picture. Paul Haggis's didactic melodrama on race relations in modern day Los Angeles is so schematic that it blunts any emotional power the movie may have had. The filmmakers tell interlocking stories about individuals of various ethnicities who are forced to confront intolerance, from others and within themselves, which often leads to anger. The coincidences that occur, and the ways different characters bump into each other, is so contrived that many of the incidents come across as unbelievable. Detailed in simplistic fashion, each character's attitude towards race appears one way, until they are forced to confront their feelings, and they act in opposition to what was first displayed. Haggis avoids subtlety and complexity. The movie spells out its themes and ideas in blunt terms. There is an attitude of self-congratulation expressed as Haggis spends an hour and forty minutes lecturing us that racism is bad and anyone is capable of acting on their bigotry. The characters are mostly types and the dialogue is frequently preachy. Some people really seem to hate this movie for some reason. The complaint usually goes somewhere along the lines of "it's not Spike Lee's 'Do the Right Thing,'" which makes me stop listening instantly because it's a stupid complaint. That's a no-win proposition if I've ever heard one: be unlike a respected movie and get panned, or be like said acclaimed film and risk being called derivative. 

I, for one, like the way "Crash" handles the subject of race relations. Lee's movies dealing with race are like portraits, filling every nook and cranny with depth and nuance; "Crash" is like a splash-panel, less detailed but flashier and containing more immediacy. Yes, it lacks the depth of "Do the Right Thing" and other, similar films, but "Crash" seems to have many more arresting scenes than its predecessors.

The movie concerns the lives of a number of multicultural Los Angeles residents, almost all of whose paths cross during a fateful 36-hour period. Not all of the connections feel organic, making "Crash" a more unwieldy ensemble-cast character-study than, say "Magnolia" or most of Robert Altman's movies. However, the real joy comes from watching the characters interact - sometimes brashly, sometimes tenderly - and navigate a minefield of cultural differences.

Frankly, I'm just happy to see a film willing to show legitimate racism without sugarcoating it via happy-crappy PC messages.
Watch this movie, think about it. You'll forget all your prejudices towards foreigners, at least for one moment.
