First of all, I want to start off this review by saying, if you have never been to Los Angeles (or any other large multicultural, metropolitan city in the U.S.), you may brush Crash off as a Hollywood exaggeration. I live in LA, and I can honestly say that this film is quite accurate (especially the portrayal of the LAPD). I, and other people that I know have personally experienced situations like the ones portrayed in the movie (obviously not exactly the same). So I connected to it on a level that stretches far beyond sheer entertainment. Now, I do not mean any disrespect to those of you who did not enjoy it, but if you could not find anything in Crash to connect with, then I'm inclined to assume that you have never experienced anything like it. Because I have, I think that this is one of the best character studies ever made, and it certainly deserved the Oscar for Best Picture (despite how great I think all the other nominees were).

I said this earlier about Burn After Reading, and I hate to repeat myself in different reviews, but Crash is so much more bloated with talent that I have to say it again. This film is a prime example of how to properly utilize an ensemble cast of talented actors and actresses. Without a doubt, this is a character driven story, so the cast had to be great. And they came through big time. Not only were all of the leads and secondary actors/actresses perfect casts, there were also a number of great names who only had minimal roles (Keith David, Loretta Devine, Tony Danza and William Fichtner, to name a few). Like I said, the lead actors were all great choices. I cannot think of a weak link in the entire movie, so if you can, please let me know.  I don't know who is best to start with, so I'll just start with the first actor to appear on screen, Don Cheadle. He played Graham Waters, a Detective that goes through enough throughout the course of this film for me to say that I'd never want his job. He was very effective, without over doing his emotions.

His partner was played by Jennifer Esposito. She's good, but nothing exceptional. The other mentionable, but not exceptional performances were; Brendan Fraser as a politian named Rick Cabot, Michael Pena as a locksmith, Larenz Tate as a young criminal named Peter, Bahar Soomekhand as Dorri (the Iranian store owner's daughter), and Ryan Phillippe as a rookie cop. And the laundry list of exceptional performances were those of Sandra Bullock as Cabot's wife, Shaun Toub as the Iranian store owner Farhad, Chris "Ludacris" Bridges as Peter's partner in crime (his philosophical speeches are what made his performance one of my personal favorites), Matt Dillon as a racist cop with a hard life at home, Terrence Howard as a television show director, and Thandie Newton as his wife. Even though I separated the good and the great performances, they were really all convincing. Some were just more engrossing than others.

A lot of people say that Crash is overrated. I respectfully disagree. I think this film is by far the best directorial effort by Paul Haggis (writer of my favorite Bond, and one of my favorite all time films - Casino Royale). Well, he really hasn't directed any other movies worth mentioning, except for In the Valley of Ellah (which I thought was also pretty good). The message in Crash is blatant and simple. All the movie is saying, is that perhaps we should all take the time to reflect on the state of race relations in, not only America, but the entire world (I wasn't trying to sound poetic). And also how harmful basing our actions on stereotypes can be. I for one, have to admit that it struck a nerve with me the first time I saw it. It's affect has worn off for the most part by now, but it's just as important today, as it was five years ago. I think everyone has to see this movie at some point in their lives.

Set in post 9/11 Los Angeles this story is about a dozen people of all different races and circumstances. Each story interweaving with the others in one way or another. One of the best ensemble performances ever on film in my opinion. Powerful scenes throughout but no more than the scene between Matt Dillon and Thandie Newton in an overturned automobile.  That said, I'm fairly certain the music running through many of the scenes had a huge effect on their impact.  It's one of those movies that you just know would come across entirely different if there were no music at all in it.
Every interaction with another race provoked some form of racism, either overt or latent.  Was the story a bit contrived?  Sure.  A little too easy for all these storylines to have intersected?  Sure.   Did I mind?  Not at all. 
This picture really should have been called Racism.  Not How To End Racism In This Day And Age.  And not Racism Is Bad So Dont Be Bad.   :)   
It basically showed the rock skipping across the pond effect of our interactions.  Each one having a ripple effect.  Sending us off in a new direction with more information that we had before.  What we choose to do with that information is up to us. 
The movie certainly wasnt trying to excuse a racist attitude and believe me they were coming from every single direction imaginable.  Duck!  Here comes some racism!  :) 
It wasnt saying this group is more guilty of it than that group. It merely showed us what could be or where someone else might be coming from.  AND It was not trying to solve anything.  There's no tidy bow at the end to wrap it all up.  In fact it is merely showing the production of and end result of racism. Leaving us to say whatever we want about any of the interactions. 
In other words, have the conversation.  I loved it. Every minute of it.

Racism is a bad thing. This is pretty much a given for any right thinking person in the twenty first century, and yet racism is everywhere. Today in the United Kingdom we are witnessing a rather disturbing rise of political parties that have attempted to stir up racial tension and create rifts between an "indiginous" white population and minority ethnic groups of people who - thanks to the efforts of the tabloid media - have become the popular societal scapegoats for any number of problems that certain folk have a tendancy to try and blame on someone else. 

In Paul Haggis' 2004 movie Crash he attempts to confront the issue of racism and the effect it has on the lives of a number of individuals in multi-cultural Los Angeles. The film is a well acted and solidly produced piece of work, which does unfortunately suffer somewhat from a lack of subtlety in getting it's message across, and a rather unlikely set of coincidences in a storyline that see the various characters bumping into each other on several occasions in the space of a couple of days in a sprawling metropolis of over fifteen million people.

Crash is an extremely atmospheric movie, and one which concerns itself more than most in attempting to elicit an emotional reaction in the viewer. Beautifully shot, and with a memorable and uplifting score by Mark Isham, it contains some very powerful and moving sequences and portrays a rising sense of tension with some style. It also gives the city of LA a rather otherworldly feel - all shimmering heat-haze and glowing neon - in a similer way to Michael Mann's features Heat and Collateral. It's a well-paced film that is perhaps somewhat let down by what could be seen as a somewhat contrived script and a storyline that seems to have been written to shove it's agenda down the viewer's throat.

As I said in my first paragraph; racism is intrinsically a bad thing. Crash wants us to be in absolutely no doubt that this is the case and is somewhat hamfisted in getting this across. I can't find fault with the movie's sentiments, but I do feel that a little more subtlety and perhaps some less heavily sterotyped characters would have made for a better movie. Still, the film does contain a number of very memorable scenes and is aiming to make it's point whilst remaining an accessible and essentially mainstream piece of work. Ultimately it is a good and very worthy movie that, whilst simplistic at times, has an important message to put across.

Moving at the speed of life, we are bound to collide with each other. A deep story that reminds you that one's inner evil can lead one's life to crash. A district attorney and his pampered wife, two carjackers, several members of the LAPD, a television director and his wife, a locksmith, and a Persian family, are all strangers in the city of Los Angeles. But the lives of these people weave together in the story of life that the shows the benefits of good actions, and the fact that bad decisions can lead life to crash in an instant. Crash is a great film, but from what I have heard through the years, it is a film that is still debated as to whether or not it truly deserved Best Picture by the Academy. Looking back now, out of the five films that were nominated for Best Picture at the 78th Academy Awards (Brokeback Mountain, Capote, Crash, Good Night, and Good Luck, and Munich), the film that still continues to be mentioned the most within pop culture is Brokeback Mountain and maybe it should have deserved Best Picture the most. Crash is a passion piece by director Paul Haggis, and although it has its flaws, it is still a film worthy of even having a nomination for Best Picture. Crash features an ensemble cast of Sandra Bullock, Don Cheadle, Matt Dillon, Jennifer Esposito, Brandon Fraser, William Fichtner, Terrence Howard, Chris "Ludacris" Bridges, Thandle Newton, Ryan Phillipe, Larenz Tate, Michael Pena, and Keith David. I'm not going to go into the detail of which character each actor plays, but overall, the performances by all of these actors is great. This great acting is due to competent writing and direction. The filmmakers understand that viewers can be affected by this film on an emotional level, and therefore took each character on a journey that tests the ideals, beliefs, ethics, and morals in varying situations. But one problem that this story had was the fact that because there is such a large cast of characters, I felt that there wasn't a good balance of screen time for each character. This problem also led to confusion as to what is exactly going on in each scene from time to time. Some time the plot shifts forward and then sometimes it shifts backward, which can make any viewer confused. A strong running theme in this movie is the notion of racial and social prejudice in Los Angeles which can be said for other major cities within the United States. A simple look at a city bus and its large windows can be seen by a black man as a window for the upper class elite to identify the people on the bus who are poor enough to ride in them. Prejudice scenarios in Crash can be provoking but also true and can force one to examine and question their own prejudices. Crash is one of the greatest in cinema history and should be watched at least once in your life. "It's the sense of touch. In any real city, you walk, you know? You brush past people, people bump into you. In L.A., nobody touches you. We're always behind this metal and glass. I think we miss that touch so much, that we crash into each other, just so we can feel something." - Detective Graham Waters

Yet overall I feel that this film tries too hard to cover what cannot be covered in a single film - that is the tumultuous, often indefinable nature of so many divergent characters. I've heard that Crash is a racist movie because it upholds the very stereotypes it rails against. However, I think that's the exact point. We can espouse our tolerant attitudes towards other races until we're blue in the face, but in the end, it's still tolerance - something icky we have to live with, abide with, put aside. This movie pits what people say against what people do. You never know what you will do in a certain situation until you're there. Just because you're a good person doesn't mean you won't do something incredibly stupid or racist (Ryan Phillippe's burdened white man). Just because you're kinduva bad person doesn't mean you can't rage indignantly about everyday injustices (Ludacris' carjacker). It's petty to tally up the racial hero points for this movie. Oh, the white man saves a black woman from burning wreckage. Well a white man also senselessly kills a black man. If anything, black and white are balanced. The Hispanic man is the only one who seems completely non-judgmental, and the Asians seem the most immoral - cashing in on human trafficking. As an Asian woman, should I be offended that the Asians are treated so cheaply? No. These are all people who end up acting against type, whether those character arcs are redemptive or damning.

It is not often that a film bowls me over. Crash not only bowled me over, but left me shrouded in disbelief & awe. Extremely controversial, especially in America, this film focuses on racism in a way that will touch everyone. As Sandra Bullock said "If you can't relate to this film, your a liar." I completely agree. 

Confronting and heart stopping, this film shines a light on the honest side of human character, culture and race. Bringing tears when the characters come to term with their faults, anger when they are ignorant and humour when they are ironic.
Several characters all collide over the course of the movie, their problems & flaws crashing & their actions having unknown effects on them all. 

Los Angeles virtually becomes a character in itself as you are invited into the world of a city that, unlike others, houses a sheltered population. Constantly in cars & refined to their neighbourhood & class system, never venturing out, separated by concrete highways, fear and ignorance of what is just across the bridge. Why do we hate for no reason & with no information? Do we choose to stay ignorant? Are we all part of the problem? These are the questions the film raised for me and no doubt it will raise different questions for you. Don't shy away, allow this film to open you and seep into your soul. 

The film absolutely exhausted me due to the emotional washing machine I found myself in. I find that these three rules may be good ones to follow. First, make sure that you are not tired when you watch it. Second, make sure you have time to relax & watch the whole thing & three, don't watch it if you know you will be interrupted or you won't get the full experience. Pay attention & keep your mind open, this film may just end up changing you.         


RECCOMMENDATIONS 


RELIGION: It's a tough one, depending on your race, beliefs and religion, you may get offended. However, the movie is startlingly honest and doesn't set out to offend but to simply tell the truth. I say challenge yourself & see how you go. 
Children: It is brilliant but it is definitely not for children, put them to bed. 
     
Watch it if you liked: This film is in a realm of it's own, have the guts to see it without a comparison.  

Don't watch it if: You have sensitive religions/cultures to take into account that you think can't handle it. You have older people to consider, people that can't follow storylines or pay attention.

The world is full of people. People we know and people we don't know. The world works by having us meet people completely by accident, hooking our lives with others. By doing so, we somehow effect other people's lives and how they live. The world sure does work in mysterious ways, doesn't it? In order to get the right idea, watch "Crash" and you'll see what I mean.

"Crash" is a powerful and gripping drama that gives us a look at people being people and how their lives affect others by being connected. The characters in the film are played off like they are actual people, just going on about their lives, not knowing who the other people are around them. The movie was written and directed by Paul Haggis, a man who knows exactly how to make characters come to life. We look at these characters lives, knowing how we can somewhat relate to them. Why? Because these kinds of people exist. 

Over the course of two days, we take a look at people living in Los Angeles, all with the effect of racism. Each of the characters are uniqe in their own sense that truly grabs your attention. They are all different with the way they live, but all of them has something in common: they have no idea who they truly are. The main idea of the movie is to truly get to know yourself. A line spoken from a great performance by Matt Dillon, as a racy white police officer, says aloud to his leaving partner, "You think you know who you are? You have no idea." 

It's true, though. How do we really know who we are, and how do we know who others are? A perfect example is in an exhilerating scene between Brendan Fraser who plays a district attorney and his wife played by Sandra Bullock, who have previously got robbed by two black thugs (played by Ludacris and Larenz Tate). They are getting their locks changed for protection, but Bullock wants them changed again in the morning. She wants this because the lock fixer, played by Michael Pena, appears to look like a Mexican gangster, having Bullock worry that he's going to take one of the spare keys and give it to his homies. Does she really know who this guy is? The audience members find out that he's just a loving father of a daughter that he lives for, seeming as if he wouldn't even harm a fly. 

The movie has a terrific, all-star cast in it, all that give powerful performances. Each of the actors and actresses truly brings real people on the screen so that we can all realte to them somehow in a sense. Paul Haggis' writing for these characters is outstanding. Just listen to the dialogue throughout the movie, and then go walk in the street somewhere and try to hear what other people talk about, because that is how the people in this movie talk. It provides the authenticity of being believable, and that is why I praised this movie so much. 

"Crash" is a movie that truly asks the audience who they really are, making us look over the course of our lives and how we live it. It also asks how we view others and what we really think of them. Do we know much about others? Do things happen in the world on purpose or do things happen completely by accident? Who is it that really controls the world? It could be fate, or it could be ourselves.

I am honestly very unsure about how to view this movie. Crash is a very dramatic film about racism and morality, but its effectiveness and level of sincerity are hard for me to read.

During the first half of this picture, I was frequently frustrated. At the one hour mark, I was ready to fail this picture. Nearly every line during the first hour of this picture is geared toward a racist message. And it got extremely frustrating. All that this film was telling me was that everyone is racist. And I do mean *everyone*. There is only one character who appears in the first hour of the movie who is not portrayed as being completely racist. Unsurprisingly, that one character--Daniel Ruiz as portrayed by Michael Pena--was the character I liked most during the movie.

This movie has a lot of anti-racism messages, but the messages are hammered in so hard that by the end of the picture, the audience is sick of them. There's a lot more hate and drama in this film than there is anything else. I don't mind being told that there are racists still alive in the world, but what's the message of the movie? What's it trying to say? That racism is bad? I'm pretty sure that any audience in the 21st century would be aware of this fact. And if the message is that there is still racism alive in the USA, we get the picture after the first half hour. I mean, seriously, it does not need to be milked so much so constantly.

Now, there are a lot of aspects to this movie I really thoroughly enjoyed. For instance, any time the film stopped focusing all of its attention at how bad racism is and more at the questions of morality, it became a far more enjoyable experience. There were even a couple scenes of the picture in which the brilliant poetry of the moments really brought tears to my eyes.

***Warning: Here There Be Spoilers***
The greatest example of this is right at the middle of the movie. This was when my entire outlook on the movie changed. During this scene of the movie, a police officer comes to the rescue of a woman who is trapped underneath her car. The twist is that this is a woman the officer had violated the previous evening. Risking his own life and limb, he saves the woman, who is, understandably, stunned.
***

Sandra Bullock plays one of the many supporting characters in this film, and she was honestly the only actor who I did not think gave a believable performance. Every other actor in this film, on the other hand, was absolutely magnificent. Brendan Fraser gives 100% in every scene he is in, Chris "Ludacris" Bridges is astonishingly good throughout the picture, Don Cheadle is able to portray a lot of the hidden depth in his character, and Matt Dillon gives one of the most moving and powerful performances in the movie.

The most interesting part about this movie is that it tells an absolutely brilliant story. It really does; but the screenplay is far from satisfactory. I hold that this is a very weak screenplay. The storyline and all of the poetic plot points were very well done--don't get me wrong--but none of the dialogue in this movie felt real or sincere to me, and it relied far too heavily on racist remarks. I felt like it was a great weakness of the film that no characters found any other ways of communicating or being able to be characterized in any way outside of their bigotry.

Now, a lot of the characters do have marvelous arks to them by the end of the film, but not all of them. In fact, only a couple of them do. Only about three of the characters have any kind of ark to them. This would not be bad at all--I'm usually more frustrated by movies who can't give me *one* character with an ark--but there were about nine or ten characters that the audience is following at all times. And it gets to the point where I'm watching in absolute frustration, begging for this movie to give me some real depth to these characters besides relying entirely on this idea of racism. I didn't get a deep sense of satisfaction with all the characters.

But the characters I *did* get that satisfaction for really had this poignant, emotional response from me. When this movie works, it works very very well. But there were still plenty of times when this movie *doesn't* work.

Still, I'm going to give Crash a marginal recommendation. The message gets a little hazy, but I do feel that the poetry of the picture is what is ultimately more important. And there is plenty of that to be had here. I cannot say that every audience will find this picture dripping with sincerity, but the astonishingly good acting and the brilliant direction is what sets this film apart at the end of the day. This is not a masterful film, but it does raise itself to an above-average level.
6/10

It's all in the title: Crash. The viewer is slammed for two hours. I realize that in order to get a message out, we can resort to yelling. But this Haggis film is frothing at the mouth. 
During most of the movie, I could not help myself from exclaiming, "Are you serious?!" It's not a problem with the acting. It's not a problem with the directing. It's a problem with whoever wrote this mess. Just when you think the ridiculous plot is over, it explodes again and again and again. And not in a good way. After Ludacris' (who did an excellent job) stolen van just happened to hold Asian slaves, I lost all hope in this movie. The message of "Crash" is invaluable, but the overkill delivery ruins the film. 

If you want to look at a near perfect example of a film critizing the values and history of an entire nation, watch Rashomon. It invokes personal reflection and critiques humanity in a "fresh" way. "Crash" has its moments, but it teeters on being farcical.

Not as strong as it could have been, and I think this is because racism is not new. The film has some really powerful pieces (and less compelling ones), but there's nothing here that is transcendent: I've heard it all before. It's still an important topic today, and it's a good "discussion movie". 

Sandra Bullock and Don Cheadle really stick out for me as standout actors here. Bullock's insidious racism I find particularly relevant today, while Cheadle's story is pure tragedy, and is easily the most sympathetic character. The acting was great overall, but I found Matt Dillon's character to be a racist without cause. The tactic of showing a character's racism, followed by a redeeming moment was a bit too easy for me: not everyone is good, and Dillon's character felt especially awful (although well acted). I can rail against the misguided motives of many of the characters, but it is still true today that racism clouds our judgment, and we'll never be a free society until we can remove it completely from our zeitgeist.

I know it's an important premise that we're suppose to suspend our disbelieve with, but as the movie went on I did find it hard to swallow that this small group of people, who were mostly strangers, were this tightly connected to so many different events. As a metaphor for "we're all in this together" its potent, but it doesn't work as anything realistic, a quality I value in any drama. I'm surprised it won the Academy Award for Best Picture: it's a good movie, but I find it hard to believe there was nothing better out that year (I haven't seen the other nominees)

I can't stand football players so if someone made a movie about showing me how wrong it is to hate football players you really think that it's going to make me change my mind, I mean seriously. The poison of racism isn't something that can be cured by watching a movie, it can only be cured by showing people how truly horrible it is whether through pictures of lynchings or just letting them listen to Rush Limbaugh but a movie being showed is just silly. 

The one drawback in the movie for me was the fact that it felt a little too preachy. I already know it's wrong to judge someone based on their flesh tones, it's the main reason why I don't vote Republican *rimshot* so a movie trying to shove a message down my throat that I already know does cause a bit of problem for me. One of the many things that the movie does right is the whole openness of it all and how every character gets their moment to shine. We don't follow just one person throughout the entirely of the movie but spread out through out the whole movie and the whole time we feel like we're visiting an old friend is fascinated to see how they've progressed since we last met them. The end of the movie is great too because you don't get a definitive "and they all lived happily ever after" but just get the sense that this is just how life is so get used to it.

I went into the movie expecting a traditional boring dramatic score but instead got one of the best musical journeys I've ever been on courtesy of Mark Isham. The score can be best described as "Princess Mononoke" meets "Blade Runner" in terms of its dreamlike quality and how it makes you feel like you're high on acid or something. If you listen to the music with you eyes closed it will make you feel like you're flying, with music like that who needs drugs to get high. For my money I'd say the cue "Sense of Touch" is the best piece of music in the movie. It's the long 6 minutes piece that accompanies the last moments of the movie and it works really well in creating this dizzying dreamlike feel. I've heard a lot of music by Isham in the past but never knew he was capable of such greatness. Hope he writes more stuff like this in the future.

But I have to admit, Crash did not deserve to win Best Picture, in my opinion. I think it should of been between Munich and Brokeback Mountain.But it has great characters and lines plus the acting is great.

I am still in shock that this dreadful film walked away with the Oscar for best picture, leaving the truly great "Brokeback Mountain" with nothing but a cold shoulder. This film is absolutely ridiculous in it depiction of racism and the characters in which these sentiments reside. 

The film has no real guts or desire to take this discussion to any honest level. Many scenes inspired my ire, but one scene in particular, which could have illustrated the truly vile nature of undeserved hate, left me with a bad taste in my mouth as well as leaves the film with a missed opportunity at dramatizing the consequential nature which imbues a lifestyle of hate.

After middle-eastern shop owner's business is vandalized with derogatory terms spray-painted on his walls (as well as a trashed storefront), the owner buys a gun determined that he will never be subject to such discriminations again. The person he blames for this incident is a Latino family man, who works as a lock repair person, who he feels did him an injustice by telling the middle-eastern owner that he could not repair his locks, but that he would need to purchase new locks for the store. After a long and convoluted mishmash of story-lines, the store owner finally has had all he can take of being pushed around and finds the the home of the locksmith, carrying his revolver along with him for the planned confrontation. The two men arrive at the house at the same time. The Latino man is greeted by his daughter, wearing a lucky amulet of some kind (I cannot remember exactly) as the two men argue their sides of the story. The middle-eastern man pulls the gun and fires out of rage, just as the little girl jumps into her fathers arms. We fear the worst has just taken place. The shop owner looks on in horror as the father grasps his daughter in his arms, weeping over the notion that she has been shot. "What have I become?" is the immediate emotion which the gun toting vigilante now expresses. Alas, the girl is miraculously alright, giving credit to the amulet which her father had, in a previous scene, bestowed upon her.

It turns out that the daughter of the shopkeeper had placed blank rounds in the firearm, taking the live ammunition from the store.

This presents many problems for me, as a viewer. For one: how stupid is the daughter of the shopkeeper that she would do such a foolish thing? Leaving her father unknowingly defenseless in a possible gun battle means certain death for her father. Yet the daughter does not hate her father and seems to be of a generally even mind when met in previous scenes.

The second issue I have with the conflict described above is the use of luck to get out of a sticky situation. When I realized that the girl had not actually been shot, but simply shot at, I felt cheated. But not only as an audience member, I felt that the movie had cheated itself out of a tough, emotional lesson-- hatred does damage far beyond those who hate and are hated. By the death of that young girl, this would have been expressed very dramatically that hate kills indiscriminately. It is like a living, breathing entity which is born within us, but takes a life of its own in the end.

There are many, many other problems which I have with the film-- such as the lack of hate found is some people groups and the lack of redemption found in others. Spike Lee's "Do The Right Thing" is a strikingly better film, as all of the racial groups hate all of the other racial groups, and there is no real tidy answer at the end. In "Crash" the last scene is basically played on the level of a joke, which conveyed to my mind that, "Everybody hates everybody anyway, so why don't we  just laugh it off."

Racism and stereotypes: the movie.  While this film is often praised for its depictions of race relations in the United States, it raises all of its questions about race in a series of implausible events.  In nearly every important scene, writer/director Paul Haggis uses contrivances and over-baked production to the point where the film almost becomes a joke.  The second act of the film plays out as a series of melodramatic vignettes in which Haggis does everything in his power to evoke emotion from his audience.  Whether it's Matt Dillon's racist cop pulling Christine Thayer from an SUV seconds before it explodes, the angry Iranian store owner attempting to shoot the Hispanic plumber, or Ryan Phillippe's younger cop talking down Terrence Howard's television producer and allowing him to go free, each scene is milked for every last drop of emotional power that it has to offer.  The music swells, the camera shows us a series of close-ups so that we can see the anguished faces, it's like a cross between Capra-corn and Spielbergian-schmaltz.   
In spite of the obvious and deliberate contrivances, however, Crash does pack an emotional punch.  Even though the technique Haggis uses to evoke the emotional responses is obvious, one cannot help but be moved by the situations created in the film.  That does not make the film plausible or narratively sound, but as a series of outlandish vignettes, the film packs an emotional wallop.
Paul Haggis has been writing for many years (although he is new to directing) yet Crash is full of clichés.  The pair of car jackers played by Ludacris and Larenz Tate are like an analytical version of Samuel L. Jackson's Jules Winfield and John Travolta's Vincent Vega in Quentin Tarantino's Pulp Fiction.  In fact, I do not believe these two characters would exist were it not for the influence of Tarantino.  Ludacris and Larenz Tate converse about stereotypes and the moral issues of modern life while performing crimes.  In this instance it lacks any irony and borders on parody, although that is clearly not the intent.  Just as Jules Winfield had a change of heart about his life's work due to surviving a barrage of gun shots, Ludacris has a moral epiphany near the film's conclusion and frees a group of enslaved immigrants.  
There is some truth to the actions and behaviors of every character in Crash.  To some extent, we all hold deep-seeded prejudices towards certain people and things due to the social constructs that have been built up around us and engrained into our very being throughout our lifetimes.  It is a natural part of life just as all stereotypes are generated from some form of truth.  Haggis very ably shows us our prejudices with all their warts, but, to a lesser degree, he also shows some of the good that can be found in us as well.  Granted, he reserves the good for only a couple of characters among the multitude, but he still makes a poignant statement about human nature.  While most of us follow the norms and harbor prejudices, we still have good in our hearts and are able to do the right thing when the situations present themselves.  Haggis has a great message and plenty of interesting material, he just lacks the skills to put them together in a capable manner.  He is simply too obsessed with old clichés and story structure to allow his ideas to grow organically on the screen.  His script falls flat and lacks the cohesiveness of the modern films which he has so clearly borrowed from, films such as Magnolia, Pulp Fiction, Traffic, and Grand Canyon.  Crash raises some important ideas and has some strong emotional moments, but it is too dependent on contrivances to be plausible and truly effective.

Racism, violence and twist after twist is what makes Crash work. Crash (Winner of 3 Academy Awards including Best Picture) follows many stories and how they all "crash" into each other. The movie begins with Don Cheadle, playing a police detective, walking towards a crime scene and then for most of the film it is in flashback mode. You see blacks, whites, spanish, chinese, basically every race and how they treat others for the rest of the film. Whether it's an Arab finding his store being destroyed or a white police officer sexually harassing a black woman, Crash is full of racism that is somewhat unpleasing to many viewers.

Crash does many things well: one of which is the cast. This cast is mainly composed of below average actors (Brendan Fraser, Sandra Bullock, Ludacris, Matt Dillon to name a few) along with some well known actors (Don Cheadle is one). What Crash does so well is actually makes their actors feel realistic. The actors work perfectly for some reason and I have no reason why. Brendan Fraser is the District Attorney while Bullock is his wife. But every character is needed to show one thing: THEY ARE ALL RACIST.

Racism is commonly used in this film. It shows how others look at one another but it also shows how different races come together. Crash nails the story aspect of the film. The movie follows different races and how each character interacts (or crashes into) another character from the film. To be honest there is no lead actor in this film. They are all supporting each other. Crash also has a few suspenseful moments, mainly involving the police. Whenever a twist comes at you, another one is right behind it giving more shock to the audience. Crash keeps you guessing which makes it a great thriller.

Crash is a powerful movie about the perception of minorities in modern society, a riff on racism that challenges stereotypes and the way in which we, as human beings, are prone to make assumptions based on the appearance of an individual, often playing off of pre-conceived idea's that have been embedded into us from an early age.

Opening with a car crash, we then backtrack to yesterday, as an ensemble cast's lives intertwine in the diverse density of the L.A. metropolis. But, unlike Magnolia, Crash is less interested in the ways in which fate and chance dictate everyday events, and more with how bigotry and racial tension exists in every corner of this multi-cultural melting pot. Where Crash is most successful is in how it challenges certain racial stereotypes and how it subsequently portrays the effects racism has on everyone's lives. It's not just a simple case of white vs. black. It goes much deeper, as we realise that intolerance is widespread and isn't confined to the white middle classes, that it exists between all colours, all races, all cultures. The finger of blame is easiest to point at somebody who doesn't look like you, who doesn't have your upbringing. Because of this, they must be in the wrong, right? Matt Dillon's veteran cop has this outlook. His father lost everything because of minority rules and he holds a deep grudge against all blacks, regardless of age, sex or profession. Yet this bigotry is awkwardly juxtaposed between his genuine care for his sick father and his honour and duty as an officer of the law, something he later demonstrates during a life or death situation. Director and writer Paul Haggis twists the stereotypical views further with the characters of Terrence Howard, a young, black film-maker and Michael Pena, who gives an outstanding & extremely subtle performance as Daniel, a young Hispanic locksmith with a wife and young daughter, with whom he shares one of the films most touching moments. In fact all of the cast do a fine job with their roles, even Chris "Ludacris" Bridges, in an attempt to branch out, providing some of the funnier moments of the movie with his musings on black oppression. And lets not forget Don Cheadle, as a cop who finds his integrity challenged after investigating a messy bout of cop on cop action.

Ultimately though, the thing that will stay with you the longest is the simple message that shines throughout the film. "Don't judge a book by its cover." Every character displays the devil inside of them but it's only one part, there is good in everyone, it just needs an outlet, an opportunity to break through. As the film reaches its climax we are forced to consider how we look at people in everyday life. How we label and pigeonhole certain cultures, certain races, into one group, with no distinction between the good and the bad. In an increasingly paranoid world, where we are being schooled in how to be suspicious of unfamiliar practices and alien customs, Crash serves as a hard reminder that while we must be careful in our own daily lives, we must be equally cautious not to discriminate and adversely affect the lives of many hard working, decent citizens just because of the actions of a few.

If there are any gripes with the film (and these will be minor) it's that what your watching is a collection of vignettes, snippets of these characters lives beamed direct to your brain for your benefit, and not a cohesive story that links seamlessly between strands, in the vein of the excellent Magnolia. At the end of the film characters have reached resolutions, but these aren't earth shattering, life changing epiphanies, rather smaller, more personal realisations that will, you assume, change their way of future thinking. Like much of the movie, it uses a lo-fi approach to the drama, making the final payoff that much more powerful and ultimately, delivering the emotional kick necessary to immerse the audience within this world

Even though all the actors did great, the other one that really stood out in my opinion was Ludacris as Anthony. It's weird, but it's almost like he's a role model, except the character does bad things. There's plenty of characters, and everyone is interesting. The story is simple, it's Los Angelas, and it shows several different characters and how they affect each others lives. Imagine a world where everybody spoke what was on their mind, without worrying about offending anyone else unless offending them would lead to negative consequences for you. Political correctness doesn't appear to exist, meaning if a thought about race, culture, gender, societal status, or anything else came into your mind, you wouldn't be afraid to state it. Now, populate that world with racists, bigots, rich, poor, thieves and police officers, and the world you imagine would probably become similar to the one that Crash represents. There are far too many characters and storylines to accurately describe them in text. All of these characters are different in their own ways, but like the point the film tries to make, all the same as well. What happens throughout most of the plot is that one character will appear, meet another character, and based on stereotypes about their race or current economic situation, will react to one another in a way that wouldn't be deemed "correct" in a polite society, even though they're almost always wrong. I'll give you a couple of examples. The first one involves a spoiled, upper class white woman (Sandra Bullock), who has just been carjacked. Upon returning to her house, with police officers from all different backgrounds present, she starts ranting and raving about seemingly every race that isn't white, with most of her insults directed toward the man currently changing the locks to her door (Michael Peña). While she does leave the room to do this, it becomes pretty clear that everyone in the house can hear her. She believes that the locksmith will go and sell the keys to her house to a gang, and demands that they change the locks again in the morning. When he leaves, we see that the locksmith isn't a criminal, but a family man, with a wife and daughter he takes care of. He even left a dangerous neighborhood to protect them. The second situation involves an Iraqi named Farhad (Shaun Toub), who opens the film wanting to buy a gun. The shop owner is less than friendly to Farhad, who is eventually thrown out of the shop due to the racism exhibited by the shopkeeper. Eventually, Farhad's daughter, Dorri (Bahar Soomekh), manages to get the gun from the abusive salesman. It turns out that the pair only wanted the gun to protect their shop, in case more thieves were to come in. That doesn't make the Iraqis innocent in this film, definitely not. Almost every character has both redeeming moments as well as inexcusable ones. For most of the time, I figured it would be one or the other; either the characters would be completely good, or completely bad, but that isn't the case. By the end of the film, most of the characters will have learned a lesson, one that can be boiled down to their prejudice being right or wrong (in their eyes, at least). What this results in are deep, realistic characters that all have problems and need to do some growing up, and learning about other cultures. In fact, most of their problems come from sheer ignorance, something relayed to us in one of the film's final scenes, where a white, off-duty police officer (Ryan Phillippe) picks up a hitchhiking black man (Larenz Tate), and they get along well enough for a while, despite the fact that one's a white cop, and the other is a black thief (although neither is aware of the others' "occupation"). I think I could watch these people for hours. This is an ensemble film, and as such suffers from the main problem that almost all films with such a cast suffer from: Not enough time is spent with each character. If Crash ended up being 4 hours, I think I'd be okay with that, because these characters are ones I wanted to watch for double the time that they got. There are a couple of characters that feel really shortchanged, only really getting three or four scenes throughout the entire picture. I wanted more, which is a good sign that the movie I was watching was of high quality. I was not bored for a single moment while watching Crash, which is praise in and of itself when you're talking about a drama. Despite that it is a drama, the amount of tension you get from each film makes it seem more like a thriller, and I was certainly thrilled. Whenever a scene started, I knew I would be in for something exciting. Crash didn't disappoint in this aspect. While I didn't get tired of the film's message, I'm sure that it might become redundant to some. It is delivered over and over again throughout the film, which is about as close as the film comes to having a problem. This can turn some people away, I'm sure, because being told multiple times that being racist and assuming negative things about people not exactly like you are bad qualities to have ends up getting stale. But I think that because the film delivers that idea with multiple ways and scenarios, it doesn't get stale, but instead, becomes stronger and will stay with you after you it, even if you weren't someone to need that being told to you. Crash is a great film that deals with racism and different societal classes. Is it perfect? Not quite, but it's very close. It gets its message hammered home in multiple ways, using realistic and intriguing characters to captivate us. It's more thrilling than a lot of thrillers, and manages to find a balancing point between being too over-the-top with how bigoted these characters are, almost always giving them a chance to redeem themselves. Definitely give this film a watch.

Crash is a good movie, but it shouldn't have won the Oscar for Best Picture over Brokeback Mountain based on two fronts. Firstly, it doesn't smoothly execute it's goal of raising a clear message. This is, after all, a message film. It's not really clear what commentary about race it's trying to make. Should we be color-blind? How should we view each other? Secondly, when trying to assign racial roles to characters, it oversimplifies the characters to the point where you can only see them as "racialized" and not really as a character--perhaps this was the film's intention, but by the end of the movie audiences get the feeling that they are being "talked to" about racial injustice, rather than by really "experiencing" racial injustice through the eyes of compelling characters. With that said, there is some good acting.. so that makes up for what is lost with the oversimplification of character roles. Crash is better off as a short film, with its poetic edginess and use of the metaphor of a car crash to symbolize the conflict of as well as the solution to racism in modern LA.

We've seen a lot of movies with interweaving narratives. We've seen a lot of movies about social & racial tensions & a great deal of them have taken place in the melting pot that is Los Angeles, California but not many of them have been this profound.

Race relations in post-9/11 Los Angles, Crash is a blunt and rather shocking outlook on people's misconceptions and prejudices regarding the people around them. Discrimination, gun crime, police intimidation, and human trafficking are among the themes focused on in this matter-of-fact drama, which provocatively addresses every racial stereotype in the book in a way which demands a certain level of recognition. The cast take to the roles with enthusiasm and ambition, and succeed in bringing emotion and depth to a subject which nobody really likes to talk about. As well scripted and acted as Crash is however, the events are a little contrived and the message is decidedly finite; racism exists and is a huge societal issue. This is something most people are well aware of already. But at the very least, Crash presents the limits which racism can reach, and forces you to be more aware; commendable, as this is no easy task.

At the time Crash came out, there was something of a backlash against it. When it received the award for Best Picture at the Oscars, many critics heckled the members of academy on accusations of homophobia, as Crash had beaten hotly tipped favourite Brokeback Mountain for the win. In fact, most critics seemed to use this entirely as their basis for Crash being a terrible film. Just recently, it was voted the worst Best Picture winner of all time. Now that it has been seven years since those awards, it seems a fair time to reassess Crash, and decide: does it hold up as a good film?

The answer is a complete yes. While I still believe Brokeback Mountain is the better film, Crash isn't far behind. Following the lives of numerous interlocking characters in Los Angeles, Crash deals with the topic of race and power. Racist LAPD officer John (Matt Dillon) abuses his authority in a groping of a black woman and her television director husband (Thandie Newton and Terrence Howard), but later gets a shot at redemption. Young officer Tom (Ryan Phillipe) is a good guy battling to lose himself of his racist partner. District Attorney Rick and his wife Jean (Brendan Fraser and Sandra Bullock) are robbed by two young black carjackers (Chris "Ludacris" Bridges and Larenz Tate); Rick doesn't see a way of pressing charges without being a racist. Farhad (Shaun Toub), a Persian shop owner, is bitter for a robbery and blames Hispanic locksmith Daniel (Michael Peña), who just tries to earn a decent wage. Finally, there's Detective Graham Waters (Don Cheadle), who's just trying to be the best man he can under tough circumstances.

As with most multi-stranded films, the acting, by statistics, is going to be good, but Crash is a very underrated film when it comes to individual performances. Just about everyone is solid in it. Top of the list is Matt Dillon as the bitter, racist police officer. It's an often thankless and unlikeable role, but he gains sympathy in his care of his ill father, and in a mid-film act of redemption. Brendan Fraser, in one of the few roles he's taken on that wasn't a franchise or kids film, is very likeable, although Sandra Bullock has to put with a poorly written character that is mostly obnoxious. Don Cheadle gives a brilliantly subtle performance as a man bitter at the mother who has all but forgotten who he is, and is actually he heart of the film. Even Chris Bridges, most famous as rapper Ludacris, gives a great portrayal of the young criminal angry at the prejudice he sees wherever he goes.

Crash is also home to many fantastic individual scenes. The highlight of the film is a car wreck that leads to one of the most heart stopping, emotional rescues in any film of the last decade. Prepare the tissues, as just about every character gets a strong emotional breakdown; Howard faces off with the police; Newton is forced to accept help from her most loathed person; and, in a complete tearjerker, Peña suffers complete grief. Possibly the saddest scene of the film for me personally was the resolution to Cheadle's storyline; subtlety is the key, and his walk away is heartbreaking.

Perhaps Crash wasn't the film of 2005, and perhaps it wasn't quite worthy of the Best Picture award, but by the end of the film, that won't matter to you; all that matters us that Crash is a sublime film, with stunning acting and beautifully written stories.

I was looking forward to my long-delayed viewing of Paul Haggis' Crash. I thought it would provide me with an experience along the lines of when I watched Falling Down, a breathtaking portrayal of societal arrogance, where I was riveted and infuriated for much of the film. Instead, Crash is a by-the-numbers film about America being a melting pot of racists, waiting to be set off in a cliche set up, and appears to be more of a stock lecture instead of a truly eye-opening film.

I must give respect and well-earned shock to the film for winning Best Picture, over critic/fan favorite, Brokeback Mountain. Its win was probably one of the biggest stuns next to when Annie Hall bested Star Wars in 1977, or when Forrest Gump stomped both Pulp Fiction and The Shawshank Redemption for the same title in 1994. Crash is definitely an interesting piece, setting its sights on the controversial nature of racism and its victims and alarmists, but manages to plod along in its runtime, rarely reaching heights of admirable status, and manages to be questionably exploitative and, dare I say, racist in itself.

The film follows numerous characters in a forty-eight hour period in Los Angeles where they are met with racial confrontations, have their personal outlooks and insights tested, and eventually, have their stories intertwined with one another in some way, shape or form, connected by the central focus; a car crash. Such characters are a black LAPD officer (Don Cheadle) who is long estranged from his mother, a white District Attorney (Brendan Fraser) and his spoiled-rotten wife (Sandra Bullock) whose car was hijacked by two young black men (Chris "Ludacris" Bridges and Larenz Tate), a racist white police officer (Matt Dillon), who molests a black woman (Thandie Newton) right in front of her husband (Terrence Howard), a Hispanic locksmith (Michael Pena) trying to keep his family business straight, an uptight Persian immigrant (Shaun Toub), and an optimistic cop (Ryan Phillippe), who works with Matt Dillon's character.

Right off the bat, there are far too many underdeveloped characters here. The way we are greeted with them is awkward, too fast, and lacks much substance. In an ordinary anthology film with intertwining characters, take Adam Rifkin's criminally underrated and near-perfect film, LOOK for example, we spend enough time to get to know the characters, form opinions about them, and actually become intrigued and somewhat astonished at how they meet and engage with one another. Crash breathlessly tries to juggle a dozen loose stories and find creative ways for them to connect with each other that it doesn't have time to adapt its subjects into believable people. It's almost encouraging its own problem by stereotyping its characters.

The film portrays all of its characters as on-the-edge racists triggered by a fairly mild, forgivable, and misunderstood circumstance where every conclusion is jumped to and nobody is smart enough to think something over before acting. Perhaps Crash is trying to show us that that, specifically, is the problem, but it is gone about in such a ham-fisted, heavy-handed way that we know what the film is trying to say, but we simply don't care and are tired of being talked down to for close to two hours.

With that being said, it must too be stated that all the actors here do a wonderful job at, at least, trying to create versatile, believable characters, although few succeed. Sandra Bullock is the standout here, simply giving it her all and showing us true character-acting versatility in not only her role-choices, but her creative and involved performances. Ludacris isn't as outgunned as I thought he'd be, Don Cheadle does exceptional work, Matt Dillon is great here, and so is the rest of the cast. But inevitably, I'm reminded of the one-dimensional characters they play and the truly vacuous background that plagues each and every one of them. A quick look at other reviewers scattered across the internet show that their shallowness has neglected people to notice the good acting behind them.

The film concludes with one of the lamest, most uncreative Hollywood endings in a blue moon, showing us easily the most schmaltzy, conventional, unbelievable, cringe-inducing ending a film about racism could possible give us. Even with dedicated performances from a barrage of different talents, Crash connects their characters' stories in such a contrived and facile way it's distracting, is plagued by levels of sheer incredulity, and occupies an end scene of complete and total folderol. As a whole, it plays like a heavy-handed lecture by a representative of the "Why Can't We All Just Get Along?" committee.

Starring: Sandra Bullock, Don Cheadle, Matt Dillon, Jennifer Esposito, Brendan Fraser, Terrence Howard, Chris "Ludacris" Bridges, Thandie Newton, Ryan Phillippe, Larenz Tate, Shaun Toub, and Michael Peña. Directed by: Paul Haggis.

Crash is a film that is as relevant now as it is as it was seven years ago.   Though the premise is pure contrivance, it's a epic one which begs for suspended disbelief.  Paul Haggis cleverly paints stereotypical portraits of this film's multiple protagonists using the prejudices and preconceptions of those who surround them, only to then turn the audience into confidants, revealing key details of the protagonists' lives unknown to those in the story.   Those intimate details and the "seemingly" random, sometimes violent interactions of the main players, oddly draw the audience in closer, created a sense of connectedness and community where one doesn't appear to exist.   

Crash is a cautiously optimistic film and an uplifting film without the traditional high fructose Hollywood corn syrup.  Yes, there are a few implausible moments, but they aren't Indiana Jones Nuke The Fridge moments, they are purposeful and meaningful.

Crash, directed and written by Paul Haggis, is one of those films whose reputation (or disrepute) is far bigger than the film itself. If the film had never won the Best Picture Oscar in 2006 (over Brokeback Mountain, which everyone considered a 100% certain winner), it would have been quickly forgotten. But ever since the visibly surprised Jack Nicholson announced it as the winner, many people have denounced it as the worst film of the decade and the worst film to ever win the award. Even in 2010s they still keep reminding us what a self-indulgent, pseudo-profound and sentimental piece of crap it was.
 
Crash has numerous storylines and characters, all surrounding the subject of racism. During 36 hours, various people in Los Angeles, including a black cop, an Iranian shopkeeper, a Hispanic locksmith, two black carjackers and a wealthy district attorney and his ever-querulous wife among others, get in touch with multiculturalism, xenophobia and their own prejudices.
 
I do acknowledge the flaws of Crash, which are many. One thing it was particularly criticized for was being preachy. It isn't that all the time, but it has moments when you feel like the message is shoved down your throat. Some of the dialogue is very heavy-handed and exaggerated and some plot points forced. And sometimes it slips to sentimentality and even feels like a soap opera.

But Crash is not a bad film. In fact, it's pretty damn good. Why? Because no matter how many faults you find from it, no matter how self-important, soapy and sentimental it may be, it does provoke thoughts and feelings. It drills deep down to the nature of prejudices, and bravely tackles on the prevalence and everyday nature of racism. It may not be a politically correct film. It deals with questions of racism directly and straight out, forcing the viewers also to ponder their own attitude towards different people.

And what Haggis really succeeds at is creating character portraits. He refuses to make any of them a stereotype or a caricature. You learn to care about the characters and their fates, no matter how unpleasant some of them may seem at first. For example, Matt Dillon's character, a policeman John Ryan, is at first shown as a racist prick, as he sexually harasses Thandie Newton's character and forces her husband to watch, but later we see him feeling anguish over his sick father, and we understand why he did such an obscene thing. The two carjackers are at first shown as one-dimensional, stereotypical hoppers, but the other one of them is apparently religious, and the other one has a surprise for us at the very end of the film. There isn't a clear protagonist in the film, and some of the characters get less screen time than others, but we can still clearly understand who they are and what their lives are like.

The film is quite cynical in demonstrating peoples' attitude towards strangers, indicating that they're always suspecting the worst about each other. But it also believes in an individual's ability to change. Many critics have asserted that the film uses an overly complex story and large character gallery to deliver a simplistic message ("racism is bad"), but there is much more below the surface; the film paints a very complex picture about human nature.

Some of the characters and situations where they learn something feel awkward; like the Iranian shopkeeper, who is mostly shown as an incredulous, hysterical, impolite freak, who learns to be more confiding and peaceful only after accidentally shooting a little girl. And it's very hard to believe that Ryan and his partner, would end up meeting the couple that Ryan embarrassed the next day in their respective situations. But these unconvincing scenes have such dramatic tension that you don't pay attention to their improbability.

The film is also well shot by J. Michael Muro, but the true star here is the editor Hughes Winborne, who carries the story (or stories) on so fluently that you aren't confused at any point. The transitions from one story to another are completely seamless, and we always get to spend the right amount of time with one character before going on to the next. Mark Isham's score is also impressive; sometimes it's frustratingly underlining but mostly very beautiful.

The performances of Crash range from terrific to plain silly. The best performances come from Matt Dillon (who also received an Oscar nomination), who is truly spooky as Ryan, who has problems to control his own prejudices, and Don Cheadle, who is very convincing as a cop looking for his criminal brother. Terrence Howard and Thandie Newton are also really good as the black couple. Keith David has only a brief role, but delivers a nice, smooth performance as a police lieutenant. Chris Bridges, better known as the rapper Ludacris, is also pretty good, while you could expect him to be absolutely terrible, as musicians who become actors often are.

However, there are some weaker performances as well. Sandra Bullock is still not convincing, even though she's clearly trying to find a new dimension from herself as an actor. Ryan Phillippe is too inexpressive in his role as Ryan's partner, and Brendan Fraser is totally wooden. But Bullock's and Fraser's characters are some of the most irrelevant of the film, so it's obvious they can't get much out of them. They are also the characters you care about the least.

Overall Crash is a film that deserves to be seen and thought about. Sure it has flaws and isn't a masterpiece that will stick in your mind forever, but it's a solid, well written, well directed and mostly well acted drama. Did it deserve to win the Best Picture Oscar or not? Who knows, moreover, who cares? The awards are a side issue. Haggis has made the film with good intentions, hoping to make people think and discuss the subject matter, and even if you find the end result clumsy, it's always better to have a story with at least some thought in it than a story left untold, right? I like Crash. I think it's a good film. And I'm not ashamed to admit it.

A worthy 'Best Picture' winner, 'Crash' is an unsuspecting masterpiece that looks at the hard truths of racial disparity in post-9/11 Los Angeles. There are so many factors at play in the Paul Haggis directed film, which boasts a multifaceted, talented cast (Brendan Fraser, Sandra Bullock, Terrence Howard, Thandie Newton, Ryan Phillippe, Don Cheadle, Matt Dillon, Jennifer Esposito), that it's hard to keep track of all the individual stories that are featured, although it's genius how they are all sewn together as the film progresses. Even though there are deep topics at the center of the film, the characters portrayed are very identifiable, and it's interesting to see how feelings change about certain characters over the course of the film. What 'Crash' really excels at is its ability to introduce thought-provoking questions that stay with you long after watching the plot unfold onscreen. To add to things, there are no issues with pacing, and the film easily keeps your attention, which is something a lot of dramas have trouble with in this day and age. Despite its heaviness and subject matter, 'Crash' is an enjoyable film that offers as many teachable moments as it does entertaining moments.

A real thought provoking film which requires a little more concentration than I originally gave it. Set in LA and starring a wealth of well known actors, it follows the lives of several different individuals, with various backgrounds, lifestyles, and more importantly, ethnicities. At first, watching the scenes flip from one story to the next was very frustrating with it becoming hard to grasp any fluency with the concept, other than the fact that black people were being treated as the aggressive race, with little respect shown for them. However, as the individuals began interlinking with one another's lives, and how one persons actions would shape another's, the clever approach this film had actually pieced together was somewhat entertaining. Clearly intent on portraying messages with regards to race equality in today's society, the events soon lead one to wondering whether people can all be judged on appearance or first impressions. Whom we perceive to be the good cop and bad cop are soon brought into debate quite literally in the scenarios the director has placed onto our screens in this finely staged spectacle. I feel I could pick up things that would have initially bypassed me on a repeat watch as the only problem is that it feels a bit patchy in the beginning with just a gangland style culture being aired for our entertainment. It's credit to the writer that several different chapters all intertwine at various stages, provoking a change in direction for our thoughts. I'll admit to still being somewhat confused as to the purpose of some of the characters but to think I'd be so keen to watch this again after the slow start I endured was definitely surprising.

Every single shot of this film is so intricate and so thought out to bring the story to life for just about anyone who watches it regardless of who you are or where you've been. I feel like no matter what your stance is on the subjects presented in this film, you can find at least a piece of you self in one or more of these characters, that in one film alone were all brought to life so vividly. I just want to mention that some of the my favourite performances personally were Sandra Bullock in her role as Jean Cabot. She makes her character so detestable in the beginning but becomes so vulnerable and allows the audience to see the awakening and growth that occurs. Don Cheadle also did a fantastic job bringing his character to life. Loretta Devine was a very small but very well executed role that brought a lot to the story. Thandie Newton gave an excellent performance in her role and really made me think and feel throughout the film. Ludacris played a very important role in the film because while, like all the characters, he had a story to tell and a way of thinking to observe, he made comic relief possible in an otherwise very heavy film. Ryan Phillippe was enjoyable in the film as someone that at first presents himself in one way but we later learn has his flaws as well. Ashlynn Sanchez also did a great job as the piece of innocence in the film. All the actors did a great job and I wish I had the time to comment on them all but I would simply recommend watching for yourself and taking the chance to connect with each character as they experience their lives and learn their lessons. While CRASH is most assuredly a technically well-made film, there is absolutely nothing it has to say that couldn't be ascertained from paying a little attention in the real world. Racism is definitely a problem in America (and the world), but all this film seems to have to contribute to that discussion is that it's bad. To make matters worse, every single character in the film is a stereotype. And there's also too many characters to begin with. You learn a little bit about them and their lives, but the running time didn't really allow for a deeper examination of these people and why they are the way they are. All of the performances were good, to be sure, but it was all in service of a heavy-handed script that approaches the issue of racism in the most skin-deep way possible. Despite the film's title, implying a certain degree of chance in one's encounters, every moment in the film felt calculated and calibrated for maximum emotional impact in a way that undermines the seriousness of the issues it wanted to address. At the end, no one really learns anything and, as an audience member, I was left wondering what the point was exactly. From a technical standpoint, though, the film is fairly solid. The movie is about, and (presumably) shot in, LA and the filmmakers did a good job of capturing it on film, especially in the night time. The cinematography was actually kind of beautiful, in contrast to the ugliness of the characters. I'll even give credit to the score for being relatively toned down, letting the rigged emotional stakes of the film stand out that much more. When all is said and done, I'm also left wondering how in the world this shallow nonsense ever won Best Picture. Although well-made and well-acted, it just seems like the Academy gave themselves a pat on the back for even acknowledging that racism exists. The subject deserves better and more thorough treatment than it got with this film.

The movie Crash is about the daily struggle against prejudice and racism in America. It starts off with several seemingly unrelated stories, which ultimately converge into a single crash after much deliberation. Although the clash may appear coincidental and even contrite at first, at a deeper level, the movie seems to suggest that there is no absolute coincidence, that the black guy shot in a car could as well be your lost brother, that the police officer teasing you in the last moment could as well be your savior, and that the person who insists on justice could as well be a murderer. None of the accidents should be surprising, since they are simply manifestations of the historical racism and cultural prejudice of America on a daily basis. Yet what really distinguishes Crash from other conventional movies that portray racism is the reconciliation part at the epilogue. Indeed, certain people may appear offensive upon first glance, yet the life stories behind them could be so sympathetic as well. All it needs to understand a person more holistically is to go a layer deeper, beyond what his deeds may suggest. Above everything, Crash is about contradiction, contradiction between people's surface and their hidden nature, between what a man has done and what he will do, between what things seem and what they actually are. At the end, the movie suggests that because people do change over time, racial stereotypes and even personal characterization can't always apply, yet love and compassion, the beauty of humanity, shall always persist and find their way in darkness.  

Although the movie depicts racism mostly in the lights of average Americans, one scene particularly mesmerizing is when the wretched Chinese are released from the car by the black fellow. On the one hand, this scene greatly resembles the enfranchisement of black men in the 19th century, the only difference being Abraham Lincoln is a black man this time. From a historical perspective, this ending points out the continuum of oppression and liberation in America, and how much progress America has made and unmade since the Declaration of Independence. On the other hand, when the trafficked Chinese step outside of the car, they look isolated, dismantled and lost. Yet the reason for their deliria is not just the fact that they don't mentally belong here. The reality is that the world immediately in front of them is so stereotypically diverse and grotesquely prosperous that it elicits fear. In the 21st century, what America really needs is to not only solve the domestic issues of racism, but also accommodate immigrants against any form of nativism.

The first time I saw Crash was a week ago in my Social Issues in Film FYE class. My teacher told us to pay close attention to how the characters related to each other and try to find the deeper meaning in the film. The actors and directors did an amazing job.  They delivered a film that was transparent and hardcore, yet relevant and thought provoking.  By the end of the movie, I was completely blown away.  I did not expect to be so impressed by this film.  Surprisingly, it left me pondering my own personal views on several cultural and social issues.  I went back to my dorm that day a watched it over and over again.  The three things I look for when critiquing a film is a good story line, believable characters, and sensible plot execution. 
The story line of "Crash is about the collision of races, cultures, and classes." (Lisa Schwarzbaum, 2005). The pileup begins almost immediately when two young black men are walking in an upscale white part of Los Angeles and talking about the perception of young black men in upscale white town. Then carjacks a Lincoln Navigator that happens to belong to the L.A. district attorney and his rich-bitch wife and Bam!, that's four people linked and unmasked, in all their ugliest prejudices and most shameful fears, by the fate of one SUV which will eventually have everything, to do with the fate of another Navigator, owned by a rich black TV director and his wife and stopped for inspection by a racist white cop and his partner .When they got pulled over the cop touch the man's wife inappropriately in front of his very eyes. This atomically catches my attention at how in the film, Crash's main white characters are depicted in comfortable positions, both socially and economically. Then in another scene , the television executive producer who tells Black producer Cameron Thayer (Terence Howard)  to make one of his actors speak "more black" because that character was "supposed to be the dumb one."  In the movie most of the minority characters were portrayed as socially powerless. "The film Crash was directed by Paul Haggis, he does a good job at showing how most people feel prejudice and resentment against members of other groups, and observes the consequences of those feelings."(Roger Ebert, 2005) This I can completely agree with this because the director, didn't hold back when showing the audience the true reality behind the social issue of racism
For me, believing in the characters helps me gain a better understanding of the film.  Whether the characters are A-list or under budget actors / actress the way they express their emotions on camera plays a major role in creating a great film. The actors and actress in this are amazing from Sandra Bullock, Ludacris Jennifer Esposito, William Fichtner and many others. Their emotions poured out through the screen, I could feel everything they felt, whether it was anger, disappointment, shame, happiness,  sadness , although I couldn't fully relate to everything presented in the film , I  could easily put myself in their shoes , all from the way they made everything feel so realistic .The characters themselves function symbolically. For example, one thing that happens, again and again, is that peoples' assumptions prevent them from seeing the actual person standing before them. An Iranian is thought to be an Arab, although the Iranians are really Persian. Both the Iranian and the white wife of the district attorney believe a Mexican-American locksmith is a gang member and a crook; however he is a family man." No matter how hard some of the characters try to disprove their own racial stereotype, in some way or form it becomes inevitable that they must live out the stereotype to exist in the society they live in. " (Justin Aptaker, 2012) The characters find themselves not only stereotyping others but also living up to their stereotypes The movie Crash is unique because instead of showing characters at their best, like most popular movies do, the characters are instead stressed out and pushed to their own emotional limits.
If the film gets my critical and perceptive juices flowing, then it generally works for me. I want the film to leave me with something to think about. This film constantly keeps you on your toes and at the edge of your seat. There is always a twist. Everyone's life stories tie into one another rand you watch at how their actions influences not only their life but someone's life. The film sets a tone of how reality truly is this and that these things really happened. The characters in the film took me on a ride of crazy emotions, yet it managed teaches me to realize that it is never too late to redeem one's self and change. In the film there is a lack of acceptance of other cultures and unwillingness to understand why individuals are the way they are. Crash demonstrates this throughout the film through every character. This is the part of the film that made me pounder on the deeper meanings and the main point the director was trying translate.
Ultimately, I believe anyone seeing it is likely to be moved to have a little more sympathy for people not like themselves. "Crash" exceeded my expectations it had a relevant story line, believable characters and a thought provoking message. The movie contained hurt, coldness and cruelty, but it still leaves you feeling hopeful. In the end, the movie conveys the importance of respecting individuality, and realizing we share similar fears and hopes. You may have to look hard to see it, but "Crash" is a film about making personal progress in the midst of unexpected pain.

There are several moments in the film when its subject matter is laid bare and leaves you questioning just how deep-seated racism is, and that we could potentially be, by our very natures, discriminatory towards those different to ourselves.
